CONFIDENTIAL. 


— a 


Correspondence respecting the Rights and Privileges of 
the Latin and Greek Churches in Turkey. 


(RASTERN QUESTION, 


PAKT V. 


No. 1. 


The Earl of Westmorland to the Karl of Clurendon.—(Received August 8.) 
(No. 292.) 
My Lord, Vienna, August 5, 1854. 

YOUR Lordship will have learnt, by my telegraphic despatch of yesterday's 
date, that Baron Bourqueney and myself had waited on Count Buol, to learn 
from him the decision His Majesty the Emperor had taken upon the documents 
which, by the orders of our Governments, we had submitted to him. 

I inclose a copy of that despatch, in which your Lordship will find stated 
the purport of the answers we received. 

The announcement of the intention of the Emperor to direct. Colonel 
Kalich to proceed to the head-quarters of the English and French armies to 
eoncert the dates and positions from which they should cooperate with the 
Austrian armies in the movements which might be decided upon, and the announce- 
ment of the intention of His Majesty, at a later period, to appoint a general officer 
to reside at those head-quarters, and to invite the appointment of officers of a 
similar rank to be placed at the head-quarters of his own army, was considered 
by us as perfectly satisfactory. 

The acceptation of the text of the notes to be exchanged between the three 
Governments, but accompanied by the proposal of the two modifications which 
were required by the Austrian Government, occasioned some discussion ; but as 
these modifications had been transmitted for the approval of our Governments, 
it was agreed that their consent to them must be waited for. 

he text of the Convention, as it was modified in Article III, by the 
reciprocal engagement of Austria to the offensive and defensive stipulations of 
the alliance, was agreed to by Count Buol; but he stated that the Emperor 
considered the modifications proposed, as to the non-acceptance of any overture or 
proposition for a cessation of hostilities, would interfere with the necessary dis- 
cretion which belonged to the Commanders-in-chief, and would more naturally 
form part of those ulterior arrangements which were stipulated for in Article [II 
of the Convention. He therefore proposed that this Ist Article should remain as it 
had been originally worded, ‘To this proposition we also replied that it would be 
submitted to our Gocenanente: 

Count Buol stated that he had already invited the Prussian Government to 
adhere to the four points mentioned inthe notes to be exchanged between the 
Representatives of the three Governments, and that upon the acceptation or 
refusal by Prussia of this invitation, and upon the signature of those notes, the 
Austrian messenger would immediately be forwarde with them to St. Peters- 
burgh, together with the instructions to Count Esterhazy; and if the Russian 
Cabinet ‘ not accept the terms suggested, and order the evacuation of the 

[47 B 


.| 
4] 


2 


Principalities within eight days, Count Esterhazy would be directed to demand 
his passports. As soon as this result was known in Vienna, the Emperor pledged 
his word to sien the Convention. 

Upon this annoucement being made by Count Buol to us, Baron Bourqueney 
and myself strongly represented against this delay in the signature of the Con- 
vention, We stated that the substance of that document had been drawn up 
and proposed by myself, and we could not, therefore, understand why 1ts 
completion was now to be delayed. We stuted that our Governments had 
already been informed that its stipulations had been nppeoveR by the Austrian 
Government; that they were waiting with impatience the announcement of its 
adoption by the Emperor, and that they looked forward to it with the greatest 
anxiety, as the completion of the alliance which had so happily been established 
between us. We therefore called upon Count Buol most carnestly to reconsider 
this determination; adding, that it was upon the signature of the Convention 
that we must make the exchange of notes dependent. 

Count Buol stated that the stipulations of this Convention could only 
become applicable after the refusal of Russia to the terms suggested, and to the 
evacuation of the Principalities; and be therefore considered that the proper 
moment for its signature would be when that refugal was made known. 

He added, that the Governments of England and France, in the apprecta- 
tion of their own interests and position, declined to notify their readiness to 
negotiate upon the guarantees contained in the notes; but the Emperor, who 
did entertain a hope that these guarantees might lead to the attainment of the 
objects for which he had engaged himself by the Protocols which had been 
signed, thought it advisable to see whether aaah a result was obtained by them, 
before he became a party to the document in question. 

Count Buol did not believe that the present abstention of the Emperor 
from signing the Convention would have any effect upon the result of the com- 
munication he proposed to make to the Russian Government, because he meant 
it should be clearly understood thet i Russia did not evacuate the Prineipulities, 
und accept the guarantees, the Convention would at once be signed. 

aron Bourquency and myself replied, that the Emperor, in becoming & 
party to the proposed Convention, might feel entire security that his interests 
would be as zealously upheld as those of the other Governments he was allie 
with: that the signature of this Convention would be the surest means of 
obtaining from Russia those objects which it was the common aim to secure ; 
that, since the Convention had been proposed by the Imperial Government, 
without the reserve at present insisted upon, to defer its signature would be 
looked upon as a change of policy which indicated a piesa of confidence im 
the Governments to whieh it had been offered; that we therefore conjured 
Count Buol to reconsider this decision; to abate at once his intention to con- 
clude the Convention as soon as full-powers for its signature were received ; and 
then to proceed to the exchange of the notes containing the guarantees. 

With this appeal to Count Buol we elosed our interview. 

Since the above was written, Baron Bourqueney and myself haye both seen

might entertain a hope that hig decision regarding the delay in signing the 
Convention is not irrevocable, |

ances on the part of the [imperial Government for the prosperity and security of 
the Turkish Empire. 

Count Buol also communicated to the Ambassador the announcement 
which he bad received from the Russian Minister, Prince Gortchekoff, that the 
Emperor Nicholas had directed Ins army smmedintely to evacuate the Princi- 
palities. of Wallachia and Moldavia; and as it appeared that a considerable 
portion of the former of these Principalities was already evacuated, the Austrian 
Commander-in-chief, Baron Hees, had dispatched an officer of his staff to the 
head-quarters of Omer Pasha, in order that he might regulate with him the 
entry into that province of the Austrian troops, according to the berms of the 
Treaty of the 14th of June-of this year, between Austria and the Porte; and 
with respect to the Principality of Maldavia, Baron Hess was now only waiting 
for further details as to the date and extent of the movements of the Russian 
armies in their retreat, to combine also with Omer Pasha the advance of the 
Austrian lorees. 

Count Buol also informed the Ambassador that as Prince Gortchakolf, in 
the announcement he had made, had stated that the evneuation of the Princi- 
palities was ado ited by the Russian Government as 2 strategie operation, he 
conceived that the Austrian Government might look upon it as directed as much 
against themselves as any of the elligerents ; they meant, however, to curry out 
the movements of their troops. which would take place in consequence of that 
operation, without unnecessarily pressing upon dhe Russian army, although 
Count Buol felt that the advance of the Austrian corps should be made with the 
least possible delay. T have, &e.

Inclosure in No. 7. 
Circular addressed to the Austrian Representatives in Germany. 


Vienna, July 28, 1854. 

BY Article LI] of the Offensive and Defensive Alliance which is adhered to 
now by the whole Germanic Confederation, the Contracting Parties have bound 
themselves, for the purpose of giving due security and force to the coniditions of 
the ‘Treaty, to keep, if necessary, at periods and at points which are to be 
determined among themselves, a part of their military force in complete readiness 
for war; and a special decision will be come to as to the time, extent and manner 
of placing these forces. 

The Courts of Austria and Prussia, in the firm hope that their efforts in 
the couse of unity will include the whole of Germany, baye already agreed upon 
the proposals to be made to the Dict respeeting the execution of these conditions 
of the Vreaty, and Baron Prokesch hus been accordingly authorized to propose, 
in conjunction with the Prussian Minister at the Diet, a military arrangement 
corresponding to said Article HL of the Treaty of Alliance; and according to his 
instructions he will consider it his duty to bring about a decision on this point 
with the greatest possible dispatch, and a rapid, energetic, and judicious execution 
of the decisions thus tuken, 

‘The most essential point of the proposal intended to be made by the twa 
Courts is that Austria is to plice 150,000 to 250,000 men, Prissia 100,000 to 
200,000 men, and the rest of the German States one-half of their federal con- 
tingent, on a war-footing. Should this proposition be assented to, two federal 
corps will be formed, the one consisting of the contingents of the 7th and 6th, 
the other of those of the 9th and 10th army corps, which could be placed in the 
most eligible positions in conjunction with the forces of Austria and Prussia, 

That the case of necessity for such military preparations, foreseen in the 
Treaty of the 20th of April, has already really occurred, surely requires no more 
apecial proots in the fee of the attitude of Russia and the preparations of that 
Power, Austria has prepared two of her armies for immediate action, and in 
Prussia the necessary orders have been given for the mobilisation of the military

No. 9, 
Sir A. Malet to the Earl of Clarendon. Received August 14.) 


(No. 84,) 
My Lord, Frankfort, August 11, 1854. 


CONTRARY to general expectation no communication whatever wits 
made to the Dict at yesterday's sitting, either of the Russian reply to the 
Vienna and Berlin notes, or relating to the mobilisation of a portion of the 
federal contingents. 

From whatever cause this delay has arisen, there can be no question as to 
the object aimed at by Prussia, viz, putting off any decision to the last moment, 
being attained; and this has been effected without its being possible to throw 
the whole blame of the delay upon the Cabinet of Berlin, 

When M. de Bismarck accompanied the King of Prussia from Munich to 
Berlin, it had been agreed between the two Governments that the communica: 
tion of the Russian answer should be made in the sitting of the Diet held on the 
3rd of August. 

M. de Bismarek on arriving at Berlin telegraphed to Baron Prokesch to 
proceed without him. It seems, however, that Baron Prokesch’s instructions 
were to act only in concert with M. de Bismarck, and he consequently abstamed 
from making the communication, 

Tt was then to be expected that-as soon as M. de Bismarck came back to 
his post, the earliest opportunity would be taken of doing what it had been 
already agreed between the two Governments should be done in this respect, as 
well as in that of inviting the Diet to put a part of their contingents on 4 war 
footing, which had been already done by Austria, through a cireular note to her 
own Ministers at the several Courts, as reported in my despatch No. 84 of 
yesterday's date, ) 


= 
a 


Such, however, is not the course which events have taken, and the conse- 
quenee is this;—If on the ard tstant the Russian answer had been laid belore 
the Diet, it would have been reported upon yesterday by the Commission, and 
whatever might have been the decision of that body, the vote of the Diet might 
have been taken in that sitting, if not opposed, or at all events in the sitting of 
the 17th. 

Now the matter will probably not be entertained (if at all) sooner than the 
17th, and the vote, or the acceptation of the Commission's report without vote, 
nay be delayed till Thursday the otst. 

I cannot but apprehend that the true reason why M. de Prokesch did not 
proceed as requested by his Prussian colleague, on the 3rd, is, that he had ascer- 
tained that the Commission would take the Prussian. and not the Austrian, view 
of the Russian answer, and that the same motive 15 still inducing him to withhold 
ull communication on the subject. 

As regards the Austrian circular to its agents, relating to the increase of the 
federal contingents, it can only be regarded as a useless, if not a mischievous, 
step, and rather caleulated to obstruct than to obtain its ostensible object. 

The execution of the measure could be ordered by the Diet alone; nor was 
it to be supposed that any single Government, with the dispositions they are 
known to entertain, would in any degree accelerate matters, by instructing its 
Plenipotentiary at Frankfort before receiving from that Plenipotentiary notice al 
the invitation having been duly made to the Diet, 

‘Austria has also contrived in this: circular to: indispose Prussia (or at any 
rute His Prussian Majesty) even more than was already the case, by assuming 
without sufficient ground, as it would appear, that the proposed measure was 
recommended in concert with the Cabinet of Berlin, and has, by addressing 
herself to the separate Governments instead of to the Diet, afforded that Cabinet 
an arin against her with the Diet, not very dissimilar ta that which brought 
about the Bamberg coalition—a nucleus of Russian intrigue, be it said by-the-hye, 
at the head of which Prussia seems about to take a stand, . 

Your Lordship will, Lmuch fear, be able to form no other judgment from 


= 


these details than that anything like prompt or energetic action on the part of 


1} 


the Diet in opposition to Prussian (1 might almost say Russian) policy, is not to 
be expected, but that, on the contrary, everything which affords a pretext for 
delay will be sedulousty taken advantage of, 
I greaily apprehend that if ever the Russian answer is laid before the Diet, 
‘tg decision will be to the effect that they do not see anything im the terms to 
induce the Diet to reply thereto, by placiug any part of their federal contingents 
on a war footing. 
T have, &e. 
(Signed) A. MALEY,

No. 10. 


Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received August 15.) 


(No. 1000.) 
My Lord, Paris, Aucust 14, 1854. 

A TELEGRAPHIC despatch of the 3rd instant received by the French 
Government from Constantinople, states that both M. de Bruck and Colonel 
Kalich, who had been sent to Omer Pasha's head-quarters, held language to the 
effect that the Austrians were to occupy the Principalities exclusively. 

Qn this despatch passing through M. de Bourqueney’s hands, he went to 
Count Buol, and reminding him that this language of the Internuncio and 
Colonel Kalich was at complete variance with all the assurances which Count 
Buol had given him, the Austrian Government having even requested the entry 
of French and Bnglish troops into the Principalities, he asked him the reason of 
this divergence of language. Count Buol replied that no attention was to be 
paid to the language of M. de Bruck ; that if that Minister had expressed him- 
self as reported, he hid done so without instructions, and that the Austrian 
Government was only bound by what he (Count Buol) stated officially on their 
behalf. 

In giving me this ‘aformation M. Drouyn de Lhuys added, that from this 
and other indications which had reached him, he could not help feeling some 
anxiety respecting the intentions of Austria in the Principalities, and he had, 
cynsequently addressed a telegraphic despatch to M, de Bourg une on the 12th 
instant, in which he stated that there were two points on which M, de Bourqueney 
was to enter Inte explicit ox nlanations with Count Buol, ‘The first, that Austria 
could claim no exclusive right to occupy the Principalities ; the second, that she 
could not oppose the march of the allies, if any one of them determined on 
pursuing the Russians through the Principalities. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys remarked that a precaution of this kind had heeome 
absolutely necessary, because Austria, by placing her troops between the Russian 
and ‘Turkish armies, gave greater liberty of-action to the former, who would thus 
be enabled to move towards. the Crimea. Besides which, in consequence of the 
dilatory conduct of Austria, Omer Pasha had entered Wallachia before the 
Austrian troops, and it could not be pretended that the troops of the Sultan 
were to be forced to retreat from territory of which the Sultan was sovereign, 

If Austria was allowed to assume the position claimed by M. de Bruck, 
there would be nothing to prevent her hereafter from playing the part of an 
armed mediator. It had become necessary, therefore, to have categorical 
explanations with the Austrian Government. 

In the course of the conversation M. Drouyn de Lhuys expressed the 
opinion that the corps of Omer Pasha should be employed, either by taking up 
a menacing attitude on the Pruth or by a descent on the coast of Bessarabia, to 
prevent the concentration of Russian troops for the relief of the Crimea. 

L have, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY,

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon. —(Received August 13.) 


(No, 1,005.) 
My Lord, ; Paris; August 14, 1854. 

M, DE MOUSTIER reports that he has had two long conversations with 
M. de Manteuffel on the subject of the answers lately returned by the French 
Government to the explanations given by the Prussian Chargé d’Affaires at 
Paris, respecting the future attitude of Prussia in the Eastern question. 

M. de Manteuifel declared that the intention of Prussia was to continue to 
act with the allies; and that he did not despair of inducing the King to consent 
to the four points which Franee, Greut Britain, and Austria had declared were 
necessary to ensure the solution of the Eastern question, but that he did not 
know how to bring this about unless some written communication was made to 
him upon the subject. M. Drouyn de Lhuys answered M. de Moustier by 
telegraph, that the French Government was resolved to make no further 
communication to the Cabinet of Berlin. 

Ifthe Prussian Government desired any information, they would probably 
obtain it at Vienna; and if they wished to join in such mt declaration as that 
which had been made by the three Governments, it must be done by an exchange 
of notes with each of the three Governments. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

No. 13. 
Mr, Magenis to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received August 19.) 


(No.4, Confidential.) ; 

My Lord, Stockholm, July 29, 185%, 
AFTER the more formal part of my audience of this day with the King of 

sweden had passed over, and | had presented to His Majesty the Queen's letter, 

His Majesty invited me to sit down, and conversed with me on the topics which 

engrogs ut this moment public attention, No one else was present, and the 

conversation lasted a considerable time. 


Ish 


One of the first subjects touched on by THis Majesty, and one on whieh he 
appeared to feel strongly, was the delay and reluctance of the Cabinet of Vienna 
to come to a decision. 1 said that I had been informed by Lord Bloomfield, on 
the 24th instant, that he that day had received the intelligence, and had 
forwarded it by telegraph to London, that the Austrian troops had entered, or 
were about to enter, the Principalities, which His Majesty doubted ; and said, 
that though reported, it had not been confirmed. 1 observed, that I believed 
Her Majesty’s Government, a few weeks ago, were satisfied with the altitude of 
Austria; and although the hesitation and intrigues of Prussia might cause delay, 
it was improbable that Austria would have gone to the expense of her vast 
armaments—an expense which she was little able at present to bear—merely to 
play the part of an armed mediator. Austria must feel, too, that she had made 
an implacable enemy of Russia; and she was, moreover, perhaps, more directly 
interested in the solution of the Eastern question than either England or France; 
and | therefore hoped that, sooner or later, she must declare for us. added, 
that, in my opinion, a bolder and more decided line on the part of Austria 
would have compelled Prussia to follow in her wake, for the latter Power could 
not, without forfeiting her position and influence in Germany, have abandoned 
Austria if attacked by Russia in her non-German provinces. J said that we hacl 
most reluctantly had recourse to arms to solve the difficulties which Russia had 
created; and it was not probable that we could lay them down unless we could 
make a peace which offered the hopes of duration. Russia, until worsted more 
than she had as yet been, would hardly consent to such a peace, and the 
moment was rather one for action than for negotiation. 

His Majesty admitted that Russia would not relinquish at present the 
viglits which she had consecutively obtained by Treaty sinee the time of the 
Empress Catherine, of interfering in Turkey—rights whieh His Majesty termed 
“an arsenal of pretexts,” and which were abrogated by the war; and he seemed 
to be of opinion that Austria would ultimately declare against Russia, but he 
still regretted the delay which probably would prevent our obtaining this year 
the results which might otherwise have ensued. 

His Majesty having informed me of the arrival this morning in Stockholm 
of General Baraguay d'Hilliers, the conversation turned to the object of the 
expedition which that officer commands, and to the war im the Baltic. 1 
informed His Majesty, that when I left London, the precise object of this expe- 
dition was oot known, and that it had been left to the decision of General 
Baraguay d'Hilliers and the Admirals of the combined fleets. His Majesty 
replied, that he wnderstood a large portion of the allied squadrons had already 
assembled at or near Bomarsund: and he consequently concluded that the 
Aland Islands would be the point selected for attack. His Majesty did not 
doubt of the success of such an attack; and in reply to my inquiry, stated that 
lie was convineed that we might hold them during the winter against ull the 
efforts which Russia could or would make to retake them. He developed at 
some length the grounds on which that opinion was formed, such as the difficulty 
and uncertainty of transporting across the ice, by the shortest winter road of 
ubout forty-five miles English, a large force, accompanied by heavy artillery, ancl 
the enormous weight of projectiles required fora siege; the shortness of the 
periad—under the most favourable circumstances, about two months from the 
middle of sie ae which such operations could be effected; the impossibility 
of opening trenches on the sea-side, and the difficulty of doing so on land, from 
frosts, &c, His Majesty added, that the capture of the Aland Isles would be of 
great importance, both because it would in some measure satisfy popular impa- 
tience in England and France as to the small results obtained by our large fleets 
in the Baltic, and because those islands would form a good basis for future 
operations. His Majesty stated, that he thought our success in the Baltic for 
the present year would be limited to this capture alone, 

During the whole of our long conversation the King expressed himself with 
moderation towards Russia, and 1 do not believe that the Emperor's name was 
once introduced, His Mijesty made no allusion whatever to a more active 
cooperation of Sweden with England and France in the present war, nor to the 
lute negotiations for that cooperation with the French Minister, M. Lobstein, 
and the Commandant Blanchard, as reported by Mr. Grey to your Lordship in 
his despatches Nos, 180 and 192 of the 24th and 26th of this month; and | 
thought it advisable on my part to leave that chord untouched, 

E 


ss 


14 


His Majesty's manner and language during the whole of my interview 
were most cordial and friendly; and had every reason to be satisfied with the 
sentiments he expressed towards England and towards myself personally. 

T have, &e 


(Signed) ARTHUR C. MAGENIS.

My Lord, Foreign Office, luguat 15, 1854. 

HER Majesty's Government entirely approve the language held by you 
to Baron Manteuffel, respecting the view taken by the Prussian Government of 
the exchange of the notes between the three Powers at Vienna, as reported by 
your Lordship in your despatch No. 446 of the 11th instant. 

The communications that have passed between the two Governments 
during the last twelve months, must have eonvinced Baron Manteutfel of the 
friendly feelings of England towards Prussia, and his Excellency therefore 
cannot doubt that it must have been both with reluctance and with sufficient 
cause that Her Majesty’s Government have found themselves compelled to 
suspend these communications ; but it is not the custom of Her Majesty's 
Government to exhibit. confidence which they do not feel, and 1 i¢ impossible 
any longer to confide in Prussia, who, by paralyzing the action of Austria, and 
exciting the German Powers against her, renders such eminent service to the 
Power with which England is at war, and who therefore can hardly now be 
considered as holding a neutral position. 

Tam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

Lord Cowley to the Karl of Clarendon, —(Received August 18.) 
(No. 1,022.) 


My Lord, Parts, August 17, 1854. 

YESTERDAY morning M, de Hitbner communicated to M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys the instructions which Count Buol addressed, on the 10th instant, to the 
Austrian Minister at St. Petersburgh with a view of informing the Russian 
Government of the terns without which no peace could be made between Russia 
and the Western Powers, and of the adherence of Austria to those terms, 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys had been prepared for this communication by a short 
despatch from M. de Bourqueney dated the 11th instant, in which that Minister 
states that he had not concealed from Count Buol his disappointment at. the 
form and tenour of his instructions to Count Esterhazy. Count Buol had 
replied that he could not employ other than courteous language towards the 
Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, and ay M. de Bourquenvy knew what the 


22 


Russian Government had demanded (among other things a joint oecupation of 
the Principalities with Austria), he would be satisfied with the language of the 
‘Austrian Government, Most positive orders had been given to Count Esterhazy 
to enter into no discussion, but to ask for a simple “yes” or “no” to the advice 
ojven from Vienne. 

To return to M. Drouyn de Lhuys’ interview with M, de Hiibner, his 
Fixcellency at once took objection to the latter part of the instructions to Count 
Esterhazy, in which Count Buol holds out hopes of u cessation of hostilities, and 
he requested M, de Hiibner to state to his Government that England and France 
would never permit themselves to be dictated to on this point; that they were 
as anxious as Austria for peace on proper terms; but that they were the sole 
judges of when and under what conditions an armistice could be agreed to. If 
Austria had any pretension to play the part of an armed mediator, it eould not 
be done without France having an encmy more to contend with. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys told me that he should write in the same strain, but 
culmly and courteously, to M. de Bourqueney. 

He then said that he hoped to send to-day for your Lordship’s considera- 
tion a project of a tripartite Treaty ; but that he was of opinion that Austria 
should not be urged to sign it; but that France and England should wait until 
she herself proposed to do 80. If she had determined to-content herself with the 
occupation of the Principalities, the overtures of the Western Powers im favour 
of a ‘Treaty would be made in vain: but if, im consequence of supporting our 
demands at St. Petersburgh, she exeited the ire of the Czar, and that hostilities 
were threatened, or attempts made to alienate her Slavonic population hy 
Russian agents, she would be the fret to ask for a ‘Treaty, and the two Powers 
might then impose their own conditions. Ee was for signing nothing which was 
not precise, clear, and positive.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clurendon.—(Received August 18 ) 


(No, 1,023. Contidential.) 
My Lord, Peris, Angust 17, 1854. 


COUNT HATZFELDT, who has been for some months absent from bis 
iat, returned to Paris on the 14th instant. THe has not been to Berlin, nor has 
le aeen the King of Prussia or any of his Ministers. He had an interview with 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys on the day after his return, when he expressed himsell as 
creatly chagrined at the course which events had taken, and at the position in 
“hich his Government was placed. He expressed himself in sinmlar language to 
me, adding that he should not have returned here had he been aware of the real 
state of attairs. 

But while admitting this chagrin to M. Drouyn de Lhuys, Count Hatzfeldt 
attempted to throw the blame of Prussia being insulated on the Western 
Powers. He said that both France and England had treated his Government 
with neither friendship nor courtesy in not communicating to them, a5 they had 
done to Austria, the observations ofthe two Governments upon the last Russian 
propositions, 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys replied that Count Hatzfeldt should recollect that the 
notes which passed at the Bamberg conference had not been communicated by 
Prussia to France and England, although the eontents of them intimately con- 
earned those two Powers, and they had been received from several of the 
smaller Gernian Courts 5 that Prussia had refused to assist at the late conferences 
at Vienna; that she had prejudged the question which it was proposed to decide 
‘nr conference, by declaring the Russian propositions to be acceptable, whereas 
the Western Powers, whom. they chiefly concerned, had pronounced them 
detestable, "The aymiposlis® of the Prassian Court and Government were known. 
to be with Russia, although their declarations had been against her ; transports 
of arma destined for Russin were allowed to pass through Prussia; finally, news 
had been just received that the defences of Dantzic were suddenly ordered to be 


23 


strengthened —against whom? not against Russia, for she had not a man-of-war 
in the open waters of the Baltic: but against the maritime Powers, whose cause 
Prussia pretended in words to espouse. Prussia ought not to be surprised if, 
under these circumstances, the three Powers had exchanged notes binding them 
to the future policy which they were to pursuc, without reference to the policy 
of Prussia. : : 

_ Count Hatzfeldt made no defence to these observations ; but he asked what 
his Government could do to extricate themselves from the unfortunate position 
in which they found themselves? 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys answered that as Minister he could give no advice, nor 
would he make any further communication to the Prussian Government; but as 
an individual he would state his opinion of the course which Prussia should 
follow. There were two ways of awing Russia—by an armed demonstration or 
by diplomatic pressure. If the Prussian Government considered that they were 
not justified in entailing wpon Prussia such an expense os calling out an army 
larger, he admitted, than the resources of the country could well maintain, let 
them act with double energy through their diplomatic arents; let the language 


H Loe el Pe i] psy ae) : r a , 
of those agents be clear and unequivocal, so that Russia might understand that the 


. - = 
whole moral influence of Prussia was against her; let them be the first to demand 
the signature of notes and ‘Treaties, If Prussia pursued neither of these courses, 
neither armed nor spoke, she would abdicate her position of a great Power, and 
she would find the most momentous question of modern times settled without 
reference to her, who was ‘par excellence " the largest Power in Germany. 

Count Hatzfeldt exclaimed that M. Drouyn de Lhuys must recollect that 
there was a national fecling and a national pride in Prussia. 

at And it is for that very reason,” said M. Drouyn de Lhuys, “that I speak 
asido, You arein danger of becoming like an individual who has allowed 
himself to be passed over, and quarrels afterwards with everybody in order to 
retrieve his honowr. When you find yourselves insulated you will not be able to 
bear it, and you will be looking out for whom you Thay attack, in order to prove 
that you are somehody. ‘There is nothing in the declarations exchanged at 
Vienna which is not in unison with your own declaration ut Bamberg. The 
evacuation of the Principalities ; the future fate of the Christians in ‘Turkey; the 
free navigation of the Danube, and the extension of German commerce in the 
Black Sea, were declared by you to be essential to the welfare of Germany. If 
you are afraid to repeat as much in conjunction with the other Powers, Germany 
will have a right to say either that you deceived her by declaring that which 
was not true, or that you prefer your own interest to hers, if you do not defend 
the latter.” z ; Bae 

After giving me this deseription of his conversation with Count Hutafelkt 
M, Drouyn de Lhuys added that he was about to call your Lordship’s serious 
attention to the hostile conduct of Prussia evinced in the fortifications of Dantzic 
and in the free passage eiven through the Prussian territories to arms and 
ammunition for Russia. He was of opinion that a categorical demand should 
be made to Prussia to puta stop to these inimical yroceedings, and that in case 
of refusal her ports should be at once blockaded, He said that if some measure 
of this kind were not adopted, We should some day find ourselves in the same 
position in regard to Prussia, as we were now in regard to Russia, that is, we 
should find her armed at all paints to dely us, Le ad

My wee’ | Therapia, August 2, 1854. 
As THE day before yesterday Marshal St, Arnaud arrived here from Varna, 
n the same day Madame de St. Arnaud paid a visit to the Sultan's harem, 


wee ae ae received by one of the Sultanas, accompanied by some of the 
ultan’s children: and on retiring, she received & present in diamonds, reported 


ee 


34 


to be magnificent, from the Sultan. The Marshal himself was invited during the 
visit, and had an audience of His Imperial Majesty, no one being present except 
the first interpreter of the French Embassy. aa 

1 am informed, though neither by his Excellency nor by M. Benedetti, that 
Marshal de St. Arnaud apprised the Sultan of the military operations about to 
be undertaken by the auxiliary armies: and requested that His Majesty would 
order his Minister to place at’ his disposal whatever he wanted for the execution 
of the enterprise. : 

If the Marshal's communications extended beyond this point, nothing, to 
my knowledge, has yet transpired on the subject. : 

On the following day the Seraskier and the Captain Pasha waited on the 
French Marshal at the Imperial country-house in this neighbourhood, which the 
Sultan has allowed Madame de St. Arnaud to occupy. According to my 
informants, his Excellency stated his wants in artillery and other objects, and 
assurances were given that they should be supplied without delay. 

Reshid Pasha has sent me word that all these arrangements took place 
without any previous knowledge on Ins part. 

I had some conversation with the Marshal when he called upon me here, 
and also when I returned his visit. 

L extracted enough from him to know that my information respecting lis 
proceedings was generally correct. He spoke with confidence of the intended 
enterprise, reckoning largely upon the good understanding und spirit of emula- 
tion existing between the two armies. He hoped that the remainder of his 
artillery would arrive in time; and that neither the cholera—though he admitted 
its ravazes—nor the suspension of the Austrian operations, would prevent the 
accomplishment of the concerted plan. ‘The hope was expressed with aniination, 
but so a5 to convey an impression of doubt. 

His Excellency returns to Varna to-night.

sir Edmund Lyons arrived here from Varna the day before yesterday, for the

Lord Stratford de Redelijfe to the Eurl of Clarendon.—(Received August 15.) 


(No. 433.) 
My Lord, Therapia, August 5, 1854. 

THE representative of Schamyl Bey in Circassia, the Naib, or Licutenant, 
as he is called, arrived in Constantinople a few days ago with a numerous com- 
any of Cireassians. The Naib previously visited the commanders of the 
auxiliary forces in Varna, and was entrusted by Lord Raglan with a letter, copy 
inclosed herewith, for me. 

| lost no time in sending a message of compliment to the Naib, with a view 
to acting in the sense desired by Lord Raglan. But three days elapsed without 
my hearing a word from him or his party. He was sent to live on a remote side 
of the capital and did not give himself the trouble of opening any communication 
with me. 

It was not till after he and the other Circassians had been received by the 
Sultan that Reshid Pasha sent a part of them, headed by the Naib, to this 
residence, 1 received them with the eustomary Enstern attentions, and, not- 
withstanding the difficulty of carrying on conversation through the complex 
medium of four languages, succeeded in obtaining some degree of insight into 
their cireumstinces and wiews. 

| confined myself to making inquiries, and carefully avoided the expression 
of any opinions as to their means of usefulness or fulure prospects. 

The substance of what IT learnt from them is now to be stated to your 
Lordship. i 

They belong to several of the tribes which form the population of Circassia. 
That population is divided into three principal tribes, which are subdivided into 
smaller ones, cach haying a lunguage or dialect of its own, wholly distinet from 
the Slavonic languages, and intelligible ina certain degree to all. 

‘Their creed, with very few exceptions, is Mahometan, ‘The chief Ministers 
of their religion are the Cadis. They build places of worship out of their own 
private funds, ‘There is no State provision for that object, and there 1s no 
metropolis in the country. 

Their law is, of course, the Mussulman law. ‘They have Mehkemeés, or 
Courts of Justice, whase decisions are enforced by the Naib’s authority. 

The families are taxed for objects of general interest, a5 occasion requires, 
each family being called upon to give its quota, There is a common Treasury ; 
but it did not appear to whose custody it was consigned, 

The land is held in various proportions by the peasantry and their chief, 
éach family having a share of it, however small in most eases. ‘There does not 
seem to be any class of labourers apart from that of proprietors. 

They boust of being able to collect a force of 200,000 fighting men, ‘They 
have no standing force ; no body of officers; no system of discipline. Each man 
provides his own arms, a rifle, a Reel a broad sword, anda dagger, They have 
au few pieces of cannon, probably not very effective, and perhaps not even 
mounted. They use gunpowder of their own making, and English when they 
can getit. They have plenty of horses. ; 

The Naib has been among them about eight years. He is a native of 
Daghestan, and came originally from Schamyl Bey, He gradually won their 
confidence, and rules among them without any formal title to their obedience. 

‘The Russians possessed the const, beenuse, huving access from the sea, they 
were able to construct forts, and to establish themselves there. ‘ 

The Turks, in former times, had a Pasha at Anapa; but he only commanded 
the fortress, and had no legal power over the inhabitants. 

With respect to the Sultan’s temporal authority there was evidently a 
difference of opinion among them, 

All had the appearance of recognizing His Majesty os their Sovereign in a 
religious sense, and so far at least they had given him token of allegiance at the 
late nudience. 

When asked whether they would like to have a French or British General 


20 


‘at their head, they replied that they would hike to have assistance; but they did 


not seem prepared to submit to a foreign commander. an 

One or two of the party showed symptoms of independence, not only in that 
respect, but as to the future destiny of their country, 

" ‘They have mountain paths of communications) into Daghestan, besides the 
military road; but the Russians have established their power between the two 
countries. | 

On the whole it may be inferred that it would be as difficult for them to 
expel the Russians without assistance, as it would be for the Russians to subdue 
them completely; that freed from the Russian yoke they would probably fall 
into separate communities, capable of being united, though undisciplined in time 
of danger, having affinities with each other, of which religion is the strongest, 
and more inclined to accept the protection, than to tolerate the authority of the 
Sultan. aie 

They expressed a certain confidence of success in the event of their being 
joined by an auxiliary force, round which they could rally, and concentrate their 
own means of resistance. < | 

It is by no means improbable that an English auxiliary force would be the 
object of their preference. are 

[think it right to observe that the form of statement which I have adopted, 
tends rather to convey a more positive and definitive impression than the 
answers of the Circassians might strictly be said to warrant. Some kind of 
abatement ought, perhaps, to be miade on this acount. 

[ have to add, in conclusion, that the Circassians are understood to have 
been somewhat dissatisfied with the manner in which they have been treated by 
the Turkish soldiery. 

I have, &e, 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redetiffe. 
(No, 485.) 
My Lerd, Foreign Office, August 18, 1854. 

WITH reference to my instructions No. 261 and No. 265 to the Earl of 
Westmorland, respecting the Austrian occupation of the Principalities, and with 
reference to Lord Cowley’s No. 1,010 of August 15 on this subject, of which 
copies were inclosed in my despatches Nos. 480 and 483 of the 16th and 17th 
instant, | have to state to your Excellency that it is the desire of Her Majesty's 
Government that no portion of the Turkish territory should be occupied by 
Austrian troops except at the request or with the entire concurrence of the 
Porte, and it will be for the Sultan’s Government to determine how far the 
proposed occupation will be safe and advantageous. 

To Her Majesty's Government it appears that such occupation would be 
safe, if its objects, civil as well as military, are clearly delined; if all intention 
of exercising an armed mediation, or interfering between the belligerents be 
distinctly disclaimed; if the right of the allied forces, as well as of the Turkish 
troops to enter the Principalities be recognized, and an engagement taken not 
to permit the Russians to return either to Moldavia or Wallachia, And under 
these circumstances Her Majesty's Government are disposed to think that the 
Austrian occupation would be ialeantaeeot as it would set free a large portion 
of Omer Pasha’s army, and enable him to cooperate elsewhere with the allied 
forees. 

Lam, Xe. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

No. 35, 
The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 


(No, 270.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, August 18, 1854. 

COUNT COLLOREDO has read to me a despatch from Count Buol, 
dated the 15th instant, inelosing a copy of a despatch which he had addressed to 
the Internuneio on the Slst ultimo, with reference toa question stated to have 
been raised at Constantinople, as to whether the occupation of the Danubian 
Principalities, after the retreat of the Russian army, was to be effected by 
Austrian troops alone, or by those troops in conjunction with the Turkish and 
allied forces. 

In this despatch to the Internuncio, Count Buol, after alluding to the 
explanations previously given as to the view taken by the Imperial Court of the 
decision of the Porte in regard to the re-establishment in concert with Austria of 
a legal order of things in the Principalities, goes on to say that although Austria 
must necessarily claim, in the settlement of that question, the share to whieh 
she is entitled, on aceount both of the special engagements which she has entered 
into with the Porte, and of her geographical position, it never entered into her 
views to give an exclusive character to her proceedings as regards the Powers 
who are acting in concert with her for the maintenauce of the integrity of 
‘Turkey. In disclaiming any such notion, even in the case of the evacuation 
being brought about by her own action alone, Austria must of course be pre- 
pared to allow the maritime Powers their full share in the settlement of the 
matter, if her operations for that object should be su yported by their troops. 

As regards Prince Stirbey and Ghyka, it was the hope of Austria that the 
result of the inquiry into their conduct would be favourable, but if that should 
not be the case, and if either of them should have given cause for suspicion’ of 
their fidelity and devotion to his Suecrain, Austria would certainly not feel 
herself called upon to support his pretensions, but would, on the contrary, have 
an interest in his being superseded by a person in whom the Divan could place 
more confidence, 

As regards Servia, Austria hoped that her representations, combined with 
the recent orders of the Porte, would induce the Servian Government to comply 
with her demands, whereupon there would be nothing to prevent the re-csta- 
lishment of relations between Austria and Servia on their previous footing. 

Count Buol, in his despatch to Count Colloreda, refers to this despatch to 
the Internuncio as a proof that Austria did not pretend to the exclusive occupa- 
tion of the Principalities, whether that operation was effected peaceably or by 
force, It was with reference to the last contingency that Colonel Katich had 
been ordered to ascertain whether, and to what extent, the Turkish and allied 
commanders would be prepared to cooperate with the Imperial troops in the 
first half of September. In the meanwhile the Cubinet of St. Petersburgh had 
announced the withdrawal of the Russian troops from the Principalities, upon 
which an Austrian officer had been immediately sent to Omer Pasha’s head- 
quarters, to concert with him for the entrance of the Imperial troops into 
Wallachia, and the return of that officer was only waited for in order to that 
measure being carried out, Count Buol goes on to say that it is evident from 
this that Austria does not look upon the Convention with the Porte of the 14th 
of June as authorising her to offer any opposition in principle to the eventual 
cooperation of the Turkish and allied troops in the oceupation of the Princi- 
palities. 


a2 


It is another question whether, in the existing state of things, it is for the 
interest of the baltivorents to insist on this cooperation, and whether, on the 
contrary, it would not be more to their advantage to dispose of their troops 
otherwise, inasmuch as the Austrian occupation of the Principalities, once accom- 
plished, would suffice to guarantee the Ottoman Empire against any fresh 
attempt at invasion from the side of Russia. 

The reasons in favour of this view of the question Count Buol says were 50 
evident, that he hoped they would be fully appreciated by Her Britannic 
Majesty's Government, and that accordingly the question of the occupation of 
the Principalities would no longer be a matter of discussion between the 
respective military commanders. 

T thanked Count Colloredo for this communication, which I said was gatis- 
factory, and particularly as regarded the Hospodars, and it was to be hoped that 
no misunderstanding, either now or at any future period, would take place 
respecting the occupation of the Prineipalities, if the interition announced in 
Count Buol's despatch were strictly adhered to. 


Lam, Xe. 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

My Lord, Foreign Office, August 18, 1854. 

COUNT COLLOREDO has read to me a despatch from Count Buol to 
Count Esterhazy, stating that the reception given to the announcement of the 
evacuation of the Principalities, manifested the hopes entertained with respect 
to that measure by the Emperor of Austria, whose confidence was proved by the 
dispositions he had taken. 

Prince Gortchakoft was instructed not to represent the movement as a 
concession, but simply as a strategical measure, and to inquire in return the 
meaning of the Austrian armaments on the frontier. 

Count Buol says that no explanation was asked of the strategical measure, 
but orders were sent to a portion of the army to halt, and that other arranges 
ments of a similar kind would be made, in the expectation that this course would 
be appreciated at St. Petersburgh, and that the proposed bases of negotiation 
would be adopted. : 

Count Buol further states that the Austrian occupation of the Prineipalitics 
was not to be subordinate to any political understanding with the Cabinet of 
St. Petersburgh, and that no condition would be made at variance with the 
position taken by Austria, and which she was determined to maintain. 

That position is one which binds her, in principle, to the three Powers with 
whom she has hitherto been joined, but leaves her action free. She had 
separately and for Austrian interests required the evacuation of the Principalities ; 
but as her proceedings with reference to that would be governed by her stipu- 
lations with the Porte, all negotiations with Russia on the subject were 
inadinissible, 

Count Buol informs Count Esterhazy that it is of urgent importance that 
Russia should accept the bases completely and without reserve, as Austria had 
engaged to adopt them as the only conditions upon which relations could be 
re-established between the Porte and Russia, Count Esterhazy is instructed to 
ask for a direct answer, and no latitude is given to him to accept any alteration 
or condition with respect to the four points, as the efforts of Austria had been 
exhausted at London and Paris, and any attempt to procure a modification of the 
bases would be fruitless. 

I said that the latter part of the instruction to Count Esterhuzy was precise, 
and would, L hoped, procure the information sought by Count Buol as to the 
real intentions of Russia; but | expressed my surprise that upon such a commu- 
nication as that made by Prince Gortchakolf, the march of the Austrian army 
should have been suspended, 


Russia retreated from the country that she had unjustly seized, and could 


oo 


» hold, but that was no reason for pursuing the course that was the 
se ee advantage. She announced that she made no concession to Austria, 
and that she was in a bad military position ; and instead of the Austrian army 
halting, there seemed to be a double motive for its advancing. If uae 
desired peace it was most unfortunate, [ said, that all her measures should ten 
to protract the war. eae 

(Signed) CLARENDON.

My Lord, Vienna, lugust 16, 1854. 

" COUNT BUOL informed me that he has proposed to the Prusstam 
Government to place all the documents relating to the late transactions with 
Prussia before the Dict, and to call upon that body to pronounce whether they 
do not feel themselves called upon to support the greater Powers of Germany 
by making some armed preparation. By the documents laid betore them the 
Dict would see that questions were at issue with Russia which might lead to 
hostilities; and it was proper that they should consider whether they would 
remain entirely unprepared to support the Austrian and Prussian Governments, 
which might Rane ta engage in them, Count Buol stated that the Prussian 
Government had taken umbrage at the circular despatch which had been 
addressed to the President of the Diet, Baron Prokeseh, and to the Austrian 
Ministers, because they had not previously been made acquainted with it. This 
circumstance, Count Buol stated, had been explained by the fact that a copy of 
that circular, for communication to the Prussian Government, had been entrusted 
to Count Esterhazy, who had been accidentally detained for a few days at 
Vienna; and it was in consequence of this delay that the Prussian Government 
had first become acquainted with the document sara an indirect source, 
The matter had been taken up with some asperity by M. Bismark Schoenhausen; 
but the explanation above given had since been made, and the fresh commun 
cation to the Diet which Count Buol had proposed to the Prussian Government 
would, he hoped, take place without delay.

(No. 305. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Vienna, August 16, 1854. 

IN a conversation with Count Buol on the present policy of Austria, his 

Excelleney stated to me that the proposed advance of the Austrian troops, 
whose movements between the Ist and 10th of September it had been intended 
to combine with those of the English and French armies, for the putpee of 
driving the Russians from the Principalities, if they had refused to conform to 
the Austrian summons to evacuate them, having been rendered unnecessary 
by the voluntary retreat of the Russian army, the Austrian Government would 
now proceed to oceupy the Principalities, with the en gement that they would 
not again permit them to be invaded by Russia. Yount Buol added that in 
taking this measure his Government did not for a moment pretend to an 
exclusive right of occupation, although they were of opinion that in such an 
operation it was wise to avoid as fur as possible the employment of troops of 
different nations. He said that all details connected with the occupation would 
be settled in the most friendly manner with the Porte. ‘Looking, therefore, to 
the carrying out this measure without opposition or delay, some of the Austrian 
corps which were still on march had been ordered to halt in their different 
positions, in order not to accumulate a greater number of troops than was 
necessary on the frontier, 
‘The Russian Government, he suid, in ordering the evacuation of the 
Principalities, had expressly stated that 1b was a strategical operation, and 
therefore they had imposed no obligation on the part of Austria in the manner 
of carrying out the occupation, With regard to what might now arise between 
Russia and the Austrian Government, it would very much depend upon the 
nature of the reply from St, Petersburgh to the last communication he had made, 
hut in the meantime his Government were carrying on their armaments, and 
were completing those which were in progress. 

I acquainted Count Buol with the importance your Lordship attached to 
the judicious execution of the measure of occupying the Principalities, so that 
rio umbrage might be given to the Government of the Porte or to any of the 
allies, and he assured me that he was fully sensible of the necessity of acting 
with the caution suggested by your Lordship. The Austrian Government, he 
said, had no other object in entering the Principalities than to aid the general 
cause in whieh the allied Governments were engaged, and as observations had 
heen made as to their not having entered them when they announced their 
intention of so doing on a previous occasion, he could not help saying that the 
suspension of the ineasure had been attributed to very erroneous grounds. 
They had been reproached, he said, with having required the Turks and allies 
to undertake that operation, but this statement contrasted singularly with the 
accusation brought against them that they wished for an exclusive occupation. 
The proposals which they had sent to the different head-quarters of the allies 
(immediately before the arrival of the announcement by Prince Gortchakoff’ of 
the evacuation) for a general cooperation for the liberation of the Principalities, 
was a sufficient proof of the inaccuracy of such an insinuation, and the 
acceptation which had been received from Omer Pasha of the proposed coopera- 
tion with his army, and the readiness with which he fixed the dates and 
positions for combined movements, was the best evidence of the confidence 
existing between the two armies, The answer to the similar proposala which 
had been made to Lord Raglin and Marshal St. Arnaud, have not as yet been 
received. 

The real grounds, however, for the temporery abandonment of the pro- 
posed occupation of the Principalities were notorious. Prussia commenced by 
urging objections to it, and she was followed in that course by other Govern- 
ments; in the meanwhile tt appeared that the Russians were not evacuating the 
Principalities, and Austria could not order a hostile movement against thom 
while she was in communication with St, Petersburgh for the purpose of settling 
some basis upon which the terms of peace might be discussed,

Inclosure 2 in No, 43. 
Extract from a Letter from Giurgevo. 


Giurgero, August 3, 1854. 

OWN the lst we made a reconnaissance about twenty-five miles on the road 
ty Bucharest, to a place called Kalagouren, where we fell in with the Russian 
outposts, a few Cossacks. The bridge, however, having been burnt, we did not 
cross the small tributary of Argesh, on which Kalagouren is situated. LT believe 
the main body of the Russians have now left Bucharest, and I should not be 
surprised if the Turks were init ina few days. It would be well, I think, if the 
Government had decided on the steps for woverning the country temporarily 
which they may intend to take. Omer Pasha is most anxious to prevent the 
Turks from doing mischief, and will, Pthink, suceeed, but he is in-very great 
difficulties from the total absence of money in the military chest. As he ought 
to pay for the things he takes and requires in the country, It seems to me of 
the utmost importance that he should receive an immediate supply of funds. 
Not a moment should be lost in remitting them to him. 

So far as lcan judge Russia is only mancuvring to gain time to get her 
reserves organized and up inte Moldavia, or near the scene of action. 

The Gth Corps, as your Lordship is no doubt aware, has entered Moldavia. 
The 2nd has moved down from Blund, and is opposite the frontier of Gallicia, 
arin the Moldavian frontiers, the frontier of the Bukovine and Transylvania. 
This does not look like peace, and | suspect we are only beginning the war, 1 
should not wonder if they intended to fall upon the Austrians single-handed, and 
then to turn round upon us. However, we have gained a great step in having 
obtained a secure base on the left bank of the Danube. Our position at 
Slohoduie is now very secure. The Pasha is exceedingly cautious, and | have 
no doubt will pley a safe game. If he advances to Bucharest, it will only, T 
think, be with a light corps. 

The troops here are in very good health, notwithstanding the great heat, 
which is rather trying.

(No. 458.) 
My Lord, Berlin, August 18, 1854. 

WHEN I went to Baron Manteuffel to-day [ took with me your Lordship’s 
despatches Nos. 220 and 221 of the 15th instant, and as I thought the 
knowledge of their contents might be useful, I read them to his Excellency ; and 
trust that your Lordship will not disapprove of my having done so. 

He maintained that there was a positive misapprehension as to the causes 
whieh led to the refusal of Count Alvensleben to attend the Conference at 
Vienna, and that the desire of the Prussian Government to hold some previous 
communication with that of Austria was the real and sole cause of the 
occurrence. 

His Excellency seemed to feel keenly the observation of your Lordship, that 
it is impossible any longer to confide in Prussia because she is rendering the 
Power with which England is at war such eminent services; and still more so 
the observations which [| made from myself, that we consider the position of 
Prussia to be one of hostile neutrality. Baron Manteuffel said, that for months 
past he had been struggling to prevent the King making a declaration of 
neutrality; that the party about His Majesty were continually urging the 
adoption of a policy which would put an end to the doubts which now existed 
ag to his future intentions; that he had hitherto succeeded in preventing any 
declaration of his views; and that if Russia refused the conditions proposed as 
bases of peace, he believed the position of Prussia must change, und that the 
moment might soon be at hand when joint action with Austria would become 
inevitable. 

I have, &e. . 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

(No. 11. Secret and Confidential.) 
My Lord, Stockholm, August 14, 1854. 
THE French Minister ot this Court, M. Lobstein, recenved on the 10th 
yatant two despatehes from M. Drouyn de Lhuys, dated the Ist and Sih instant. 
The former was brought by Count de Larochelambert, an Attaché of the French 
Mission at Berlin; the latter by the Commandant Blanchard, who arrived here 
by the same steamboat, Upon a comparison of dates—M. Blanchard having 
reached Paris and seen the French Minister for Foreign Affaire on the evening 
of the Bist ultimo—it appears that both these despatches were written alter 
ML. Drouyn de Lhuys had received M. Lobstein’s Bea pai les the substance of 
which has been brought to your Lordship’s knowledge by Mr. Grey, in. his 
despatches No. 189. of the 24th ultimo, and No. 192 of the 23th ultimo. 


43 


M, Drovyn de Lhuys' second despatch, however, was written after the Emperor 
Napoleon had been made acquainted with the substance of M, Lobstein’s 
communications. 

In the despatch of the Ist, M. Drouyn de Lhuys communicated to 
M. Lobstein the project of a Treaty offensive and defensive, which had been 
presented to him by the Austrian Minister at Paris, as well as his own eounter- 
project, agreeing as to the “fond,” but differing as to the form by which it was 
to be effected, and adds that M. de Bourqueney had obtained Count Buol’s 
consent to the proposed alteration of form, subject to the Emperor of Austria's 
approval, and had asked for his full powers to sign by telegraph on the 41st. 

It is unnecessary for me to allude further to these two documents, which 
are of course in your Lordship’s possession. M. Lobstein was instructed to 
obtain the accession of Sweden to the ‘Treaty about to be signed with Austria in 
the first instance, and to let it he amderstood that the Separate Treaty with 
Sweden might be regarded as a corollary of the former; and he was farther 
directed to reply to the confidence already shown by the King of Sweden to the 
French Government, by placing before His Majesty in person this despatch and 
ils inclosures. 

In the second despatch M. Drowyn de Lhuys informs M. Lobstein that the 
Emperor “a accueilli avec la plus grande satisfaction les propositions émancées du 
Roi de Suéde ct les approuve;" that he was ready to accord to His Majesty the 
supreme direction of the campaign in Finland, it being of course understood that 
the immediate command of the Trench troops was to be vested in General 
Baraguay d’Hilliers. 1 remember nothing more of importance in this despatch, 
which M. Lobstein’ read to me, which it is necessary to report to your 
Lordship. ; 

M. Lobstein had an interview, which lasted two hours, with His Majesty at 
Haga on the 12th instant, and submitted to him these documents, which at His 
Majesty's request he left in_ his hands till this morning, when he was promised, 
with their restitution, His Majesty's final answer. 


The King stated frankly that he thought a campaign in Finland was out of 


the question for this year, He said he hed fixed the 20th August or the Ist 
September as the latest period at which such @ campaign should commence, but 
he would have required some previous time to put his army on war footing ; 
and he thought it al ny for Franee to bring 50,000 men into the field in 
sufficient time. His Jujesty acknowledged that on the previous occasion he 
had admitted the possibility of a commencement this year, and taking up winter 
quarters ; but that he no longer thought it advisable. [is Majesty then added 
that though he was opposed to action his opinions as to an allianes remained 
unchanged ; that 15,000) French might winter in the Aland Islands, and might 
defend themselves against all the efforts of Russia; the casemated barracks there 
would hold 4,000, and with the abundince of wood on the islands, the remainder 
might be housed round the forts; that they would have a support in the 
alliance with Sweden; and that on the Ist of May next year the joint operations 
might commence, 

His Majesty expressed a reluctance to accede to the Project of Treaty 
between Austria, Great Britain and France, which M. Drouyn de Lhuys hacl 


drawn up, unless a separate Treaty, such as he had proposed (the substance of

contained nearly the first paragraph of his own, but his second paragraph was 
wanting. | may here state that in Mr. Grey's report of the Treaty, for the

IN fulfilment of the promise made by His Majesty to M, Lobstein, 35

the conclusion of a Treaty with Great Britain, France, ‘nd Austria, Mi. Lobstein 
had requested it might be in writing, and he copied it from M. de Manderstrém’s 
dictation. 

The following, if not an accurate translation of it, 18 very nearly so, and 
certainly contains its strict sense, It states: 

The King cannot change the conditions which His Majesty has already 
stated, namely, that His Majesty requires that the guarantees, which are sought 
for in the North, should have been formally apts en and adopted by the 
Contracting Parties (Great Britain, France, ant Austria) before the united 
kingdoms (Sweden and Norway) take part im the Convention agreed on between 
them. 

This may be effected in two ways, cither by their insertion in the Treaty 
under discussion (the Treaty with Austria), or by additional Articles, acceded to 
by Austria, which should be presented simultaneously to His Majesty, with the 
invitation to accede to the above mentioned Convention. 

If ‘une invitation pure et simple” to accede to the Treaty, of which a copy 
was inclosed in M, Drouwyn de Lhuys’ despatch of the Ist, and which the King 
has perused, was made to His Majesty, His Majesty would feel himself “ dans 
in ndcessité regrettable” of declining such invitation until the moment arri 
when the eventualities with regard to the political position of the North were 
more explicitly defined and agreed on. i 

‘The King thinks it is preferable, in consequence, in every respect, that the 
two arrangements above mentioned should be concluded at the same time, 

It is understood that stipulations respecting gubsidies, “et frais de la mise 
en campagne,” &c., should be treated in separate Articles between the King and 
the two murilime Powers. 

M. de Manderstrdm, after communicating the above decision of His Majesty; 
‘aformed M. Lobstein that his Government had sounded the Cabinet of Vienna 
us long ago as June last, Bs to the possibility of its being unable to preserve its 
neutrality in the present war, The similarity of the Austrian ant Swedish 
positions was divelt on, and the general desire to follow Austria hinted at. 
M, de Manderstrém states that this overture was favourably received by Count

Duchies, are subduing their natural antipathies, and finding a point for agree- 
inent in their sympathy for Hussian principles. As these parties, even united, 
would still be very weak, they must look around for support, and the sentiments 
of His Prussian Majesty and the Kreuz Zeitung Party, naturally attract them 
to that quarter. These inclinations, if they have not yet led to any agreement 
on measures In concert, cannot fail to give currency to reports like those I have 
above alluded to; and I therefore trust that my noticing them may not be 
altogether out of place. 

Connected with these surmises, I beg to inclose to your Lordship an 
article from the * Altonaer Zeitung” of yesterday, the 23rd August, to the 
effuct, that the British Government cannot desire Denmark to depart from her 
neutrality; that no German could desire to see more German unity established 
than the Danes do; and “in regard to the Prussian Cabinet, the highest 
acknowledgements of her moderation and prudence are often heard.” This 
* Altonaer Zeitung" received a regular subvention from the Danish Government; 
but it has, as is said, been lately withdrawn, It is certain that it no longer 
publishes articles offensive to the English and French Governments. 

Whilst addressing your Lordship respecting these rumours, it may not be 
amiss that I should refer to a conversation which I had lately with Count 
Reventlow Criminil, the member of the Danish Cabinet and Minister for 
Holstein. On my way to the Travemiinde, on the 1th instant, it so happened 
that I was placed in # carriage in which there was no one but the Count and 
inveelf, Te began the conversation by deploring the calamitous effects of the 
war, especially for Denmark and Sweden, whose true policy, he maintained, was 
that of vigid neutrality. Upon my alluding to the difficulties that might arise 
to them therefrom, and remarking that it appeared to me that Denmark 
especially would be exposed to less danger from an alliance with England and 
Franee than from one with Russia, he replied, “As I said before, our policy is 
that of strict neutrality, and that we must use every effort to adhere to.” To 
this observation I made no reply, and our conversation turned to other 
subjects. 

LT have, &c. 


(Signed) G. LLOYD HODGES.

No. 66, 
The Earl of Westmorland to the Karl of Clarendon.—{ Received August 28.) 


(No. 314.) 
My Lord, Vienna, August 23, 1854, 

1 CONSIDERED the most satisfactory mode of bringing before Count 
Buol the views entertained by your Lordship as to the present position of the 
Austrian Government in relation to the affairs of the East, was to send to him 
the despatch No. 262 of the 15th instant, which your Lordship had addressed 
to me, 

Count Buol expressed his satisfaction at your Lordship’s remarks upon the 
signature and the exchange of the notes which had taken place between himself, 
M. de Bourqueney, and myself, and which was an evidence that the evacuation 
of the Principalities by the Russian Government had not affected the’ policy of 
Austria, which was to cooperate with England and France for the attainment of 
the objects the three Governments had in view, and with respect to which they 
were happily agreed, 

Your Lordship is aware that, although the Austrian Government consider 
the evacuation of the Principalities as an important object to have been attained, 
yet the terms in which it has been announced to them, as a stratesical measure, 
has imposed no obligation as to the mode in which they have decided (in accord- 
ance with their Treaty with the Porte) to carry out the occupation of those 
Provinces. They do not consider this measure to have been adopted in 
satisiaetion of the demands of Austria; but they look upon their own aavlarstion 
that they will resist the reoceupation of these Principalities by the Russian 
armics as a satisfactory security against their return. 

I have already informed your Lordship, in my despatch No. 305 of the 16th 
instant, of the feelings of Count Buol as regards the signature of an offensive 
and defensive Treaty of Alliance with England aud France, and of the conditions 
upon which lie considers that it must now be made dependent. He expressed 
himself as equally convineed with your Lordship of the importance of such a 
Treaty, and stated his readiness, whenever the oevcasion for the application of 
those conditions should arise, to adopt it, in support of the engagements which 
he had taken with England and France and with his German allies. Count 
Buol received with great interest your Lordship's declaration that the Govern- 
ments of England and France were willing to agree that the conditions contained 
in the note signed by M. de Bourqueney and myself should be regarded as the 
bases of negotiation with Russia, Se considered this assurance as very satis- 
factory, in as far as it was an aceeptation of those conditions of negotiation 
which hitherto had only in # negative form been assented to by the two Govern- 
ments. He said he should make no use of this declaration until he had received 
the same declaration from the French Government; and, with regard to the 
conditions attached to it by your Lordship, he considered the first, “as to those 
Governments having been no parties to their transmission to St. Petersburgh," 
as already fulfilled by the communication with which he had submitted them to 
the Russian Government; and with regard to the second, “that hostilities

should not be suspended until the preliminaries of peace are signed,’ he thouglit,

Russian Government accepted the proposed basis, it might be considered as 
tantamount to preliminaries, and would, in such a case, avoid the delays 
attendant upon the assembly of Plenipotentiaries. Count Buol, however, merely 
suggested this idea as a means by which a decision might be accelerated ; but 
he was satisfied that it was a question with regard to which a perfect under- 
standing between the allied Governments would be arrived at. 

I have communicated your Lordship’s despatch, and Count Buol’s remarks 
upon it, to M. de Bourqueney, who has not yet received any instructions from 
his Government upon this subject, but who (as soon as they reach him) will act 
upon them as I have done. 

1 impressed upon Count Buol your Lordship's forcible arguments, lest, by 
the movement of the Austrian troops, the Russian Government should be able 
to derive political advantages, from their present bad military position, by being 
relieved {rom all apprehension as to the security of their frontier—a result by 
which, if obtained, they would secure a great advantage, while a great disservice 
would be rendered to the allies. | . 

Count Buol stated that it was impossible not to admit that the Austrian 
and ‘Turkish armies concentrated upon the Prath and in the Bukovine, with the 
great vesources of the Principalities (of which the Russians would have been 
deprived) in their rear, and with the means of immediately operating, if so 
required, within the southern provinees of the Russian Empire, were in a much 
more menacing position than that which they had hitherto occupied in the rear 
and flank of those Principalities, and with the Turkish army on the banks of the 
Danube, which army would have become entirely charged with the defence of 
Bulgaria. From this advanced position on the Pruth, the Austrian Government 
were requiring from Russia the consent to those conditions of peace which had 
been agreed to by the three Powers, and which had now been accepted by 
Eneland and France as the basis of negotiation with that Government; and 
while awaiting the answers which would be returned to the communication of 
these conditions, the Austrian army, amounting to upwards of 300,000 men, 
conjoined with the Turkish army under Omer Pasha, were in so menacing a 
position, that it would be impossible for the Russians to detach any effective 
portion of troops from the army with which they had to watch the movements 
of so formidable a force. He must, therefore, consider the advance of the 
Austrian army, in connection with that of Turkey, upon the frontiers of Russia, 
as the most effective operation (short of direct hostilities which might hereafter 
be determined upon by the Imperial Government) which could at present be 
adopted in support of the general objects of the allied Governments.

My Lord, Vienna, August 23, 1854. 


WITH reference to your Lordship’s despatch No. 260 of the 15th instant, 
I feel it my duty to state that no such communication as the one said to have 
been made by the Internuncio and Colonel Kalich, as to the intention of the 
Austrian Government to occupy exclusively the Principalities upon their evacua- 
tion by the Russian troops, was ever made to me by Count Buol. I therefore 
consider the expression of your Lordship’s satisfaction at learning that that 
communication was unauthorized as entirely justified. 

I have stated to your Lordship in my despateh No. 305 of the 16th instant, 
the positive assurance of Count Buol that his Government has put forward no 
such pretension as that of an exclusive occupation, that they had no intention 
of carrying that occupation into execution but with the eoneurrence of the 
Porte, and that as the Principality of Wallachia was now in’ part oceupied by 
ihe Turkish armies, the Austrian Government had no design of impeding or 
opposing them from pursuing the Russians through the Prineipalities if they 
thought it advisable so to do. 

Count Buol has also stated that all the questions relating to the Austrian 
occupation of those Principalities were at present entrusted to the arrangements 
of the Austrian military authorities with Omer Pasha, with whose approbation 
the entry of the Austrian troops into Wallachia had already taken place, and the 
dislocation of the troops of the respective armies would be settled between those 
authorities with the view of combining the separate positions in which each army 
was placed with their mutual convenience. 

‘The Austrian army was about to occupy the Principalities im accordance 
with the stipulations of the Treaty with the Porte of the 16th June, 1854, and 
‘+ was the firm intention of the Imperial Government to adhere religiously 
to the engagements therein contracted. ;

arguments of persuasion only pourtray a servility and pandering. to Russian

propositions, it terminates with an allusion of a reproachful nature to the 
Western Powers. : Putbet .

(No. 445.) 
My Lord, Therapia, August 11, 1854. 

THE Servian Agent has called to apprise me, in substance, of what he is 
charged hy his Government to communicate to the Ottoman Secretary of State. 

It appears from his statement that Prince Alexander has decided on 
complying unreservedly with the requisitions of Austria and the counsels of the 
allied Powers. ‘The Servian militia is to be dissolved; the martial exercises 
practised of late are to be discontinued ; and the attitude of the Principality 
is to be such as to manifest reliance, not on Russia, but on the Porte and 
its allies. 

M, Niecolayevitch assured me that, in reality, his Government had never 
entertained any plans inconsistent with its duty to the Sultan; and that the 
circumstances, whieh at one time had encouraged the contrary supposition, were 
the mere results of anxicty as to future events, and of a desire, natural to every 
‘dividual existence, not to compromise its safety by acts of unnecessary or 
premature decision. 

It is probable that Reshid Pasha will give me a copy of the Servian 
despatch, which, in that case, Tshall forward to your Lordship by the earliest 
opportunity. 

T have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.
