Inclosure 4 in No. 75. 
Colonel Gordon to the Duke of Cambridge. 


Sir, Camp, Gerrekler, Augual 5, 1554. 

IN’ compliance with the orders of your Royal Highness, I went yesterday, 
and on two previous days, through some of the Bulgariin villages in the neigh- 
bourhood, accompanied by Mr. Dickson, for the purpose of inquiring inte the 
cause of the disinelination of the inhabitants to bring supplies into the eamp, and 
the reason why some of them had refused to sell their craps to the Comunssary 
of the division, but had begged him to take what he wanted by force, and pay 
them for it afterwards. : 

Having found some of the leading men amongst the Christians, and gained 
their confidence by friendly conversation of some duration, we obtained the 
same information from each, and heard cach express the same hopes and wishes, 
although they were examined separately and witheut their haying had any means 
of communicating with one Gee ore 

They all state that notice has been cireulated through the district for the 
inhabitants not to sell their gram or forge to either English or French troops, 
for fear there should be none left for the Turkish army. We endeavoured to 
ascertain the name or rank of the officer who gave the notice, but our informants 
took fright at such questions, fearing the consequences to themselves from the 
Turkish authorities being in general the Christian chief of a village, or his 
deputy ; and for the same reason I omit the nanes of the villages where we 
obtained our mftormation, 

One man stated that an officer had come round with the notice, Another 
that the Turkish soldiers, who are quartered in the best house, and living at free 
quarters in every village, had given them the notice, In one village, on the 
morning of the same day we were there, the Turkish cavalry had threatened to 
break the vessels in which the inhabitants sold us milk, which they said ought 
to be made into cheese for them during the winter. 

They cach asked if we could do nothing to protect them from the Bashi 
Bozouks and the Turkish rebbers, who live in the Turkish villages, and occasionally 
assemble to plunder the Christian villages, ‘This is their grent fear; and they 
fully expeet that next winter, when we have left, they will be forced to give up 
the money iow obtained liy the sale of their produce tous. These Turkish 
soldiers sometimes enter the village in a body, and drive away eattle, &e,; buta 
more common way is to carry off the child of any man whom they think rch 
enough to pay a ransom; if the ransom is not paid they put the child to death. 
Only a fortnight since a Bulgarian boy, about twelve years old, was carried off 
from a village we visited; the father sold his cattle, &c., and realised G00 prastres 
to ransom him, but the Turks demanded 3,000, which the father was quite 
unable to pay—the boy's throat was cut and his limbs cut off. This must lave 
been done almost in sight of the English camp. Against these robbers the 
Bulgarians have no protection or means of redress, for they are not allowed to 
carry fire-arms or swords, which every Turk does, and the ‘Turkish soldiers 
quartered in the villages will never interfere to apprehend a Turk accused of a 
crime against the Christians; in fact, the condition of a Bulgarian is little better 
than that of a slave, and those we spoke to all expressed their great desire that the 
Russians would come and occupy the country permanently, for they could not 
be worse treated than they are at present, and there would be at any rate 
community oF religion, \ 

With reference to the complaint from the Civil Governor of Varna of what 
occurred at Soumbey, it appears that the two batteries of the Ist Division 
encamped near that village (which is a Turkish one) on the 25th ultimo, and ho 
previous arrangement for obtaining forage having been made, the Commissary of 
the Artillery pureliased seven loads of barley, for which he paid on the spot 
174 plustres, six loads were taken away to the camp, and on four artillerymen 
returning with an arabe to fetch away the last load, which had been paid: tor, 
nine of ten armed Turks came up and forced them to desist, unloaded the araba 
and drove away the artillerymen, who haying no means with them offered 10 
resistance, . opt 
On the same day that this occurred the water of the only fountain in the

village ceased to run, so that the artillery had to go up the hill nearly two miles 
fora very small supply of water, rendering it almost impossible for them to 
remain at that place, On thefollowing morning between 4 and 5 the water was 
running from the fountain, and Turkish women were seen getting water at that 
hour; but soon afterwards it ecased to run, and remained dry until the artillery 
left next day. Two days afterwards 1, myself, saw the water running as 
usual. ‘This does not actually prove anything, but it seems most probable that 
the Turks eut off the supply of water in order to compel the batteries to change

Inclosure 5 in No, 75. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to Reshid Pasha, 


Therapia, August 12, 1854. 

THE Undersigned is again placed under the painful necessity of calling the 
Porte’s attention to circumstances which form a just ground of complaint an the 
part of Her Majesty's army in Bulgaria, They are of an extremely serious 
nature. ‘They not only corroborate the truth of previous reports from the same 
quarter, but exhibit in strong colours the manner in which the same perversion 
of authority that leaves unpunished the most outrageous acts of cruelty tends 
also to exclude the British soldier from local means of subsistence, and exposes 
the great cause for which he has staked his life to the most perilous chances, 

The Ottoman Secretary of State has only to read the accompanying paper's 
in order to-satisfy himself that the Undersigned, in thus stating lis impressions, 
wives way to no ¢xageerated views, Whiether his Highness considers the 
purport of Lord Raghin's despateh accompanying this official note, the facts 
wrought to light in Colonel Gordon's report, or the sentiments expressed by His 
Royal Highness the Duke of Cambridge, he cannot but recognize the gravity of 
the complaints in question, and the urgent obligation of removing their cuuses 
with the least practicable delay, 

It is not enough on such an oceasion to address particular cases of 
erievance, antl to punish the convicted offenders. The Sultan and his Ministers 
uvust feel thatafer such afflicting disclosures, contidence can only be restored by 
the enforcement of remedial measures calculated to secure a free command of 
provisions on purchase to the auxiliary armies, and to protect the peasantry wha 
supply them trom hindrance and outrage. 

The Undersigned abstains purposely from enlarging on so painful a subject. 
He is willing to believe that the Porte, instead of seeking to palate the atro- 
cities complained of, or to cast 1 doubt on their reality, will be no less anxious 
than himself to justify the sympathies of Europe, so warmly displayed in its 
favour, and to wipe out the double stain which lawless subjects and ill-advised 
functionaries have in their several ways endeavoured to fix upon its adminis- 
tration. 

The Undersigned, &c. : 

(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE. 


Tnclosure 6 in No. 75, 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe co Lord Raylan. 


My Lord, Therapia, August 14, 1854. 
YOULL despateh of the Sth instant, containing an inclosure from Lieutenant- 
General His Royal Highness the Duke of Cambridge, and a report from the 
Lonourable Colonel Gordon, had. no sooner reached me than | called upon the 
Ground Vizier, and after putting him in possession of the painful circumstances 
related therein appealed to his judgment, experience, and feeling whether such 
ucts o° baseness and atrocious cruelty were to be tolerated by any Government 


a 


Ok 


having the slightest pretensions to honour and humanity. I disclaimed all 
intention of accusing the Turkish Ministers of complicity in the acts complained 
of, but I also stated my expectation that adequate measures should be forthwith 
taken to protect the unfortunate peasantry from outrage, and to secure for the 
British army free access to local means of subsistence on terms of fair purchase. 
His Highness made no direct objection to my demands, though the explanations 
which he offered had a tendency to weaken their impression, and to make redress 
an object of difficult attainment. 

With respect to the assertions of the peasantry that they were secretly 
discouraged from supplying the British army with provisions, he ascribed an 
unwillingness, which they might have betrayed on that seore, to a misapplication 
of the Porte’s restrictions on the sale of provisions for exportation from districts 
occupied by the allied armies, As to the practice of kidnapping, of extorting 
money by terror, and of murdering by instalments, he classed them under the 
common head of brigandage, and stated broadly his conviction that Turk, 
Greck, Bulgarian, and Cingaree, the four races in Bulgaria, partook in equal 
share of the criminality. 

His Highness admitted that the prevention of such atrocities was a deside- 
ratum, and, to exeuse the authorities for not finding a remedy, stated that the 
trustworthy and experienced policemen employed in time of peace had been 
drafted into the army, and replaced from necessity by others of inferior 
characters, and for the most part wholly destitute of the required qualifications. 

[neither disputed nor admitted the correctness of these statements, but 
insisted on the urgency of putting m some way or other a check upon the 
grievances so justly reprobated, of leaving no room for mistakes which could 
not be repeated without endangering the most important interests. 

M., remonstrances, ‘vested with a more formal shape, accompany your 
Lordship’s despatch and its distressing disclosures before the Council; and as 
soon as L sueceed in obtaining any satisfactory results, | shall venture to bring 
them to your Lordship’s knowledge. 

T have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Inclosure 7 in No, 75. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to Lord Raglan. 


My Lord, Therapia, August 15, 1854. 

SINCE I had the honour of addressing your Lordship yesterday on the 
subject-matter of your despatch of the Sth instant, | am informed officially by 
M. Pisani that having read and explained to Reshid Pasha, agreeably to my 
instructions, the official note by which I comuunicated to the Porte your Lord- 
ship's correspondence, he received fram his eee the assurance that the 
Pasha of Varna, by whom it is presumable that he means the Civil Governor. 
shall be removed, and also that it 1s his Highness’ intention to obtain the 
appointinent of a Commissioner having full power to act, and who will be charged 
to inquire into the cases complained of, and to have condign punishment inflicted 
upon the offenders, “A general firman addressed to the several Governors in 
Bulgaria, and describing the extent of his powers, will be given to this Imperial 
Commissioner, 

It is the more destrable that the proposed measure should be rendered 
effective, not only for redress, but for prevention in future, as the retreat of the 
Russians from Wallachia, and other simultancous operations, may leave the 
peaceable, and in particular the Christian, inhabitants of Bulgaria more than ever 
exposed to the cupidity and violence of their lawless neighbours. On this 
account [ venture to request that your Lordship will favour me with any 
suggestions which your practised judgment and local observation may supply, 
and with this advantage I should not despair of inducing the Porte to act on the 
oeeasion with that degree of vigour and combination which is necessary to 
produce a real and lasting result. 

T have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

Inclosure 2 in No, 76. 
Consul Neale to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Varna, August 9, 1854, 

WITH reference to my despatch No, 94 of the 7th instant, wherein I had 
the honour to state to your Excellency that I had been informed that the French 
troops had sustained a loss of 800 men by sickness and privations in the 
Dobrutscha: I now have to acquaint your Lordship that I am assured, by those 
who are better informed upon that subject, that the number of deaths among 
the French troops on the occasion referred to amounted to upwards of 1,600. 
An oe number have died from cholera at Varna. 

The number of deaths by cholera in the British army, according to the best 
information which is accessible to me up to this date, does not exceed 800. 

The number of cuses generally has been fewer within the last two or three 
days, and the disease has assumed a milder form, 

_ Thave, &e. 
(Signed) EDWARD ST. JNO. NEALE.

My Lord, Therapia, August 15, 1854, 
THE Sultan's Commissioner to Wallachia is to start to-morrow for Omer 

Pasha's head-quarters. His departure has been deferred by the temporary 

suspension of the imilitary operations announced by Austrian. The appointment

has been given to Dervish Pasha, who was formerly employed on the Turco- 
Persian boundary. A better selection might, in some respects, have been made ; 
but those who might have been preferred, were prevented by special circum- 
stances from being named, and Dervish Pasha has at least the merit of being 
attached to his country, and of having much decision of character. 

His instructions are founded upon the communication made to Count Buol 
through the Turkish Ambassador to Vienna, They were stated by me to your 
Lordship at the time; and Thad the satisfaction of learning that they were 
approved by Her Majesty's Government. A proclamation, which the Commis- 
sioner will be authorized to address to the Wallachians on his arrival among 
them, is prepared. [have been careful that so important a paper should be in 
strict accordance with the principles which, under present circumstances, ought 
to be kept in view. Tansladons of the instruction and proclamation shall be 
forwarded to your Lordship by the next messenger. 

‘A Turkish foree under Halim Pasha entered Bucharest several days ago. 
The retreat of the Russians on Busco, in the line to Fokshant, was the imme- 
diate cause of that movement. Prince Gortchakolf appears to have expected it, 
for he wrote to Omer Pasha recommending to his indulgence some Kussiins, 
wounded or sick, whom it was necessary to leave there. 

The Generalissimo himself remained at Rustechuk or Giurgevo with the 
principal part of his troops. It 1s not improbable that he will visit Bucharest im 
person, before his army advances in force in that direction. Reshid Pasha 
affirms that he will not put his army in motion without fresh instructions from 
the Porte, and a thorough understanding with Lord Raglan and Marshal 
St. Armaud. 

Mr. Colquhoun being, on the 7th instant, at Rustehuk, on his way from 
Bosnia te Constantinople, Omer Pasha prevailed on him to return to Bucharest, 
attaching apparently much importance to his presence there at su critical a 
juneture. 

I hope that Mr. Colquhoun will be able to render good service by exercising 


a salutary influence over the local authorities. He ‘enjoys the advantage of 


knowing the place well, and of having witnessed the conduct of Prince Stirbey, 
when ordered by the Porte to withdraw from Wallachia. 


The Internuncio, who called here just now, has every appearance of 


expecting an early declaration of war against Russia on the part of his Govern- 
ment. He assures me that, if Austria decides on that course, such part of her 
army as may be charged with the occupation of Bucharest will he separate from 
the principal force destined to operate from the Bukovina, and to act against 
Russia, should that Power determine to make a stand for the continued 
possession of Moldavia. 
I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

General Klapka’s intended mission is finally dropped. The Porte was 
willing to send him to the armies at Batoum and Kars with some diminution of 
attendance and expense, The General himself was still prepared to lend his 
services, if required. He was, however, of opinion, that the lateness of the 
season presented serious obstacles to his obtaining any efficient result during 
this year. The deficiencies of the army at Kars are already known in detail to 
the Turkish Government. In spite of those deficiencies it appears, from the last 
reports, that the troops were in condition to take the field, and the Porte has 
determined on removing the Commanders-in-chief of both its Asiatic armies. 

Under these circumstances I could not but acquiesce in the expediency of 
dropping a mission of inspection which, at an earlier period, offered a fair 
prospect of advantage, but which had been rendered useless by a series of delays 
and obstructions more difficult to explain than to lament.

I have also the honour to forward herewith in copy the proclamation which 
Dervish Pasha is to publish in Wallachia, and an instruction which | have 
addressed to Mr. Colquhoun on the supposition of his having repaired to 
Bucharest agreeably to his declared intention. 

This morning [ have received despatches from Mr, Colquhoun to the 13th 
instant. 

Colonel Simmons was then at Bucharest with that part of the Turkish 
army which Omer Pasha had selected to occupy thateity, [t appears that some 
doubt was entertained as the real evacuation of the Principality by Prince 
Gortchakoff, and some anxiety as to the result of the movements made beyond 
Bucharest by the Turkish cavalry, 

The prospect of Prince Stirbey’s return to power apne to have been 
viewed by the population generally, and even by some of the more influential 
Boyars, with dislike and apprehension. 

A petition numerously signed is on its way to the Sultan through Omer 
Pasha, for the purpose of objecting to the Prince's restoration. . 

| have reason to believe that Omer Pasha will give the weight of his opinion 
to the object of the petition, and that the Embassies of France and England at 
Constantinople are expected to take the same line. 

lor my part I conceive that the petitioners are substantially right, and 1 
sincerely regret that the support given to Prince Stirbey by the Cabinet of 
Vienna should have placed the Porte in a false position respecting him, 

I venture still to hope that some better arrangement may be made, and 
that facilities in that respect may be derived from the retirement of the Russians 
behind the Prath, supposing the Austrian army not to enter the Principalities in 
that case. 

The language, however, of the Austrian Internuncio, as stated to me ina 
message from Reshid Pasha, points to a different contingency, Tt appears that 
M. de Bruck, in speaking of the evacuation, said that even if it had extended to 
both Principalities, the policy of Austria would be unchanged, and her troops 
would enter Wallachia, 

There is, nevertheless, a remainder of doubt which has induced Reshid 
Pashu to think it better that the Sultan's Commissioner should not enter upon 
his functions at once, and in this sense he has written to Omer Pasha. 

It is probable that in the course of a few days the whole mystery will clear

Inclosure 2 in No. 87. 
Extract from Private Correspondence. 


Trebizond, August 10, 1854. 


BY the Turkish post which reached this afternoon from Eraeroom, we hear 
of the occupation of Bayazid by the Russians on the 29th July. 

There are many stories about at Erzeroom, and all agree that the Turks 
under Selim Pasha, on the advance of the Russians, left Bayazid without firing 
a shot, and fied in great disorder over the lnlls to Kara Klissia, and across the 
mountain pass to Vau where Mahomed Reshid Pasha had taken the command, 
and having reinforced the army with 12,000 Arabs, was contemplating @ march 
on Bavazid. ‘The Russians found in Bayazid very large supplies of bread, flour, 
ammunition, hay, tents, and camp furniture, the greater part of which were Taid 
up for winter stock. Some Bashi Bozouks made a stand, and joined by some 
Rediffs fought nobly, and although many were killed, they committed great 
havoc amongst the Russians; they did not belong to the Bayazid division but to 
the Kars army, and merely met the Russians by accident, 

The road to Persia is intercepted by the Russians, who have also sent a 
detachment to occupy the quarantine station at Kissil Diazel. Many caravans 
had halted, and the people of the adjoining villages, panic-stricken, had fled in 
all directions. ; 

Erzeroom was alarmed on the 3rd by news of the approach of the Russians; 
the bustle and confusion was very great until the report was contradicted, 

General Guyon was nigh taken by a party of Russians near Hagee Veli 
Kivi; he owes his escape to having cut off the top of a Cossack 's lance with his 
sword, and the speed of his horse. ‘The day following, Iskender Bey and 
Mr. Dunean, the “ Chronicle” correspondent, were also near falling inte the 
hands of the Russians; they galloped up to the Russian outpost at Koorook 
Derch, and, after taking a good look at the Cossacks, were gallopmg back, when 
a shower of musket-balls were sent Aying after them; a ball struck close to 
Mr, Duncan’s stirrup on a stone, and several went over his head within half-an- 
inch. 

The English courier from Persia had not yet made his appearance, and 
fears were entertained of his safety. Mr. Baltour, the * Times ” correspondent, 
died a few days since, at Erzeroom, of rapid consumption. The rowils between 
Erzeroom and Trebizond are infested with brigands. a 

The army at Choorooskeo is in a miserable plight; even after recetwing 
large reinforcements from Varna, it is again reduced to 41,000 men, and if 
attacked by the Russians must be totally annihilated, The fever carties off 
hundreds daily, nod Selim Pasha does nothing to render the sickness less 
dangerous ; he amuses himself in his tent, at some distance trom the camp, with 
a host of boys and Georgian girls, and from over-exerhon suffers from pain in 
the back and weak legs, and makes these latter pretexts for not visiting the camp 
oftener, ‘The doctors have ull resigned except one; and the dead are buried or 
rather half-buried wherever they chance to full. The stench from the bodies is 
awlul. sian tace 

The fever is also committing ravages at Redout Kaleh, Captain Chapman, 
who commanded some 140 Engineers and Sappers and Miners (English) stationed 
there, embarked on board the * Wasp” in a very poor state of health. Captain 
Gordon, who was ut Sookoum Kaleh, was obliged to leave on account ol il health. 
Lieutenant Lampierre, R.E., now at Redout Kaleh, has caught fever, The 
“ Purious” and “ Firebrand” are sounding off Anapa. Captain Brock was. at 
Bardan, and the * Wasp” was gone to him; he had not heen able to reach 
Schamy 1, | 

Some forty Circassian chiefs reached ‘Trebizond som days ago, and went 
onto Varna, and among them was Schamyl's Deputy:Naib, ‘They go to Varna 
to consult with Lord Raglan and Marshal St. Aroaud as to the future. Phey 
object to be put under Turkish yoke, and will be independent or unier England ; 
without some such promise they will not stir against the Russians, but take theit 
chance. If their terms are accepted, they engage to furnish at once 80,000 
iifantry and 20,000 cavalry, | 

The ex-French Consul at ‘Tiflis arrived here yesterday, and goes on fo 


re

Trebizond, August 12, 1851. 
ISKENDER BEY, a Hungarian in the Turkish service, who fought so 


nobly at Sockbatan, arrived here this day from Kars in four days, bearer of 


intelligence of a bloody battle fought on Saturday the Sth of August, between 
Kajee Veli Kioi and Koorock Derch, ‘The details. as given by Iskender Hey 
are as follows; on the 4th instant, the Turkish force, all but five battalions and, 
twenty-four cannon, left Kars, and marching through Veli Kioi halted before the 
Russian outpost of Koorook Derch. The Turks, counting that evening 30,000 
atrong, divided into two divisions, commanded the first by Kerim Pasha, and the 


second by Vely Pasha, with General Guyon as Chief of the Staff, and Aan 


Mustapha Pasha as Commander-in-chief and Generalissimo. Hassan Pasha, 
Commander-in-chiet’ of the Arabistan Irregulars, commanded the reserve division 
in the field, and Pasha commanded the reserve division in Kars; Kmety 
commanding the advaneed guard. During the night of the 4th, the Russians 
advanced to their outposts and took wp a position on the plain, about 400 yards 
from the ‘lurks, and exactly on the spot where their outpost stood the might 
hefore; they were commanded by General Prince Beibitoft, and General Prince 
Dolgorouky Baratinsky, Chief Staff Officer. At 5 a.m.,on the Sth, a general 
action commenced; at 9 o'clock the left Russian wing commenced giving way, 
but heing yeinforced soon revived: at 11 both sides got so close that they 
charged each other with bayonets ; and at 12 the action ceased as if by mutual 
consent. The Turks, leaving 6,000 dead on the field, retreated ina very orderly 
manner, except a small part of Kerim Pashua's division, whieh went rather 
hastily and chimsily to work, and retired helter-skelter, 

The whole force got to Kars early in the afternoon, when the wounded 
were immediately dispatched to Kraeroom; these amounted to about 3,000, 
The Russians left 6,000 dead on the field and carried away about 2,500) 
wounded ; one of their Generals was killed and a great many officers. Among 
the Turks killed was Hassan Pashaof the reserved division, Among the wounded 
Mustapha Pasha, Cochiminsky, a Hungarian Colonel, in the neck. Iskender 
Bey had a horse shot under him, and cut his forehead in the fill, All the 
European officers, from General Guyon downwards, behaved with great coolness 
of mind, courage, bravery, and activity, as did also Mr. Duncan, the “ Chronicle” 
correspondent, During the battle the Russians had six guns dismounted, anil 
the Turks ten, The Russians on the afternoon of the Sth surrounded these 
wuns with cavalry, and walked the whole sixteen guns off to Koorook Derch, 
alter doing which they retired to their former camp, leaving a small force at one 
hour's distance, and exactly opposite Hajee Vely Kioi, where the Turks left twa 
regiments of Cavalry and sowie Infantry under the command of General Kinety. 
For once in a way the Bashi Bozouks hehaved well, and only about 600 fled to 
their homes, 5 deserted over to the enemy before the action commenced, and 
| after all was over. The Russians also had several deserters over to the Turks 
before and after the action. Both armies fought nobly and bravely, and although 
in strict military language the Turks may be said to have lost the battle, still the 
Russians suffered greatly, and every bit us much as the Turks, The day 
following the battle Iskender Bey went to General Beibitoff, by orders of the 
Mushic, and both sides agreed to allow each other tondvance end bury their dead. 
The Turks and Cossacks consequently met alongside of one another, and appeared 
quite friendly. Zarif Mustapha Pasha’s ¢ocrage and presence of wind did much in 
keeping the army from giving way. The old man was in the heat of the tire

(No, 287.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, August 31, 1854. 

YOUR Lordship's despatch No. 814 has been received and laid before the 
(lueen. 

Her Majesty's Government apprave of your having sent to Count Buol my 
despatch No, 262, and they eoveive with satisfaction the fresh assurances of his 
Excellency that the re-occupation of the Principalities by the Russian armies 
will be resisted by Austria, and that he is convinced of the importance of a 
Treaty being signed in support of the engagements taken by Austria with 
England and France; but your Lordship will inform Count Buol that it is quite 
impossible for Her Majesty’s Government to adopt his Excellency’s suggestion, 
that if by any official act the Russian Government accepted the proposed bases 
it might be considered as tantamount to preliminaries ; for Count Buol will doubt- 
lesa admit that these bases, although most useful asa point of agreement between 
Austria, England, and France—although indispensable as guarantees for the 
future peace of Europe—yet require to he both more fully developed and 
more accurately defined in order to fulfil the intentions of the three Powers ; 
and in the improbable event of their beng accepted with good faith and sincerity 
by the Emperor of Russia, they might when negotiations commenced be found 
more comprehensive in their nature, and more restrictive of the power of Russia, 
than His Imperial Majesty has been led to except from the notes exchanged 
between the three Powers. 

Her Majesty’s Government would be as little disposed to give an enemy 
just cause for complaint as an ally, but on the other hand they are determined 
to give no undue advantage to their enemy, and the adoption of Count Buol’s 
proposal, leading, as it would do, to an arinistice, would be a great and exclusive 
benefit to Russia. 

My despatch No. 262 was ex jlicit upon this point, and your Lordship 
could have no doubt respecting the ¢ etermination of Her Majesty's Government ; 
but you will again announce to Count Buol that England and France cannot 
permit hostilities and be dependent on negotiations, and that they are firmly 
resolved not to lay down their arms until preliminaries of peace with Russia are 
signed,

No. 89). 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received August 31.) 


(No, 467.) 
My Lord, Berlin, August 28, 1854. 

BARON MANTEUEFFEL mentioned to me to-day that he had received 
despatches from Baron Werther at St. Petersburgh, who reported that Count 
Nesselrode had expressed much annoyance at the communications from Berlin 
in support of those lately forwarded from Vienna, and that he had especially 
observed on the tone in which the King of Prussia had written to the Emperor, 
urging His Imperial Majesty to accept the proposals which had been made as the 
bases for a negotiation for peace. ; 

His Excellency said that the Russian Government had not yet decided on 
the answers to be returned, and that Count Nesselrode’s observations to Baron 
Werther were yery vague, but they left the impression on the Prussian Minister 
that the questions of the navigation of the Danube, the revision of the Treaty 
of 1841, and the protection of the Christian subjects of the Porte, might be 
accepted ; but the remarks of Count Nesselrode on the proposed future arrange- 
ment for the government of the Danubian Principalities led to the belief that 
they could with difficulty be entertained on account of the state of national 
feeling on this subject. 

Baron Werther added that the Chancellor spoke of his desire that any con- 
cessions compatible with the honour of his country should be made, and the 
Prussian Minister seemed to hope something from the fact that Count Nesselrode’s 
influence was said again to be in the ascendant. 

_ Baron Manteuffel said to me that the Chancellor had observed that the 
Vienna communications did not contain the assurance that the four points 
named were proposed to Russia by England and France as the bases on 
which the Government of these countries offered to negotiate for peace, and 
sae it might be considered doubtful whether these proposals were binding on 
hem. 

1 replied to his Exeelleney that it was perfectly true that we had made no 
proposals to Russia, nor ha we any intentions of making any to a country with 
which we were at war, but that Count Nesselrode might rest assured that if the 
Emperor consented at once to the terms which have been made known to then 
by the Cabinet of Vienna, the British and French Governments would not fail 
to abide by their engagements with Austria, and be found disposed to enter 
upon negotiations. 

I then said that I apprehended Count Nesselrode had only raised this 
question because he had no better reason to offer for his hesitation to agree to 
the proposed terms, 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

No. 96, 


Lord A. Loflus to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received September 4.) 


(No. 53.) 
My Lord, Berlin, Seplember 21854. 

ON my waiting on Baron Manteuffel this day his Excellency informed me 
that Baron Budberg, the Russian Minister at this Court, had communicated to 
him a despatch from Count Nesselrode, in reply to that which his Excellency 
had addressed to Baron Werther on the [3th ultimo (of which a copy was 
inclosed in Lord Bloomfield’s No. 465 of 25th ultimo), instructing him to 
support the conditions submitted by Austria to the Imperial Cabinet. 

Baron Manteuffel stated that the answer of the Russian Cabinet to those 
proposals had been forwarded to Vienna, and a copy of Count Nesselrode’s 
despateh to Prince Gortchakoff was inclosed for communication to the Prussian 
Government. His Excellency first remarked that Count Nesselrode had 
expressed to Baron Budherg his great annoyance and displeasure at the support 
which Prussia had given to the Austrian conditions, and likewise to the terms in 
which that support had been expressed, 

He then informed me that the despatch to Prince Gortchakolf conveyed the 
Emperor of Russia’s refusal to accept the condition submitted by Austria; it 
stated that the Emperor had made concession after concession, and that he could 
not yield any further; that he should evacuate the Principalities and withdraw 
his forces within his‘own froutier, and assume the defensive; that he was not 
indisposed to negotiate, but that he did not think that the present was the 
moment, and he should therefore await in his strong defensive position a more 
favourable one, and the march of events. 

Baron Manteuffel, on mentioning to me the displeasure which the Emperor 
had expressed with respect to the terms of the despatch to Baron Werther, 
observed to me that Count Bernstorff had reported that your Lordship had 
equally found fault with that despatch, and that it was singular that it had 
neither pleased the English nor the Russian Cabinets, I replied that perhaps 
his Exeelleney would permit me to remark that in this respect the despatch 
might be # faithful representation of the Prussian policy, which it appeared had 
not the good fortune to please either party. 

His Execelleney informed me that he had left Putbus before Count Ben- 
chendorff's arrival, and before His Majesty had been made acquainted with the 
Emperor's intentions. 

L endeavoured, but in vain, to extract an opinion from his Excellency as to 
the course which the King would now pursue, and as to whether any hope 
could be entertained of the adoption of a more decided policy. He only repeated 
what he had previously expressed to Lord Bloomfield, that he did not think that 
any change would take place during this year, adding that it would be an 
illusion were he to state that Prussia would be found marching in our ranks, 

I stated to his Excellency that the refusal of the Emperor to accede to the 
conditions proposed by Austria, and supported by Prussia, would, I trust, open 
the eyes of the King to the deceptive and ambitious policy of Russia; that the 
question was now clearly no longer un Oriental question—it was an European 
one, in which all the Great Powers were bound to coalesce to preserve the balance 
of power; that in former periods of history such coulitions had successfully 
combated against the aggressor and perturbator of the peace, and that T did not 
doubt but that on this oceasion the same spirit would be awakened in Europe 
imainst the common enemy. 

I remarked that duties were imposed on great Powers which they could 
not abandon without forfeiting their rank in the scale of nations, and that in 
ihe present erisis it was impossible that a country geographically situated as 
Prussia, with her large extent of territory and military forces, could remain 
inactive or neutral. Such neutrality would virtually imply nu'lity, and an 
wutire sacrifice of all influence, rank, and participation in the great policy of 


‘Europe— position which L could never believe would be borne by the Prussian 


nation, 


8. 


His Excellency listened attentively to my observations, but. maintained a 
placid reserve, without offering one word of comment or explanation. ‘ 
I am informed that he maintained the same reserve with the Marquis de 
Moustier. 
I have, &c. Mpc Se 
(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS.

Inhabitants of Wallachia and Moldavia! 

IN consequence of an agreement concluded by His Majesty, my most gra- 
cious Lord and Master, the Emperor, with the Sublime Porte, the Tinperial 
Austrian troops enter the Principalities. | 

They will remove from you the hardships of war, and restore to you the 
blessings of peace. me Sled 

Receive these hostages for your future tranquillity and secunty with love 
and confidence; they will deserve it by their correct conduet, by u constant 
display of order and discipline. + Wik Hs (Ses 

~ The privileges secured to you by the Sublime Porte remain in full force, but 
T expect on the part of your authorities every assistance for quartering and 
provisioning the troops, for whose wants a compensation will always be given ; 
and on the part of the people tranquillity and order, for any disturbance or even 
threat of it by uproarious individuals or parties will be put down with all the

BY the best information which | can obtain of the dispositions of the 
members of the Diet im reference to the Eastern question, more particularly 
with respect to the policy of the two great German Powers, the actual situation 
may be described as follows : ; 

It is thought that Russia by declaring that she will evacuate Moldavia and 
Wallachia, gives a sufficient satisfaction to Austria, and consequently to 
Germany, provided the declaration is honestly fulfilled within a reasonable 
period, —say the end of September. Spt oo) 

Anustria’s declaration that her o¢cupation of the Prineipalities on the retreat 
of the Russians, is not to be regarded by the Czar as a hostile measure, 1s 
senerally approved, 

If by undue delay of the Russian troops in the general measure of 
evacuation, or by their attempting to hold some strategic point within either 
province, the Austrian troops come into hostile collision with them, the Diet 
will not be inclined to consider auch collision as & necessary casus belli for 
Germany. a . | 

If ‘Austria occupies the Principalities without obstacle, but then puts 
forward further demands on Russia, the Dict will not support such demands. 

If, on the other hand, Russia attacks, either in the Principalities or 
elsewhere, especially in the latter case, the Diet will make common cause with 
Austria. ‘The latter supposition indeed brings the Treaty of the 20th April 
into play, but I am here referring rather to matters of inclination than of 
Treaty engagements, and much as I see the powers that be in Germany inclined 
to eschew a state of warfare a5 long as possible, 1 am equally convineed that 
the danger of a foreign attack on German territory would wnite them in

hetween our own country and France, and its probable consequences on their

her neighbour on the other side of the Rhine. 

Tt may then be surmised that if Austria connects herself more closely with 
the Western Powers and with Turkey, this apprehension and fear of the future 
will be considerably angmented, and will lead to one of two things—either a 
desperate resolution to take part with Russia, or the more rational decision to 
act with the rest of Europe against the Northern Power. 

As it may be presumed that natural connection with Austria would in such 
case have some influence, it will perhaps be the most reasonable to expect that 
‘nthe last resort Prussia as well as the rest of Germany would march against 
Russia, but she will do it (as far at least as her Government is concerned) 
most reluctantly, and with many an uneasy look towards the western frontier. 

In laying these considerations before your Lordship, I leave wholly out of 
sight the efforts of Russian or any other diplomacy, merely looking to general 
results which will, as I conceive, hardly be affected in the end, though they 
may be delayed in their progress by any efforts of intrigue or influence, excepting 
by warlike successes or the contrary on one side or the other, 

1 will, however, permit myself to observe that in the intercourse which | 
have with my colleagues, and with other persons in this residence, I distinguish 
with regret a greater degree of general mistrust and want of confidence towards 
England than existed previously to the commencement of the war. Iam bound 
to add, that the inaction of our joint armaments has created impressions of our 
inability to coeree Russia, almost countervailing the altered opinion now con- 
ceived of that Power since the non-success of her operations on the Danube. 

At this moment the Russian reply to the noted four points is still unknown 
here; it may produce a considerable change in the position, and if as reported, 
it proves decidedly unfavourable, will tend more to strengthen Austrian policy 
than any event which has occurred within a long period, : 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) A. MALET.

Inclosure 2 in No. 103. 
Fice-Congul Stevens to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Trebizond, August 12, 1854. 


TWO Aide-de-camps in charge of despatches for Constantinople reached 
this to-day from Kars, which place they left on Tuesday last. On the Saturday 
previous (the Sth instant) a terrible battle was fought at Koorook Dereh, situated 
Hearaan Hadji Velli Khoi and Gumry. ‘The Turks in two bodies commenced 
the attack at 5 o'clock in the morning, and were composed of 22,000 infantry, 
4,000 regular cavalry, 4,500 irregular cavalry, 5,000 Bashi Bozouks and Reditls, 
with 52 field-pieces. A reserve corps of 5 battalions of infantry and four field- 
hutterics were left in Kars. ' 

The first body was commanded by Kerrim Pasha, the second by the Mushir 
Zarif Mustapha Pasha, and General Guyon acted as Chief of the Stafl. 

The Russians, on the other hand, consisted of 25 battalions of infantry, 
4 regiments of Don Cossack cavalry, 2 regiments of Circassian Cossack cavalry, 
2 regiments of dragoons, 6 regiments of irregulars, and 60 spb under 
General Prince Bebitoff, seconded by General Prince Dolgorouky Baratinski. 

Both sides seem to have fought bravely, and all did their duty, save the 
Turkish cavalry, which proved very inferior. 


80 


The loss on either side was considerable, and is estimated at 5,000 to 6,000, 
besides 2,000 wounded. 

After five hours’ fighting, the Turks retreated in tolerable order to Kars, 
leaving Ismail Pasha (General Kmeta), with two regiments of cavalry and nine 
ficld-pieces, to watch Hadji Velli Khoi. 

The Russians retook their first position. Ten Turkish and six Russian 
suns were dismounted, and owing to the superiority of the Russian cavalry 
were finally carried off the Russians. Bul for the loss of these ten guns, and 
the fact of the Turks having abandoned their position by retreating to Kars, the 
battle might have been considered as drawn. ‘Those two circumstances unfor- 
tunately give Russia the right to the victory. 

Amongst the Turkish officers killed was Hassam Pasha, belonging to the 
reserve. Mustapha Pasha, of the Arabistan troops, was wounded; as also 
Colonel Tufan Bey (Cochiniski, a Pole). On the Russian side a General fell, 
as well as many olficers. 

The sick and wounded had commenced reaching Erzeroom when the Aide- 
de-camps let the city last Thursday. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) F. A. STEVENS.

foreigners. Owing to its haying lost its way in the night the left wing arrived 
two hours later than the right, which at daybreak occupied the heights above 
the enemy's camp. Instead of surprising the enemy, the latter were discovered 
drawn up in full force in battle array, whilst the baggage and tents had been sent 
to the rear across the Kars-tchai. Either by their spies or through treachery, 
the Russians were perfectly acquainted with our movements, and fully prepared 
to sive battle. Kerrim Pasha seeing that the second division, or left wing, did 
not approach, took up his position and awaited its arrival. ‘The Russian General, 
Bebitoff, perceived the forlorn position of this corps, and at once attacked it 
with the whole strength of the army. 

After a sanguinary struggle, the Turkish right wing, left to its own resources, 
crushed by cavalry charges and torn by grape, gave way and disbanded. Whole 
battalions ran away, not in a mass but in units. The whole place was covered 
with dots representing men, and Russian dragoons committed sad havoc amongst 
this living crowd. A more shameful sight could not be seen; officers set the 
example of flight, and the display of cowardice was incredible, ‘The pursuit of 
the Russians was stopped by the arrival of the Turkish left wing, which now 
appeared, and attacked the Russian right. The enemy here gave way, but 
being reinforced by the dragoons, who returned from the pursuit, returned with 
vigour to the fire. ‘The Turkish cavalry soon gave way; the artillery followed, 
which accounts for their not being captured; and the infantry disbanded, as was 
the case with the vight wing. The Russian dragoons, mad with drink, here 
hewed down hundreds, whilst the cannon poured in grape on the retreating mass. 
The Russians suffered severely, for they soon desisted from the pursuit, which, 
had they only continued a little longer, would have resulted in the total capture 
of the Ottoman army, with arms, baggage, and cannon. The stream of fugitives 
extended from the camp to Kars, a distance of five hours. 

‘The defeat must be attributed chiefly to the want of punctuality on the part 
of Vely Pasha, whereby the enemy was enabled to combat with full foree each of 
the two divisions, and also to the intense cowardice of the Cavalry and Reditt 
regiments. The latter were mixed up with the good regiments, and drew them 
away in their flight. The garrison of Kars was under arms, aud prevented the 
entry into the town of Bushi Bozouks and fugitives, who would otherwise have 
pillaged the town, Last night we expected the Russians, who, however, did not 
appear, Should the enemy appear, not a man will show fight, and Kars with 
Ierzeroom will fall. 

In my opinion the policy of Russia, at present, in Asia is not to advance 
into the Turkish territory, but to act there strictly on the defensive. A few 
days will show what we have to expect. 

Exeuse, my Lord, the haste with whieh I write this, but, as 1 mentionedt 
above, I am tired to death; we were seventeen hours on horse, without food or 
witer, 

I have merely given your Lordship an indistinct account of the action, but 
it will suffice to clear up many exaggerations which will be current in Stamboul. 
The Turks were 25,000 strong; the Russians 21,000, Our loss is of course not 
known, but J imagine it to be about 1,500 killed and wounded, 2,000 prisoners, 
and 5,000 who have passed Kars and returned to their homes. The army is 
completely lost and demoralized, They say 5 cannons are lost, but I believe 
more than 20 have fallen into the hands of the Russians. 

The Russians must have lost about 1,200 to 1,500 men.

‘The announcement by Count Neseelrode of the decision of the Russian 
Cabinet to reject all the terms which had been proposed by the note of Count 
Buol to Count Esterhazy of the 10th ultimo, as bie sis upon which he would 
desire that a negotiation for peace might be established, was received by Count 
Buol (alter the information which has previously heen transmitted from Berlin) 
with sone surprise; and in announcing that he should immediately transmit 
copies of this document to London and to Paris, he said that he should accom- 
pany it by the reflections which the new state of things created by the decision 
of the Emperor Nicholas had suggested to him, 

He said that the engagements which had been entered into by Austria with 
the English and French Governments could in no way be affected by this 
decision ; that it was only necessary still more to fortify the position which had 
been taken by his Government by obtaining the sanction of Prussia and the 
German States to the guarantees which had been adopted by the Allied Govern- 
ments as the basis of any future negotiation, He was anxious upon this point, 
and was expecting a reply to the communication which he had already made 
with regard to it to the Cabinet of Berlin. | 

2 C 


“a

ha | 


98 


He considered the position in which the allied Governments were placed at 
the present moment was satisfactory, All the points contained in the guarantees 


which were required were in their possession: the Principalitics were evacuated, 
and were about to be entirely occupied by the Austrian and Turkish armies, who 
would defend them against any future fggression on the part of Russia; the 
mouths of the Danube were almost entirely in the power of the allies ; the 
Black Sea was under the control of the Western Powers: and if the Russian 
fleet was captured in Sebastopol, their influence there would be wholly destroyed ; 
the Russian Protectorate of the Greeks was also annihilated; and under these 
great disadvantages, Russia had retired within her frontier. 

I stated to Count Buol that I felt sure that your Lordship would be 
anxious under the present state of things to draw closer the bonds of alliance at 
present existing between the allied Governments and Austria by the signature 
of an offensive and defensive Treaty of Convention, such as had been already 
proposed: but Count Buol answered that until he had received the reports from 
Count Esterhazy at St. Petersburgh, and those he expected as to the attitude 
which Prussia would assume, he was unwilling to enter into any new negotii- 
tion « that he had explained the position which his Government would maintain 
‘1 his communications to Count Golloredo and M. de Hibner, and that he 
should await the replies he should receive from them; but he repeated the 
assurance he had already given that his firm determination and that of the 
Imperial Government was to maintain every engagement he had taken with the 
allied Governments, and act in entire concert with them for the attainment of 
the important interests they lad bound themselves to secure,

My Lord, Berlin, September 8, 1804. 

I HAD an interview with Baron Manteuffel on Tuesday lust the oth 
instant, and T opened the conversation by calling his Excellency’s attention to 
the striking contradiction which ts contained in the despatch of Count Nesselrode 
to Prince Gortchakoll, conveying the refusal of the Russian Government to 
accept the terms which had been submitted by Austria, I! observed to his 
Excellency, that in the preamble of that despateh great stress wos laid on the 
concession whieli Russia had professed to yield to the remonstrances of Austria 
and Germany by the evacuation of the Principalities, whilst at the conclusion 
of the despatch Count Nesselrade states in unmistakeable terms, “que des 
motifs uniquement puisés dans nos nécessités stratésiques,”” had induced the 
Emperor to withdraw the troops within his frontiers 

In drawing his Excellency’s attention to this striking discrepancy, 1 stated 
my hope that it might be the cause of opening the King’s eyes to ihe duplicity 
of the Russian policy towards Germany, His Excelleney perfectly concurred in 
this view, and remarked to me that it had not eseaped his notice. 

I then stated to bis Excelleney that 1 well recollected the great weight and 
value which he attached during the course of last winter to the concert of the 
four Powers. J expressed my regret that lutely Prussia had for some not clearly 
explained reason withdrawn from that concert. 1 laid before his Excellency the 
sreat importance at this moment (since the Emperor had rejected the counsel of 
Germany) of reuniting the voice of Europe, and of proving to the Emperor that 
Germany condemns his obduracy, which was the sole obstacle to the restora- 
tion of peace, | represented here as forcibly as 1 could that no more favourable 
opportunity could occur for Prussia to regain the ground she lind lost; that 
she could do so now by a-voluntury act, ‘such as the formal adoption of the 
four conditions lately submitted to the Imperial Cabinet, and by her declaring 
them to be the indispensable conditions of a future peace.” 

L told Baron Manteuffel that it was but the necessary corollary to the 
step which the King had lately taken ut St. Petersburgh, and that such a 


99 


measure would not only produce the best effect in Europe, but would prove of 
the greatest benefit to I russia. In an European light it would re-establish her 
good fivith and confidence with the three Powers. Ina German sense it would 
regain for her the position which she had abdicated, and would harmonise her 
policy with that of Austria. 

__ His Excellency replied that he had already spoken with the King on the 
subject even previous to the arrival of the Russian answer; that the King had 
raised objections on the score that these four conditions were not definitive on 
the part of the Western Powers, but were dependent as.to their extension on 
the future eventualities of the war; that on this account he did not like to bind 
himself, and he was moreover indisposed to take any engagement which might 
foree him into war, or oblige him to take an active military part. 

T observed to his Excellency that there was a difference to be drawn 
between belligerents and non-belligerent Powers. We were actually at war, and 
therefore could make no proposition, or authorize any to be made, to Russia. 

_ We had only expressed to Austria certain conditions, the acceptation of 
which we laid down as indispensably necessary previous to the coinmencement: 
of any negotiations. Austria had aceepted those conditions as her own, and had 
engaged herself to them ; Prussia, on the other hand, had only approved of them 
and counselled their acceptation at St. Petersburgh. By accepting them in the 
came formal manner as Austria had done, Prussia would only bind herself to 
terms of peace, for the attainment of which the King of Prussia had alwavs 
expressed the greatest anxiety. "i s. 

_ As His Majesty had supported those conilitions at St. Petersburgh, it 
might be supposed that he could have no insuperable objections to a formal and 
official adoption of them. They did not bind him to go to war, but they would 
have a vowertul weight in giving an assurance to the Western Powers that 
Prussia did not withhold her moral assistance from them, though she at present 
denied her material aid. . 3 

__1 must do Baron Manteuffel the justice to say that he appeared really 
anxious to adopt this course, and informed me that le would submit the measare 
lo the King, and counsel its adoption. He seemed to think that TnL 
difficulties would be raised, but 1 could perceive a ray of hope that he mi rit 
bring the King to accede to it. : : 

I finally remarked to Baron Manteuffel that His Majesty, who was so 
known for his devotion to pence, might be induced likewise to refleet that it was 
possibly in his power to circumscribe and shorten the war; but that he might 
be assured that if he wished to do so and to prevent such future complications 
as might lead te a general conflagration, his only course was to act in union 
with the three Powers, and by entering the European coalition to reduce the 
Hrmperot ot Russia to mush concessions as would restore peace. ot

(No, 1,107. Confidential.) 
My Lord. Paris, September 11, 1854. 


M. DROUYN DE LHUYS received, while at Boulogne, a despatch from 
M. de Moustier, recounting a conversation which he had had with Baron 
Manteuifel, respecting the present position of Prussia in the Eastern question. 
Baron Manteuffel appears to have expressed to M. de Moustier, his regret at its 
being supposed that the Prussian Government was ilLdisposed towards the 
Western Powers. What, he asked, could be done to prove the contrary t It 
seemed out of place now, either to exchange notes with the two Powers, us had 
heen done with Austria, or to express the adherence of Prussia to the contents 
of ‘those notes. Was there ho other way of re-establishing an understanding 
with Great Britain and Mrance? j “ 

Having given me this ‘aformation M. Drouyn de Lhuys added, that it 
acemed that the refusal of the Czar to accept the bases of peace propased by 
the Cabinet of Vienna had had a beneficial effect upon the King of Prussia, anc 
had opened his eyes to the danger of the situation; that it would be well to take 
alyeninge of this change, and that he would tell me in confidence that he 
intended to desire M. de Moustier to reply to the Prussian Prime Minister, that 
the French Government was pleased to find that the Prussian Cabinet was 
desirous of noticing that unanimity of action among the four Powers which had 


een unfortunately impaired by the conduct of Prussia; that perhaps an 


exchange of notes, or au adherence, on the part of Prussia, to the engugements 
entered into by Great Britain, France, and Austria, was not the best mode of 
procses ene at this late hour: but why should not Prussia propose some other 
course; for instance, the signature of a Convention, or of some instrument of a 
more solemn character than a note? 

Your Lordship will observe, that this instruction coincides with the 
language held by M. Drouyn de Lhuys to Count Hatzfeldt, as reported in my 
despatch No. 1,025 of the 17th August. His Excellency added that, in case 
M. de Manteuffel should catch at the idea, and inquire what sort of Convention 
was desirable, he should furnish M. de Moustier with a copy of the Convention 
which the two Governments had proposed for signature at Vienna, and direct 
him to propose it, at a favourable opportunity, as an elaboration of his own. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) COW LEY.

Mr. Buchanan to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received September 12.) 


(No. 257.) 
My Lord, Copenhagen, September 6, 1854. 

GENERAL OXHOLM spent a few days at Copenhagen last week. 
During his stay he stated to me, and also, | understand, to several other 
persons, that Her Majesty's Government were perfectly satisfied that Denmark 
should remain neutral during the present war, and that they had no wish whiat- 
ever to secure her support and alliance, As this language id not appear to me 
to be quite consistent with your Lordship’s opinions, T was glad to receive, by 
the messenger Webster, your despatch No, 107 of the 17th ultimo, acquainting 
me with what had passed at General Oxholm’s interview with your Lordship 
previous to his departure from London. M. de Bluhme, however, was again 
confined to bed, and I could not see his Excellency until yesterday, in order to 
correct any erroneous impressions which he might have received on the subject ; 
but in the meantime | mentioned to M, de Quaade, that T feared General 
Oxholm had misunderstood your Lordship’s observations respecting it. 

M. de Bluhme assured me that he had not understood General Oxholm to 
say more than that Her Majesty's Government did not intend to urge Deninark 
to'abandon her neutrality, I said, in that case General Oxholm had correctly 
reported the intentions of Her Majesty's Government ; but that, with a view to 
his Exeellency’s more complete su alacies with their sentiments, 1 would read 
a despatch which I had received from your Lordship, coutaining your own 
statement of what you had said to General Oxholm. I then read your Lordship’s 
despatch No. 107, and his Excellency seemed much gratified with the assurances 
ind expressions which it contained with respect to the immediate question at 
icsne, He observed, however, with regard to the latter part of the despatch, 
that he could not believe Denmark’s claim to have her neutrality guaranteed 
hy the Great Powers in the same manner as Switzerland, would be strengthened 
by her taking a part as 4 belligerent in the present war. He said also, that, 
independently of this consideration, he did not suppose the Great Powers would 
enter into such an arrangement out of pure benevolence towards Denmark ; but 
that they would be in some degree influenced by what they might consider 
conducive to their own interests. I therefore replied, that whatever considera- 
tion may have hitherto induced the Great Powers to enter into arrangements of 
the kind, it was not to be denied that a guaranteed neutrality was @ great boon 
fon feeble State; and that the obligations which it imposed on the Powers 
undertaking it might become, under inany circumstances, a cause of embarrass- 
ment and inconvenience to them. If such a boon, therefore, I added, were 
desired by Denmark, she could only expect to obtain it through the friendship 
and goodwill of the Powers whose influence would predominate in the general 
arrangements for the reestablishment of peace. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) ANDREW BUCHANAN,

My Lord, Stockholm, September 2, 1804. 

[ INFORMED your Lordship in my despatch No. 22 of the 30th ultimo 
that the French Minister at this Court had, by the instructions of his Government, 
submitted to the King the course which the French Government thought the 
most advisable to pursue in the negotiation for an alliance with Sweden, and 
had been directed to inquire whether that course met with His Majesty's 
approbation. . 

As I brought to your Lordship’s knowledge in my despatch No, 22 the 
march proposed by France, it 18 unnecessary to repeat it at present. : 

The IInd Article of the project of a Treaty submitted to the King, which 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys applies to the particular position of Sweden, states: © Les 
Hautes Parties Contractantes s'étant réservées le droit, en dehors des guaranties 
d'un intérét Européen qu’elles doivent s’employer a obtenir, de poser encore, le 
cas Gchéant, d'autres conditions résultantes de leurs positions particuliéres, et 
des sacrifices qu’elles se sont, ou se seraicnt imposts, elles s’obligent, jusqu au 
rétablissement de la paix générale, ih nentrer dans aucun arrangement avec Ja 
Cour Impériale de Russie avant d’en avoir délibéré en commun.” 

Baron Stierncld read to M. Lobstein on the Ist instant His Majesty's 
answer to these proposals, and the latter copied it from the Swedish Foreign 
Minister’s dictation. M. Lobstein was good enough to communicate it to me, 
but | was unable to obtain a copy of it; its sense, however, was as follows + 

The King thinks that, with respect to the project of a Treaty now 
submitted to him, it is impossible to modify the opinions which His Majesty has 
already expressed with regard to the Treaty proposed by Austria (those opinions 
are reported in my No. 12 of August 14). His Majesty must at the same time 
acknowledge that he sees, “avee un profond déplaisir,” in the [Ind Article of 
the present Project, that the question of Finland is looked on by France as “en 
dehors des garanties d’nn intérét Européen.” His Majesty, on the contrary, 
regards the weakening of Russian power in the North as an indispensable 
euarantee of future peace, and consequently of European interest. 

With regard to the withdrawal of the allied fleets from. the Baltic, His 
Majesty admits that if the Alond Islands be evacuated, he sces no necessity for 
the flects wintering there; he urges strongly, however, that they should remain 
until it be nolonger possible for the Russian fleets to leave Cronstadt or Sweaborg. 
His Majesty advises, consequently, that the three-deckers and large classes of 
sailing-vessels should be sent home, but that a sufficient force of steam-vessels 
and frigates should remain to keep the Russians in check; these vessels, His 
Majesty thinks, might safely eruize off Gottland at first, and find harbours of 
shelter. on the southern Swedisa coasts and in Denmark till they left the 
Baltic. . 

The intelligence received by this Goveroment both from St, Petersburgh 
and from Berlin represent the peace party at the former capital in the ascendant, 
and it is thought in consequence that the answer to the Austrian note of the 
18th August will not positively reject the four conditions laid down in that note; 
it is further felt that the season is too far advanced for a campaign in Finland, 
and His Majesty not uonaturally is unwilling to declare himself at present, 
The steadiness with which he holds to the original terms proposed by him 
is thus explained ; and I think it improbable that he will make ony concession 
in those terms for the present, His Majesty has stated more than ance to the 
French Minister that his alliance was first sought by us, and not ours by him ; 
he also says that he is not anxious for conquest, and he desires that the taking 
of Kinland from Russia, and its reannexation to Sweden, should be declared 
a guarantee of European interest to justify his forming the alliance, aa well as 
perhaps to offer greater chances of its accomplishment. 

I have, &e, 
(Signed) ARTHUR C. MAGENIS.

COUNT COLLOREDO communicated to me, on the LOth instant, a 
(despatch from Count Buol dated the 3rd instant, adverting to the return to 
Bucharest with the Turkish forces of individuals compromised m the troubles of 
the vear 1848, and to the mischief which had already resulted from their 
presence ; though admitting at the same time that Omer Pasha, in conformity 
with a promise which he gave to the Austrian Consul-General, had taken steps 
to remove agitators from Wallachia. . 

The interests of Austria however, Count Buol observes, preclude her from 
allowing revolutionary intrigues to be concocted on her frontier and under the 
eye of her troops. She is bound by ‘Treaty to the Porte to concert with that 
Power for re-establishing a regular administration, and the attempt to do so 
could not fail to be impeded by those restless spirits who advocate ill-digested 
measures of reform, and seek to support them by unseasonable demonstrations. 
The removal of such persons from the scene of action is consequently a common 
henefit to all Powers interested in the common cause, and Austria does not 
doubt that, sharing these views, the British Government will instruct its agents 
in ‘Turkey to assist in giving effect to them, ft 

1 asked Count Colloredo whether the persons alluded to by Count Buol 
were Wallachians or foreigners, and what were the objects they were supposed 
to be aiming at. He said they were Wallachians, and mentioned the names of 


Constantine Rosetti and Nicolas Galeno as the principal agitators, nnd their 
object was to excite the peasants against the proprietary class. 

I informed Count Colloredo that I would instruct Her Majesty’s Consul- 
Soneral at Bucharest to make inquiry, and to communicate with Omer Pasha 
upon the matter, |

Pasha to name an Austrian Commandant de Place at Bucharest; and that 
General Hess has issued a proclamation inviting the authorities to address 
themselves for the future to Count Coronini or to the persons named by him. 

It would thus appear that the first step of the Austrian Commander-in-chiet 
on entering the Principalities was to mark his disregard for the sovereign autho- 
rity of the Sultan, and to ignore the presence of the Turkish Commissioner then 
at Bucharest, and of the Turkish Commander-in-chief, who, with his victorious 
army, had established a state of things satisfactory to the people of Wallachia, 

It appears also that the request of Omer Pasha, that the publication of the 
document should be delayed, was refused by General Popovich, and that it had 
actually been posted at various places along the Austrian line of march trom 
Puthenthurm. 

Her Majesty’s Government consider that General Hess, in adopting this 
decided course of policy, must have acted under the express orders of his 
Government, and they are further confirmed in this belief by hearing that Omer 
*asha was required to withdraw his forces from Bucharest, and to occupy merely 


_ the positions of Giurgevo and Kalarasch, as such a movement would add weight 


to negotiations which Austria might be carrying on, notwithstanding that Omer 
Pasha had come to Bucharest with his army at the express request of General 
Hess, communicated to lim three weeks before by Colonel Kalich and General 
Lowenthal, and on the engagement, approved of by the Commanders-in-chiel of 
the allied armies, that his advanced posts should, by the 5th of September, be at 
Bouzeo, and that his army should be in and around Bucharest. It could only, 
therefore, have been by positive orders to that effect that General Hess departed 
from his own arrangement, and addressed to Omer Pasha a demand which that 
General properly resisted as offensive to his Government, and derogatory to his 
character as the Turkish Commander-in-chief. . 

But these proceedings on the part of the Austrian military authorities are 
altogether at variance with the assuraices which the Austrian Government have 
xiven voluntarily, as well as in answer to the specific inquiries of Her Majesty's 
Government respecting their intentions in occupying the Principalities, and the 
character which that occupation was to assume; and although Her Majesty's 
Government have been informed that in consequence of Omer Pashn’s refusal to 
fall back on Giurgevo and Kalarasel, the Austrian demand to that effect has 
been withdrawn, they still feel entitled to request from the Austrian Government 
an explanation of the course pursued by General Hess, and to inquire whether 
that course has been disapproved, and what instructions will be given him for 
his future guidance,

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received September 15.) 


No. 1,112) 
a fond Paris, September 13, 1894. 


1T would be a waste of your Lordships time to call your attention to the 
substance of the communication made by M. de Hiibner to M, Drouyn de Lhuys 
respecting the future intentions of Austria m regard to the astern question. 
Count Colloredo must have made a similar communication to your Lordship. 
But | have less scruple in recounting the substance of the observations made to 
M. de Hiibner by M. Drouyn de Lhuys after hearing the explanations and 
‘atentions of the Austrian Cabinet. * 
ve M. Drouyn de Lhuys said that he could not but regret a decision. which 
was eo contrary to the spirit.of the assurances made until now by Austria, anc 
so incompatible with the interests of Germany, and he must add, that ake 
publicity whieh the Austrian Government had given to. their resolution not to 
‘ttack the Russian troops beyond the Pruth, was deserving of severe condenmma- 
tions, It was tantamount to informing the Russian Government that they 
might employ all their forces against the allies, as they had nothing to fear trom 
the hostility of Austria, | - 

MM. de Hubner did not gainsay these assertions; but he observed that the 
position of his Government was very delicate and difficult, and was rendered 
doubly so by the isolated position in which Austra was placed, in consequence 
of the expedition to the Crimea. 

* No. 121. 


111 


M. Drouyn de Lhuys replied, that the difficulty was of Austria’s own 
creating. He called to M. de Hiibner’s recollection that, for more than six 
months, the maritime Powers had been urging the Austrian Government to 
come to an understanding with them respecting future operations ; that he 
himself had told M, de Hiibner, when hostilities became inevitable, that there 
were two ways of prosecuting the war—one upon the Danube, the other upon 
the Black Sea; that to make a campaign upon the Danube, the cooperation of 
Austria was necessary; while the maritime Yowers, if left to themselves, must 
carry on their operations in the Black Sea. Over and over again the Austrian 
Cabinet had been pressed to say when and under what circumstances they would 
join the allies. Count Buol had invariably refused every explanation, and had 
‘at last himself admitted that the allies were free to choose their own point of 
attack. Inno way could the situation of the two parties be compared together : 
that of the allies was active warfare; that of Austria, next akin to neutrality ; 
and the result was, that the active hostility of the allies drew upon them the 
resources which the passive neutrality of Austria permitted Russia to dispose of. 
He feared that the policy of Austria would lead to consequences that might 

rove most disastrous to herself, A little firmer language on her part in the 

inning would have preserved peace—a little more decision later would have 
circumseribed the war within its proper limits. Let her beware, lest her present 
attitude, which freed so large a portion of the Russian army, did not lead to 
erayer consequences and a wider extent of the war; lest the troops thus freed 
did not use their freedom to rouse the Slavonic tribes to arms, and to excite 
them against the German race. If Austria hoped, by her present attitude, to 
divert the wrath of Russia, he thought she would be fatally deceived. ‘The same 
weapons which had been tried by Russia against Turkey, namely, creating tlisal- 
fection in the Sultan's subjects, might be turned against Austria ; and in trying 
to avoid a war in defence of justice, and for the protection of the oppressed, she 
might find herself involved, by the oppressor, in a war of nationality. 

1 understand it to be M, Drouyn de Lhuys’ intention to embody these 
arguments in a despatch to M. de Bourqueney, which will be communicated to 
your Lordship. 

M. de Hiibner appears, in the course of the conversation which I have 
recounted, to have attempted to make M. Drouyn de Lhuvs understand that the 
present attitude of Austria was but temporary; that she had contracted no 
engagement not to attack Russia; and that circumstances might yet force her 
todo so. But M. Drouyn de Lhuys said that such observations had but little 
value for him: that he looked to facts; that he contrasted the language of the 
Austrian Cabinet before the conditions of peace were sent to St. Petersburgh, 
with their eonduct now; that the Russian answer had, in fact, been more 
peremptory and insolent than Austria could ever have expected it to be; that 
no one point had been obtained, for in the evacuation of the Principalities, on 

-strategical grounds only, uo guarantee was given that they were safe from 
‘avasion for the future; and the result was that, from the attitude assumed by 
Austria, Russia was relieved, to the detriment of the allies. ;

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clurendon.—( Received September 15.) 


(No. 1,119. Confidential.) 

My Lord, Paris, September 13, 1854. 
IN the course of the conversation with M. de Hibner.to which my preceding 

despatch refers, M. Drouyn de Lhuys stated: to the Austrian Minister that he 

must be permitted to observe that inasmuch as there was a choive between a 

war on the Danube and a war in the Black Sea, so ulso there might be a jieace 

concluded on the Danube or a peace concluded in the Black Sea. If Germany 


took no active part in the war, neither could she expect her interests to be 
consulted whenever peace was made, 


112 


_ _M. de Hibner observed that the notes exchanged between Austria and 
the Western Powers provi’ed for the conditions of peace; but M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys replied that in his opinion these notes could not be considered binding on 
the Western Powers if Austria persisted in giving them no help beyond an armed 
occupation of the Danubian Provinces. The notes were exchanged under the 
supposition that a further Convention would be signed binding Austria to aid: in 
bringing about such a peace as she herself had deemed essential to the future 
wellare of Europe. It could not have been intended then, and could not be 
pretended now, that France and England were to shed their blood for what was 
recognized by the German Powers to he essential to the interest of Germany, 
while Germany remained a passive spectitor of the contest. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys observed to me that he had not been sorry to have an 
opportunity of saying this much to M. de Hiibner. He had, however, touched 
the subject very lightly, and solely with the intention of letting M. de Hitbner 
see that there were two ways of viewing the engagements contracted between 
the maritime Powers and Austria. 

‘To me, however, he must express the conviction that the time would come 
when it would be necessary for the maritime Powers to let Austria clearly under- 
stand that the engagements contained in the notes referred to the eventuality of 
war. 

If Austria was not at war, she would have no Treaty of Peace to sign, and 
could not pretend that she should be consulted by those who were at war 

The notes were part and parcel of a general transaction; an exchange of 
notes was to be made, and a Convention founded upon the coniitions which they 
contained was then to be signed; but as the latter part of the transaction had 
not been executed, it followed that the former part became a mere record of 
opinions exchanged, and that those opinions might be modified as circumstances 
dictated. 

I have, &c.
