No. 139. 
The Earl of Westmorland to the Barl of Clarendon.—(Received September 17.) 


(No. 848. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Vienna, September 13, 1854. 

IN conformity with the instructions contained in your Lordship’s despateh 
No. 288, | waited upon Count Buol, in company with M. de Bourqueney; and 
I submitted to him that despatch, and placed in his hands the copy of the 
project of Treaty which was inclosed in it. 

M, de Bourqueney had already communicated the substance of the despatch 
he had received from his Government upon the same proposal, for the signature 
of an Offensive and Defensive Treaty, and had delivered to Count Buol a copy 
of the proposed Treaty. | 

M. de Bourqueney and myself, in the fulfilment of this duty, accompanied 
it by those expressions which we considered the most adapted to impress Count 
Buol with the importance our Governments attached to the adoption of a 
measure by which the bonds of alliance already existing between our Govern- 
ments would be drawn closer, und a greater effect would be given to the policy 
upon which the three Powers were so happily agreed, and a further security 
bused for the attainment of those guarantees for the future tranquillity of 
Europe, which they had pledged themselves to regard as indispensable. 

Count Buol replied that, notwithstanding the absenee of the Emperor, who 
had left Vienna for Ischl, he felt himself in a position to state that his Govern- 
ment received, with feelings of the most entire satisfaction, the offer of eooperi- 
tion made by the Governments of England and France in the eventuality of 
Austria being engaged in hostilities with Russia; but by the ‘Treaty which was 
now submitted to him, the near approach of that eventuality was so clearly 
indicated as to attribute to the Government of Austria a position towards Russia 
more advanced than that which they had assumed: for if it held out the 
prespect, that they would consider the rejection of the four Articles of the 
proposed guarantees as a caste belli, it would convey a meaning which was 
contrary to their intention; for it was fitting that the Imperial Government 
should openly aud distinetly declare, that not huving made the acceptation of 
those articles by Russia a condition of the maintenance of peace, they could not 
make their rejection a ground for the commencement of hostilities, What they 
proposed to themselves was, at all risks, to an out immediately the entire 
pcoupation of the Principalities, and to defend those provinces against all 
ageression. 

The Imperial Cabinet feel that, by signing the proposed Treaty, they would 
expose themselves to questions as to its import, the answers to which would weaken 
or destroy all the importance which might be attached to it, Nor could they 
become parties to this Treaty wonder an apprehension of an attack from ussio at 


a IN Lar i ee 
. , cast : / f Fay ar ‘ | 
ee Ye ee Fr Meteo): Sethe aS ot a pe 


115 


a time when that Government had declared, in the most formal manner, that 
they assumed an entirely defensive attitude within their own frontiers. 

If Austria, under these circumstances, was to sign this Treaty; she would 
be placing arms in the hands of the Governments of Germany who were adverse 
to her policy, and who would accuse her of having produced an irritation in the 
Russian Government destructive of all hopes of peace by negotiation, without 
adding to the general power of offensive action in case a peace was only to be 
obtained by war. 

Count Buol stated that the Treaty would add nothing to the engagements 
which had already been taken by his Government with the allied Powers, to 
which, and particularly to those taken by the note of the 8th of August, he 
most steadfastly adhered, notwithstanding their rejection at St. Petersburgh , 
and, in exchange for the proposed Treaty, he would submit a project by the 
adoption of which the fidelity of his Government to these engagements would 
be still further demonstrated, and to which he anxiously desires the most 
serious attention of our Governments. 

He would propose that England, France, and Austria should invite the 
Prussian Government to take part in a Conference in Vienna, to which a 
Plenipotentiary from the Porte should also be invited, and which should have 
for its object to discuss and define in separate Acts the questions of internal 
organization which are referred to in the four Articles, But, as we could only 
bring into such a Conference a power which was entirely engaged in the support 
of the principles laid down im the notes of the 8th of Aaggust, the Prussian 
Governuient would be required to engage themselves by an Act to acknowledge 
and adopt those principles, from which no deviation would be admitted. 

If the Prussian Government should refuse this invitation, they would place: 
themselves in an isolated position, but Count Buol does not consider that this 
should interfere with the determination of the other Governments, and he is of 
opinion that the meetings they would hold might be designated, if so judged 
advisable by the Cabinets of England and France, asa Congress for the regulation 
of the pale involved in the four Articles. 

The tirst object would be to regulate the organization of the Principalities 
under the collective Protectorate of the four Powers. The privileges and 
‘mmunities would be examined and defined in relation to the action and position 
of the Sovereign Power. The questions as to the military and civil: adminis 
tration would be diseussed and settled, and registered ina document which would 
be sanctioned by the guarantee of the Powers who took part in the discussion, 
The freedom of the mouths of the Danube would be secured by regulations andl 
stipulations adopted by the Congress, and the mode of testing and securimg the 
observance of these reculations would then be established. 

The Article relating to the revision of the Treaty of 1841 would also con- 
stitute an object of discussion for the Congress, although at the present moment 
any decision with regard to it must be subject to the result of the operations 
which are now in the course of being carried out. : 

Lastly, the Congress would enter upon the consideration of the position of 
the Christian subjects of the Porte, and in the same apirit in which the Acts 
upon that subject have hitherto been framed, the Representative of the Sultan 
would be invited to make such proposals as would accord with the just solicitude 
which on all sides has been manifested upon this question. 

By the adrian of these measures, Count Buol conceives that the great 
objects of the alliance will be placed on a footing of security, and that by the 
sisnature of the different Acts which will emanate from this Congress, a settle- 
ment of the future peace of Europe will be secured upon a ‘firm and permanent 
footing, and will be relieved from those dangers and doubts which, by the passi- 
bility of disunion amongst the most influential Powers, might at one time have 
been apprehended or calculated upon,

Inclogure in No. 140. 
Circular addressed to Prussian Representatives in Germany. 


(Translation. 


SHORTLY before the Diet temporarily suspended their sittings, the 
Eastern question was brought before the respective Committee, but no resolution 
was passed, the different Ministers not being provided with su ficient instructions. 
Asit may therefore be expected that on the recommencement of the sitting of 
the Dict the united Committee will again occupy themselves with this important 
question, His Majesty the King, &e., considers it a duty enjoined by the con- 
fidential relations he entertains with his German allies, with perfect frankness to 
communicate to their Governments the views which guide and will continue to 
cuide his further conduct in treating these affairs. 

Since the above-mentioned sitting of the Committee, the Royal Govern- 
ent have received from the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh the answer to the 
Austrian despatch of August 10, which we supported on the 13th ultimo, It is 
contained in a despatch of Count Nesselrode to Prince Gortchakoff, dated the 
14th ultimo, which was communicated to us in a short covering despatch, in 
reply to the steps we had taken at St. Petersburgh. I inclose, herewith, copy 
of the said despatch to Prinee Gortchakoff, and request that you will eommu- 
nicate it confidentially to the Government to whom you have the honour of 
being accredited. 

We regret that His Majesty the Emperor Nicholas did not consider himself 
to be in a position to accept a basis of negotiations of peace, which, if it had 
been accepted and in so far as hostilities might have been arrested and 4 peace 
prepared by those means, would have responded to the wishes and objects of 
our Royal master, and which he, precisely on that account, had recommended at 
St. Petersburgh. But whilst we impartially examine the position caused by this 
rejection, and whilst we more particularly take into consideration the declaration 
at the end of the Russian despatch, according to which the Russian troops, with- 
drawn within the territory of the Empire, will there hold themselves in a strictly 
defensive position, still we cannot lose sight of the great importance which is to 
be attached to this declaration, both as regards its value in a military and in a 
political light, with regard to the German interests, which are protected by our 
alliance with Austria and the other German States. : 

We believe that all apprehension of a Russian attack in general, and more 
tepeninyy on Austria, is entirely removed by 80 clear a declaration. ‘That Russia 
atill declures her retreat to have been directed by strategical mutives, cannot 
diminish the practical value of that step. The Cabinet of St. Petersburgh had 
already, in their declaration of June 4%, given up the theory of holding a plerge, 
when they desoribed the ocoupation of the Principalities as & purely military 
position, At present she does not only really evacuate them, but she also 
declares that she will confine herself to the defensive within the Russian terri- 
tory. ‘To persist, in spite of this, in considering the danger of a possible 
reoccupation of the Prineipalities as a permanent peril to German interests, und 
in deducing therefrom a military obligation, would lead to the aradoxical result 
that while all Europe, the Western Powers included, at the time did not 


Ll7 


consider the fact of the occupation of the Principalities as constituting a casus 
belli, it is now thought necessary to discover one in the fact of their having been 
there. | 

On these considerations it is His Majesty the King’s conviction that the 
Additional Article of the ‘Treaty, which referred to positive and real conditions, 
must be looked on as annulled; but the answer to the question as to the 
necessity of any further protection of German interests, if really endangered, 1 
accordance with Article II of the Treaty, renders a previous agreement of the 
Contracting Parties necessary. 

In applying this to the well-known four points, the question arises whether 
they in so far relate to the interests of Germany as to render it advisable to the 
members of the Alliance to adopt them as the exclusive basis of future nego- 
tiations. If one could be certain of the adoption of this basis, not only by Russia 
but also by the Western Powers (which from many symptoms appears More than 
doubtful}, and if it had been followed by negotiations of ee with suspension of 
hostilities, such a result would have been well adapted to counterbalance the 
uncertainty which still exists as to the practical meaning of the four points with 
regard to the interests of Germany, I refrain from entering more particularly 
into the scruples which might be raised in this respect ; [only observe thereon, 
that the difficulties which mizht be connected with the common protectorate of 
the Principalities, as well as of the Christian Rayahs, could easily assume i 
character anything but advantageous to the interests of Germany; end I also 
remark that although we are willing to look on the entry of the Austrian troops 
into the Principalities as a guarantee for the energetic vindication of the general 
German interests in that country, still the simultaneous advance of Turkish, or 
perhaps other foreign troops into those countries, and the establishment of such 
elements in them, cannot be considered asa state of things favourable to the 
interests of Germany, irrespectively of the military complications which arise 
from it. 

This basis being rejected by Russia, and there being no doubt that, even if 
the Western Powers recognized it as binding on themselves, which is not the 
case, immediate negotiations of peace would not be attained, His Majesty the 
King, however ardently he may have desired an immechate negotiation on this 
basis, and had with particular satisfaction punporied at St, Petersburgh the 
despatch of the Cabinet of Vienna which referred to it, still cannot reconcile it 
with his conviction to recommend to bis German allies the adoption of the four 
points, i a manner which would and must entail burdens and obligations on 
them which do not appear enjoined by the spirit and object of the alliance. 

The more strictly His Majesty the King intends to persist in a firm and 
undeviable execution of the Treaty, as a guarantee of an independent neutrality 
[Machtenhaltung (?)] on the part af Germany, the more conscientiously he 
believes it his duty to remove from its sphere all obligations which are not 
dictated by clearly recognized and general German interests. 

His Majesty hopes to agree with his German allies in these views. He feels 
entire confidence that His Majesty the Emperor of Austria will not only enter 
into them with heart and soul, but also as a German Prince participate in them. 

The wisdom, moderation, and love of peace of His Imperial Majesty afford 
to the King an increased guarantee that Austria, insured by the declarations of 
Russia against attack, will refrain from assuming any aggressive attitude against 
her, and thus avoid complications, a necessity for which cannot be found in the 
protection of the interests of Germany, and to which Article II of the Allianee 
would not be applicable. 

The Roya Minister ut the Diet will be instructed to. conform his language 
in the Committee, as well as in the Dict, to these considerations, and to seek to 
give them due appreciation, 

When you inform the Government to whom you have the honour of being 
accredited of this, by communicating to them the present despatch, you will also 
express the great importance we attach to being informed, as soot as possible, 
that its Representative at the Diet has been provided with instructions based on 
the same principles. 

Berlin, September 3, 1854.

complete contradiction to what Baron Manteuflel had expressed to the Austrian

explanatory of this extraordinary and deceptive conduct of the Prussian

es Se ae this, Baron Prokesch, without having previously mentioned

event of the rejection by Russia of the conditions required. have the honour 
to forward to your toeatie herewith a copy of these seven questions, . 
M. de Bismarck Schonhausen was excessively incensed at this proceeding ol 
Baron Prokeseh, and declared that he was wholly without instructions. He 
immediately started off for Putbus; represented lo the King the imminent 
danger to Germany and Prussia, if, in the event of a refusal of the four pomts, 
Austria was to declare war against Russia; and excited the King to take sone 
counteracting step with the smaller German States. This, consequently, gave 
birth to the Prussian circular, the aim of which was to paralyze the independent 
action of Austria, and to thwart her influence with the other German States. 
When, however, it was discovered that Austria had no intention ot declaring 
war against Russia, or indeed taking any precipitate step, it was feared that the 
circular, when brought to light, would greatly compromise the Prossian Govern. 
ment with the Western Powers; and thus it was that Baron Manteutfel con- 
vinced the King of the necessity of taking some step In order to counteract the 
bad effect of the circular, On the 8th instant, therefore, Baron Manteuffel 
expressed to Count Esterhazy, M, de Moustier, and myself, his intention of 
making a communication to the three Courts, declaring that the Prussian 
Government were willing to give their adhesion, under a certain reserve, to the 
four conditions of peace which they had lately supported at St. Petersburgh. 
I believe, my Lord, this statement to be the true key to the double policy 
which Prussia has attempted to play. The real fact is, that, to maintain himeell 
in power, Baron Manteuffel 15 called upon to make large concessions to the 
King, and the party who enthrall His Majesty; in. return for which he ocea- 
sionally obtains a certain sacrifice on their part. But 1t must be remarked that 
the concessions wrested from Baron Manteutfel are of the largest magnitude, 
and wholly partake of a nature defensive of Russia.

Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon. —(Received September 17.) 


(No, 78.) 
My Lord, Berlin, September 15, 1854. 

I HAD an interview with Baron Manteuffel this evening, and expressed to 
his Excellency the thanks of Her Majesty’s Government for the intention he 
had expressed to me of using his best endeavours to obtain the liberation of the 
British subjects arrested by the Russian authorities near Memel. 

I then stated to Baron Manteuffel that I had been much embarrassed since 
I had last had the honour of seeing him, on being made acquainted with a 
circular addressed by him to the Prussian Ministers at the German Courts, 
which was in complete contradiction with the assurances which he had expressed, 
not only to myself, but to the Austrian and French Ministers. I stated that I 
was placed thereby in a false position with respect to my Government, having 
reported to your Lordship the assurances which I had received from his Excel- 
leney that Prussia was wine to give a declaration of her adhesion to the four 
points of peace she had lately supported at St. Petersburgh; whereas the dacu- 
ment he had signed a few days previously had positively stated that Prussia 
could not recommend the German Confederates to adhere to them. 

His Excellency was much embarrassed, and at first seemed indisposed to 
allow that the circular did contain any such statement; but on my repeating to 
him the phrase, his Excellency remarked that the circular ‘‘ was merely addressed 
to the German States, and was a reply to certain propositions which Baron 
Prokesch had subinitted to the Diet without consulting them; that it did not in 
any way change the assurances which he had given to the Austrian and French 
Ministers and to myseli’; and that Count Bernstorff was already instructed to 
make a communication to your Lordship in the sense of this assurance.” 

I understood his Excellency to mean, that Count Bernstorff would commu 
nicate to your Lordship the willingness of the Prussian Government to adhere 
to the four conditions under a certain’ reserve—that they would not oblige the 
King to go to war. , 

His Excellency further informed me that Count Arnim had made the 
communication to Count Buel, who had expressed himself much satisfied 
with it. 

| then inquired of his Excellency whether the declaration which the 
Prussian Government was ready to make would annul the circular addressed to 
the German States. THe replied, ‘How can you ask me to annul a document 
which bears my signature?” I replied, that j was ata loss to understand the 
Prussian policy, when, in the course of a few days, two such contradictory 
statements had been put forth; and that, for my own part, I had felt it a painful 
duty to have to address to your Lordship two contradictory reports within the 
space of a few hours. I then remarked to his Excellency on the nature of the 
circular, saying that itoffered a new proof of the endeavours of Prussia to thwart 
our policy with Austria and Germany. I stated, that it was a document 
decidedly hostile to us, and defensive of Russia; that we did not wish to dictate 
to Prussia what policy she should pursue, but that we had a right to expect that 
it should not be hostile to us; and that if she desired to be neutral, her 
neutrality could only be a total abstention from any interference between the 
belligerent parties. 

I then took occasion to read to his Excellency your Lordship’s despatch 
No. 2 of the 3lst of August, relating your conversation with Count Bernstorif. 
He only observed, that there were many points to which he could reply, and he 
expressed himself as entertaining no fear that Prussia would be excluded from 
taking her part at the conclusion of peace. 

The impression which I received from this interview is, that Baron 
Manteuffel is personally extremely annoyed and embarrassed at the publication 
of the Prussian circular, and that he has done all he could to-retrieve the inju- 
rious effect it will produce in London and Paris. He finds himself powerless, 
and unable to prevent evil; and all his endeavours are devoted to repair the

The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 


(No, 306.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, September 19, 1854. 

COUNT COLLOREDO communicated tome onthe Sth instant a despatch 
dated the 3rd from Count Buol, stating that before his Exeellency can form a 
correct opinion upon the Russian answer, it will be necessary to wait for the 
report of Count Esterhazy and the information which the Cabinet of Berlin 
muy be able to furnish, but that such explanations as may be received shall at 
once be made known to Her Majesty’s Government, and will always be matter 
for common deliberation. 

Count Buol considers that the objects of the notes exchanged on the 8th of 
August have been partly realized by the evacuation of the Principalities; for the 
Protectorate hitherto exercised by Russia over these Provinces has de facto 
ceased; the Austrian occupation will present a barrier against any future inva- 
sion, and the integrity of ‘Turkey in that quarter will be secured by the present 
shite of things: therefore a defensive position towards Russia is assigned to 
Austria, but at this moment there is no political or strategical motive for 
assuming an offensive attitude, 

The navigation of the Danube, which ts the second point in the notes of 
the 8th of August, will now be free from all obstacle, with the exception of the 
short passage between Reni and the mouths of the river which form the Turco- 
Russian frontier, 

The third point in the note will be greatly facilitated if the expedition of the 
allies against the Crimea is successful, 


— += = —- 


122 


With respect to the fourth point, which excludes Russia from any official 
Protectorate over the subjects of the Porte, Count Buol observes that such # 
Protectorate is now by the present state of things completely interdicted, and 
he considers that it is of great importasice that the Powers friendly to the Porte 
should come to an understanding as to the means of inducing the Ottoman 
Government to take the initiative in permanently settling the religions rights of 
the different Christian communities, because that question once determined, 
Russia could not fail to recognize a fact of which the advantage, while it ren- 
dered any special protection unnecessary, would be shared by the Greek com- 
munity. 

Lastly, Count Buol thinks that Russia will more resign herself to make 
peace by adopting the guarantees which are essential to peace, in accordance 
with the notes of August 8, if these guarantees, by the irresistible force of 
things, had become accomplished facts. . 

T told Count Colloredo that I had listened to this despatch with great sur- 
prise and disappointment, as Count Buol's language appeared to indicate a 
change of policy that would secure to Russia the “neutralité bienveillante” she 
had all along insisted upon with Austria. Austria, | said, had made known to 
the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh the bases that she considered indispensable for a 
solid and lasting peace, and they had been rejected in terms which clearly proved 
that the pretensions and ambitious views of Russia had undergone no nee: 
but Austria in return declared that she had no motive for assuming an offensive 
attitude, and that she should merely occupy the Principalities, which for strate- 
gical reasons alone, and not as any satisfaction to Austria, had been evacuated 
by the Russian armies. I could not, | said, agree with Count Buol that by this 
movement the abjects of the notes exchanged in August 8 were in any way 
realized; for Russia had not renounced her Protectorate over the Prineipalities, 
and Prince Gortchakoff had declared his intention of returning there, which 
intention he would probably carry into effect if the Austrian troops withdrew 
before the conclusion of a peace, which the present policy of Austria would 
indefinitely postpone, There was no security, therefore, as to the first point, 
except by a prolongation of the war, and finally compelling Russia to abandon 
all claim to interfere in this as in every other portion of the Turkish territory, 

As regarded the second point, I could not understand how the navigation 
of the Danube could be considered free as long as tL was in the power of Russia 
to obstruct the mouths of that river, and Austria appeared to have no intention 
of interfering with impediments the removal of which was a question of vital 
importance not only to herself but to the whole of Germany. 

With respect to the third point, I said I earnestly hoped that the operations 
of the allies might be crowned with success ; but so far from these operations 
being assisted by Russia they were endangered, because Russia being now secure 
from hostility on the part of Austria mighit detach a large portion of her army to 
attack the allies in the Crimea. 

As to the fourth point, I did not think that the moment was op ortune for 
pressing the Porte in the manner desired by Count Buol, and 1 aad attach no 
weight to the argument used by his Excellency in support of the measure, 
namely, that it would render the Protectorate of Russia unnecessary, a8 Russia 
had no right to exercise any such Protectorate, and had only put forward the 
claim asa pretext for interfering in the affairs of Turkey, and acquiring an 
ascendancy that would be fatal to ber independence, 

T could not therefore but consider that matters stood in a Worse position 
than before the Austrian Government had made known their demands to the 
Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, and that the Emperor of Russia would be encouraged 
to persevere in his course by the conviction, that however indispensable Austria 
might consider the proposed bases of bases of peace, she never would assume an 
offensive attitude for the purpose of obtaining them. 

‘This, L added, would also be an encouragement to Prussia and to the German 
Powers who were in league with her not alone against the Western Powers but 
aainst Austria, and must tend to prolong the war, which, however, would be 
carried on with unabated energy by England and France, and with all the means 
at their disposal, until they secured for themselves a just and honourable 

HAL. 
! Count Colloredo said thatas Austria had at great expense made complete 
preparations for war, and had rendered it impossible for the Russian armies to

remain longer in the Principalities, her position towards Russia could not be 
considered either friendly or neutral. 
IT have to instruct your Lordship to read the present despatch to Count 
Buol, and should he desire it to furnish his Excellency with a copy.

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord A. Loftus. 


(No. 51.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, September 19, 1854. 


COUNT BERNSTORFF has communicated to me the substance of a 
despatch from Baron Manteuffel, stating that the King, without considering the 
four points as the exclusive basis of all negotiation, nor consequently intending 
to contract any fresh obligations with regard to them, is yet of opinion that they 
furnish the substance (noyau) for future arrangement ; and in that point of view 
His Majesty will always be prepared to give them his moral support, and thereby 
to prove, as far as Prassian interests vermit, his desire to concur with other 
Powers in effecting a speedy but aeanbes peace. 

Baron Manteutfel added, that the Cabinet of Berlin was not opposed to a 
fresh meeting of the Conference at Vienna if it was desired by the other Powers, 
and that the King would not then hesitate to declare, by a Protocol, that the 
four points should have his moral support and good offices; with the clear 
understanding, however, that he contracted no engagement to enforce them by a 
military cooperation against Russia. 

— I told Count Bernstorff that Baron Manteuffel had had many proofs of the 
value attached by Her Majesty's Government to the alliance with Prussia, and 
of the satisfaction with which they had, at the beginning of the present crisis, 
cooperated with Prussia in support of principles which it was alike the duty and 
interest of honest Governments to uphold; hist they had regretted the alienation 
which the unfortunate policy of Prussia had since produced, and that they would 
on every account rejoice that better relations were established between the twu 
countries, and that Prussia should cease to occupy the isolated position in whieh 
she had placed herself; but that it was quite impossible to take advantage of the 
proposal now made by Baron Manteuttel. 


Bogland and France, 1 said, had agreed with Austria respecting certain, 


bases indispensable for negotiation, but without pledging themselves that these 
bases would be the limits of their demands on Hussia, which would be determined 
by the events of war; and they at the same time declared that they would be 
no parties, directly or indirectly, to any communication with Russia. Austria 
liad, however, thought proper to make these bases known to the Cabinet of 
St. Petersburgh, and Prussia had thought proper to support them: they had 
been peremptorily rejected by Russia, and it would he the height of absurdity on 
the part of England and France; they would cover themselves with ridicule, if 
they consented to call together the Conference in order that the King of Prussia 
might announce his moral support of the bases, which had already been treated 
with contempt by the Emperor of Russia, and might declare his resolution not to 
act against Russia, which, in a variety of ways, His Majesty had already made 
notorious to the world. : 

Besides, Ladded, even if these reasons did not forbid the acceptance of 
Baron Manteuffel’s proposal, the circular recently issued to the Representatives 
of Prussia in Germany, of which a copy was inclosed in your Lordship's No. 70, 
had destroyed all hope of united action. In that circular not only was the 
conduct of the Emperor Nicholas defended, and that of the Western Powers 
alluded to in terms that were offensive ; not only were the bases of negotiation 
to which Prussia was now, for the second time, offering her moral support 
severely criticised, but Prussia had laid aside her character and her functions as 
an European Power, and had restricted the great question now at issue within the 
selfish and narrow limits of German interests. ‘The policy of Prussia must, there- 
fore, have undergone a complete change; or else, if she had from the first enter- 


124 


tained the views announced in the circular, she was not justified in entering upon 
negotiations which she must have intended to defeat, and adopting principles 
that she did not share with Powers whose policy she well knew was European, 
and whose objects were not exclusively confined to Germany. 

Count Bernstorit here observed, that the circular was addressed exclusively 
to German Courts, and German interests could alone be treated of in such a 
communication. 

[said L could not fora moment admit such a reason, The German States 
constituted a large portion of Europe; they were interested in the general 
policy of Europe ; they were interested in the maintenance of international law, 
and of the distinctions between right and wrong, between justice and violence ; 
and above all, they were interested that weak States should not with impunity 
be averieved by their more powerful neighbours, and if they were insensible 
to their own manifest interests, it would become:a great German Power, when 
addressing them, to lay down certain broad principles for their guidance. 

Be that as it may, however, I said, that England and Free, far less 
immediately concerned that Germany in the issue of the struggle, had embarked 
in this war on principle; they were determined to maintain the balance of power 
by maintaining the Ottoman Empire; they were determined to protect Europe 
from the aggressive and unscrupulous policy of Russia; and they were resolved 
not to lay down their arms untila peace which they considered jusb and honour- 
able was concluded; but so little mindful were they of their own exclusive 
interests, that their first step was to enter into a solemn and binding engagement 
not to derive any advantage for themselves, 

In circumstances, therefore, so widely different, ] lamented to think that 
whether in conducting the war, or in negotiating for peace, there could on the 
part of England and Franee exist neither cordiality nor united action with 
Prussia, who have appeared to have abdicated ber position as an European Power, 
and to content herself with a fallacious immunity for German interests. 

I am, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON. 


P.S,—Your Lordship will communicate this despatch to Baron Manteutffel.

Lord Cowley to the Earl af Clarendon.—(Received Seplember 20.) 


(No. 1,134.) 


My Lord, Paris, Seplember 18, 1854. 

M, DROUYN DE LHUYS received yesterday morning, through M. de 
Bourquency, the details of the fresh proposition made by the Austrian Cabinet 
forgiving greater effect to the engagements recorded in the notes exchanged 
hetween Great Britain, France, and Austria, on the 8th ultimo, This morning 
the proposition was made in a more formal manner by Baron d’Ottenfels, the 
Austrian Chargé d’Affaires, during the temporary absence of M. de Hitbner. 

Your Lordship will have heard the project in detail trom Count Colloredo. 
| confine myself, therefore, to remarking that Austria declines signing the 
Convention offered for her consideration by Great Britain and France, but she 
proposes that the three Powers should invite the Prussian Cabinet to renew the 
Conferences at Vienna, in order to discuss and settle the details of the four 
points recorded in the above-mentioned notes, by putting them in such a shape 
as will fit them for becoming acts of international law. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys told M. d’Ottenfels that he could give him no answer 
until he had consulted with Her Majesty’s Government, but that he would 
make no seeret that, in his personal opinion, the project was inadmissible, 

In giving me yesterday the substance of the despatches received from 
M. de Bourqueney, M. Drouyn de Lhuys added that the erinerae being in Paris 
he had had an opportunity of at once toking His Majesty's orders. That the 
the Emperor's opinion, in which he eoincided, was that the Austrian Government 


should be told shortly and decisively, first, that as far as Great Britain and 
France were concerned, this was the moment of action and not of deliberation: 
secondly, that the war was not sufficiently advanced to enable the belligerents 
to put forward practical, definitive, and special conditions of peace; thirdly, that 
those conditions must be settled by those Powers which had taken part in the 
war, for it could not be pretended that the decision of the belligerents should be 
in any degree made subordinate to the will of those who had remained at peace. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys expressed great anxiety that your Lordshiy should 
take the same view of the Austrian proposition. He said that he would send to 
London, by to-night’s mail, the dra of a despatch to M. de Bonrauens 
embodying the reply which he proposed to make to it, for your Lordship’s 
approval; that he thought it of essential importance that Count Buol should 
yeceive an early answer, as it would show that there had been no hesitation as 
to the course which it behoved the two Governments to take. ; 

L observed to M. Drouyn de Lhuys that there appeared to me to be a still 
stronger objection to entertaining the new proposition than any he had 
mentioned, What was to happen if, as would probably be the case, we should 
find ourselves at issue with Austria on matters of detail? Suppose Austria to 
insist on one view and we on another, might not Austria sec in such a divergence 
of opinion reason for drawing again nearer to Russia? If there could be any 
hope of an carly peace, differences of opinion might give way for the attainment 
of an object which all actuall desired, but there would be little chance of such 
moderation when the war could hardly be said to have commenced. But even 
admitting that a general agreement as to the meaning of the four points could 
he attained, would Austria bind herself to assist the Western Powers in obliging 
Russia to accept them? Nothing of the kind was promised, or even hinted at. 

I saw M. Drowyn de Lhuys again this morning, when he stated to me that 
the intelligence which he had received f the conduct of the Austrian authorities 
in the Principalities, and to which T allude in another despatch, had confirmed 
him in the opinion which he had Cs aa to me yesterday; and he again 
evinced the greatest anxiety that your Lordship should partake his view. 

T have, &c. 
(Signed) COW LEY.

My Lord, Pera, August 31, 1804. 

IN pursuance of your Excellency’s instruction of yesterday's date I applied 
officially to Reshid Pasha on your part, and requested him to acquaint me, for 
your Excelleney’s information and that of Her Majesty's Government, whether 
it be true that the Porte had taken some step tending to annex Circassia, in 
whole or in part, to the Sultan's Empire, or placing the Circassians under his 
jurisdiction. In reply to my demand, his Highness wished me to assure your: 
Excellency, most formally, that the Porte has never contemplated any measure, 
nor does she entertain any scheme to annex the whole or any part of Circassia 
to the Turkish dominions, or placing its inhabitants under the Porte’s jurisdic- 
tion. But what the Porte heartily wishes is, to see the Circassians reseed from 
the grasp of Russia, free and independent. . 

With reference to the French Agent now here, destined for Circassia, or the. 
Court of Schamyl Bey, Reshid Pasha told me that neither the French Embassy 
nor Marshal St. Arnaud ever made any communication to the Porte on the 
subject of that Agent; but the lutter called one day, and acquainted his 
Highness that he is charged with a mission on the part of the Emperor to 
Schamy! Bey, and that he was preparing to go with Mustapha Pasha; his name 
is not known to Reshid Pasha.

( Translation.) Auguat 24, 1854. 

1 HAVE your Excellency’s note dated the 12th August, inclosing several 
despatches from His Royal Highness the Duke of Cambridge, and from Lord 
Raglan and Colonel Gordon, respecting certain reprehensible occurrences. In 
Bulgaria; representing the necessity of promptly redressing the complaints in 
question, and requesting that strong and peremptory meusures should be taken 
for securing the free purchase and procurement, without obstacle, of the pro- 
visions to be purchased for the auxiliary armies, and for protecting against 
injury or pupression the inhabitants of villages furnishing provisions to those 
troops; and I have given the note in question, and the inclosures, my full 
consideration, 


eR iF 


——— ae —_— 


128 


The views and efforts of the Sublime Porte are directed solely to the general 
welfare, and your Lordship kuows how sincerely and deeply afflicted His Imperial 
Majesty is on the occurrence of these atrocious acts, Owing to the present war 
the military authorities are all taken up with military matters, and the civil 
authorities are likewise fully oecupied in their own districts ; and it would be a 
useful and very efficacious plan, to appoint especial officers with reference to 
occurrences of this nature. The Sublime Porte has, therefore, resolved on 
appointing two Commissioners with full powers, who will not reside in any 
particular place, but go wherever it may be necessary. On the oceurrence of 
acts of the nature in question, the culprits will be arrested on the spot; after 
examination they will be put upon their trial, and punished by the Commis- 
sioners without delay according to law, and without a reference for leave to 
Constantinople being necessary. ‘They will likewise take measures for facilitating 
by every possible means the supply of provisions, and other wants, to the 
auxiliary forces in Bulgaria, There will be a separate Commissioner for the 
other side of the Balkan, and one for the country lying between the fort of the 
Balkan and Varna.

(Signed) RESHID.

No, 152. 


Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved September 18.) 


(No. 485.) 
My Lord, Therapie, September 5, 1854, 

THE most urgent want of the army at Kars at this moment is a Com- 
mander-in-chief. Seeing the doubts entertained as to General Guyon's capacity 
for the chief command, the difficulty of making a satisfactory appointment 
from France ind England, the impossibility to all appearance of finding a 
Purkish General possessed like Omer Pasha of the requisite qualifications, and 
having a favourable opinion of General Klapka, founded on his reeorded acts 
and personal qualities, 1 haye long inclined to the opinion that the Porte would 
give itself the best chance of success on the Asiatic frontier hy appointing the 
lust-mentioned General to the chief command of the army there. g 

The objections to such an appointment were that it might give umbrage to 
Austria, that it might be irreconcileable with General Guyon's position, that the 
Turkish officers would be unwilling to second a Christian commander, and 
that General Klapka's ignorance of the Turkish language would furnish an 
insuperable barrier, 

These various considerations occasioned much delay, and finally produced 
the substitution of a mission of inspection by General IKlapka, in place of his 
elevation to the chief command. . 

_ ‘The arrangements necessary to carry this limited idea into effect became in 
their turn matters of doubt and difficulty, till the course of events and the 
arrival of detailed information from Kars, combined with economical considera- 
tions, left little room for the motives which orivinally suggested the proposed 
mission to prevail. i | | 

General Klapka expressed, nevertheless, his readiness to undertake the 
charge if I continued to recommend it}; but when I lett the decision to his own 
judgment, he stated enue that, although his services were still at the dis- 
posal af the Porte, he thought the season to be too fir advanced to allow of 
his acting at present with any prospect ofa really beneficial result, | 

In this view I thought it wasonable to acquiesce. The General parted 
from me with the declared intention of going to Switzerland, where he said 
that he should always be ready to obey 4 summons, if 1 thought that his services 
could be made available on a proper and efficient footing. 


130 


Intelligence of the disasters at Bayazid and Kooroak Dereh arrived soon 
alter, and it heeame more than ever desirable that a competent General should 
be placed in command of the discomfited army at Kars. 

The Porte on this cecasion revived its former intention of sending Ismail 
Pasha to supersede the present Mushir, but at the same time declared its 
readiness to appoint any French and British General to the command of divisions 
under him, whe might he recommended by the respective Governments. 

This idea presented more than one prominent objection, and it was a relief 
to me when [found that Lord Raglan was reluctant to support it, and that his 
Lordship was impressed with a conviction that neither in his own army nor mM 
Engane would it be found practicable to realize it in a satisfactory manner. 

Marshal St. Arnaud expressed Ins willingness to acknowledge cither a 
french or an English General at the head of the army at Kars. He mentioned 
General Youssoul; he mentioned also General Cannon; and he declared that he 
had no objection to the appointment of General Klapka. 

In this manner the name of General Klapka was again brought under 
consideration, and I must confess that, without presuming te form any military 
opinion, I saw enough to satiafy ne that on the whole the Turkish Ministers 
would put the best chances on their side if they resolved to select him for the 
command in question. 

In the meantime General Klapka had embarked for Malta, and it required 
an early decision in order to overtake him there. I pointed this out fo Reshid 
Pasha, who professed himeel! well disposed to the appointment. It was to be 
vemarked that the Internuncio had never objected tothe selection of emigrants 
for command out of Europe; that the elements: of discord at Kars were likely 
to cease on the recall of those officers who, on sundry accounts, were summoned 
to Constantinople ; and that, as to the supposed feelings of the army, and the 
General’s ignorance of Turkish, the necessities of the case might well be made 
to ride over such objections. 

Last night the Ministers bad oa meeting, at which this question was 
discussed. M. Pisani reported to me this morning, on Reshid Pusha's autho- 
rity, that the Grand Viner alone made difficulties ; that he wanted to make 
General Klapka the second in command; that he stated Ismail Pasha to have 
been already named by the Porte; and that he thought the chief command 
would be better in his hands. 

Having received in the interval from Lord Raglan a confirmation of what 
1 have before stated as to his ‘nelination, and that of Marshal St. Arnaud's, in 
favour of General Klapka, I sent a message direct to the Grand Vizier, repeating 
my proposal in the form of 4 recommendation, and reminding him that the 
rejection of General Klapka, under present circumstances, would be without 
remedy for the present as far as he was concerned ; and that his Highness, if he 
persisted in his objections, would necessarily remain under a heavy personal 
responsibility. 

The appeal was not successful ; and it appears that Ismail Pasha is to take 
the command of Kars, and to act entirely on the defensive. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received September 21.) 


(No, 82.) 
My Lord, Berlin, September 17, 1854. 

COUNT ESTERHAZY, the Austrian Special Mnvoy at this Court, had 
an interview with Baron Manteuffel last evening, He first expressed the surprise 
and pain with which his Government had received communication of the Russian 
circular of the Srd instant. He stated that the circular was in direct contradiction 
to the assurances he had given him, and which he had also learnt he had given to 
M. de Moustier and myself, Baron Manteuffel endeavoured to refute this 
assertion, by denying that the circular contained any refusal on the part of 
Prussia to adhere to their conditions; but Count Esterhazy refuted the truth of 
this statement by immediately producing the cireular, and reading the paragraph 
proving the assertion. Baron Manteullel remarked to him that he was aware 
that he had held conferences with M. de Mousticr and myself; to which Count 
Esterhazy replied that we certainly saw each other every day. Count Esterhazy 
then stated at some length the objects which the Austrian Government had in 
view in submitting the late proposals to the Diet; assuring him that Austria 
had no desire to impose immediate sacrifices on the German States; but that 
as an attack on Austria, on the part of Russia, could be scarcely doubted (était 
presqu’indubitable), it was of the highest importance that Germany should be 
prepared for such an eventuality by the adoption of an united policy. Ele was 
therefore charged to invite the Prussian Government formally to support the 
proposal which would be submitted to the Diet, of an unreserved adhesion to 
the four conditions. Count Esterhazy, on learning that Baron Manteuffel would 
sec the King to-morrow, observed to his Excellency that he would detain his 
courier for Vienna until to-morrow night. Baron Manteuffel replied that he 
should not be enabled to receive him till late in the evening; when Count 
Esterhazy stated that he should then detain the courier till the following evening, 
and requested his Excellency to inform him in writing of the reply of the 
Prussian Government to this invitation. Iam informed that in this interview a 
question was addressed to Count Esterhazy by Baron Manteuffel, which tends 
to prove what has been hitherto a surmise, and has been only indirectly alluded 
to in the public press. Your Lordship may have been informed that one of the 
great wishes of the King of Prussia has been to act as mediator between Russia 
and Austria, To this intent it is stated that His Majesty wrote secretly to the 
Emperor of Russia, saying that if he would promise not to attack Austria, His 
Majesty would also exert his influence to prevent the Emperor of Austria from 
drawing the sword against him, 

Baron Manteufiel (when Count Esterhazy referred to the possibility of an 
attack on Austria by Russia) asked, ‘Mad not the Austrian Government 
received a promise from the Emperor of Russia that he would not attack 
Austria? Count Esterhazy indignantly replied, ‘that if such had been given, 
they would have immediately conveyed it to the knowledge of the English and 
French Governments, and to that of Prussia; for had they not done so, it would 
have been an act of bad faith of which Austria was not capable.” 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS.

Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon,—( Received September 21.) 


(No. 84. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, Septenther 17, 1854. 
AS I am uncertain whether Count Bernstorif will have lett in your 
Lordship’s hands a copy of the communication which he has been instructed 
to make with respect to the declaration of adhesion by the Prussian Government 
to the four points lately supported at St. Petersburgh, | have the honour to 
transmit to your Lordship a copy or the despatch addressed by Baron Manteuffel 
to Counts Bernstorff and Hatzfeldt on this subject, which has been confidentially 
communicated to me. . | 
It will readily appear to your Lordship from this document that the first 
and chief desire of the King of Prussia is to reenter on his own terms the 
European concert from which he had himself withdrawn, and that his present: 
object is to do so without incurring any fresh obligations. It appears to me 
that the declaration which the Prussian Government should in fair reason be 
called upon to give, ought to be an unconditional and binding engagement to 
the four conditions, In the same manner’ as Austrin has done; the declaration, 
accompanied with the reserves which she now proposes, appears to me of little 
value, and to offer no guarantee to the Western Powers that she will steadily 
and cordially support the policy to which she affects to give her approbation. 
No important result will be gained by such a declaration as she now proposes 
to give, except to herself, as she hopes thereby to reinstate herself in the 
European position which she had abdicated by her own vacillation and 
weakness. In all their arguments and public documents, the Prussian Govern- 
ment have invariably treated this quest ion as if it alone affected German and 
Prussian interests, and not as one in which the balance of power and the safety 
of Kurope are vitally concerned. If, therefore, Prussia desires: to resume her 
place among the great European Powers, she must indubitably subscribe 
unconditionally and without reserve to those terms to which they are bound, or 
she must be content to confine her political action and influence in Hurope to 
that of a merely German Power. 
~ It is but too evident that great mortification is felt here, at the cessation of 
confidential communication with the English and French Governments, and the 
dread of isolation has worked, and is continuing to work, beneficially on the 
Royal mind, 
a I have, &e. | 
(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS.

My Lord, Berlin, September 22, 1854. 
ON waiting upon Baron Manteuffel this evening, I found his Excellency 
silent and reserved, He informed me that he had received despatches from 
Count Bernstortl; but us he seemed disinclined to refer to their contents, | 
thought it most prudent not to press him, They had evidently produced an 


unfavourable impression, if 1 may judge from the extreme coldness of manner 
and reserve which his Excellency evinced, 


138 


I first inquired from his Excellency (on the grounds that my interpellation 
referred to a great European, and not a purely German question) whether the 
Prussian Government had come to any agreement with Austria with respect to 
the propositions which Baron Prokesch had lately submitted to the Diet. His 
Excellency informed me, in few words, that they had not yet agreed upon the 
course to be pursued, but that he hoped an understanding would be come to. 

I further inquired whether the seven questions which Baron Prokesch had 
laid before the Diet were still to be considered as awaiting solution. His 
Excellency replied that he was not aware that Austria had withdrawn them. 

I then expressed to his Excellency my regrets that the relations between 
England and Prussia had ceased to be of that cordial and friendly nature which 
had hitherto existed. I endeavoured to explain to his Excellency that we were 
engaged in a formidable struggle, and were interested to know upon whom we 
could reckon as our allies; that all we had hitherto asked from Prussia was her 
moral support—that support which would have cireumseribed and shortened the 
war; that the war on our part was not one of conquest, for we had formally 
bound ourselves to derive no exclusive advantage from it; and I expressed my 
surprise and regret that Prussia should not have cordially united with us in 
support of those principles of which she had acknowledged the justice. 

His Excellency regretted likewise that the relations between the two 
countries should not be of a more cordial nature; adding, that without incul- 
pating either party, “they must be content to bear with it”’ (qu’il fallait le 
subir). He stated that they had to consider their own interests, and that no 
State could be blamed for doing so. [replied to his Excellency that this principle 
might be applicable to smaller States, but it was not a statesmanlike principle 
for a great European Power, for that the duty of the great Powers was to wateh 
over the public law of Europe, to defend the weak against the strong, and to 
maintain the balance of power; and that it was a dereliction of duty if they held 
back from incurring sacrifices which their position rendered imperative. 

His Excellency expressed himself as perfectly informed of the feeling which 
existed in England against the Prussian Government; and remarked to me that 
had he not used his influence, affairs here would have gone to greater lengths. 
| replied to him that I was quite aware of the difficulties he had to encounter, 
and of the opposition to us on the part of the Court party; and IT further 
remarked to his Excellency that it was impossible for us to have any confidence 
‘nthe Prussian Government as long as His Majesty was surrounded and 
counselled by persons who were openly and undisguisedly hostile to England. 

1 have thus given your Lordship the general tenour of our conversition, 
which was carried on without any anger or bitterness, but rather in a tone of 
mutual regret that a better unanimity did not exist between the two countries, 

On taking leave of his Excellency, I assured him that 1 should gladly hail 
any event which might produce a salutary change in the policy of Prussia, and 
rectore the cordial relations and good feelings which till now had ever existed 
between the two Governments, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS.

Circular addressed to the Austrian Ministers accredited to the Governments of

(Translation.) Vienna, September 14, 1854. 

AT’ the time when the Courts of Austria and Prussia jointly communicated 
to the German Federal Assembly, in the session of the 17th of August, the 
negotiations upon the Bastern question, important overtures had been sent to 
the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, on the part of the German Powers, in the view 
of a peaceful understanding, whilst the Envoy of the Emperor of Russia made a 
preliminary announcement to us of the intention of Russia to withdraw lier troops 
from the Danubian Principalities. 

Since that time the declaration of the Court of Russia upon our propositions 
‘of peace have reached us through the despatch of Count ¢ eavale to Prinee 
Gortchakoff, which is sent herewith. It is decidedly a rejection, but it confirms 
the fact of the evacuation of the Principalities. I also inclose the despatch to 
our Minister at St. Petersburgh, in which we reply to that declaration, together 
with a second despatch, intended merely as an instruction for guiding Prince 
Esterhazy in his communications, the object of which is to show in its true 
light our share in the last negotiations, in correction of the very erroneous ideas 
of the Russian Cabinet thereupon, 

Previously to communicating to our German confederates our ideas of the 
present state of affairs, we wish to understand how this state is looked upon at 
the Court of Prussia, and as soon as we are made aware of the views of that 
Court, we shall make it our duty to diselose fully to the Federal Governments 
the opinions which we have formed to ourselves, in order thereby to induce them 
at the same time to give a further consideration as to the resolutions which they 
may think the German Confederation is called upon to frame under present 
circumstances, 

His Majesty the Emperor and his Court most deeply regret that the Court 
of Russia has not felt itself in a position to enter upon negotiations for peace 
on the bases which he, in union with the Courts of France and England, have 
admitted as being the necessary conditions of any resumption of pacific relations 
between Russia and the Porte, for the acceptance of which His Majesty the 
King of Prussia also has interested himself. The Imperial Government, on its 
part, cannot recede from those conditions, to which alone can now be attached 
any hopes of peace, and of security for the future; and it wishes that the period 
may not be distant when Russia also will no longer refuse to join in the now 
rejected negotiations upon these points. 

On the other hand, His Majesty the Emperor cannot but admit the political 
importance which is undeniably to be attached to the declaration of Russia, 
insomuch as it has removed the immediate danger of a conflict between the two 
Empires. The withdrawal of Russia from the Principalities had previously been 
announced to us merely as an exclusively military measure, which carried with 
it by no means the character of a political concession, ‘The Court of St. Peters- 
burgh repeats now, it is true, that the gathering together of its forees to its own 
territory comes exclusively under the point of view of a strategic necessity ; but 
xO 4 


i40 


yet, at the same time, it represents this withdrawal as a great sacrifice made to 
the interests of Austria and Prussia, and it expressly adds, which is true, that 
Russia, not gratuitously intending to increase the complication of aliairs, but 
resolved to defend her territories against every ageression, from whatever quarter 
it may come, will remain within her frontier in a defensive attitude, until fair 
propositions shall allow her to manifest her desire of peace. By this a political 
situation is no doubt indicated, and not a military one only, Russia has declared 
that her intention is for the moment not only to abstain from all attacks upon 
Austria, whether on the territory of the Empire or in the Prineipalities, but also 
not to eross again the Turkish border, intent only on the defence of her own 
COUNTY. 

By this time the evacuation of the Principalities ig probably fully completed, 
and this is inthe first place an important result, brought about by a cooperation 
of causes, among which we may consider our continued forbesratee of active 
steps as one of the most decided. The occupation of the Principalities by 
Russia has been declared by the German Conrts to be incompatible with the 
‘aterests of Austria and Germany; it ap saved not less so to the belligerent 
Powers, as well as the origin of the war, ant as the first obstacle to every 
pacific arrangement, which was, under all circumstances, necessarily to be 
removed, Russia has now withdrawn the fatal step, and the importance of this 
fact is already felt in its immediate and nearest consequence, the limitation 
of the scene of land-operations to a scale quite within the hopes of pence. We 
chall certainly not omit anything which may conduce to render this now 
accomplished fact productive of all results favourable to the objects of 
reconciliation, 

But, on the other hand, we cannot delude. ourselves as. to the fact that the 
declaration of the Russian Cabinet carries with it nothing definitive; that nothing 
assures to it a value extending beyond the circumstances of the moment. Even 
when ltussia wasin occupation of Moldavia and Wallachia, and still, when the 
Porte had already declared war, she announced the intention to remain in a 
defensive position and not to cross the Danube. Circumstances soon changed 
this resolution. Russia has not hitherto given up any of her claims; she has 
offered no securities for the maintenance of ‘the interests of Europe and Germany. 
Should things turn out in ler favour, she may even seize upon that piuirantce 
which, yielding to necessity, she hus now resigned, In looking to this, we ure 
constantly thrown back upon, our own energies to fulfil the duties we owe to the 
Pawers who have jomed us for & common object, and to ourselves also. We 
have incurred no obligation to hasten a final decision by an actual advance 
against Russia, but we must remain strongly prepared and perlectly free mn our 
resolves, in order to be assured that our important interests may be properly 
attended to under every change ‘of circumstances, und that afterwards, in the 
negotiations upon the restoration of peace, our efforts to bring back a seeured 
condition of law and peace may be successlul. 

But if Austria, for the defence of those interests which Germany shares with 
her, finds reason to persevere in the armed attitude which she has assumed; if, 
for the attainment of a truly German object, she wishes: to act in union with 
Germany, she may fairly claim to receive an ample and powerful support from 
the confederate Governments. What the state ol Germany [may require? ], if a 
condition of complications which we do not anticipate, and shall try to prevent 
vo fir as in out power, should compel us to ussume O coercive position, 1s a 
question not now before us, wid the special Conventions vet concluded would 
not certainly extend to such a ease. aut that Russia, so long as we do not 
nttuck her, could not make otir occupation of the Principalities a ground of 
rittack upon us, without finding all Germany united with us, this is what, in the 
atate of uncertainty which still subsists, we must wish to see placed beyond a 
doubt, and made a matter of obligation. We might dwell upon the question, 
what force of obligation would in such case still remain in the Additional 
Article to the Treaty of the 20th April? It appears to us, that in this Article, 
secording both ta letter and spirit, the alternative is siwply that either the 
anyplest securities must be given that the war will not he extended nor the 
Pyincipalities occupied, or else that our occupation of these countries 1s placed 
under the guardianship of mutual obligation (salidaritit) founded upon the 
confederation, But we believe that we need not go upon this point, because we 
ure satisfied that every fresh investigation into the matter, on the basis of the 


11 


provisions of the principal Treaty, must lead to the same result, We maintain 
the rights of Europe by advancing to the Principalities, and therefore, in 
principle, we may not, by our occupation, exclude others who are entitled [to 
the same]. But while we protect the integrity of the Turkish Empire, in con- 
nection with the Sultan and his allies, against every new attack on the Prinet- 
pilities, we gain at the same time hereby, and hereby only, 4 weighty security 
for the preservation of the interests of Austria and Germany, as well in the 
course of events as in the future arrangements. The Jonfederation certainly 
cannot but approve of our proceeding in this matter, even if already this were 
not really shown with sufficient clearness by the Conventions and declarations 
hitherto made. 

The King of Prussia has also promised to the Binperor, as a member 
of the Confederation, the powerful aid’of Prussia in case any attack be made 
upon us, and has secured it to us by a binding obligation, In the supposition 
that Austria should not take ashare in the offensive war against Russia, for 
instance should not pass the Russian frontier, Prussia would see, in an attack by 
Russia upon the territory of Austria, a danger to her own interests and to those 
of Germany, and would support Austria with all the means at her disposal. 
Prussia has, in this matter, expressed to us her conviction that the other Princes 
of Germany also would not, im such ease, shrink fram any saerifice to avert from 
the closely-connected Austria the dangers which menace her, and therewith from 
Germany also. We cherish the same conviction, and we hope that this conti- 
dence will be responded to by the resolutions new about to be passed at 
Frankfort. If the German Conlederation, by its declaration, gives us a pledge 
of its support, then, and then only, could we, as a German Federal Power and 
as a Contracting Party to the Alliance of the 20th April, even without any 
equivalent tnilitary dispositions on the part of the Confederation, feel outselves 
in tranquillity at least for the future, although we should then have to bear 
exclusively those sacrifices and those efforts without which, in the present state 
of the world, Germany could not be secure. 

Proceeding from these considerations, we have proposed to the Cabinet of 
Berlin to lay before the Federal Assembly, through a Representative of both, the 
despatch trom Prince Gortchakoff; with a joint declaration, that although 
now, after the evacuation of the Principalities, the state of affairs does not 
imply the necessity of an innmediate exhibition of the defensive power of the 
Confederation, yet that it affords an opportunity of declaring, that any uppre- 
hension of an attack by Russia upon the territory of Austria, would call forth in 
a common bond of defence all the Governments who shared in the alliance: of 
the 20th April. 

further, we would hesitate to bring to discussion before the Confederation 
the difference in the attitude of Austria and Prussia in regard to the bases: laid 
down for the future peace, and for a definite proposition for adopting the four 
points in the whole extent of the obligation incumbent upon us + it certainly 
seemed to us very desirable that Prussia, whase position in regard to Euro ev 
has hitherto always rested on the same foundation with ours, would also in the 
iuericn of guarantees place herself on exactly the same line with us, and that 
the same course should be pursued by the whole ef the Confederation, In the 
meantime Prussia has on ber part warmly recommended in St. Petersburgh the 
acceptance of the four points which have been derived by the three other 
Powers from the principles of the Vienna Protocols; and it is satisfactory to us 
to have learned from the very last communications of the Cabinet of Berlin, that 
His Majesty the King, without contracting a binding obligation to iilitary 
cooperation against Russia—an obligation which doves not exist even for Austria— 
will further grant at all events lis full moral support to the four points, and 
that he has made the like declaration to the other sharers in the Vienna Con- 
ference also. We may therefore, in furtherance of the work of peace, reckon 
upon the adoption by Prussia also of the same bases ns those which we have 
agreed to, and in this respect also we look for counsel, with just confidence, to 
the cirele of our contedentes. ie 

As we have the fall conviction of having wrought for the interests of 
Germany, together with our own, by our influence in determining the poitits 
whiel we, with France and England, haye set forth as the condition of peace— 
ns these points especially tend to the furtherance of German interests in one 
part, and ure nowhere in opposition to them, we must consider them to be of 


142 


great value; we even think it due to the dignity of the country that it should 
not only express the fullest acknowledgment of our proceedings, but also that 
it should aid our efforts to restore peace pon those bases by the weight of its 
suffrages, and in a suitable case by its action. 

The required guarantees afford on one land the necessary seope for future 
negotiations, und on the other hand they express with all precision what 15 
required for Germany especially. If the Confederation, however, wishes, with 
a full approval of the four points, to make a distinction between the general 
interests of Europe and the particular interests of Germany, pronouncing espe- 
cially in favour of those conditions which regard these Jast interests, that is to 
say, the discontinuance of the Protectorate hitherto subsisting in the Danubian 
territories, and the freedom of the trade of the Danube, we should make no 
essential objection to such a treatment of this matter. 

You are solicited to communicate this despatch, with its annexes, to the 
Government to which you have the honour of being accredited, The present 
moment will certainly appear highly critical in the eye of all the German 
Fovernments, and they will be very desirous to contribute by their suffrages to 
strengthen the attitude of the Confederation, as towards other countries, through 
the measures which they adopt, and thereby to inerease the friendly feelings of 
confidence between its members as such. It will give us the greatest satisfaction 
if you are able speedily to report to us that the overtures with which you are 
entrusted have been favourably received by :

(No. 93. Confidential.) 
My Lovd, Berlin, September 22, 1854. 

| AM privately informed that Baron Manteuffel has submitted to the 
King’s approval the answer which is to be given to the invitations lately 
addressed to this Government by Count Esterhiy, as reported in my despatch 
No, 82. It is drawn up in the most courteous und friendly terms, but the 
Prussian Government declines to accede to the proposals submitted by the 
Austrian Minister. 

| cannot very correctly state to your Lordship what are the exact proposals 
which have been made by Count Esterhazy, but the substance of them is, [am 
‘aformed, an invitation to Prussia to pursue an identic policy with Austria on 
the Bastern question, and to support the adhesion to the four conditions of peace 
to be submitted to the Diet. 

It is evident that, if Prussia continues to refuse her assent to these pro- 
positions, and if Austria is unwilling to recede, a trial of strength will take nee 
at the Diet: and it is generally believed that Prussia will command the majority. 
{am not, however, inclined to think that matters will be brought to this issue, 
The dificult question will be to find some form of agreement by which the 
Austrian policy will be confirmed by the Diet, without. Germany and the Minor 
States being bound by any obligations of a military nature, 

The position of Prussia, as fur as [can learn, is as follows :—She recognises 
the validity of the Convention of the 20th of April, in as far as the mutual 
guarantees of the respective States are concerned. But she considers the cases 
laid down as obliging her to render military assistance to Austria as abrogated 
by the evacuation of the Principalities. She will now take no new obligations 
of any sort. If Austria should assume the offensive against Russia, she will do 
so at her own risk, If Austria, however, should be attacked by Russia in the 
Principalities, Prussia will come to her assistance; but she will do so voluntarily, 
spontaneously, and will make her co-operation the subject of future arrangements 
to be then settled between them, 

The present crisis, therefore, is one between Austria and Prussia. Tt i a 
trial of strength in Germany for German influence. It is a reaction to the 
‘Treaty of the 20th of April between the two States, which was so discordant to 


14a 


the feelings of many of the Prussian statesmen, and Prussia feels herself now 
relieved [rom a position which placed her in an inferier line to Austria. 

But it may be regarded as certain, that if in this instance the Southern 
States of Germany accede to the Prussian rather than to the Austrian policy, it 
is solely for the purpose of preventing any aggtessive action, present or future, 
of Germany against Russia. They will never desert Austria; nor would they 
lo 80 in the present instance, were they not actuated by interested and selfish 
motives; and | firmly believe, that if Austria had the courage to pursue her own 
policy, she would soon rally Germany to her standard. 

1 have, &c. 
(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS.

I WAITED this day upon Count Buol to acknowledge the written com- 
munication I had received from him last night, and which 1 immediately 
transmitted to your Lordship by telegraph. Count Buol, in referring to that 
communication, assured me that his Government had till yesterday been in 
wntire ignorance that any diseussion, which had taken place between General 
Coronini and Omer Pasha, as to the distribution of the Austrian and ‘Turkish 
troops in the Principalities, had referred to anything but the convenience anil 
advantage of settling the different garrisons they were respectively ta occupy ; 
but from the moment that the Emperor had learnt, in consequence of the 
representations that M. de Bourqueney and Thad made upon the subject, and 
which, according to his promise, Count Buol had brought befure His Majesty, 
that Omer Pasha had contemplated, by a movement of his army upon Ibraita 
and Galatz, tomake a demonstration against the Russian army in Bessarabia, 
His Majesty had immediately directed General Hess, by telegraph, not to 
interfere in why way with that movement, or with any operation Omer Pasha 
might contemplate, which had for its ohjeet to prevent the Russian Generals 
from detaching any part of their army, lately in eceupation of the Principalities, 
to the prejudice of the allied armies at present acting in the Crimea,

Count Buol stated that he was very anxious that this intention of the 
Emperor should be most scrupulously carried out, and I consequently arranged 
with M. de Bourqueney that he (having a eypher to commumieate with the

announce to Colonel Dieu, who was with Omer Pasha, the determination which 
had been taken by the Emperor, and the consequent order which had been sent 
to General Hess, and to desire him (Colonel Dieu) to press upen Omer Pasha the 
advantage of a forward movement on ihe part of his army, which might operate 
most favourably for our expedition in the Crimea. 

Thave the honour to inclose a translation of the despatch above referred to,

which T trust that we shall avert any danger which might have threatened our 
armies in the Crimea by the detachment acuinst them of any portion of the 
Russian troops now concentrated on the Pruth.
