The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 


(No, 311.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, September 26, 1554. 
COUNT COLLOREDO read to me, on the 99nd instant, a despateh from 
Count Buol similar in all respects to your Lordship's No. 348, with respect to 
the reasons which have induced the Austrian Government to decline the 
offensive and defensive Treaty which your Lordship and M. de Bourqueney 
were instructed to propuse; and stating the grounds upon which his Excellency 
suggests that a Congress, where Prussia and the Porte should be invited to take 
part, should meet at Vienna, in order fo diseuss and define in separate Acts the 
questions referred to in the notes exchanged between Austria, England, and 
ranee, on the 8th of August. 


147 


I told Count Colloredo that Her Majesty’s Government had proposed the 
Treaty as a necessary consequence of the nates, and in the firm expectation that 
if the bases of negotiution contained in these notes were rejected by Russia, 
Austria was determined to take active measures for securing an order of things 
which she herself considered indispensable for the future tranquillity of Europe. 
It was (roc that Auscria did not say that at any particular moment, oF for any 
special reason, she would declare war; but in expecting that she would do 5a, 
we were justitied by the firm and decisive language of Count Buol respecting 
the policy of the Emperor of Russia; by the great military preparations made 
at such vast expense, and by the position which the Austrian army occupied on 
the Russian frontier; by the demand addressed to Prussia to adhere to the four 
bases, and the instructions to the Austrian Minister at St. Petersburgh to 
decline all modification of them, and to require a categorical answer; and lastly, 
by the proposal for a combined military operation made by General Hess to the 
British, French, and Turkish Commanders-in-chief, 

As, however, the peremptory rejection of the bases by Russia is not 
considered to be a casus belli, and as the Austrian Government sees no political 
or strategical motive for assuming an offensive attitude, and appears to think 
that advantages gained by war, and which ean only be maintained hy the 
continuance of war, are equivalent to conditions recognized by a ‘Treaty of Peace, 
Her Majesty’s Government can no longer attach the same importance to the 
Treaty proposed by England and France; ani it only remains for them to 
accept the assurance given by Count Buol to your Lordship, that the Treaty 
would add nothing to the engagements which had already been taken by his 
Government with the allied Powers, to which, and particularly to those taken by 
the note of the 8th of August, he most steadfastly adhered, notwithstanding their 
rejection at St. Petersburgh. 

With Rereeh however, to the Congress proposed by Count Buol in lieu of 
the Treaty, 1 told Count Colloredo that, in the opinion of Her Majesty's 
Government, the time for conferences and deliberations had long gone by, and 
that we tmust look alone to vigorous and determined action for the results 
which Austria, equally with England and France, wits interested in obtaining ; 
that the answer of the Emperor of Russia destroyed all prospect of a specdy 
termination of the wat; and it was useless, therefore, to discuss the conditions of 
peace, which the events of war right materially alter, and to which, even if they 
were arranged by the Congress, Austria gave neither guarantee nor assurance of 
active support. 

The proposed Congress, I added, would consist of three belligerent Powers, 
aud of two non-belligerent, one of which was not prepared to make war, antl the 
other had declared that it never would make war against Russia; and it was to 
be apprehended, therefore, that in debating the conditions of a distant peace 
grave differences of opinion might arise between Powers so differently situated, 

It appeared, moreover, hopeless to expect that any discussions in which 
Prussia took part, could be brought to a satisfactory conclusion; as for months 
past she had rendered services fir more important to Russia, than by openly 
taking part with her; for she had succeeded in paralyzing the uction of Austria 
with the Western Powers, and in thwarting the policy of Austria in Germany. 
She had abdicated her position as an European Power, by restricting the great 
questions upon which the future destiny of Europe depends within the narrowest 
limits of German interests; and at the very moment when she was renewing in 
London and Paris her offer of moral support to the four bases, she was bitterly 
criticizing them in her cireular to the German Courts. 

When the position of the different Powers concerned shall be more clearly 
defined by the progress of the war, and when peace has become possible, & 
Congress will doubtless be necessary for the regulation of the various 
interests and questions that will then be pending ; but at the present moment It 
could lead to no permanent settlement, while it night tend to disturb the good 
understanding with Austrin, which it is the eamest desire of Ter Mujesty’s 
Government to maintain and to improve. 

And it is with that object, which cannot but be promoted by the frank 
interchange of opinions, that your Lordship is instructed to submit to the 
consideration of Count Buol the views of Her Majesty's Gonerament upon the 
present position of affairs, with reference to the policy of Austria,

The Western Powers have agreed to four conditions, which Austna 


considers indispensable for a solid and durable peace. Russia, on the other

are unchanged, and she evidently looks to,—Firstly. A restoration of her Pro- 
tectorate of the Principalities. Seeoncly. The command of the navigation of 
the Danube. ‘Thirdly. The monopoly of force in the Black Sea. Fourthly. 
Che exclusive protection of the Christian subjects of the Porte professing the 
Greek religion. | 

_ ‘These points are all consistent with the future peace of Europe and the 
maintenance of the Ottoman Empire; but upon none of these will the Emperor 
vield unless defeated, and it would seem therefore to be the obvious interest of 
‘Austria to disable him, and thereby put an end to the war. She has the means 
ut her disposal; her magnificent army is move than sufficient for the purpose ; 
and England and France, when, a8 it is to be hoped, the expedition to the 
Crimen has been crowned with success, are really to cooperate with her for the 
common object. Austria can no longer hope to restore peace by negotiation ; 
and her hesitation to make war may, in some measure, be caused by her appre- 
hension of the neutrality, if not the hostility, of Prussia and of Germany. 

But Prussia is hound to defend Aus:ria if attacked, and would not venture 
to evade the obligation; and the smaller States of Germany, although now 
averse to engaze themselves 1s parties to the war, would hasten to the support 
of Austria if she were in danger. 

There are evils, however, to be incurred hy prolonged inaction, 

lhe inactivity of Austria, and her recent deelaration that she has no cause 
of war with Russia, add to the number of troops with whieh England and Mrance 
have ta contend in the Crimea; and she is, therefore, passively favouring 
Russia, ; 

I'wo of the conditions agreel to by the Western Powers, are more favour- 
able to the interests of Austria than to those of England and France; but if 
Austria still stands aloof she must expect that England and France will insist 
upon arrangements more in accordance with their own interests and with the 
great sacrifices they have made, and will continue to make, in order to check 
the aggressive power of Russia, and to wphold the principles of international 


justice. 
Your Lordship is instructed to read this despatch to Count Buol.

Mr. Magenis to the Rarl of Clarendon.—(Received September 26.) 


(No. 33.) 
My Lord, Stockholm, September 19, 1854. 

1 HAVE learned from various sources deserving of credit, that the warlike 
preparations of this country are carried on with as great activity as 1s possible, 
without wishing to excite too much public attention. 

The gun-boat flotillas of Gothenburg and Gottland have been or are about 
to be concentrated here, and the Minister of Marine informed me that there 
were 100 of the smaller class carrying one heavy gun, end 60 odd of the larger, 
armed with two guns, one of which was of the largest calibre at Stockholm. 

The military preparations are on a more unusual scale, ‘The aceoutrements 
for an army of 60,000 men are prepared, and winter ereateoats for 40,000. 
New swords and pistols are shortly to be given out to the army, and 6,000 new 
Minié rifles for distribution to the infantry, and am told that all of the latter 
arm embodied are about to be exercised at ball practice. Parties of 100 men of 
the Guards, relieving each other, are employed in making ball-cartridges for 
twelve hours daily in this capital, and [am told can make 60,000 a-day, and 

have already completed 7,000,000 cartridges. I hear also that several new 
cannon have been ordered, and supplies of shells have arrived at Waxholm. 
These armaments can hardly be required for the internal defence of the 
country, or to ensure respect to ‘ts declared neutrality; and though perhaps 
they might be accounted for by the wich of His Majesty to put himself in such 
a state of defence as would forbid any aggression or pressure on the part of 
Russian when the allied fleets withdraw from the Baltic, they appear to me 
rather to indicate that Sweden feels she may be culled on to take a more active 


cooperation in the future campaign. 
I have, &e. 
(Signed) ARTHUR C. MAGENIS.

My Lard, Therapia, September 9, 1854. 

TAM informed that Ismail Pasha is ordered up from the Danube to take the 
command of the army at Kars. ‘The Turkish Government declares its inten- 
tion of keeping that army on the defensive. The retirement of the Russians, 
and the approach of winter, are in themselves sufficient securities that no 
forward movement will be attempted. 

On further communication with Reshid Pasha I learn that his personal 
opinion is not so favourable to the choice of General Klapka for the ehicf com- 
wand at Kars as I had been led to suppose. In a conversation which I had with 
him yesterday, he seemed to have adopted the Grand Vizier's opinion, according 
to which General Klapka might have the second but not the chief command. 
The reasons given for this distinction are, that a knowledge of Turkish 1s 
necessary, and that certain collateral duties to be performed by the Commander- 
‘nechief require that he should be a “Mushir.” Jam inclined to think that 
the real difficulty lies ina deep-rooted jealousy of foreigners, which nothing but 
repeated disasters and a sense of imminent danger will entirely overcome. 

The dead season, should war continue, will afford time for deliberation on 
the whole of this matter, and the reports of Colonel Willianis may be expected 
to assist Her Majesty's Government 1m coming toa decision as ta what may hest 
be done in order to make the next campaign in Asia more auecesstul than the 
last.

No. 174. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received Septamber 7.) 


(No. 494.) 
My Lord, Therapia, September 10, 1854. 


I WAS informed, some little time ago, by the Commander-in-chief of Her 
Majesty's army in Turkey, that the plan of having a corps of Bashi Bozouks, 
paid by Great Britain and organized under the command of General Beatson, 
was to be relinquished by his Lordship’s direction. 

[have since received letters from General Beatson, expressing much dis- 
appointment on account of that decision, and a strong conviction, founded on 
his late experience, that there is nothing in the character of Turkish irregular 
partisuns to prevent their being brought into order, and rendered usetul for 
military operations, | ; 

It js evident that the question thus raised does not belong to my province 
ander the present instructions; and even ifit did, my reliance on the soundiess 
of Lord Raglan's judgment would mae me slow to entertain any separate 
impressions on such a matter. It has, indeed, occurred to me that the failure in 
Ceneral Youssouf’s ease may be traced to special causes; and I have seen it 
stated that le has himself made admissions to that effect mast ereditable to his 
sense and candour. I have also been struck with the evidence afforded in favour 
of the Bashi Bozouks, and their susceptibility of organisation and management, 
by persons who have served with General Beatson, and who witnessed their 
sonduet under severe privations, It would appear that such of them us were 
sent to that officer by Omer Pasha, were in a condition which implied no great, 
inclination on the part of the Turkish Commander to facilitate the success of his 
undertaking; and in fact it may be alleged, without fear of contradiction, that 
the experiment, in so far os British management is concerned, has never been 


fairly tried. 


151 


I make a point of writing to your Lordship upon this subject by to-day’s 
messenger, because I understand that the Honourable Mr. Walpole, who has 
been with General Beatson on the Danube, coming last from Bucharest, takes his 
passage for England by the French packet, with the view of submitting personally 
to your Lordship euch information as an eye-witness fresh from the scene of 
aeclion can alone supply. 

It is not for me to determine whether a corps of ‘Turkish Irregulars, Tis 
placed perhaps in Europe, might be available in Asia, and whether General 
Beatson's experience in India, and national habits, may not fit him for a service 
which in other hands has caused disappointment and loss. But your Lordship 
is well aware that the question is not destitute of political bearings, and with 
respect to them I may be allowed to offer a few remarks. 

Among the circumstances which tend most powerfully to keep this len pire 
in a state of comparative barbarism and disorder, are the unruliness of those 
wild mountaineers of whom the irregular soldiery 1s principally composed, and 
that jealousy of foreign interference which characterizes all Governments of 
Tatar origin, Great Britain by showing the Porte in what manner these ride 
people, however accustomed to independence and stimulated by want anid 
cupidity, may be tamed into order and rendered serviceable to their own satis- 
faction, would confer an inestimuble beneft upon this Empire, setting an example 
capable of being followed out, after a time, by the Porte itself on a larger seale, 
and with proportionate consequences, The comfort obtained by those who had 
the first experience of our treatment, founded, as it is, on providing for the 
wants of the men, respecting their religious prejudices and national usages, 
encouraging good, and never compromising with bad conduct, attending to them 
in sickness, and leading them gallantly into battle, could not fail of spreading a 
salutary contagion among the whole race, and disposing them for that state of 
discipline and submisson to regular military service which the interests of 
Turkey so loudly demand. 

The field of improvement ig one where humanity walks hand-in-hand with 
true policy, In proportion as the wild tribes are reclaimed from their savage 
habits, the peaceful population have less to apprehend and more to enjoy, 

The Government also would be gradually weaned from that mistrustful 
dread of foreigners which, however disguised and softened down, continues ta 
exert an unhealthy influence, and to neutralize many important benefits neces- 
sary to the advancement of Turkey. 

| confess that views of this description are a wide radiation from the 
establishment of a single corps of Bashi Bozouks under General Beatson, But 
the consequences are not the less deducible from the premise. Engaged as we 
are in a war against power, tending to shut out Westorn liberality and European 
improvement from this fine portion of the elobe, advantage may surely accrue 
from viewing every measure with reference to. those interests, and striving to 
make them all converge in their operation towards the sume beneficial and 
indispensable result, 

T have, &e. 


(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Inclosure 1 in No. 175. 
Dervish Pasha to the Qttoman Porte. 
(Translation.) September 1, 1854. 


TH Administration formed by the Russians at Bucharest was naturally 
broken up on the occasion of the Province of Wallachia being rescued from their 
hands under the august auspices of His Imperial Majesty the Sultan. 

By the tenor of a Vizirial despatch, dated the 19th Ausust, addressed to 
hia Highness Omer Pasha, and communicated by him to me, the invitation to 
Stirbé Bey which I had been instructed to make, was to be put off for a while, 
But were such an extensive province to be lett without a Goyernment, affairs 
would fell into arrears to the prejudice of the inhabitants; and although the 
presence of Omer Pasha at Bucharest would naturally invest him with the reins 
of government, his Highness is already sufficiently occupied with the important 
charge confided to him, and would have no time in the midst of so many Brive 
eceupations to attend to all the details of the Administration as it behoved tim. 
With the view, therefore, of transacting the more important lnusiness under my 
superintendence according to ‘nstructions, and with his Highness’ sanction, and 
on the other hand for the settlement of routine business and of the important 
affairs of government in this quarter, &e., of the people under the Royal auspices, it 
was found expedient to constitute a little Administration under the title of Pro- 
visional Government. 

Although it is clear that Kantacouzine, one of the first Boyars who came 
forward, who was appointed President of the Council by the Russians, is a 
Russian partisan, and that most of the actual members (of the Administration) 
are of the same category, there are no others at present among the Boyars 

epable of earrying on the Government, : 

With the view, therefore, of obviating difficulty in the conduct of affairs for 
the time being, and pending the receipt of the Porte's orders, the old Assembly 
has been temporarily confirmed in office under the Presidency of the aforesaid 
Kantacouzine. ‘The Minister of Justice, however, Argyropulo, being @ pro- 
claimed Russian partisan, and having thrown ue his place on the withdrawal of 
the Russians from Bucharest, and gone with them and subsequently returned, 
the President's eldest son, Jean Kantacouzine, was appointed Minister of Justice 
‘n hig place, with the concurrence of his Highness Omer Pasha. 

The necessary formalities were gone through, as your Highness will see by 
the inclosed paper, drawn up in French,

No. 178. 
Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clurendon.—-(Received September 27.) 


(No 501, Most Confidential.) 
My Lord, Therapia, September 10, 1854. 


AMONG the British officers whom I have presented for employment in 
the ‘Turkish service, by far the greater number have been accepted; and 
certainly those whose merit has heen tried on the field of battle have given the 
Porte no cause to repent of its confidence. I have been careful never to recom- 
mend on insufficient grounds, and, alter all, the number of applicants has not 
been great. 

Since the retirement of the Russians Thave found a diminished willingness 
to receive my recommendations, and the Seraskier, secking to excuse: himself, 
sent me several days ago a letter addressed to him by Omer Pasha. Of this 
letter, which | must request your Lordship will consider as strictly confidential, 
a translated copy is inclosed herewith. The off-hand and indiscriminating manner 
in which the Turkish Generalissimo has thought proper to express himself 
of British officers recommended to him by the Seraskier ig as misplaced as it is 
unjust, and augurs, if it be not attributable to temper, an early forgetfulness of 
services which have covered his head with laurels ungathered by his own hand, 
and saved him, as I well know, in more instances than one, from the conse- 
quences of his own temerity and thirst for distinction. 

Ignorance of the Turkish language is, no doubt, a fair obstacle to the 
employment of foreign officers in the Sultan's service, but the knowledge of it 
has never been a condition of their acceptance. 

1 purpose writing contidentially to Colonel Simmons upon the subject of 
this despatch, 

1 have, &e.

(Translation. ) Rustehuk, August 15, 1854. 
YOUR Excellency is aware that a number of English officers are sent from 
the capital to be employed in the Imperial army at their request. The fact is 
that they are unacquainted with the Turkish language, which is difficult of 
acquirement, and are of no use whatever here (so let it be). In the midst of the 
multifarious occupations of the army I am incessantly intruded upon with their 
visits; and I therefore beg it as a favour that no more of them may be sent in 
future, in order that 1 may be relieved from their extreme importunities.

| RECEIVED this morning through Vienna your Excellency’s despatches 
from No. 486 to No, 501, both inclusive, the last of the 1Oth instant, 

With reference to the observations contained in your despatch No. 489 of 
the 9th of September, respecting the appointment of Ismail Pasha to command 
the Turkish army at, Kars, and the oljections stated by the Porte to the chief 
command of that army being entrusted to General Klapka, I have to state to 
your Excellency that Her Majesty's Government have little doubt that a deep- 
rooted jealousy of foreigners is, a5 you suppose, the main cause of the neglect of 
the army in Asia; but the suicidal indulgence of that feeling ill becomes 
Govermnent whose very existence depends upon the support of foreigners. 

Repeated disasters may possibly overcome the feeling, but these disasters 
must prolong the war at the cost of the blood and the treasure of England; and 
as Her Majesty's Government will not submit to disaster or disgrace that 
common precautions may avert, your Excellency will inform Reshid Pasha of 
the great dissatisfaction which all the proceedings in connection with the army 
of Asia have caused to Her Majesty's Goverment, who must insist that their 
advice shall be taken if their support is to be continued,

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Receted September 29.) 


(No. 515.) 
My Lord, Therapia, September 14, 1854. 

THE day before yesterday. in the afternoon, I received despatches to the 
9th instant, from Her Majesty's Consul-General at Bucharest. They gave an 
account of unpleasant differences of opinion between the Austrian Commander 
on oneside, and Omer and Dervish Pashas on the other. ‘Two matters remained 
after much discussion unsettled, and were held, by agreement, in suspense for 4 
few days, until reference could be made to Constantinople. One of the points 
at igsue was the Austrian proclamation, to which the Turkish General and the 
Turkish Commissioner equally objected. The other was the return of Prince 
Stirbey. Dervish Pasha, acting in concert with the Ottoman Commander-in- 
chief, was so apprehensive of endangering the public tranquillity by that 
measure that he determined on leaving out of his own proclamation the passage 
relating to Prince Stirbey, and on making an appeal to his Government belore he 
forwarded the intended invitation to Vienia. 

AAs these opinions accorded sufficiently with my own anticipations, I lost no 
time in waiting on Baron Bruck for the purpose of making him acquainted with 
the substance of Mr. Colquhoun's reports. 1 found M. Benedetti already with 
the Internuncio, He had received, as it appeared, advices similar in their 
general substance to mine, and had waited upon the Austrian Minister with the 
intention of prevailing upon him to take them into favourable consideration, 

A discuseion ensued, of which | have not time to relate the particulars, and 
Baron de Bruck persisted, to the close of it, in maintaining opinions opposed to 
ours. His Exeellency stated that he was without advices of the same date as mine, 
and that he was in expectation of despatehes from Count Coronini, by the hand 
of one of his attachés, Count Ludolt, who had accompanied Dervish Pasha to 
Bucharest. 

On leaving his house I went to Reshid Pasha, and put him also in possession 
of what L had learned from Mr, Colquhoun. His Highness viewed, as L clic, with 
recret, the differences which had arisen, and expressed a desire to support 
Dervieh Pasha without exciting unfriendly sentiments on the part of Austria. 
When [left him he had made up his mind to propose an amendment, or an 
explanation, according to orcumstances, of the Austrian proclamation, and to 
invite Baron de Bruck toa meeting at which the lrench Representative and 
myself might endeavour, in coneert with him, to bring his Excelleney into a way 
of thinking more aecordant with ours. 

Yhis meeting, to which the Internuncio gave an accidental character, took 
place to-day, aud the question of Prince Stirbey’s recall was fully discussed 
without any apparent change in Baron de Bruck’s opinion, who treated the 
mensure ag one to which the Porte was bound by a positive agreement, and 
which could not be departed from, or deterred, without embarrassing the Court 
of Vienna, and compromising the Commander of its troops ut Bucharest. 

Reshid Pasha finally threw out an idea which promised to remove the 
existing difliculties in a great degree, and to couciliate our conflicting opinions. 


161 


He proposed that Dervish Pasha should forward his intended invitation to 
Vienna without further delay, addressing it to the Turkish Ambassador, who 
would be instructed not to deliver it to Prince Stirbey without previously 
making known to Count Bool, Lord Westmorland, and Baron de Bourqueney, 
the objections entertained at Bucharest to the Hospodar's return by Omer 
Pasha, the Turkish Commissioner, Mr. Colquhoun, and the French Agent, to 
say nothing of Prince Alexander Ghika and a considerable number of Ins 
countrymen. Baron de Bruck was not inclined to accept even this very 
moderate proposal, and 1 was finally obliged to leave the mecting with the 
expression of a hope that he would be able ta take a more favourable view of it 
on further deliberation with Reshid Pasha alone. 

T have sinee learned from M. Pisani, whom I sent to ascertain the final 
result, that it has been agreed between the Pasha and Baron de Bruck that, with 
respect to the proclamation, it shall be amended or publicly explained in 4 sense 
satisfactory to the Porte according as it may have been published, or not, before 
the arrival ofa fresh instruction to Dervish Pasha; and, with respect to the 
return of Prince Stirbey, that the invitation shall be forwarded im the way 
proposed by Reshid Pasha, if General Coronini consents to the arrangement in 
virtue of the observations which Baron de Bruck undertakes to address to him 
with that view. 

The time for reference which has been allowed is so brief, that an express 
steamer must be dispatched to Varna this evening; and purposing, if possible, 
to avail myself of the opportunity for writing to Mr. Colquhoun, | transmit this 
hurried despatch without apology, relying on your Lordship’s indulgence,

COUNT COLLOREDO has this day communicated to me the substance 
of the letters which Count Coroni and Dervish Pasha have respectively 
addressed to Prince Stirbey, 

In the first Count Coronini, after alluding to the terms of the Treaty 
between Austria and the Porte of June 14, observes that the first object of that 
‘Treaty having been effected by the retreat of the Russians, the Emperor of 
Austria had directed a portion of his army to enter the Principalities with a 
view to the second object of the Treaty, namely, the re-establishment, in concert 
with the Ottoman Government, of the legal order of things in the Provinces, 
and that Count Coronini was directed to put himself inte communication with 
the persons entrusted by the Porte with the duty of cooperating with him for 
the re-establishment of order and the maintenance of tranquillity. “That both 
Austria and the Porte had deemed it necessary, with a view to this object, in the 
first instance to replace the Government of the Provinces in the hands of their 
legitimate Princes, and so enable them to heal the wounds from which they 
are now suffering. 

Count Coronini therefore invites Prince Stirbey to return without loss of 
time, and he would receive @ cimilar invitation from Dervish Pasha, in virtue of 
the instructions which he had received from the Porte, and specifically in virtue 
of an order of the 31st.of August. 

Dervish Pasha’s invitation says that as the Sullan is desirous of re-esta- 
blishing order in the Principalities, and thereby providing for the well-being and 
peace Gf his subjects; and as for the attainment of that object it is requisite 
‘1 the first instance, and as soon as possible, to restore the old system of udmi- 
nistration, whieh will be effected by the return of the Princes, and their 
reinstatement, Dervish Pasha was directed to invite Prince Stirbey to return to 
Bucharest, and there await the further directious of the Porte.

Count Buol goes on to say that Austria does not pretend, under her Con-

Smpire, and has engaged by implication to defend them from fresh invasion, she

‘n the Crimea, or be transported to Asia for the purpose of acting in that

1 told Count Colloredo that it was not alone the interference with the

rities since the occupation of Wallachia, that had produced a painful impression 
upon Her Majesty’s Government. A marked disregard for the Sultan’s autho- 
rity had been exhibited; his victorious troops had been treated as intruders upon

Province by Austria alone, and not in concert with the Porte as stipulated by

were of a nature to alarm the Porte as to the actual, and still more as to the 
future, intentions of Austria. 

Count Buol, 1 said, must therefore not be surprised that Her Majesty's 
Government are unable to reconcile the difference between the conduet of the 
Austrian Agents and the assurances of the Austrian Government, and that they 
should earnestly desire the termination of that difference. | ; 
___ For the accommedation and supply of his army, the Austrian Commander-

the enemy of the Sultan, so far from being impeded, should receive every facility

purpose of aiding his cause. | |

object in view would be sent to the Austrian authorities in the Prineipalities. 
Such instructions will be in accordance with the avowed policy and intentions of 
Austria, and cannot but preter the good understanding and cordial cooperation 
between Austria, England, and France, upon which a speedy termination of the 
war may in a great measure depend, |

My Lord, Paris, Seplember 26, 1854, 

I MENTIONED yesterday to M. Drouyn de Lhays that your Lordship 
had had a lengthened conversation with Count Walewski respecting the future 
destiny of the Crimea, should victory place it within the power of the allied 
armies, | took this course with the hope, in which I was not disappointed, of 
leading the French Minister for Foreign Affairs to express his opinion upon this 
very important matter. . 

_M. Drouyn de Lhuys said that there were three points connected with the 
subject which | had brought under his notice :— 

|. Supposing Sebastopol to be ie was it to be oceupied or abandoned ? 


164 


9 Ifit was determined to occupy it, was that oceupation to be limited to 
the place itself; or to extend over the Crimea? 

4. Were the defences of Sebastopol to be maintained or destroyed t 

Upon the first of these questions he observed that, in whatever light he 
viewed it, his opinion was that the allied armies, if victorious, should winter in 
the Crimea. ‘The climate of the southern portion of that peninsula was healthy 
and fertile; the port of Sebastopol would be a constant refuge for the fleets ; 
from no place could further enterprises in the East, to whatever pont directed, 
be more advantageously undertaken; the moral effect of wintering on Russian 
ground would be immense ; and the armics would be removed from the chance 
of contemplating the cruelties and misgovernment still practised in Turkey, 
which had made so unfavourable an impression upon them during their oceupa- 
tion of Varna. Sree at 

All these things spoke in favour of the armies wintering in the Crimea,— 
nothing as far as he was aware, against it. | 

With respect to the second question which he had raised, whether the 
occupation was to be limited or extended to the whole Crimea, he observed 
that this was a matter which depended on atratezical measures, and could only 
be decided by the Commanders-in-chief of the armies; but he should be glad to 
find that their decision was in fivour of the whole of the Crimes. 

With regard to the third point, namely, the preservation oF destruction of 
the fortifications of the Crimea, particularly of those of Sebastopol, a greater 
difference of opinion might prevail, because, if they were destroyed, and a neces- 
sity for them discovered afterwards, they were not so easily reconstructed ; while 
if they were temporarily preserved, they might be destroyed at any moment. 
Nevertheless his impression was that they ought to be destroyed at once. Three 
eventualities were possible in disposing of the Crimea: It might be restored bo 
Russia; it might be again placed under the rule ot the Sultan; or it might 
remain in the possession of the French and English. In neither of these cases 
would there be any necessity for preserving the fortifications. If the Crimea 
was restored to Russia, it must be restored shorn of that which gave Russia such 
preponderance in the Black Sea, If it was to. be again placed under the rule of 
the Sultan, it would not be prudent to place the Porte in possession ofa place of 
such military importance: as the Russian fleet would be destroyed, the Porte 
would have nothing to fear from outward attack, and would have no need of 
such defences as now existed. Lastly, if the Crimea was to remain in the hands 
of the French and English, as they would have nothing to fear from maritime 
ueressions, it was clear that they could do without impregnable fortifications. 
Ror all these reasons he should prefer to see the defensive works of the Crimes 
destroyed at once. =. of 

Teaid that with regurd to the allied armies wintering 1 the Crimea, 1 had 
veason to believe that Her Majesty's Government concurred in. the opimon 
whieh his Excellency had put forward; that as to the second point, ik Was 80 
clearly a matter which must be referred to the decision of the Commanders=in- 
chief, that there could be no difference of opinion between the Governments at 
home; but that with reference to the third point, namely, the destruction of the 
fortifications of the Crimea, I believed that it had been a question with Her 
Majesty's Government whether it might not he prudent to presery® the works 
which had been raised to defend Sebastopol against an attack by land, but to 
destroy those which rendered it so formidable a fortress by sea. 1 could only, ! 
said, contemplate two out of the three contingencies adverted to by his Excel- 
loney, a8 possible with regard to the Crimea—that it should be restored Lo 
Russia, or replaced under the authority of the Portes tor as France and England 
jad declared that, in engaging in this war, they renounced beforehand all advan- 
tage to themselves, they could hardly keep possession ol the Crimea, or ol any 
part of it, without placing themselves ‘1 contradiction to this declaration. 
There were many reasons, | thought, why, if the two Governments decided that 
in no ease should the Sebastopol of to-day be allowed to remain’ in either 
Russian or Turkish hands, that. that fortress should be dismantled as soon 8s 
Providence placed it in our power. Delays were proverbially dangerous. If the 
destruction of the fortification was postponed until the period came for evacus 
uting of the Crimea, might not unforeseen difficulties then oreur ? 

Supposing Russia were to accept all other conditions of peace, but to 
demand, ag a gine quad nom, the restoration of the Crimes, with its fortified places 


165 


uninjured, and that she should be supported by Austria and Prussia, how greatly 
should we regret that we had not forestalled the question by destroying them at 
once! Supposing also (for no Power should be so. arrogant as not to contem- 
plate the possibility of misfortune) we, in our turn, were dislodged from the 
Crimea, would not the reverse be doubly bitter if we had neglected, while it was 
in our power, to take every possible security against the future? These contin- 
gencies, | was aware, were improbable, but stranger things had happened in the 
world's history; and as I could see no motive whatever for preserving works 
from which the two Governments would not even desire a temporary benefit, 
and which they might hereafter bitterly repent not having destroyed, I trusted 
that if our arms were blessed with victory, the first use we should make of that 
Mito would be to destroy the stronghold of the aggressor for ever; ince, it 
once destroyed, it would be our own faults if it was rebuilt, Ofcourse, I said, 
1 was not presuming to give an opinion upon the preservation of such defences 
as were necessary for the safety of the allied forces; and, L added, I begged 
M, Drouyn de Lhuys in general to understand that 1 was only giving an 
individual opinion, and that | had no authority from your Lordship to enter into 
any discussion of the question with him. 

M. Drouyn de Lhnys replied that he was in the same position; that he had 
not taken the Emperor's orders ; and that his observations must be considered 
as entirely personal. But so much impressed was he, he added, with the neces- 
sity of commug to some distinct understanding with [Her Majesty's Government 
ona matier of such paramount importance, that he should consign his ideas 
upon it to a despatch, which, if it received the Hmperors approbation, should 
be sent to Count Walewski.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received September 29.) 
(No. 1175.) 


My Lord, Paris, September 28, 1854. 

THE day before yesterday, and yesterday, M. de Hiibner had interviews 
with M. Drouyn de Lhuys for the purpose of entering into some explanations 
with his Excellency respecting the present attitude of Austria towards the 
Maritime Powers, and with reference to her position in the Principalities. 

M. de Hitbner complained that the conduct of Austria had not been 
appreciated as it deserved, He maintained that she had faithfully observed the 
engagements into which she had entered with Great Britain and France, and he 
assumed that she had rendered great services to the general cause, inasmuch us 
the stratezical position taken by her armies had forced the Russians to evacuate 
the Principalities, 

M. Drouyn de Liinys would not admit M, de Hitbner's statement to be 
correct. He maintained that Austria had pledged herself to sign a Convention 
with the Maritime Powers, if Russia refused to accept the four points; that 
Convention ought to have been signed, the answer of the Russian Government 
having been a direct refusal. And although he admitted that the evacuation by 
the Russians of the Principalities was in a great measure due to the strategical 
measures of Austria, yet he could not look upon it as a service rendered to the 
allies, since Austria in occupying the Principalities had given Russia clearly to 
understand that she would not pursue her successes further, and would on no 
aceount attack the Russian troops; the consequence was that the army in 
essarabia could be sent without danger to Russia into the Crimea. It was 
impossible, moreover, to look at the conduct af the Austrian authorities 10 the 
Principalities without being convinced that they were acting, however uninten- 
tionally, for the interests of Russia. 

_ M, de Hiibner explained why it had been impossible for Austria to sign the 
Convention at the present moment, and complained that the substitute of a 
further Conference or Congress which she had proposed had not been adopted, 


166 


M. Drouyn de Lhuys showed, as he thinks, even to M. de Hiibner’s satis- 
faction, the unsatiaiactory results to which such a Congress must have led; but 
as there was nothing new in the arguments of either one side or the other, I 


need not repeat them.

Tnclosure in No, 198. 
Instructions addressed by the Porte to Omer Pasha, 


(Translation. ) Seplember 15, 1854, 

1 HAVE received your Highness’ despatches reporting the communications 
which had taken place with Count Coronini; and subsequently, between his 
Excellency on the one side, and your Highness and Dervish Pasha on the other. 
As some of the matters in question were settled there, I have to remark that the 
passage contained in the proclamation of the Austrian Commander-in-chiel, 
namely, that reference was to be made by the local authorities, in all matters, 
to his Excellency, does certainly impair the sovereign rights and authority of 
the Porte; and it is of great importance that an amendment should be intro- 
duced into it, namely, that it should be clearly explained that the real object of 
such reference was connected with matters concerning the Austrian troops, It 
has been therefore agreed upon with the Austrian Minister, that if the proclama- 
tion in question has not yet been published, the passage in question should be 
altered in the above sense; and that if it has been published, you should enter 
into communication with Count Coronini, and frame a new proclamation to be 
signed collectively by the Count, your Highness, and Dervish Pasha, in whieh 
the meaning of the passage in question should be properly set forth. Your 
Highness is therefore requested to act in conformity therewith. With reference 
to the second point referred to Constantinople, namely, the subject of Stirbé 
Bey, the best endeavours were used to prevent the return of that Prince into 
Wallachia, and of whieh, the proceedings had at Bucharest, evincing the 
(public) distaste thereat, and the documents in my possession, came in support. 

ron de Bruck, however, represented that he had also reliable information on 
this subject; that there was a good deal of personal animosity mixed up with 
it; and that it was not right that such hesitation should be shown with regard to 
it, after the receipt of the last instructions of the Porte at Bucharest. In short, 
there was no persuading his Excellency to the contrary. 

We suggested, in the presence of his Excellency Lord Stratford de Redclitle 
and of M. Benedetti, that the aspect of the question having changed since the 
occurrence of the last events at Bucharest, which had been reported to Count 
Buol and to the foreign Representatives at Viera, reference should be, at all 
events, made to Vienna for a fresh decision respecting the return or not of the 
Prince, and that the ietter inviting him to return should be sent to the Ottoman 
Minister at Vienna, in order that he might proceed accordingly; but the 
Austrian Minister persisted in saying that the dignity of Austrin requived that 
the original arrangement should be carried out, and that the fermentation 
which would ensue at Bucharest, until an answer could be received to the 
reference to Vienna, would more particularly place Count Coronini in w difficult 
position; he could not, therefore, agree to my suggestion. The Austrian 
Minister, however, at length gave strong assurances that if Dervish Pasha were

written to-again to send the letter inviting Prince Stirbey to return into Wallachia, 
according to his instructions, and that the Pasha were to make his remarks to 
Count Coronini on the subject, he would use his endeavours that the question 
should be again referred to Vienna for decision, if Count Coronimi had no 
objection to make on the score of his own position, and of the state of matters 
at Bucharest. 

On the other hand, 1 declared that if Count Coronini were to consent to a 
fresh reference to Vienna on this oceasion, and insisted on Prince Stirbey’s return, 
and that anvthing sinister should occur at Bucharest in consequence, the 
Austrian General would be responsible for it; and that, however it might be, 
Prince Stirbey’s return was a temporary measure; and that the Porte might, in 
conformity with her sovereign rights, change and dismiss him, if it should be 
necessary, after inquiry to be made, at any time. 

| informed the Austrian Minister that in neither case would the letter of

No, 199, 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Karl of Clarendon.—(Received September 30.) 


(No. 525.) 
My Lord, Therajia, September 20, 1854, 

JUDGING from appearances, I find it difficult, with every disposition 
fairly to appreciate the embarrussments and intentions of Austria, not to recur 
in some degree to the impression originally made upon me by the terms of the 
Austrian Convention with Turkey, The course pursued by General Coronim, 
necording to the latest advices from Bucharest, corresponds not a little with 
that reality of an exclusive occupation which Baron Bruck in conversation with 
me has more than once endeavoured to substitute for the principle of a joint 
one accepted by Count Buol, as that which, together with other wholesome 
principles, was to prevail in the operation of rescuing Wallachia and Moldavia 
from Russian usurpation, At all events it is certain that if the plan reeom- 
mended by the Austrian military authorities be carried into effect, as matters 
now stand, the Austrian army will occupy exclusively the two Principalities, 
interposing, de facto, a pacific though armed authority, between the two 
principal belligerents, and if Baron Hess's proclamation be literally maintained, 
assuming for the time that very position which Russia has reluctantly given up 
from, motives of strategic necessity, teas oa 

The Porte is fully in possession of your Lordship's views on this important 
and delicate subject, nov is there any backwardness on the part of its Ministers 
to acknowledge their soundness, But, practically, the course pursued by 
Austria, with the reluctant acquiescence of Turkey, hus very much the air of 
leading to consequences not easy to be reconciled with the principles laid down 
by your Lordship on the part of Her Majesty's Government.

No, 205, 
The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received October 2.) 


(No. 362.) 
My Lord, Vienna, Seplember 27, 1854. 


T SUBMITTED your Lordship's despatch No. 301 of the 14th instant to 
Count Buol, and left it with him in order that he might, after considering it, 
sive me the explanations required by your Lordship as to the conduct of the 
Austrian general officers tawards the Turkish authorities in Wallachia. 

Count Buol said that with regard to the proposals of Colonel Kalich, as 
reported in Mr. Colquhoun’s No. 36 of the 25th of August, he must state that 
he had already early in September explained to me that these proposals had 
been withdrawn, and that although some misunderstanding had arisen, the 
matter had been settled by General Popowitch, and, with the full consent of 
Austria, had been referred for final decision to the Porte, ‘This explanation I 
reported to your Lordship unofficially on the (th of September, 

With regard to the proclamation of General Hess, it had been drawn up 
and published by him at a time when it was not known that any Turkish troops 
or authorities were in the Principalities, and it applied to the reference to the 
Austrian General in all things relating to the Imperial troops, and the represen- 
tations which had been made against it had heen superseded by its correct 
publication by the Wallachian authorities and Council in Bucharest, 

With regurd to the invitation which had been addressed by General Hess to 
Omer Pasha to withdraw with his forces from Bucharest, and to occupy the 
positions of Giursevo and Kalarasch, as detailed in the letler of General 
Coronini, whieh is inelosed in the despatch of Mr. Colquhoun No. 51 of the 
6th instant, Count Buol stated that it was dictated only by a wish to arrange 
in the most convenient manner the dislocation of the forces composing the two 
armics, and to avoid the inconveniences which always must attend the joint 
occupation of the sume garrisons by the troops of different nations, but not at 
all upon political grounds, os stated by General Coronini, who had nothing to 
do with any such considerations. 

With regard to the allusion made by Omer Pasha as to his having formerly 
been invited by General Hess to occupy Bucharest, and advance upon Busco, 
this invitation had been addressed to him at the time the Austrian army was 
preparing, in conjunction with the allies, to march against the Russian forces 
in the Principalities, and drive them by foree of arms from the positions they 
were occupying, As soon as the declaration that the Russtuns would evacuate 
these Principalities was made by Prince Gortchakotl, this proposed operation 
was naturally put an end to, und could have no reference to the movements 
which had afterwards been recommended, or had taken place. If Omer Pasha 
had regarded the proposals of the Austrian Generals as an attempt to interfere 
with his projected strategical movement on Tbraila and Galatz, his Highness 
would have been perfectly reassured by the orders which had been transmitted 
to General Hess in no way to impede the movements of the Turkish army ; 
orders which his Government had forwarded immediately to the Austrian 
Commanders on receiving notice of the construction which was put on the 
advice tendered by them to Omer Pasha, which had been understood as an 
endeavour to prevent the Turkish troops from following the Russian army, and 
thus enabling it to march to the Crimes, to the prejudice of the ullied forees 
now operating against Sebastopol. 

Count Buol said that nothing could be more painful to his Government 
than that any suspicion of such a nature should be entertained; and while he 
knew that those who understood the policy of his Government must at once 


‘have rejected il, he trusted that the orders sent s0 promptly to General Mess 


would have effectually refuted the representations of those who appeared always 
willing to decry the policy of Austria.

The Earl of Westmoriand to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received October 2.) 


(No, 364.) 
My Lord, Vienna, September 27, 1854. 

IN obedience to your Lordship's instructions, I communicated your 
despatch No. 206 to Count Buol, and left a copy of it in his hands. 

_ Count Buol begged me to delay any discussion with regard to it till he had 
time to consider it, and I therefore returned to him. this day for that purpose. 
Count Buol said that he had observed with preat pain that your Lordship had 
expressed your general disagreement with the policy which had been pursued by 
the Imperial Government, and it was with equal regret that he had received an 
expression of the same feeling from the French Minister, M. Drouyn de Lhuys. 

He stated that although in the despatch from Paris some points were 
referred to which were omitted in the one from your Lordship, yet the two 
documents might be considered as so nearly identic, that he would read me the 
despatch he had ilready written, and was about to address to M. de Hiibner, the 
general arguments and statements of which he should embody in his despatch to 
Count Colloredo, to be placed in your Lordship's hands. 

Count Buol said that your Lordship stated you considered the language be 
had used in his despatch ta Count Colloredo. as indieating a change of policy, 
which would secure to Russia the “ neutralité bienveillante’’ which she had dll 
long insisted upon from Austria. He said that he deprecated this inference alto- 
gether; that the Imperial Government had no such feeling towards Russia, and he 
had never given any countenance to such an assumption, which he hoped, there- 
fore, that your Lordship would discharze from your mind; and he was very 
certain that the Russian Government did not indulee in any such delusion, as 
was proved by a despatch which he had within these few days received from 
Count Esterhazy, which stated that Count Nesselrode, in comp aning of the 
continued concentration of Austrian troops in the Bukowina, had not disguised 
from him that the corps of Guards which had lately been marched from 
St. Petersburgh were ‘A Vadresse de l'Autriche.” 

Your Lordship stated that the Austrian Government had made known to 
Russia that the refusal of the conditious of negotiation which had been proposed 
to her did not give them any motive for war. 

Count Buol said that he knew of no such declaration having been made to 
Russia; he had certainly informed his ‘lies, as he felt he was bound to do, that 
his Government would not willingly commence a campaign in the Russian 
provinces in the month of October, but what he told to those he was in alliauee 
with he did not intend as general information, and lie had made no communica 
hon to this efleet to the Russian Government, 

With respect to your Lordship’s belief that by the posture which Austria 
had assumed, the prolongation of the war would be entailed: Count Buol 
rephed that no Government could suffer more from such prolongation than thut 
of Austria, and that therefore her pveatest interest would be to bring it to a 
speedy clase, He said the Austrian Government had not declared war, though 
they had offered many occasions to Russia upon which that Government might 
have declared it against them, but they did not wish to enter at this moment 
upon t contest which they felt would be attended with every disadvantage, 

As to assisting the allies in their expedition against Sebastopol, for the 
success of which he most ardently wished, Count Buol said that the Iniperial 
Government had never pretended that they could be able to offer any more 
effective cooperation with the allies than by the concentration of their troops on 
the fronticr of Bessarabia; but they did pretend that by the assembly of their 
great army in the Bukowina, and by placing the Russian army in the impossi- 
bility of undertaking any offensive operation to the south of the Danube, or of 
remaining in the Principatities, they had facilitated the great operation which 
had now been undertaken by the English and French Governments. 

With respect to the discussion of the immunities to be granted to the 
Christians in accordance with the benevolent. intentions of the Sultan, Count 
Buol stated that he could not but still consider that the present moment might 


175 


be advantageously employed in communication between the allies upon this 
subject, while the pretensions which had been put forward by Russia were 
entirely done away with by the state of war; but he would of course conform 
himself upon this subject to whatever should be agreed to by the Governments 
engaged in the discussion. 

have faithfully reported to your Lordship the language held by Count 
Buol in his conversation with me, and which will probably be repeated with more 
detail in his despatch to Count Colloredo. Your Lordship may be sure that 1 
shall not cease to urge upon Count Buol the importance of a closer union ol the 
three Powers, and of the more active employment of all the means at their 
disposal to bring to a termination a war which might lead to the most disastrous 
consequences to Austria,

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received October 2.) 


(Telegraphic. Vienna, Octuber 1, 1854. 


COUNT BUOL decided three days since to transmit to London and Paris 
a communication having for its object to re-establish the good understanding 
between Austria and the Western Powers, which recent circumstances appear to 
have disturbed, The Cabinet of Vienna acknowledges the necessity to unite the 
action of all the Powers by a common Act of which the bases will be submitted 
to your Lordship, This document would avoid whatever France and England 
have objected to in the late Austrian propositions, and all other details would be 
embraced in the same Treaty of offence and defence.

Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon —(Received October 2.) 
(No. 97.) 


My Lord, Berlin, Seplermber 29, 1554, 

| WAITED on Baron Manteutfel on Monday last, and in conformity with 
peur erdenies instructions, | read to his Excellency your Lordship’s despatch 
No. 51. 

Baron Manteuffel stopped me at its commencement to remark that Prussia 
had never declared that she would not act against Russia, 

I replied to his Excellency that I received his observation with satisfaction, 
and would faithfully report it to your Lordship. 

Tig Excellency further remarked, with reference to the Prussian circular of 
the 3rd instant, that it must be borne in mind that that document was a commu- 
nication to their German confederates. 

Lobscrved to his Excellency that at all events it might be expected that 
Prussia would advise her confederates to adopt the same course which she hac 
professed the readiness to pursuc herself: and I intimated to his Excellency that 
your Lordship’s reply to a similar observation of Count Bernstorit's (which | 
was about to read to him in continuation of the despatch), most unanswerably 
refuted any such attempt to excuse the Prussian circular. 

His Excellency made no further observation during the reading of this 
despatch, and its termination did not offer any further remark upon it. THe 
informed me, however, that he had received a “good despatch” from London 
that day with respect to a Prussian vessel (the “ Louisi,” I believe), which 
had been seized and afterwards liberated ; and he told me that this had produced 
n good impression on the King. 

a A 


178 


We had subsequently some conversation with respect to the negotiations 

with Austria, His Excellency remarked that he desired nothing better than to 
come to some agreement with her, but that it was easier to give expression to 
the feeling than to effect it. He complained that she was susceptible, and in 
mentioning her circular of the 14th, stated that it was very unclear and unde- 
cided; that at the commencement she recommended the four points, and after- 
wards withdrew them; and he finally remarked to me that even England and 
France ito longer cared about them. 
___Lreplied to his Excellency, that with respect to these points he must bear 
in mind that two of them, and these more especially referring to German and 
Prussian interests, were already achieved—tirst, the Principalities were in_ the 
occupation of the Turkish and Austrian troops; and secondly, the mouth of the 
Danube, or at least the Sulina branch, was in our hands, It appeared to me, 
therefore, that if Prussia and Germany were really anxious for German interests, 
their only and best policy would be to act in union and harmony with Austria 
and the Western Powers, as their interests would certainly not be advanced in 
acting in opposition to us, 

His Excellency seemed to recognize the justice of these observations, but 
appeared jealous and suspicious of Austria, and fearful that a conflict might yet 
arise in the Principalities between Austria and Russia, which, if Prussia entered 
into any fresh positive engagement, might entail upon her active military 
assistance. 

I found his Excellency at this interview more conversible and friendly than 
I had reason to expect, nor did he evince any soreness or anger during the com- 
munication of your Lordship’s despatch. Of a naturally cold and reserved 
temperament he seems determined to carry out at all price the inert policy of 
his Sovereign, unmoved by the difficulties of his task and the dangers which 
menace the peace of Europe, 

I have, & 


Ac. 
(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS.

No. 215. 
The Rarl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 


(No: 590.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, October 6, 1854. 

I HAVE received your Excellency’s despatch No, 525 of the 20th of 
September, respecting the course Sey by Austria in the Prineipalities ; and 
it would appear from your observations, that while acknowledging the soundness 
of the views entertained by Her Majesty's Government in regard to the Austrian 
occupation of those Provmees, as set forth in my various despatches to Lord 
Westmorland, of which copies have been communicated to you, the Turkish 
Ministers reluctantly acquiesce in the course pursued by Austria, although that 
course may have the appearance of leading to consequences not easily to be 
reconciled with the Pees laid down in my despatches. j 

The views and principles of Her Majesty’s Government as explained in 
those despatches were, that the oecupation by Austrian troops of the Prinei- 
alities should not be of an exclusive character; that no interpretation of the 
Treaty between Austria and the Porte would justify the Austrian Government 
in demanding the withdrawal of the Turkish forces, against the consent of the 
Porte, nor, under such circumstances, would Her Majesty's Government recom- 
mend the Turkish Government to comply with the requisition ; that the march 
of the allied troops should neither be apposed nor embarrassed, if they deter- 
imined on pursuing the Russians through the Principalities; and that England 
and France would not consent to Austria assuming 4 position which would 
enable her hereafter to exercise an armed mediation, 

The views thus entertained by Her Majesty’s Government have more 
recently been impressed on the Austrian Government with reference to the 
proceedings of the Austrian Commander-in-chief on entering the Principalities, 
as your Excellency will have seen by my despatch to the Earl of Westmorland, 
No. 301 of the 14th of September. 

Assurances, upon the whole satisfactory, have been received from the 
Austrian Government in reply to the several communications ; but Her Majesty’s 
Government have seen no reason to alter the opinion expressed in my despatch 
No. 485 of the 18th of August, as to the conditions upon which alone it 
wppeared to, Her Majesty's Government that the Austrian occupation of the 
Principalities might be safe and advantageous to the Porte. 

Tam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

(No. 111. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Frankfort, September 30, 1854. 

A DAY or two after I had the honour to receive your Lordship’s despateh 
No, 94 of the 22nd ultimo, inclosing your Lordship's despatch No. 51 of the 
19th, to Lord Augustus Loftus, | called upon Baron Prokesch, and found the 
Representatives of Bavaria and Saxony with his Excellency. When they had 
taken their leave, I said that I hoped my having found those gentlemen at his 
Excelleney’s house was a good sign, and that there might be some foundation 
for the reports that Bavaria and Saxony were more disposed than they had 
recently shown themselves towards Austrian policy, 

Wi. de Prokesch answered that such was not by any means the case. 
MM. von der Pfordten and Beust pursued their course; the latter especially, 
said his Excellency, aims at taking a high place in European politics (veut faire 
de la haute politique), and that there was, in reality, no nearer approach, on 
the part of either State, to Austrian views on the Eastern question. 

M. de Prokesch went on to say that he found the Diet so averse to 
pronouncing themselves in any way in the sense he and his Government desired, 
that he found it desirable to continue the same conduct which he had adopted 
respecting the question of putting the Federal contingents on a war-footing ; 
namely, to allow the questions as to adhesion to the ‘Treaty of the 20th of April, 
and all other subsidiary ones relating to Eastern affairs, to remain undecided, 
and to put off receiving the reports of the Committees, 

M. de Prokesch was full of invective against Prussia, and repeated what he 
has often already said to me, that Austria could not feel assured of not finding 
that State arrayed in hostility against her. 

M. de Prokesch, on our conversation turning upon the recent correspond- 
enee of M. de Manteuffel with the Prussian Representatives at St. Petersburgh, 
Vienna, and London, read to me the note addressed to M. de Bernstortf, whieh 
drew forth your Lordship’s despatel: to Lord Augustus Loftus, No. 51 of the 
19th ultimo. This despatch Thad with me, and allowed MI. de Prokeseh to 
jeruse it. ‘The contents appeared to afford him considerable satisfaction ; and 
iis Excellency then showed me copies of the despatch addressed by Count 
Nesselrode to Baron de Budberg, by which that Minister was instructed to 
signify to the Cabinet of Berlin the Czar's rejection of the four points; and also 
the despatch which M. de Manteuffel had written to Baron Werther in_ reference 
to Count Nesselrode’s communication. 

These State Papers have no doulit been before your Lordship, and [ neeil 
only remark in relation to then, that the point to which M. de Prokescl espe- 
cially called my attention was the assertion made in the note of Count Nessel- 
rode, by way of reproach to the Cabinet of Berlin, that the support given by 
His Prussian Majesty to the four points had much surprised his Imperial 
Master, as the demands they embodied were altogether bevabd and at variance 
with the propositions antecedently made by Austria, which demands (if | 
recollect the wording of the despatch rightly) were asserted by Connt Nesselrode 
to have been framed “sous In dictée de Ia Prusse.”” 

In the desputch from Baron Manteutfel to M. de Werther, this observation 
of Count Nesselrode’s was replied to in a way that fully admitted the gravamen 
af the charge of dictating to Austria, if such it can be styled; and Baron 
Prokesch seemed to think it deadly offence to his Cabinet that M. de Buol 
should be supposed te have written anything whatever under the influence of 
Prussian inspirations, 

His Excellency told me that it was incorrect to say that negotiations were 
at present going on between the two States; the dissidence was great, and the 
present efforts of Prussia were all directed to circumseribing and defining the 
uction of Austria in the Danubian Principalities within limits favourable to 
Russia. Prussian was at present demanding eategorical explanations from 
Austria as to her views and intentions in holding the Principalities, Would 
Austria, for example, allow the Turks (no allugion, I believe, is made to the 


187 


allied forees) to attack the Russian Province of Bessarabia? What would the 
Austrian Corps of Occupation do in ease of Turkish suceesses or reverts: 
Would they permit the Turks to be reinforeed ? Would they allow the Ruseins 
to pursue the Turks, if repulsed, into Moldavian or Wallachian territory? 

These queries, M. de Prokesch said, were in view of the counsels which 
Prussia would give her German confederates as to their adherence to Austrian 
views in respect of the four points. Thad previously heard that Austria hed 
expressed herself as only requiring the Dict’s adhesion to two points, pene 
first, the free navigation of the Danube and Black Sea; and secondly, the 
cessation of Russian Protectorate over the Principalities, and consequent sanction 
of Austrian occupation. | , 

I put then the question directly to M. de Prokesch as to the foundation 
for such an assertion. w.. . 

His Exeelleney did not explicitly reply to my query; but Tam inclined to 
think from what he did admit, that this assertion of Austria’s requirements from 
her German confederates is essentially correct, and is in fact the extent of eon- 
cession to Prussia whieh it is thought prudent to make. It is sought hereby to 
extend the federal obligations of mutual defence to the Danubian occupation, and 
that a Russian attack on the troops of Austria in those Provinces should entail 
the same consequences asin aggression on any other Province of the Empire 
comprised in the Germanic Confederation. : 

I thought, I said to M. de Prokesch, that in order to secure the really free 
navigation of the Danube, it would be necessary to exclude the Russians entirely 
from the banks of that river; it might perhaps suffice to draw a line from 
Akerman, or some point agreed upon on the Black Sea, to the Pruth, effectually 
to obtain that object. 

On this Baron de Prokesch said that his plans went far greater lengths ; 
that he would deprive Russia of the whole of Bessarabia, and restore it to 
Turkey; that he had already suid as much to his Ministry, and made no seeret 
of his opinions, of his personal fecling of hostility to [ousst, 

I remarked that some disappointment had very naturally been felt in 
England and France at the recent decision of Austrit not to consider the rejee- 
tion of the four points by the Emperor of Russia us a cusus belli, "That in 
weighing the conduct of Prussia, which his [Excellency appeared to consider m 
nearly the same light as I did myself, it seemed to me that the divergence 
might and ought to have induced Austria to take her own line. No doult 
could be reasonubly entertained that Mnghind and BPrance, determined as they 
were to obtain a secure peace, were able to compass that object without aid from 
any quarter; but that if Austria had resolved to take an uctive part against 
Russin, there could not exist any difference of opinion as to the desired object of 
the war being likely to be more speedily obtained. Surely, T said, Austria could 
rely not only on our ¢arnestness in pushing hostilities to the utmost, but on our 
ood faith and abnegation of all aims at aggrandizement as consigned in our 
‘Treaty engagements with France. 

‘To this M. du Prokeseh promptly replied that this was not enough; that 
between individuals perfeet reliance on good faith might subsist, and responsi - 
bilities be entered into accordingly; but with States it was otherwise, and 
nothing but the guarantee of written engagements sufficed in such emengencies. 
He had, he declared, advised his Government to enter into such engagements 
with the Western Powers, and said that had he himself been Minister, he would 
ere this have taken steps to enter into negotiations for an alliance irrespective of 
Prussia and her policy, which he characterized as donble-dealing and insincere. 
Such are the main points of M. de Prokesch’s conversation and remarks 
upon this occasion, His Excellency’s character and dispositions are already sa 
well known to your Lordship, that it is not likely that you will attach an undue 
value to them, or be led to think that the opinions of the President of the Diet 
will have much weight with Count Puol, 

Anything that for the moment opposes his own peculiar views hecomes 
on the instant the object of Baron Prokeseh’s virulent enmity. ‘Thus lussia, 
whose policy he had formerly to combat at Constantinople, and whence he lis 
consequently received proofs of his having made himself personally obnoxious, 
is not likely to be spared, if he had it in his power ta wound her. 

Our swn country came in for a large share of similar feeling when his

My Lord, Stuttgardt, October 3, 1854. 
IN conversing yesterday with Baron de Linden upon the Eastern question, 

| hud oceasion to observe that no Government desired peace more than that of 

Her Majesty, as their whole conduct had shown, when his Excellency remarked, 

that if peace was the object, the terms demanded should not be humiliating. 


191 


inguired if his Excellency saw anything humiliating in the four points, when he 
replied in the negative; but added, that we had not bound ourselves not to go 
beyond them. I replied, that the longer the war continued, the more stringent 
might be our terms; that, for example, although the capture af Sebastopol 
might possibly find us still willing to accept the four points as the basis of peace, 
such might not be the case if a continuance of war in the spring were to bring 
about, through an expedition both military and naval, the capture of Cronstadt. 

His Excelleney expressed the opinion, that perhaps the fall of Sehastopol 
might lead us to insist less strongly on the four points; but I replied, that I 
considered we could never depart from them in the sense of diminution. 

Baron de Linden further observed, that the explanations respecting the sail 
points, which had been requested of Austria by Prussia, were necessary to the 
formation of a complete opinion regarding them. 

It is to be presumed that this Government will follow at Frankfort in the 
wake of Prussia. 

Baron de Neurath, the late Minster of Foreign Affaire, recently told my 
informant that his return to office was rendered impossible by this Government's 
adhesion to Prussia’s view of the Eastern question, 

It is remarked that the language of Count Seckendorff, the Prassian 
Minister, has become less anti-Russian since his return to lis residence about a 
month ago. 3 

Of the feeling here, it may, perhaps, be said, that the upper class shows 
more Russian sympathy, and that the middle and lower classes show less 
Russian antipathy tina they feel. | 

As partly indicative of this state of feeling, I may mention that Baron 
Handel, the Austrian Minister, has censed to visit the Club here, on account of 
the hostile sentiments displayed towards his Government, 

A natural reason for the smaller German Courts to look up to Russia, 
would seem to be, that all the Great Powers but Russia look down on them. 

T have, &e. 
(Signed) G, S. & JERNINGHAM.

THE slow progress made by the two great German Cabinets in the prelint- 
nelry yaaa which the nature of the projected communication to the Diet 
at Frankfort, in respect to their future attitude in the Eastern question, has 
rendered indispensable, has greatly ‘nereased the difficulty of pronouncing a 
decided opinion upon the possible ulthmate conduct of the minor States of the 
Confederation, when the expected propositions shall be made to them. ‘The 
great apprehension they entertain of becoming involved in a war, for objects in 
the attainment of which they, singularly enough, still persist in asserting that 
they are but remotely interested, REFUraly inclines them to side with the policy 
of whichever of the two Great Powers seems most likely to promise them the 
longest reprieve from the hard fulfilment of their Federal obi rations, and the 
atill more unpleasant prospect of finding themselves arrayed against & Sovereign 
whom they have long been accustomed to look upon in the light of a protector, 
und the preserver of order in, burope, At this moment there can be no doubt 
that they all give evidence of a leaning to Prussia, because they ealealate that 
by aiding her to thwart and control the movements of Austria, they will 
aueceed in preventing the lmperial Cabinet from committing them to any 
positive engagements, until the approach of winter shill render active hostile 
measures altogether out of the question for this years and they hope that when 
the season shall be so fir advanced as to oppose in obstacle to the further 
proseeution of warlike operations, means will be found for reverting once more

This view of the motives which guide the policy of the minor States in the

mind a-strong impression that every expedient would be resorted to for putting 
off any decision of the Diet, until a more fixed and explicit basis for the conclu- 
sion of peace than is contained in the four points specified by the British and 
French Governments, should be brought forward. Tndeed, he admittted that he

M. Von der Pfordten made an attempt to defend that policy, apparently 
from the convietion thar, by carrying it out, there still remained some slight 
chance of eseapinge from any participation in the struggle for preponderance 
in the East, which he says is the sole question at issue between Russia and 
the Western Powers; and he avowed, without hesitation, that the object of 
Prussia, in common with the minor States of Germany, was no. other than to 
avoid being drawn inte the complications in which the recent steps taken by

thouglit proper to bind herself, From all 1 could collect, the Governments of 
the smaller States are extremely dissatisfied at the little account taken of them 
hy the Imperial Cabinet during the course of the transactions which have led 
to the present situation of affairs, It is. reproached with ignoring the very 
existence of the Diet; until it is in want of the material aid of its federal-alhes 
to further its own ambitious views of conquest, for to that end they maintain 
its efforts are now directed: and admitting this ta be the ease, they bitterly 
inquire whut wdvantage is to acerne to them, and what return they are to 
expect for the sacrifices they are eilled upon to make. They say that not 
liaving been even consulted upon all these matters, the results of which were 
only communicated to them months after they became public, they cannot 
and will not permit themselves to be made responsible for, and bear the burthen 
af, the consequences ; anid that us‘they resisted the attempts of Prussia to make 
them subservient to her exclusive policy three vears ago, so will they now 
pursue the same course in respect to Austria. 

My conversation with M. Von der Pfordten having taken this direction, I 
ventured to remurk that, in the abstract, | could not blame the minor States for 
acting in the manner they thought most conducive to their own interests, 
provided they were strong enough, and united enough, to maintain their 
position; but 1 said that so miuny other consid¢rations, and such important 
principles of international justice, which so nearly touched all weak States, were 
mixed up in the present quest ion, that | thought it behoved them well to consider 
whether they bad not as anuch miscalculated their true interests as they undoult- 
edly had thete power. M. Von der Pfordten asserted, and I believe with great 
truth, that there isin Germany no sympathy whatever for Russia; but this must 
be understood toapply to the population, and not ta the Courts and Governments, 
whieh are unquestionably more or less alternately influenced by their dread and 
adoration of the Emperor Nicholas, The same may be-stated of the: press, 
which is unceasingly at work to distort facts, and to keep up the prestige of the 
omnipotence of His Imperial Majesty; for instance, two articles, cither, as 1 im 
dssurcd on the best authority, fiom the pen of M, Von der Pfordten hinigell, or 
written under his especial direction, have recently appeared in a popular journal,

THE attitude of Prossia in this great political drama merits the greatest 
acknowledgments. So long as there was a question of representing real and 
positive German interests, Prussia was seen in the closest union with Austria, 
determined to use every means to defend and protect those interests; and all 
the other States of Germany were found ready to accompany them in this path, 
When, however, these interests, as has been above observed, do not appear to he 
in any immediate danger, all ground oy aye demonstrations aguinst Russia

(fensive and Defensive Allianee with the Western Powers; und Count Buol is
