reign Tights against the demands of the Court of Russia, and to protect andl 
watch over his ‘aterests—interests common tO US, his faithful and obedient 
subjects, and in the prosecution of which we are engaged 1 full liberty and 
freedom from molestation under the Imperial auspices, and in the enjoyment of 
political and spiritual privileges granted to us without stint, . 

Of such important character is the present contest, in which the allied 
Western Powers have embarked, regardless of pecuniary and personal saer- 
fice, and for which they are met with the above ungenerous and unprineipled 
requital. 
~ Having thus shown to what extent we owe a tribute of gratitude to the 
friends and allies of our Monarch, it become our duty, in which we do not fail, 
to exhort paternally and in decided terms by means of this ceclesiastical letter, 
those among you, our kindred, who have been guilty of ucts 80 unseemly and 
at such viailance with your character as Christians and subjects of the Porte, to 
desist for the future, and: to conduct yourselves in a friendly and becoming 
manner, thereby affording sincere proof of your eratitude for the countless 
services und dangers undergone ‘1 order to maintain the rights of the Porte 
against Russia; which latter Power, under the pretext of protecting the 
Orthodox Church, cherishes, as we have on many occasions exposed, seeret and 
political designs ; while working for a pernicious and destructive purpose, she 
proclaims & different language in nae und endeavours to seduce the more

simple among us bY these delusive proclamations, and by so doing has become 


the cause of such dangers and calamities through nearly the whole world, and 
lias brought universal distress upon the poor, who are barely able to obtain a 
living. 

But the Almighty Judge, who is alone acquainted with the secret thoughts 
of man, has not suffered the world to be afflicted with the scourge of a war 
raised for ambitious designs without retribution, but has declared himself for the 
right cause, and has granted his blessing upon the Imperial and allied armies. 
He has accorded them a complete victory over the enemy's foree at Silistria ; he 
has broken them and put them to flight, and dispersed them beyond the 
boundaries. 

Being, therefore, clearly convinced of the deceitful policy of that country, 
do not give, any of you, the least faith or attention to the above delusions, 
unworthy of the notice of any prudent man, but remain as heretofore faithful to 
the Imperial Government, preserving pure and intact your sentiments of obe- 
dience, submission, and devotion to the supreme and benelicent power set over 
us from on high. 

It is for you on the present occasion to redouble your proofs of complete 
obedience and sincere devotion to that Power which has not ceased to extend its 
fostering care aver all classes of its subjects, and under whose protection we 
live in full enjoyment of the national and spiritual privileges accorded to us of 
old, which our gracious Sovereign has lately confirmed and secured to us by 
his Royal sign-manual, under the impulses of his natural benevolence, 

Similarly, 1 the fulfilment of a Christian duty, cherish sentiments of 
sincere friendship towards the friendly and allied Powers, which have ranged 
themselves in sincerity fora good cause alongside our Government, Wherefore, 
you will not only abstain from affording their soldiers any cause of dissatisfaction, 
ns has been done by certain ill-advised persons, but will behave ina conciliatory 
spirit towards them, and become thereby the object of the common regard antl 

woodwill of the Porte and the allied Powers; discharging with Christian zeal 
your imperative duty of offering up prayers for the salvation and prosperity of 
our most gracious Monareh, for the success of his arms, and the astablichinent 
of the long-cherished peace and tranquillity, as result of the contest now under- 
taken with the blessing of God. May Ie also grant the allied Powers a worthy 
recompense for their efforts, and confer His grace upon all who cooperate with 
zeal in the humane and sagacious views of our Sovereign, Heaven grant it!

My Lord, Varna, September 21, 1854, 

T HAVE the honour to report to your Lordship that, yesterday and to-day, 
several British and French transport steamers and vessels have arrived in Varna 
from the Crimea, to embark the troops remaining here, Some vessels will also 
proceed, I understand, to Bourgas, to embark the French cavalry hitherto 
stationed at Aidos, Her Majesty's steam-ship “Spiteful” also arrived this 
morning from the Crimea, to expedite the embarkation of the four regiments of 
British cavalry. . 

I am informed that the allied armies had advanced towards Sebastopol, and 
that an encounter with the enemy was expected to take place yesterday or 
to-div. 

The only deficiencies stated to be experienced by the troops was that of 
wood and water.

Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received October 8.) 


(No. 539.) 
My Lord, Therapia, September 25, 1854. 
YOU can hardly fail to have anticipated me when I state that the commu- 
pications between the Austrian and Ottoman Commanders in Wallachia, on the 
one hand, und the military bearings of the policy pursued by the Court of Vienna 
rowards Hussia, on the other, warrint an apprehension of serious complications 
and untoward contingencies. f 
It may be inferred from the language of Austrian agents, that Austria looks 
to maintaining relations of peace with Russia, rounded on the evacuation of the 
two Principalities by the Russian army, and that she reckons upon being allowed, 


209 


in reality, to enjoy the exclusive occupation of these Provinces without firing « 
shot for their delivery or in their defence. 

‘The Porte, informed by its Commander-in-chief and Commissioner, looks 
with repngnance, not unallied to mistrust, on this course of proceeding, She 
approves Omer Pasha’s desire to take up positions at Galatz and Ibraila, with a 
view to further eventual demonstrations against Russit. She can support her 
awn view of the case by referring to the earlier propesals of Austria, intent, in 
appearance, at that time on active and combined operations, She can also call 
to her aid the opinion of Marshal St. Arnaud communicated through MM. Bene- 
detti, and intimating, on military grounds, an apprehension of Russia's being 
enabled, by the prolonged inactivity of Austria, and the withdrawal of the 
Ottoman urmy, to detach a powerful remforeement from Bessarabia to her troops 
in the Crimea. 

The Turkish Ministry summoned to decide between the conflicting dangers 
of indisposing the Austrian Cabinet and leaving the allies in an exposed condition, 
naturally appeal to the Representatives of those allies. 

Partaking the anxieties created by so doubtful and embarrassing a question, 
Lagreed with my French colleague to reserve our opinion till after the arrival of 
the accelerated steam-packet yesterday. Unfortunately no clear light is thrown 
upon our uncertainty by the correspondence then received. What information 
has reached us tends rather to inerease our apprehension, and is certainly not 
eatenlated to remove our embarrassment, 

Your Lordship can hardly be surprised if under such critical circumstances 
we prolong our hesitation until we can discuss the matter at leisure in all its 
bearings, and agree on what advice it will be most prudent to offer to the Porte. 
My own inclination is to avoid every abrupt or hazardous preceeding not 
warranted by a distinct and urgent necessity ; butat the same time not to shrink 
from maintaining the full rights of the Porte in active operation, if such a course 
be deemed, on mature reflection, indispensable to secure the allied armies in the 
Crimea from any additional danger. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

My Lord, Bucharest, September 15, 1854. 

I AD the honour to inform your Lordship in my despatch No. 35 of the 
oth instant, that it had been decided at a conference held on the preceding day, 
between Omer Pasha and General Coronini, that a considerable portion of the 
‘Turkish force should move upon Ibraila, in order to occupy the Russian army 
lately withdrawn from the Prineipalities. I have now to inform your Lordship, 
that before carrying this operation ito effect, General Coronini communicated 
with the Baron von Hess, who has sent a reply through him, a copy of which 
I herewith transmit to your Lordship, as trans ated from German into French 
by one of his Highness's secretarics, 

His Highness being desirous that thia communication should reach your 
Lordship and Marshal St. Arnaud with the least possible delay, Colonel Dieu 
has charged Captain Jumell, of the Etat Major of the French army, who will 
kindly take charge of this to convey it to the head-quarters of the allied forces. 

His Highness feels that the positions taken by the Austrian forees in Walla- 
chia are such, that he cannot make the contemplated diversion under existing 
cireumstances, and finding his army paralyzed and unable to operate upon the 
plan whieh he understood to have been agreed upon, after the communication 
which passed between Colonel Kalich and the Baron Liwenthal, on the part of 
Buren von Hess, your Lordship, Marshal St. Arnaud and himself, at the com- 
meneement of the month of August, he ig anxious to acquit himself of the 
responsibility of not acting up to this arrangement. ‘The propositions made by 
hin would, he considers, have the effect, if adopted, of preventing at lenst 1 large 
portion of the Russian forces from being moved towards the Crimea and the 
chores of the Black Sea; an effect which would be particularly useful, if it should 
Le in the contemplation of your Lordship and Marshal St. Arnaud to operate 


211 


vpon any other point on the shores of the Black Sea west of the Crimes, after 
completing the operation now i execution by the English and French araes. 
Tam to inform your Lordship that his Highness, being about to leave this. 
place for Rustchuk for a few days, has deferred replying to the einai con 
tained in General Coroninis communication, thinking it probable that 1 the 
meantime information may be received relative to the operations of the allied 
armies which may materially affect the position of affairs in the Principality. 

In the meantime his troops remaining in the positions before taken by 
them, will be ready to. continue their movement to the front, or io make any 
other which the eventualities of the moment may require. _ 1 propose, however, 
to report to your Lordship a few of the remarks which his Highness made to me, 
relative to the communication in question, new 

His Highness considers it @ duty which he owed to your Lordship and 
Marshal St. Arnaud, to use his utmost endeavours to act up to the arra ngement 
concluded in the beginning of August, and from which it may enter 1nto the 
caleulations of your Lordship and Marshal St. Arnaud that the Russian army 1 
and near the Principalities would be oceupied in this direction, whilst the English 
and French armies were operating upol! the rear of that army. 

Instead of this being the case, information has arrived here, which appears 
to be of a positive nature, that the greater part of the Russian army 18 moving 
upon Odessa and towards the Crimea, leaving only the ath Corps d'Armée under 
General Liiders, between the Pruth and the Dniester. 

His Highness also considers that until Austria declares war, the Russian 
army is not kept in check by the Austrian forees sufficiently to prevent a large 
portion of them from being moved towards the shores of the Black Sea, and 
that an advance of the ‘Turkish army could not fail,even if the contrary were the 
case, to add to the Russian force which would thus be kept in check ; whereas, 
if the proposition now made by Baron von Hess were carried into effect, the 
Turkish army becomes altogether paralysed, and has little or no effect upon the 
operations of the war. ; 

His Highness also feels, that although the complete evacuation of the 
Principalities is in great measure due to the attitude assumed by the Austrians, 
it cannot be entirely attributed to them. 

He cannot forget that the preparations made by your Lordship and Marshal 
St, Arnaud, and the position of the Turkish army, brought about the abandonment 
of the siege of Silistria, the evacuation of Little Wallachia, and the concentration 
of the Russian forces on the left bank of the Lower Danube ; that subsequently 
the forced passage of the Danube by his troops, and the fortifying of a secure 
position on the left lank of the Danube at Giurgevo and Slobodzie, placed 1b im 
the power of the allied forces at war with Russia; to cross the Danube and 
carry the war into Wallachia that it was only after these operations had been 
effected, that the roposition of Baron vou Fess was made, and that appearances 
led to the belief ‘hat the Austrians were going take a decided part in the next 
struggle. 

His Highness also observed that in carrying into effect the operation 
proposed, through Colonel Kalich and the Baron Léwenthal, by Baron von Hess, 
the Turkish army was for some time exposed to attack by the forces of Russia, 
then concentrated in his front; the Austrian army being too far distant and not 
in a condition to render him any assistance, not being at war with Russia. 

His Highness further remarked that instead of preventing any attempt at 
negotiation, any movement which could have the effect of harassing the enemy, 
or rendering greater the probabilities of success against him in any other quarter, 
must tend to make him more ready to aecept the terms required of him by the 
allies. 

‘The movement proposed by his Highness would also have the advantage of 
not being attended with risk, und would place his army in such a position, that 
if thought desirable 4 junction with it of the English and French armies under 
your Lordship and Marshal St. Arnaud, could be effected by sea, 

- “These are in brief the observations made by his Highness, with which I 
think it right. your Lordship should be acquainted ; his answer however to the 
communication of General Coronini will not be sent for a few days, 
Lam, &. 
(Signed) J. L. A. SIMMONS,

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarencon—(Received October 9.) 


(No, 1220.) 
My Lord, Paris, October 8, 1854. 

M, DE SEVRES, the Freneh Secretary of Legation at Vienna, arrived in 
Paris late on ‘Thursday evening with despatches from M. de Bourqueney dated 
the 2nd instant. ‘These despatches relate to the fresh propositions which the 
Governments of England and France had been led to expect would be made to 
them hy the Cabinet of Vienna in regard to the Wastern question. ‘The nature 
of the propositions themselves is to be found in Lord Westmorland’s confidential 
despateh No. 365, also of the 8nd instant, which T had the honour to forward to 
vour Lordship on the 6th instant. It would be superfluous, therefore, for me to 
zo into any details of them. Twill only remark that M, de Bourqueney hits 
necompanied his statement by a * Projet de Traité.” 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys bemg in the country, the despatches were sent to 
him, and I was unable to ask his opinion of them until yesterday afternoon. 

His Excellency said that he had just come from a council at St. Cloud, and 
that he was enabled to speuk the Emperors sentiments, as well as lis own; that 
he thought the propositions detestable (détestables), and that they could not he 
seriously entertained, He proceeded to recapitulate them seriatim as contained 
in the * Projet de Traité,” and remarked that they were in general a repetition of 
what the allied Governments had refused in another shape. England and France, 


‘he observed, were required to consign to a Treaty the une embodied in the 


notes exchanged on the 8th August. What advantage would they derive from 
such a proceeding which they did not possess already? ‘They were asked to 
define more precisely the character of the Austrian aecupation af the Principalt- 
ties; but this was already defined hy the Convention of the 14th of June, signed 
hetween Austria and the Porte, A pretension, indeed, was put forward that if 
the allied armies entered the Principalities to attack the Russians, their move- 
ments should be continued in concert with the Austrian Commander-in-chier : 
thut is to say, the allies, who had a signed a Convention with the Porte per- 
nitting them to occupy, during the war, any part of the Turkish territory which 
suited their strategy, or their convenience, were to make their entry into the 
Principatities to depend in some measure 08 the permission of Austria, The 
propesal of a Conlerence or Congress was equally inadmissible, Tt was tanta- 
mount to preparing a Treaty of Peace in the midst of war, and to place a non- 
bolligerent on a footing of equality with belligerents. 
But the worst clause of all was. that whieh stipulated tor an alliance, 
offensive und defensive, between the three Powers, In case Austria, im conse- 
quence of her occupation of the Principalities, should be attacked by Russia, 
That is, the allies were called upon to sign a ‘Treaty which should sanction the 


theory maintained by Austria, that as long as she was not attacked by Russia, 


there existed no casts belli for her. 

Your Lordship will be good enough to recollect that 1 have not seen the 
Projet de Traité,” and can only report M. Drouyn de Lhuys' appreciation of it. 

His Excellency concluded, therefore, and so had the Emperor, that the 
propositions could not be entertained. But another question remained for 
consideration. 

M. de Bourqueney’s despatches showed that both the Emperor of Austria 
and Count Buol were most anxious that they should be accepted; and the 
former had expressed himself with same sensitiveness respecting the suspicions 


re ie 


to which his conduct had given rise ‘1 London and Paris. [f these frealh 
overtures on his part were rejected at once, might there not be danger of his 
becoming alarmed at the estrangement evinced towards him by England and 
France, and might he not seek to draw nearer again to Russia t Under this 
apprelicnsion, M. Drouyn de Lhnys continued, he had been considering it what 
way the proposition could be refused without giving offence, and it appeared to 
him that, as the last accounts which he had received, both frou Constantinople 
and Bucharest, showed that the Austrian agents at those places were acting in 
direct opposition to the stipulations which the Treaty proposed to consecrate, 
an answer might be returned to the Auetrian Government that so long as these 
crying acts of injustice were not remedied, the allied Governments could not 
entertain the fresh overtures made to them by Count Buol. 

1 asked whether this would not imply an engagement that, the evils once 
remedied, the propositions would be entertained ; while, if 1 had understood 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys rightly, he was of opinion that they could be uceeptable 
under no circumstances. 1 was confident, I added, that Her Majesty’s Govern- 
ment would feel, equally with him, the necessity of replying to Austria with all 
possible courtesy ; but might not this be done by acknowledging Count Buol’s offer 
to be a pledge of the desire of the Emperor of Austria to draw closer the bonds 
of his alliance to Great Britain and France? by pointing out the disadvantage to 
which the stipulations of the Treaty would subject the allies 7 and by proposing 
a counter-project, in which a clause might be introduced hinding Austria to 
declare war against Russia in the spring, if a peace on the basis of the four 
points had not been previously concluded 2 This would give the two Govern- 
ments an opportunity of reassuring Austria by showing that they still adhered 
to the four points, while it would not bind them unnecessarily for the future. 
If Austria accepted this counter-preject, well and good; if she refused, she 
could not take it amiss if we, on our part, declined to agree to her conditions. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys appeared ‘nelined to abide by his own idea, and | 
said no more; the more particularly as f could not tell what might be your 
Lordship’s impression. But on eoing to him again this morning I found that he 
preferred the plan which I had ventured to suseest. Ele had seen M, de 
Hiibner, he said, who had communicated to him: Count Buol's despatches, upon 
the subject to which this despatch relates, and he told him that he could give 
him no answer until he had taken the Emperor's orders, and had consultect Her 
Majesty's Government, but he had allowed him to sce that his personal opinion 
waa not favourable to the project. 

M. de Litner, however, did nat allude te any « Projet de ‘Traité,” and hard 
merely spoken in general terms of what might he done. 

Count Walewski will receive by tomorrow's nessenger a despatch for 
communication to your Lordship, detailine at length the opinions of Nis 
Government,

Nesselrode, in which the Chancellor had stated that Russia was not indisposed

Cabinet by Austria, namely, that relating to the future Protectorate of the 
Principalities, provided that the rights and privileges of the Provinees should 
be respected, and that the Protectorate should be given over to the five Powers 
collectively. j 

Baron Manteuffel, in mentioning this cireumstance to Count Hsterhazy, 
and in requesting him to convey it to Count Buol, particularly desired that it 
might not be thought that he was the promoter, or even the direct channel of 
communication, of this proposal. He merely wished to transmit the information 
as it had reached him. 

Count Esterhazy, 1 communicating this ‘nformation to me, requested that

The more sincerely we desire a union with Prussia and the other Governments 
of Germany, the more decidedly important do we consider it that our declarit- 
tions be guarded from all misunderstanding. 

We have not said, nor can We 5a), that by the retreat of the Russian troops 
from the Danubian Prineipalities, the danger of a conflict between the two 
Empires bas been removed. We said this of such immediate danger only. 

In calling to recollection that the occupation of the Prineipalities by Russi 
was the origin of the war, and that the German Courts: had declared that the 
continuance thereof was incompatible with the interests of Austria and Germany, 
in admitting the consequent importance of the fact of the evacuation, we were 
still very far from considering that evacuuition to be equivalent to 8 maintenance 
of those weighty interests: we rather loaked upon them as deeply engaged, #0 
long as Russia does not rive securities for the establishment of a sure aud listing 
pence, 

We mentioned the narrowing of the theatre of war as au immediate conse 
quence of the evacuation of the Prineipalities, In so doing we had in view the 
fact that Russia has withdrawn her army fem Wallachia and Moldavia, and that 
Austria is invited to protect those countries from a second invasion, . But we 
have not arrogated to ourselves 4 right to separate the Principalities from the 
ere open to warlike operations, and we are not in a position to claim auc li 
a right.

Count Buol to Count Esterhazy.—(Communicated to the Marl af Clarendon by 
Count Colloreda, October 9.) 


(‘Translation,) Vienna, September 30, 1854. 

WE will add to the preceding despatch o few observations a5 to our 
relations with the belligerent Powers. 

‘here are two points which ave more or less explicitly demanded of ws fron 
Berlin. It is believed that we ought to close the Principalities against oflensive 
operations against Russia on the part of the Turks or their allies; ancl it is 
wished to obtain from us an assurance that if Russia does not uttack us, we shall, 
on our side, not proceed to aggressive incusures. 

Either supposition is, however, decidedly inconsistent with our position, 
We do not consider ourselves warranted to impede in the Principalities the 
operations of the belligerent Powers ; aud we ean in no case renounce the right 

3 i 


294 


ae 


to change our present attitude of an armed expectation for a participation in the 
war. 

We will not dwell at length on this latter point, It 1s self-evident that we 
cannot expect to attain the peace that we require through the exertions and 
combats of others, nor ean we take the engagement to bear for an unlimited time 
the heavy suerifices which so passive an attitude must entail; it is therefore only 
as regards the first point that we eonsider it expedient to state lo your Excellency 
the grounds of our decision. 

"We can only consider ourselves as entitled to the cecupation of the Prinet- 
palities. under the condition that we will defend them against every attack by 
Russian arms, and that we shall not oppose the military measures of the Allied 
Powers. 

‘This is the necessary consequence of our Treaty with the Porte, and it is 
likewise in complete unison with what we have always maintained and declared, 
ax well to Rugsia as to others. When we demanded the evacuation of the 
Principalities, we expressly stipulated that no condition, the fulfilment of which 
would be beyond our power, should be attuched to this evacuation, Russia on 
this declared herself ready to evacuate, but at the same time demanded guarantees 
of'us that she should not be exposed to the pursuit of the enemy and to further 
attack. This we refused: for Husa had in the first instance declared that it 
was her intention to retreat from purely stratemical motives, and she therefore 
avoided a conflict which must have followed the irrevocable decision we had 
taken, Russia consequently did not deliver the Principilities up to us, but 
merely left them to their fate. We occupied them because we had received the 
authority of Turkey so todo. ‘The ‘Turks enter in consequence of their military 
operations, and the French and English, owing to thei Treaty of Alliance with 
the Porte, may follow them. 

We consequently have the right to be in the Prineipalities, but nowise the 
obligation to exclude thenee by force any but the enemies of the Porte. Still 
loss uve we entitled to preseribe to the belligerent Powers for what military pur- 
poses they should be at liberty to advance, We could not advance such a 
pretension without giving just cause for remonstrances against our proceeding. 

It cannot be denied but that this state of things involves some difficulties, 
but. these may be overcome by a frank admission of the limits of our rights, and 
by amicable representations made in the form of negotiations, 

It will only be in such manner, and in the interest of the Principalities 
themselves, that we shall be able to use our influence that these districts may be 
freed from the operations of war. 

It thenee further follows, with reference to the validity of the Treaty of the 
20th April, that no distinction can be made whether an attack, in which we do 
not share, be made on Russian territory, or not. If we have not the right to 
hinder such an attack, neither does it follow that by allowing it we change our 
position to the offensive. But Russia will on its part be compelled te confine 
herself to resistance of attack on the Pruth, if she wishes to avoid «a conflict 
with Austria. Prussia and Germany will consequently, if they generally acknow- 
ledve our advance into the Principalities to be dictated by German interests, not 
be able to except from their promise of assistance a contingency, the occurrence 
of which our position does not warrant us i Oppesing. 

Your Excellency is authorized under fitting circumstances to make use of 
this despateh, and not to allow any doubt to prevail, that with respect to the 
above mentioned two points we are determined in no wise to recede from the 
position which we have deliberately assumed. 

Receive, &e. 
(Signed) BUOL.

IT would seem that something untoward and ominous hangs over that 
unfortunate army at Kars. Ismail Pasha, who was lately appointed to the 
command of it, has been taken ill here. His complaint is an inflammation of 
the eyes, which may endanger his sight. A provisional commander, by name 
Shukri Pasha, is appointed in consequence, with the rank of General of Division 
‘To me the individual and his name are alike new. He is said to have been 
strongly recommended by Omer Pasha, and ulso by Ismail, to whom, when with 
the army, he is to act as Chef d’Etat Major, superseding in that capacity General 
Guyon, and having as second in command a certain Hassan Pasha, who is stated 
to fave heen serving with Omer Pasha as General of Brigade, The arrival of 
these two officers will be followed by the departure of Mustafa Zaviit Pasha 
Kerim Pasha, and other superior officers, including General Guyon, for Con- 
stantinople, where they will be submitted to a court of inquiry. : 
Colonel Stein, who has turned Turk, assuming the name of Ferhad Pasha 
is attached to the Seraskier's staff, He was removed from the army at Kars at 
iny suggestion, a8 a man suspected even by his countrymen, and neutralizing by a 
spirit of intrigue the effects of his natural capacity and professional knowledge.

removul of Zariff Pasha is indeed a most laudable measure ; and an inquiry into

INCLOSED for your information are translated copies in print of a Vizirial 
firman, and instructions to a Commissioner appointed by the Sultan in colse- 
quence of my representations to enforce His Majesty's commands for the protec- 
tion of his subjects of all classes against the lawless and sanguinary roffians 


who, under the name of Bashi Bozouks, or as simple brigands, have of late 
committed so many outrages in the European provinces of Turkey. 

I have to call your attention to the proceedings: of the Commissioner and 
local authorities in the execution of their respective instructions, conceiving 
that no small advantage may result from their sense of having to act under your 
ahservation, with the certainty that while your good offers, when at all 
seusonable and useful, will never be withheld from them, any remissness in the 
performance of their duties will be brought, in its true colours, under the notice 
of Her Majesty’s Embassy and that of the Supreme Government.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon. —(Received Oetober 10.) 
(No. 1,226. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Paris, October 9, 1854. 

IN the report made by Marshal St. Arnaud to the Emperor of the events 
connected with the battle of the Alma, a copy of which was inclosed in my 
despatch No. 1.216 of the 7th imstant, the Marshal, after representing that the 
division of the French army commanded by General Bosquet had marched at 6 
o'clock in the morning to turn the left wing of the Hussiuns, makes the following 
statcment 

 Javais engagé les Angluis & se prolonger sur leur gauche pour menacer 
en méme temps la droite des Russes, pendant que je les occuperais au centre, 
mais leurs troupes ne sont arrivées en ligne qu’ dix heures et demie, Elles ont 
bravement réparé ce retard,” 

T have remarked that since the commencement af active operations on the 
part of the allies. the public reports of the French Commanders-in-clief suggest 
» evrtiin dilatoriness in the proceedings of Her Majesty's forces. 1 had reasoll 
to believe that the difference of time which is referred to in Admiral Hamelin’s 
despatches, between the disembarkation of the first French and of the first 

British soldiers in the Crimea, had been occusioned by a proceeding not altogether 
fair on the part of the French Admiral ; and General Rose’s interesting reports of 
the battle of the Alma, joined to a short conversation which I had with Lord 
Burzhersh on his passage through Paris, convinced me that the reproach con- 
veyed in Marshal St. Arnnud’s despatch quoted above, was unmerited. 
resolved therefore to call M, Drouynde Lhuys’ attention to this matter. 

Had known when L sought M. Drouyn de Lhuys with this intention yesterday 
afternoon, that the hand was cold which had penned the lines on which Twas 
‘about to animadvert, | should certainly have abstained from my purpose, But 
strange to say, the intelligence of Marshal St. Arnaud’s death had not then 
reached Paris. At least, nothing which fell from M. Drouyn de Lhuys gave me 
reason to suppose that he was aware of it. 

| began the conversation by saying that if was a great relict to me to feel 
that I could speak with his Excellency on all subjects without reserve, or without 
a fear of giving oftence. 1 then read to him the passage in Marshal St, Arnaud’s 
despatch quoted above, and 1 expressed my regret that it should have been 
published with the sanction of the French Government. There were, Dsaid, two 
facts implied by the paragraph in question. Virst, that the Marshal had the 
direction of the movements of Her Majesty’s forces, and secondly, that the 
fortunes of the day wereto a certain degree compromised by the delay which 
was eaid to have occurred in the advance of the British troops; for the use of 
word “rgparer”’ could not but imply that a fault had been committed. 

It was impossible, | continued to remark, to prevent the French Com- 
mander-in-chief, or the French Admiral, writing what they pleased ; ut if was 
clearly the province of the Fyench Government to take eare that nothing offen- 
sive to theirallies was published by their authority. 

I then went into some details respecting the disembarkation and the battle 
of Alma, to shew that there were two sides to nll stories, and T said that if there 
had been any delay in the advance of the ritish troops on the Alma it was 
beeause they hud to bear the brunt of the action, the Russian main pasition 
having been in their front, while General Bosquet had nothing to confront but 
some dificult ground. , 

I said that | made these observations because I fett certain that, unless 
more care was taken by the French Government in publishing the reports which 
they eegeived from the East, serious consequences might ensue. A Government 
might be ealm and prudent enough to overlook such matters, but when these 
reports went hack to the Bast, not all the ealm and pradence that the Com- 
ruanderein-chief could exercise woulil prevent young otlicers from showing their 
indignation at such language. Answers would be made, quarrels would ensue, 
and all cordinlity cease between the two armies. | therefore entreated M. 
Drouyn de Lhuys to speak to the Empevor and to his colleagues of the War 
aid Navel Departments to prevent a Resuerenes of such publications,

It gives me great satisfaction toadd that M. Drouyn de Lhuys received 
my observations in the most courteous manner, He said that he had himself 
remarked and regretted the publication of the paragraph in question, and that 
he had stated as much to the Emperor, and he quite admitted the necessity of 
rreater care in future. The Emperor's anxicty to give’ the country the earhest 
news of the success of the expedition had led His Majesty to order the imme- 
diate publication of the Marshal's report; but he (M. | rouyn de Lhuys) would 
much prefer that the publication should be retarded for four-nnd-twenty hours 
than that expressions calculated to give pain to the allies of France should be 
permitted to go faith. But, he added, he could assure me with truth that the 
conduct of Her Majesty's troops had been the admiration of the whole French 
army ; the steadiness with which they hid advanced under it most calling fire 
azainst a most formidable position was mentioned on all sides with the warmest 
praise, and he was certain that the Marshal had net intended to convey the 
shadow even of a reproof. | 

| eaid that I was perfectly sure that the reproach was not intentional, but 
that I thought that for the future the reports published on so delicate a matter 
as the participation of two armies in one great enterprise, should be confined as 
much as possible to facts. 

The conversation was carried on between M. Drouyn de Lhuys and mysclt 
in the most friendly tone, and T trust that your Lordship will not disapprove the 
step which | have taken. I have remarked among the Knglish here great 
disgust at the general tone, not ony of the reports to which T have alluded, but 
of the public press in Prince, which would seem to ighore that such 4 thing as 
an English General or an English army existed im the Hast, With the latter of 
course I do not pretend to interfere; but I humbly conceive not only that 
have been: justified in pointing out, but that it was my duty to point our, the 
consequences whieh might ensue, if expressions derogatory to the character of 
the British army were allowed to be published as proceeding from the French 
Commanders, 

Your Lordship will have no doubt remarked that there were other expres- 
sions i Marshal iS) Arnaud’s reports, besides the paragraph to which I have 
ulluded, whieh it would have been wiser to have suppressed, but as they were 
offensive only from inference, I did not consider it worth my while to mention 
them. | : 

As a further sample of the extraordinary inexactitude of the French reports, 
Ldo myself the honour to inclose herewith the copies of two plans of the battle 
of the Alma, which were published by order of the Minister of Marine, with the 
“ Moniteur” of this morning, in one of which the English army does not even 
find a place, while in the other it is made to occupy a very different position 
from that which, to judge from the accounts 1 have read, it must have

My Lord, Foreign Office, October 10, 1854. 

[LER Majesty’s Government approve the language which your Excellency 
held to M. Drouyn de Lhuys, as reported in your despateh No. 1,225 of the 
8th instant, regarding the new Austrian propositions for a closer alliance with 
England and France, and the project of Treaty sent home by M, de Bourqueney 
aud Lord Westmorland, and they concur generally the objections rised ly 
M. Drouyn de Lihuys to the terms of the Treaty. 1 haye held similar language 
to Count Colloredo, adding, however, that any proposition emanating from the 
Jabinet of Vienna, and particularly one to which it attached so much import. 
ance, would not fail to receive from Her Majesty's Government the most 
iitentive consideration ; but that, by reason of the importance as well as of the 
difficulties which presented themselves to its realization, i was impossible for 
me to give an answer without consulting my colleagues, and ascertaining the 
views of the French Government, 


aaah 


I told Count Colloredo that the Cabinet would probably meet in a few 
days, and that the delay could be of no consequence, as there was no immediate 
necessity for coming to a decision. 

I inclose herewith copies of Lord Westmorland’s despatch No. 865 of the 
2nd instant, to which your Excellency refers, and of his despatch No. 360 of the 
same date, inclosing the project of Treaty*; and your Excellency will observe 
to M. Drouyn de Lhuys that that project purports to be drawn up by Lord 
Westmorland and Baron de Bourqueney, und that we have no reason to 
suppose that it has been submitted to Count Buol. In the event, therefore, ol 
the two Governments acceding to a Treaty, it would be open to them at the 
same time to propose their own project, and the onus of objecting to it would 


then be thrown upon Austria.

No. 260. 


The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 
(No. 606.) 


My Lord Foreien Office; October 11, 1854. 

WITH reference to your Excellency’s despatch No. 546 of the 27th of 
September, respecting the differences which have arisen between the Austrian and 
Ottoman Commanders in Wallachia, I have to state that the copies of my 
despatches to Lord Westmorland will have placed your Excellency in possession of 
the views of Her Majesty’s Government upon the conduct adopted by the Austrian 
authorities towards those of the Porte in Wallachia; and 1 have on several 
oceasions and in strong terms remonstrated with Count Colloredo upon the 
subject, and upon the difference that existed between the language of the 
Austrian Cabinet and that of its agents at Bucharest and Constantinople. | 
warned him that such a state of things was destructive of confidence, and must 
lead to very serious results; and I have no doubt that Count Colloredo fulfilled 
his promise of faithfully reporting my observations to his Government. 

Your Excellency is also now aware of the positive instructions sent to 
General Hess not to interfere with the military movements of the Ottoman 
Commander-in-chief; and Her Majesty's Government have been given to under- 
stand that General Hess-and Baron Bruck had not acted in accordance with the 
intentions of their Government. 

It is to be hoped, therefore, that our representations and those of the 
French Goverament may have produced the desired effect; but in the mean- 
while I have the satisfaction of informing you that Her Majesty’s Government 
approve the advice which your Excellency has given to Reshid Pashu, as reported 
in your despatch No. 546 of the 27th ultimo. 

Lan, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

Mr. Buchanan to the Ear! of Clarendon.—(Received October 11.) 
(No. 290.) 


My Lord, Copenhagen, October 7, 1854, 

YESTERDAY being the King's birthday, His Majesty held a levée at 
Christiansborg Palace, to receive the congratulations of the Court and of the 
officers of State and other public functionaries, Audiences for the sume purpose 
were also granted to the members of the Diplomatic borly. 

When I had the honour of waiting upon His Majesty with the gentlemen 
of the Mission, His Majesty, in. referring to the events which have taken place 
in the Baltic during the summer, requested me to convey to the Queen his 
grateful acknowledgments for the respect which Her Majesty's Government had 
paid to his neutrality, and for the friendly manner in which they had acted 
towards the Government of His Majesty since the commencement of the war. 

__ In expressing my satisfaction at being charged with such a commission, | 
suid I felt assured that the Queen and Her Majesty's Government felt grateful 
to His Majesty for the good offices which his servants had always been ready to 
render to Her Majesty's ships when in the waters of Denmark, ; 

_ To which the King replied that it had been his wish that Her Majesty's 
ships should find a hospitable reception in Denmark, and he hoped that they 
had done so. : 

_ His Majesty then adverted to reports in circulation, and which were only. 
officially contradicted later in the day, of the eapture of Sebastopol by the allied 
army in the Crimen, ‘The King said that as he was neutral in the war, the 
sentiments which he would express to me on the subject must not be considered 
as those of the King of Denmark ; but at the same time he would not conceal 
from me his desire and hope that the reports which had reached Copenhagen

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 
(No. 611 


My Lord, Foreign Office, October 12, 1854. 

I HAVE to acquaint your Ixcelleney that Her Majesty’s Government 
have again had under consideration the reports of Colonel Beatson respecting 
the Bashi-Bozouks, and relying upon the knowledge and explanations of that 
distinguished officer, as well as upon the information that the Duke of Newcastle 
and I have reecived from Lieutenant Walpole, Her Majesty's Government 
consider that there is no reason to doubt that, at a comparatively small expense, 
a very efficient corps of Irregular Cavalry may be organized. 

Tt has not been the purpose of Her Majesty's Government to grant a 
subsidy to the Sultan, nor to take any portion of the Turkish army into the pay 
of England; but their intention was, that the corps of Bashi-Bozouks, to be 
raised by Colonel Beatson, should be attuched to the British army, and placed 
under the command of Lord Raglan. This intention, however, has not hitherto 
heen carried into effect, as Lord Raglan declined the services of men who had 
made themselves notorious by their lawless conduct and the outrages they had 
committed on the peaceful and loyal subjects of the Porte. 

Lord Raglan’s decision was also confirmed by the determination of Omer 
Pasha to get rid of the Bashi-Bozouks, and by the unsuceessful experiment 
made by General Yussuf, who disbanded the Bashi-Bazouks for their misconduct 
on his return from the Dobrudscha. But Lord Raglin, whose opinion has 
of course great weight with Her Majesty’s Government, only knew these men 
by their habits ina wild and undisciplined state. Omer Pasha had not the 
means of paying or feeding them, nor consequently of checking their out- 
riges, 

General Yussuf admitted he did not know how to command them, and 
his corps was handed over to him by Omer Pasha, and was not composed of 
volunteers. 

But the men whom Colonel Beatson desires ta enrol, would all be 
volunteers, and all are cager to enter the British service, and to be commanded 
by British officers; and Colonel Beatson reports, that if they are well treated 
and duly paid and cared for, the Bashi-Bozouks can, in his opinion, be formed 
into a most elicrent and servicenble body of Irregular Horse, and, as such, 
render most valuable assistance to the allied armies in the field. 

Under these circumstances Her Majesty's Government have determined to 
authorize Colonel Beatson to select 4,000 of the best men he can find among 
the Bashi-Bozouks; but such a corps cannot be attached to the British army 
which is absent in the Crimea, no, for the reasons | have above stated, can it 
properly be attached to the army of Omer Pasha; and still less can it act asa 
corps independent of either army. Fler Mijesty’s Government propose, there- 
fore, that Colonel Beatson should proceed with the organization of the corps, 
which, it is to be hoped, will be ina state to render efficient service next spring 
under the orders of Lord Raglan; and that, in the meanwhile, Colonel Beatson 
should consider himself under the command of Omer Pasha. 

Your Excellency will therefore request that orders to that effect may be 
sent to the Turkish Commander-in-chicf, who, doubtless, will lear with 
satisfaction that he is to be relieved from the task of superintending men for 
whiose existence he has no means of providing, 

An officer of the Commissariat Department will be sent to Bucharest, 
where it appears that the greatest faeilitics exist for paying and providing for the 
proposed corps; and to that officer, as wellas to Colonel Beatson, Her Majesty's 
Consul-General will be instructed to furnish all the assistance in lis power, 

lam, Xe, 
(Signed) CLANENDON,

ARTICLE 1X. 


Duke of Neweastle respecting the wants of the English military hospital at 
Selimnié, I feel that it is quite unnecessary for me, in transmitting to you this 
letter, to furnish your Excellency with any precise instructions on the subject, as 
four own feelings of humanity and the deep sympathy you entertain for the 

rave men who are now suffering from the casualties of war, will have induced 
you even to anticipate the wishes of Her Majesty’s Government that everything 
should be done to alleviate their condition. 

To relieve your Excellency, however, from any responsibility which, in the 
absence of instructions, you may have undertaken in their behalf, I have to 
authorize you, on communication and in concert with the medical authorities, 
to obtain for the sufferers whatever Constantinople or its neighbourhood can 
supply in the way of comforts or sustenance; and I have, moreover, to instruct 
your Excellency to report to me at the earliest moment what further assistance 
may be required from England to supply any local deficiencies, in order that no 
time may be lost in sending stores or other articles which may be wanted from 
this country. 

Your Excellency will keep a separate account of the expenditure which you 
may incurunder this instruction, which will eventually be repaid by the Army 
Department. 


Tam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received October 16.) 


(No. 115.) 
My Lori, Berlin, October 13, 1854. 


ON my waiting upon Baron Manteuffel this day, I commenced by 
expressing my regret that Thad not been fortunate enough to see him at my 
last visit, and with a view of giving him an opportunity (if he desired it) of 
conveying some compliment on our victory on the Alma, I remarked to his 
Excellency that great events had passed since I had last had the honour of seeing 
him. His Excellency raiiearned silence, carefully abstaining from any allusion 
whatever to the events which had passed in the Crimea. 

I then observed to his Excellency that 1 had again to call his notice to the 
passage of a large quantity of lead from Bromberg into Russia, which was 
evidently destined for the allies in the shape of bullets. IT remarked to his 
Excellency that it was perfectly fruitless to make any further representation to 
the Prussian Government on this subject, as they appeared to be wholly intent 
on furthering the cause of Russia against us, but that | begged to read to him a 
despatch (your Lordship’s No, (2 of the 10th instant) in order to prove to him 
that we were perfectly awure of the aid and assistance which Prussia was render- 
ing to Russia in thus permitting the transit through her territory of munitions of 
war, to be used against the allies. His Excellency appeared a good deal discon- 
certed by this: communication, but searcely vouchsafed to make any remark, 
merely observing that he was perfectly ignorant on the subject, and that we 
appeared to be more informed than he was, I merely referred his Excellency for 
further information to the Berlin ‘ Press,” in which the statements on the 
subject were most detailed and circumstantial, 

I then touched upon the late Austrian note, and inquired whether the 
Prussian Government had yet made any reply to that communication. His 
Excellency replied that the answer would be transmitted in a few days, and 
expressed himself as most anxious that un agreement should be arrived at, 
assuring me that kis strenuous endeavours would be directed to this end; but 
he remarked that Austria rendered it very difficult to them. 

L observed to his Excellency that the Prussian despateh to Count Arnim of 
the 21st ultimo, assuming the pretension to demand of Austria the exclusion of 
the allied troops trom the Prineipalities (as was natural to be supposed), had 
created the worst possible impression in London, His Excellency replied that 
no such demand was contained therein; but that, as Prussia was liable to he 
called upon by Austria for succour in case of attack, Prussia had merely wished 
to know the conditions on which she oceupied the Principalities, 

I did not enter into any discussion on this subject, but I took oceasion to 
inform his Excellency that Her Majesty's Government were quite tired of the 
Prussian attempts to favour Russia, and that an avowed hostility on the part of 
Prussia would be far preferable to one of masked neutrality. [ said, that as 

Prugsin had chosen to abdicate all pretence and right to deal with European 
questions, we should neither consult her during the war, nor at the conclusion of 
the peace ; and that she had entirely effaced herself as a Great Power, 

Baron Manteuticl coolly remarked that we might do as we pleased ; adding, 
‘Que nous forcerons personne de traiter avec nous.” 

While expressing my deep regret that Prussia had thus alienated herself from 
us at the moment of a great European crisis, | endeavoured in a mild and quiet 
manoer to open Baron Manteutfel’s eyes to the dangerous position to which the 


4

Prussian policy was advancing. | remarked that from havi 
with us, Prussia had passed to

Excellency made to my observations was, “that there were dangers on all 
sides.” 
Linquired of his Excellency what effect the success of the allied troops m 
the Crimea had produced on His Majesty. He replied that the King had from 
the first predicted that the allied armies would be victorious, and had been 
prepared for their successes. 
During my interview, Baron Manteutfel was ealm and composed, but T was 
unable to extract from his Excellency a single expression which could throw 
light on the present state of the political relations of Prussia, or which could give 
the smallest indication of the future, I beheve that he is almost without 
‘nfluence on the King, and that he has become the mere instrument of a party 
in whose hands the destinies of this country for the moment are unfortunately 


placed.

My Lord, Berlin, October 18, 1854. 

‘THE glorious victory gained on the Alma must inspire every loyal subject 
of Her Majesty with gratitude and thanksgiving to the Almighty Disposer of 
events, and | beg permission humbly ta express to your Lordship on my own 
art, as well as that of Her Majesty's Legation at this Court, our sincere anc 
heartfelt felicitation on the brilliant success which has attended Her Majesty's 


arms and those of Hor Majesty’s allies, 
It would have afforded me great gratitication had 1 been enabled to report 


to your Lordship that the triumph of the allied armies had elicited any 
sympathetic expression on the part of the Prussian Government, Neither the 
French Minister nor myself have received the smallest inark of satisfaction, or 
any expression of congratulation from any oficial personage, military or civil, of 
this Government. I believe, on the contrary, that the Court party, and all 
those more or less under their influence, deeply deplore the reverses which the 
amperor of Russia has gustained, and, in daily expectation of learning the fall of 
Sebastopol, are crestfallon and despondent, But on the other hand, | have 
much satistaction in stating that beyond the pale of this narrow circle the joy 
und satisfaction of every class ut Borlin at the defeat of the Russians has been 
unbounded, and Lam credibly informed that on the evening when the reported 
imielligence arrived here of the taking of Sebustopol by the allied armies, the 
delight and satisfaction of the public was evinced to a remarkable degree at all 
the places of public resort, which were crowded, and where repeated toasts were 
drunk to the health and success of the allies. 

Count Esterhazy, the Austrian Minister, M. Liebe, the Brunswick Minister, 
and Count Lannay, the Sardinian Minister, are those of the foreign Ministers 
who have expressed their felicitations ut our sucecss. The Hanoverian Minister, 
Count Knyphausen (who is certainly not Russian), and Baron Nothomb, the 
Belgian Minister, are now absent from Berlin, ‘The Wurtemberg Minister, 
Count Linden, the Hesse Cassel Envoy, M. de Wilkens, Count Hohenthal, the 
Saxon Minister, M, de Sehimmelpenninek, the Dutch Minister, and the other 
German Ministers, are all more less devoted to the Russian cause, and T can 


perceive that our successes ire harrowing to. their feelings, and are viewed with 
a jealous eye, if not with a deep regret. ‘The other foreign Ministers are 


decidedly in fayour of the Western Powers.

Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received October 16.) 
(No. 121. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Berlin, October 13, 1854. 

_ COUNT ESTERHAZY called upon me to-day, and told me that he back 
just had an interview with Baron Manteuftel. His Excellency informed him that 
the reply to the last Austrian communication was to be submitted this day to 
the King for His Majesty's approval, and that he hoped to send it ina day or 
two to Vienna. Fis Excellency said that it was “ satistaisante.” Count Ester- 
lazy remarked to me that Baron Manteuffel waa excessively reserved, and 
little communicative to him. . 

__ A report has heen in cireulution that the Prince of Prussia was to go to 
Vienna on a spe mission, but Baron Munteuffel contradicts this report both 
to Count Esterhazy and myself, 

_ Count Esterhazy expressed a belief that the Prussian Government would 
be inclined lo come to an agreement with Austria os yegards the occupation of 
the Principalities, and to give the required assurance of her support to Austvia 
if attacked by Russia in those provinces ; but in returm they expect that Austria 
will come to some arrangement with them at Frankfort, and on this latter point 
the chief anxiety of the Prossian Government appears to vest, With respect 
to the former, the engagement amounts to a very improbable contingency as 
the Prussian Government will take care thut Russia shall not be the first 
aggressor against Austria in the Principalities, On the latter point will exist 
the chief difieultics; both parties have taken up their separate line of policy 
and have appealed to the support of their German confederates. Tt has thus 
become # question of honour, which renders it difficult for either party to recede. 

Hes 


Let 2. 


258 


‘The position of the two States inay be defined as follows: Prussia regarded 
the Convention of the 20th April as a means afforded her of continually checking 
the Austrian policy, and of restraining her from taking any agressive. part 
against Russia. Austria, on the other hand, sought by this Treaty to attach 
Prussia to her, und in case of need to oblige her to afford material aid. 

Roth States have -been constantly endeavouring to influence the Dict in 
their own sense. Both have been more or leas deceived by each other in the 
object they had in view, and the differences which lave since arisen on this 
account between them have now been extended to the Diet, | have seme 
reason to suppose that Austria will be catistied if the Diet will formally approve 
her occupation of the Principalities, as being in the defenee of German mterests, 
and if the Diet will accept and formally adhere to the two: first conditions to 
which Austria is bound by her exchange of notes with the Western Powers. 

It remains to be seen whether Prussia will accede to any such terms or 


arrangements, or whether che will maintain her ground and thus force matters 


to an open rupture between the two States, 

Your Lordship will probably receive a copy of the Prussian reply to the 
last Austrian communication from Her Majesty’s Minister at Vienna, but I 
shall use my best endeavours to procure one and shall transmit it to your 
Lordship by the earliest opportunity. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS.

No, 277. 


Mr. Bligh to the Earl of Clurendon.—(Received October 16.) 
(No. 95.) 


My Lord, Hanover, October 14, i854. 

I TOOK the earliest opportunity that presented itself, after I had received 
your Lordship's permission so to do, of communicating to M. de Lenthe the 
despatch to Her Majesty's Chargé d'Affaires at Berlin, of which [ received a 
copy in your Lordships despatch No, 31 of the 23rd ultimo, telling his Exeel- 
leney, at the same time, that this permission had been granted to me as a proof 
of confidence in the Hanoverian Government. 

The communication itself, and the reasons given for making it, produced 
the effect which Thad expected; and his Excellency charged me particularly to 
convey to your Lordship his warm acknowledgments, and assurances’ of his 
desire to merit and to reciprocate the confidence thus placed in him, 

A long conversation ensued between us, in which were discussed the various 
points connected with the Eastern question; the course which England was 
decided upon pursuing respecting it; and that which it would be the interest of 
Germany to enter upon in concert with her: but, as in my former reports | 
have detailed what may have passed between usin other conversations respect- 
ing these matters, I shall not trouble your Lordship by useless repetitions, more 
especially as (if faith can be placed in the most explicit assurances) we may rest 
sutishied that Hanover will not be found wanting whenever her voice shall 
definitively be required to join in the concert against the disturber of the world’s 
peace, In the first place, M. de Lenthe informed me in confidence, that this 
Government had, after some hesitation, decided upon answering the invitation 
of the Cabinet of Vienna to pronounce as to the course which Hanover would 
take in the Diet upon the Kastern question; that they would vote for aiding 
Austria, in case of her territory being attacked by Russia on account of her 
occupation of the Prineipalities, and would support the Austrian interpretation 
of the two first of the four points which had been declared by the ‘Treaty af 
April 20 to be the sine gud non basis of an accommodation with Russia; namely, 
those relating to the Danube and to the Principalities, which, his Excellency said, 
was all that the Cabinet of Vienna would require from the Diet. Certain 
explanations, however, would be asked for by the Hanoverian Minister, as to the 
nature of the oceupation of the Principalities. In short, caid his Excellency, 
you mayassure Lord Clarendon that Hanover will go along with Austria, and 
that no reports to the contrary are to be credited. ‘That observation was 
doubtless elicited by my having just before communicated to his Excellency, for 
the purpose of provoking some such declaration, what L had heard from Her 
Majesty's Chargé d’Alfuires at Berlin, that Hanover was counted upon there as 
a sure card in the Prussian sense. 

J did wot fail, in the course of this conversation, to impress. upon hia 


a ¥ 


ee 
] 


262 


Excellency, as authorized by your Lordship, that even those who might be well- 
wishers of Russia would be serving her badly by encouraging her in resistance to 
the Western Powers, whose demands would rise in proportion to the duration of 
the contest, ‘his I did, not because doubtfal of the assurances of M. de Lenthe, 
which TL have just reported, but from my knowing his Excellency to belong to a 
party or class which has hitherto looked to Nussia for support; which fears the 
increase of French power and influence from the humiliation of Russia; and 
which is at last beginning to recognize the prestige of the unassailable supe- 
riority of Russia, to have been the beeen of a well-contrived system of 
deceit which strenuous action could destroy, and I took this, as I shall every 
opportunity, to assist M. de Lenthe and his party in recovering from their 
delusion. 

As regards M, de Lenthe, also, | would observe that, although for the 
reasons given above, he may have been, until lately at least, Russian in his 
predilections, he has a still stronger aud more enduring bias—one almost 
universally prevailing amongst Hanoveriaus, and indisposing them to follow any 
line of policy which might fend to increase in Germany the authority and 
influence of Prussia, against which Power there exists n widely spread and deeply 
rooted jealousy and dread, On the other hand M. de Lenthe, and all who 
pretend Lo be statesmen, know that they have nothing to fear nul everything to 
hope for from England and Austria, and will consequently endeavour at every 
important crisis, such as the present, to be in strict alliance with those Powers. 
He also is strongly in favour of united action cn the part of Germany. He 
apprehends that the machinations of Prussia, even if they should be abetted by 
the minor States of Germany, will no longer prevent an independent course 
being taken, if necessary, by Austria, Vor all which reasons 1 cannot doubt 
the sincerity of the assurances which, as above related, he charged me to give to 
your Lordship. 

M. de Lenthe told me that he should communicate to the Prussian Chargé 
d’Afaires, the decision which this Government has come to upon this point. 
The answer of Brunswick has been an unreserved sequiescence in all that 
Austria has required. ‘That from Oldenburg has been delayed, upon the plea of 
the Grand Duke's absence in Holstein; but from its close union with Prussia it 
ig not ta be expected that, in that quarter, the wishes of the Cabinet of Vicnna 
will be responded to. 

I have, &e, 
(Signed) J.D. BLIGH.

The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 


(No. 826. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, October 16, 1854, 

COUNT COLLOREDO communicated to me in strict confidence, on the 
I4th instant, the contents of a despatch from Count Buol to M. de THiibner, 
dated the 10th instant, in which Count Buol, referring to the instructions piven 
to Baron de Hess not to interfere with the free movement of the Turkish forces 
in Moldavia and Wallachia, and to maintain the best understanding with Omer 
Pasha and the Commanders of the allied armies, observes that Omer Pasha is 
consequent free to undertake any operation in the direction of Beasarabia, and 
that the intelligence of an opposite tendency which has reached the French 
Government is only the result of a misunderstanding which will speedily be 
cleared up. ; 

But the Austrian Government is of opinion that a good understanding 
between the respective Commanders would best be secured by a Convention 
between the several Powers, and by the establishment of a common centre of 
diseussion in the immediate vicinity of the theatre of war, by which among other 
things the continual bickerings between the Austrian ant Turkish authorities 
would be obviated, which are so little in accordance with the harmony which 
prevails between the Internuncio and the Porte. 

The Internuncio reported on the 28th of September, that Omer and Dervish 


263 


Pashas had received orders from the Porte, on the 15th, to come to an under- 
standing with Count Coronini as to the passage in General Hees’ proclamation 
requiring all communications to be addressed to the Austrian Commanders ; that 
the Pashas had thereupon proposed to make a collective proclamation explanatory 
of the passage ; that the Austrian Commander had objected to this, but offered, 
instead, to write to the Administrative Council to say that the Emperor of 
Austria could never depart from his purpose to re-establish, in concert with the 
Porte, the legitimate order of things im the Principalities; that Dervish Pasha 
having been appointed Turkish Commissioner, the authorities would naturally 
have to apply to him likewise, until the full restoration of a regular administra- 
tion of the country, in conformity with its established privileges, in order to 
settle all important points by common agreement between the Austrian and 
Ottoman authoritics. | 

Count Buol was of opinion that Count Coronini’s suggestion was the best. 

As regards Prince Stirbey’s recall, the Internuncio wrote that Omer Pasha 
had been informed that as the result of a conference between the Internuncto, 
Reshid Pasha, and the Representatives. of England and France, the former had 
undertaken to request Count Coronini to diseuss with the Porte’s Commissioner 
whether Prince Stirbey’s reeall should be rade subject toa previous under- 
standing between the Imperial Cabinet and the ‘Turkish Ambassador at Vienna, 
upon which Dervish Pasha, whose invitation to Prince Stirbey had wlready been 
sent off, announced to Count Coronini that he would write to Vienna to delay 
his departure. 

The fact, however, Count Buol says, is that Arif Effendi, who bad already 
forwarded the invitation to Prince Stirbey, had never mentioned te him (Count 
Buol) that he had received further instructions on the matter. 

The Internuncio further states that Omer Pasha had been strongly urgelto 
maintain the best understanding with the Austrian Commanders 

Count Buol says upon this, that while the Austrian Cabinet lias reason to 
be satisfied with the instructions given by the Porte to its Representatives in the 
Prineipalities, the manner in which these instructions are carried) out is mot 
equally satisfactory. . 

Meanwhile Prince Stirbey arrived at Bucharest on the Sth of October, and 
was received in a proper manner by the populace and Wallachian authorities, 
while the Turks kept aloof from hin. 

1 told Count Colloredo that as an improper proclamation had at first been 
issued by General Coronini, the best course would have been to issue another 
that should leave no doubt as to the ‘atentions of the Austrian Government in 
the Prineipalities ; but that the point of real practical importance was the inter- 
ference with the military movements of Omer Pashia, and 1 feared there eould be 
né doubt that the Austrian authorities had thereby rendered an essential service 
to Russia. 

I am, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received October 17, 
10:25 A.M.) 


(Telegraphic.) Vienna, October 16, 1854. 

A ‘TURKISH courier who left Constantinople on the 9th, has brought the 
order to Arif Effendi to require a distinct declaration on the part of the 
Austrian Government relative to the liberty of the movements of the Ottoman 
army in the Principalities. M, de Bourqueney and myself have supported by 
all means in our power the step taken by the Ambassador. Count Buol’s reply 
is perfectly satisfactory, and we have dispatched by telegraph to our Agents at 
Bucharest, directions to inform Omer Pasha that he 1s at liberty to carry on 
offensive operations against the Russian territory, that he may exeeute them by 
Galatz and Ibraila with the number of troops he may consider necessary. If he 
wishes to croas-the frontier at any other point, he will come to an understanding 
upon the subject with the Austrian General, who will, on his part, take the 
measures rendered necessary by this movement. Instructions for M. de Bruck 
will be forwarded to him by Count Buol this day, with the view of directing the 
Liternuncio in the policy of his Government.

My Lord, Paris, Oclober 17, 1854. 

1 SAW Marshal Vaillant this morning just after his Excellency had received 
his detailed reports from General Canrobert of the rd instant, 

It would appear from what the Marshal recounted to me that the allies had 
found Sebastapak more formidably defended on the south and cast than they 
had hoped would have been the case, The artillery of the Russian fleet had 
been pluced in position, and the crews landed to serve it; 23,000 Russians were 
supposed to be in the place, and about 40,000, under Prince Menchikolf, on the 
road to Simpheropol, about ten miles from the allies. 

The allies had divided their forces; two divisions of each army were 
appointed to attuck Bebastopol, and two other divisions of each force were 
ordered to protect the besieging arty. The remainder of the allied troops, with 
the Turkish division, were placed between the besieging and the covering armies 
so ng to uct as a reserve to either, 

General Canrobert computed the heavy guns of the allies to amount to 160, 
The French army was beginning to want provisions, and unfortunately 


266 


nothing had been heard of the ships which had been sent back to Varna from 
Kalamita Bay on the 17th ultimo, to fetch the remainder of the French army 
and a further supply of provisions.

It is very desirable that the Pasha of Erzeroom should be encouraged in

From want of proper care in these respects last year thousands perished in’ the

The pay of the soldiers is greatly in arrear; only 10,000 purses have been

ensable. 

No winter clothing has been yet sent, though the application for it was 
sent to Constantinople some time ago. ‘This want must be supplied without 
delay, or the consequences may be fatal. Everything aimmounces an ealy and 
severe winter. 

Wheat and barley are wanted from Sivas, Kharpoot, Diarbekir, &e. ; 35,000 
Kars samars of wheat, and 60,000 of barley. ‘This want is also urgent.

should be sent with all speed. The importance of this cannot be exaggerated. 

Mustapha Liva Pasha and Enim Bey are highl commended. If the 
former were made Ferik, and the latter promoted, the service would gain, 
and others would be encouraged. I hope these recommendations will be 
attended to.

nople, leaving the mode of execution to military judgment,

270 


with respect to Austria, and she would be at full liberty to concentrate her forces 
and her enerwies against England, France, and Turkey. Ausiria, I added, was 
of course only guided by her own interests, and was the best judge of what 
would most conduce to them, but | must be permitted to observe that a longer 
perseverance in her present course could have no other effect than to retard the 
peace of which she, in common with England and France. ardently desired the 
restoration. She had declared that certain conditions were indispensable for 
peace, she had pledged herself not to negotiate upon any others, and yet if she 
remained passive, if she was not to take steps for bringing about the arrange- 
ments she meant to insist upon, it was clear that the whole brunt and burden of 
the war would fall upon the allies, and that it must then not only be protracted, 
but might, or 1 should rather say certainly would, acquire a development beyond 
what Austria contemplated ot desired, as the result of events that she would be 
unable to control, ‘Ten months ago the Emperor of Russia might have renewed 
the old Treaties with Turkey ; three months azo he might have negotiated on the 
bases of the notes; six months hence conditions of a far wider scope, and 
embracing territorial changes, may become indispensable. England and France, 
I said, a8 was well known to Austria, had embarked in this war unwillingly and 
disinterestedly, but they were determined to carry it on with the utmost energy, 
wntil they brought it to a close by a just and honourable pence. If they were ta 
depend upon their own resources alone, the duration of the war would be pro- 
tracted ; but it would then rest with them alone to fix the conditions of peace. 

The position of Austria with respect to Russia was no longer one of 
neutrality, and she had not hesitated to make that manifest in her reeent com- 
munications with Prussia and the German Courts, and that position would be 
weakened rather than improved by a Treaty with England and Franee, which 
would not in reality draw the three Powers closer together, nor pledge them to 
united action, A Treaty of offensive and defensive alliance should be more 
positive, more binding, and better adapted to the great crisis upon which Europe 
was about to enter, than that which appeared to be contemplated by the Cabinet 
of Vienna. 

Austria might have her own sufficient reasons for not at once declaring war 
against Russia, but she cannot disguise from herself that it is inevitable, and 
that the time is not far distant when her own dignity and interests will prescribe 
a more decided course of action. 

Your Lordship will read this despatch to Count Buol. You will renew to hts 
Excellency the assurances of the sincerity with which Her Majesty's Government 
desire the cooperation of Austria, and you will state how thoroughly they feel 
the expediency and the advantage of fixing the period when that cooperation 
shall heeome active, and of contracting by a Treaty reciprocal obligations an 
terms of complete equality.

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clurendon.—( Received October 2 1.) 


(No, 387.) 
My Lord, Vienna, September 1G, 1854. 

| CAN conceive nothing so truly astonishing as the communication | have 
this day received from Lord Stratford, by which T learn that Baron Bruck hail 
decidedly objected to the instructions proposed to be sent to Omer Pasha by 
his Government, to advance into Bessarabia; to which Count Coronini had 
already declared his opposition. Baron Bourqueney had received a similar 
report from M, Benedetti. 1 therefore proposed that M. de Bourqueney and 
myself should proceed together to Count Buol, in order to express to him the 
surprise and resentment which we felt at this conduct, and at the manner in 
whieh we were requited for the confidence which we had reposed in the assur- 
ances we had received from him, and which we were under the necessity of 
declaring were in the most direct ‘contradiction to the language which Baron 
Bruck was reported by Lord Stratford and M, Benedetti to have held at the 
Conference which had taken place between them and Reshid Pasha, 

With the view of bringing the matter clearly before Count Buol, we rend 
to him extracts from the despatches which we had received from the British and 
French Representatives at Constantinople, as well as from the instructions which 
had been addressed to Arif Effendi, the. Ambassador at this Court, and from the 
other documents inclosed in the above-cited despatehes. From these documents 
we brought before Count Buol the following important statements of all the 
proceedings we came to him to complain of, some of which had been already 
the subject of discussion with him, and had received explanations which we had 
considered as satisfactory: first, that the Austrian Commander-in-chief had 
opposed the movements of Omer Pasha in the Principalities; secondly, that it 
appeared that Austria intended to hold the line of the Sereth and the Prath 
with their army, to serve as a barrier between the Russian and Turkish forces, 
and that she would oppose any movements of the allied troops through the 
Principalities ; thirdly, that Baron Bruck had stated that an advance into

Bessarabia by Omer Pasha would be objected to, if not resisted, by General
