army from the Prineipalitics. . 

We stated that the impressions produced by these fucts had been sanctioned 
by the language of General Buron Hess; we added that the statements we had 
thus made were supported by such evidence and authority that we were com- 
pelled, notwithstanding their total disagreement with the assurances and decta- 
rations which Count Buol had on 50 many occasions repeated to us, to bring 
them before him, and to call upon him to farnish us with such explanations as 
night remove the doubts and mistrust which acts and proceedings so contrary to 
the reports we had made to our Governments were calculated to inspire. Count 
Buol replied that he received these communications with the greatest surprise ; 
that he was not cognizant of the greater part of them; and he remarked that 
many of them referred to what had taken Sa before he had forwarded, on the 
2]st of September, the rstructions which he had reported to us; he had since 
that time been informed by Baron Hess that he had stuted to Omer Pasha that 
he was perfectly free to occupy Galata and Ibraila, and that he was ready to 
remove the Austrian garrison to make way for the passage of his troops, but 
that he had since learnt that Omer Pasha had renounced his intention of entering 
Bessarabia, and that he was to occupy Ibrailas but that if any doubts could 
exist upon these subjects, he stated to us most distinctly, authorizing us to 
convey his declaration to our Governments, to. our respective authorities in the 
Principalities, and to our Representatives at Constantinople, that the Austrian 
Government did not pretend exclusively to hold the line of the Sereth and the 
Pruth, or to employ their arniy to serve as oh barrier between the Russian and 
Turkish forces, or to oppose any movement of the allied armies through the 
Principalities ; that they entirely admitted the complete freedom of the move- 
ments of the Turkish troops im. the Principalities, who would only be expected 
to coinbine those movements with the Austian Commanders where Austrian 
garrisons were ulready existing ; that they recornized that the Convention with 
the Porte did not give them any exclusive maht of occupation in the Princt- 
palities, and that English and French troops, by the Convention of their Govern- 
ments with the Porte, had a right to march into the Principalities. 

Count Buol also stated that since there had appeared sufficient ground 
upon which these representations had been made to him, he-would immediately 
repeat the orders he had already transmitted to the officers in the Prineipalities, 
and he would call upon them in the strictest manner to conform to them, and to 
carry them into execution, while he would also demand the fullest explanations 
of the transactions which had taken place in the Principalities, and which had 
viven rise to the remonstrances which had now been made with regard to them, 

‘A(ter we had received these communications from Count Buol, 1 thought 
‘+ wag essential to bring strongly belore him the language which Lord Stratford 
reports Baron Brack to have held at the conference with Reshid Pasha and 
M, Benedetti, by whieh, alter objecting ta the advanee of the ‘Turkish troops 
into Bessarabia, he had refused to canction the transmission to Omer Pasha of 
the instructions which his Goyernment had drawn up for him, and had only 
udimitted the propesal of Lord Strattord that the question might be referred to 
Vienna, by which the asperities whieh had existed at a previous interview had 
heen mitivated, but that he hud vehemently complained of the canduct of Omer 
Pasha and of Dervish Pasha, and had pressed fora disapprobation of their pro- 
ceedings, which Reshid Pasha had ssa and Inad ony, expressed to shag 
persovs his regret at any disagreements which had taken place at Bucharest, and 
he desire of the ‘Turkish Government that their authorities should act in a 
frank and cordial spirit with those of Austria, 

Count Buol, in order to explain the conduct of Baron Bruck, read to M, de 
Bourqueney und myself a portion of the despatches he had just received from 
him, and which referred to the transactions ‘alluded to in Lord Stratford's reports , 
and in commenting upon some of those despatches, he did not hesitate to 
condemn the arguments Baron Bruck had used, and the declarations he had made, 
as contrary to the views of the Lmperial Government, and to the instructions 
which had recently been transmitted to him. Count Buol expressed the greatest 
regret at this circumstance, which he hoped would already have been remedied 
by the lust communications which had been sent to the Internuncio, and whieh

he believed would certainly be so by those which would be transmitted to him

With respect, however, to the operations which had been proposed by 
Omer Pasha, Count Buol declared he had never clearly understood why that 
officer had not originally pursued the plan of attacking the Russian army in 
Bessarabia at the time he had followed it from the neighbourhood of Giurgevo 
as far as Busco, where he arrived as carly asthe 10th or Lath of August. 
Count Buol stated that Omer Pasha was at that time in the command of 2 
force of not less than 80,000 men; that he was alone in front of the 
Russian army, who shortly afterwards abandoned Galatz long before any 
Austrian troops entered Moldaving that there could at that time have been no 
impediment to this movement of the Turkish army to the Pruth, near Rent; 
and that it was after that time only when the Austrian troops were about to 
enter Galatz and establish a garrison there, that any question had arisen upon 
the subject. Whatever were the reasons which during that time had prevented 
Omer Pasha from carrying into effect the operation he now proposed, Count 
Buol hoped that the renewed instructions he should transmit to General 
Coronini would so entirely remove any of the” obstacles he had compluined of 
from the Austrian authorities, that he would at once effect the movements 
which were in contemplation. 

With respect to the question which 1s asked by the Turkish Government, 
whether the Austrians will be content with remaining im_the Principalities, and 
if so, whether they would oppose any attempt of the Hussians to cross the 
Pruth, Count Buol repeated the declaration he had so often made before, that 
his Government unhesitatingly adhered to the engagements they had entered 
into to defend those Provinces from any invasion by the Russian army; that 
they had no right, and would never attempt, to prevent the entering into those 
Provinees of the ‘Turkish forces, or of those of their allies; that af the move- 
ments of these troops should bring them inte contact with the Austrian canton- 
ments, the Austrian Government would require that such movements should 
he concerted with their officers, but that they considered their right of inter: 
ference with the operations of their allics was confined to these contingencies. 

Baron Bourqueney and myself stated to Count Buol, after we had received 
these explanations from him, that we were desirous of giving every support in 
our power to the representations which the Turkish Ambassador was instrueted 
to make to bim upon the same subjects which we had now brought 
before him, and that we hoped he would give to the Ambassador such assur 
ances ag would serve to tranquillize his Government upon the points which he 
waa now directed to submit to him, and we reeeived from Count Buol the 
assurance that it was hia greatest abject to act towards the Turkish Govern- 
ment in the strictest amity, and upon the terms of the most entire confidence ; 
and we have since learnt from Arif Effendi that he was) perfectly satisfied with 
the assurances he had received from Count Buol, and that (upon the military 
questions) he had transmited to Omer Pasha the telegraphic message, 2 copy 
of which L transmitted to your Lordship in my despatch No. 386 of to-day, 
and of the purport of which I informed your Lordship in my telegraphic 
messaze of thisafternoon, 1 now also inclose a copy of the joint communica- 
tion which Baron Bourqueney and myself addressed, by telegraph, to the 
English and French Consuls at Bucharest. i 

[ sincerely hope that by these repeated orders from the Imperial Govern. 
ment to therr military authorities in’ the Principalities, the inconceivable and 
reprehensible obstacles which have beon opposed to the movements of the 
lurkish army in those provinces may now be put an end to. 

L have, &e. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND.

Inclosure | in No, 294, 


General Lord Raglan to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 


My dear Lord Stratford, Balaklava, Octoher 5, 1554, 


YOUR letter of the 30th ultimo has just been sent to me by Admiral 
Hamelin. 

In it you say that the greater part of the Turkish troops at Batoom are 
ready to join me sO s00n as Leend for them, with means of conveyance; and, 
morcever, that you have been assured by Reshid Pasha that a reinforcement. of 
8,000 or 10,000 men is in preparation at Constantinople, if wanted. 


Qa 


It is of the greatest importance that every effort should be made to 
augment this army as speedily as possible, and with this view steamers will be 
immediately sent to the Bosphorus, capable of conveying 3,000 Infantry (we do 
not want Artillery), in the hope that that proportion of the 8,000 or 10,000 men 
stated to be in course of preparation, will be embarked without the loss of a 
moment aud sent up here, 

If, however, that number should not be ready, and could not be got ready 
in a shorter time than the steamers would take to go round by Batoom, the 
vessels should at once be sent there with a peremptory order for the embarkation 
of as many men as could be taken on board, although I cannot but hope that, 
through the exertion of your influence with the ‘lurkish Ministers, one or more, 
ifnot the whole, of these vessels may have orders to receive on board an efficient 
body of troops from Constantinople without having to go to Batoom for them ; 
and I would recommend, that whatever troops are sent through your suggestion 
should be held distinet from the Turkish division already here, and placed 
exclusively under my orders. 

A copy and translation of the instructions given to the senior officer should 
be sent to me, in order that it may clearly be understood by all parties how they 
stand with regard to me. . 

The troops should bring their own armomunition, and arrange for thetr 
provisions according to their habits and convenience. Our rations are’quite at 
their service, but they may not suit them, 

Sir Edmund Lyons will direct Commander Hoseason to wait upon you with 
this letter, and he will direct Admiral Boxer to place himself in immediate 
communication with you on the subject of it. 

[ hope that the Turkish authorities, and Admiral Boxer, will feel that time 
is everything. | am certain that you will do all you ean to make them sensible 
of this important fact. 

We are still busily occupied in getting up our guns and warlike stores, and 
the navy are working with hand and head to the sume end, having landed many 
runs, and meaning to take an active and, you may rely upon it, glorious part 
in all important operations of the siege. 

Believe me, &c. 


(Signed) RAGLAN,

Inclosure 8 in No, 294. 
Tnetructions addressed to Rustem Pasha. 


(Translation. } 


THE six battalions of troops added to the British army at Sebastopol by 
His Imperial Majesty’s orders, having been embarked on steamers, accompanied 
by the aforesaid Pasha, it will depend upon cireumstanees of time and place 
whether these troops are to be employed im conjunction with, or separately 
from, the auxiliary forces; but they are to act in all military movements, and 
under all cireumstances, according to the opinion of the Commander-in-cluet 
of the auxiliary forces; and the Pasha will direct antl employ the Imperial 
troops in such manner as Lord Raglan, the British Con:mander-in-chiel, may 
deem fitting. 

The troops are to march on whatever point he may direct, and the Pasha 
will be constantly vigilant in defending and protecting them against the enemy, 
and in providing for their comfort, so that they may suffer from no difficulty 
or want, 

The ammunition and matériel of the troops is to be kept in a safe place, 
and to be guarded ayainst every danger of destruction. The Pasha will be 
careful not to neglect his duty in these respects. 

‘The Pasha will continue to report to Constantinople, in the best way he 
ean, on the manner in which the troops are employed and administered, Se , 
and on any occurrences of interest. He will equally report on the same subjects 
to Lord Raglan. 

Although instructions like these may he compared to a key, the officer to 
whom they are addressed is held bound to do his duty to the best of his 
ability, according to time and cireumstances. The Pasha will be therefore held 
responsible, like any other functionary, in the event of his tranagressing these 
‘astructions, or any which he may reeeive from General Lord Ruglau. 

The Pasha will be, as above stated, under the direction aml superintendence 
of Lord Raglan, and will act according to his directions. But if his Lordship 
should deem it advisable thut the troops under the Pasha’s command should be 
stationed and employed at any place a5 a detached force, the Pasha will then 
have to receive instructions from Lord Raglan on the course to be pursued by 


eee SOMA od 


him; and he will report to this place, as well as to his Lordship, on his military 
proceedings as on other matters. 

The necessary ammunition, provisions, and winter clothing, has been 
provided for the troops during the appointed time of their service, and a 
sum of 2,000 purses has been also given, im case it should be required, 
A Mouhassebidgi has been likewise appointed to superintend the expenditure 
and chancelry of the force. It will be the duty of the Pasha to see that the 
aforesaid ammunition, provisions, and clothing are properly served out and 
used: and if it should be necessary to purchase provisions or other necessaries 
for the troops at the place where they may be stationed, a council to be held 
with the other olficers of the force, the Mouhassebidgi being present, and care 
‘is to be taken with reference to the necessary outlay, as well as to the purchase 
to be made, according to the preseribed Chancelry forms. 

On the arrival of the troops, the Pasha will put himself into immediate 
communication with General Lord Raglan, announcing his arrival, will ask for 
instructions concerning his movements, and act conformably therewith. It will 
be, in short, the duty of the Pasha to act in no manner against the directions 
and advice of Lord Raglan. 

The greatest attention must be paid to the comfort of the troops. 

With the help of God, suecess will thus attend the Imperial troops com- 
manded by the Pasha, under the direction and superintendence of Lord Raglan. 
At whatever place the troops may arrive, any of the inhabitants coming under 
the shadow of the Imperial shadow, are to be considered as worthy of the same 
degree of full protection enjoyed by the people and inhabitants of the Ottoman 
Empire. The Pasha will Attend carefully to the means of secunng them full 
protection for their lives and property.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received October 21.) 


(No. 477.) 
My Lord, Therapia, October 10, 1854. 

THE unquiet state of the population at and near Scutari, in Albania; the 
accasional incursions of the Montenegrins; and the active measures employed 
by the Austrian Government, with the apparent view of extending its protection 
and religious influence over the Catholics, as well in that quarter as in the 
neighbouring Province of Bosnia, concur to attract a more than usual degree of 
attention. 

| have lately received, in confidence, from Reshid Pasha the draft of a note 
to the Internuncio, requesting that the territory of Montenegro may be occupied 
by Austrian troops. 1 have given it as my opinion, that if the Porte has need 
of foreign aid on that side, she ought to be careful, when applying for it, to 
specify the object, to regulate the mode, and to limit the terms of the occupation. 
lam not aware that the application has yet been made. 

On the other hand, M. Bonatti states that the Montencgrins, headed by 
Prince Daniel, have failed in their attack on the Sultan's territory ; and that the 
late Pasha of Scutari has departed, on the arrival of his successor, without 
occasioning any tumult or disorder in the town. 

An extract of his last despatch to me is inclosed herewith. 

‘As to the movements: of Austria, for the extension of her influence by 
means of religious education, 1 submit to your Lordship’s notice herewith a 
statement extracted from the correspondence of Tevtig Effundi, the Sultan’s 
Commissioner at Scutari, and communicated to me from the Porte, 

I have, &c. 

(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Inclosure 1 in No, 297, 


Abstract of Consul Bonatti’s despatch No. 37 to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe, 
dated Scutari, September 30, 1254, 


ACCORDING to despatches arrived from Podgoritza and Spux, and 
communicated to M. Benatti officially by Osman Pasha, it appears that on the 
19th September, Prince Daniel attacked the town of Spux with 2,000 Monte- 
negring, but was met by an animated resistance on the part of the inhabitants, 
and a body of ‘Tosk Albanians who formed the garrison. The combat lasted 

4 


282 


four hours, and terminated in the repulse of the assailants. A simultaneous 
attack was made by the Montenegrins of Piperi upon the town of Podgoritza; a 
vigorous resistance was offered by Dilaver Bey, with a battalion of Regulars and 
two guns, and these Montenegrins were equally forced to retreat, In the 
combat at Spux seventeen Turks were wounded ; in the Podgoritza action, three 
killed and four wounded. ‘The number of casualties on the Montenegrin side is 
supposed to be greater. 

On the 22nd, Raghib Pasha arrived; and on the 2rd his predecessor, 
Osman Pasha, left Scutari. They were respectively escorted ont of and weleomed 
into the eity by deputations of the pane people, &c. Some merchants, 
however, refused to attend Osman Pashia’s deputation, and even wished to 
impede his departure till he had paid certain accounts with the custom-house ; 
they made representations on the subject to the new Governor, who referred 
them to the Divan, transmitting their memorial to Osman Pasha. The latter at 
once declared himself ready to satisfy their claims, upon their being laid and 
substantiated before the Divan, 

A fresh body of Seutarines is about to start to relieve those who have been 
in Spux.

Lieutenant-Colonel Simmons to General Lord Raglan, 


My Lord, . Bucharest, September 28, 1854. 

I HAVE the honour to inform your Lordship that on the day following 
that on which L informed your Lordship that Omer Pasha had ordered a move- 
ment upon Tbraila of a corps of 40,000 men, this movement was counterordered, 
in consequence of a communication which his Highness received trom Baran 
Hess, based upon written instructions which he had received from Vienna. 

These instructions were to the effect that the Austrian Government desired 
that the occupation of Tbraila and Galatz should be effected jointly by the 
Austrian and Ottoman forces. As a joint oceupation by tue Austrian troops 
with a considerable corps of the Turkish army cannot be effected, on account of 
the difficulty of finding accommodation for the troops, his Highness decided only 
to send a brigade of the Ottoman army to Ibraila, with the regiment of Cossacks 
under Aadik Pasha to Galatz. 

Your Lordship will not be surprised to hear that the instructions sent by 
the Austrian Government to Baron Hess, being ofa Estoy ciepren’ nature from 
the communication relative thereto made to Colonel Dieu by the French Ainbas- 
sador at Vienna, have somewhat confirmed the Pashain the doults he entertained 
as to the sincerity of the Austrian Government, 

These doubts have, I regret to add, been strengthened by the manner of 
the Austrian Commander-in-chief, the Baron Hess, who, in a conversatim with 
Dervish Pasha relative to the explanations to be given on the subject of the 
Austrian proclamation, and which had been under discussion at Constantinople, 
observed to the Pasha, upon his objecting to the explanations which he proposed 
to give, “* Nous sommes forts, vous étes finbles; et c'est inutile de lutter contre 
nous.”” 

Dervish Pasha expressed his surprise at hearing such language from his 
iixcellency, and observed that it wale tend to lessen in the opinion of Europe 
the merit which might attach to any ussistanee which Austria might send to 
the Sultan, 

As tending still farther to show the tone assumed by the Austrians, 1 would 
inform your Lordship that Omer Pasha gave a dinner last evening to Baron 
Hess, at which about sixty persons were present, 

His Highness, after several other toasts, propared the allies of the Sultan, 
which was responded ta in a few words by Mr, Colquhoun, who invoked the 
favour of Divine Providence on the great enterprise which has been undertaken 
by the allied armies under the command of your Lordshipand Marshal St Arnaud, 
and expressed a hope that it might meet with that suceess which all sincere 
friends could desire. 

After retiring from the dining-room, the expedition to the Crimea being the 
subject of conversation between Omer Pasha and Baron Hees, the latter 
observed; “We do not desire the success of the allies, nor that they should 
receive a severe check, What we desire is, that the expedition should have nu 
decisive result, for if successful, the allies will gain too high an ascendancy.” 

T repeat this observation, as twice stated to me this morning by Omer 
Pasha,as 1 think it most desirable your Lordship should be intimately aequainted 
with those events which occur here, and may enable your Lordship to judge of 
the real position of affairs on this seene of operations, 

If necessary I could multiply facts which show that similar sentiments 
pervade the Austrian army, who have eome here more with the attitude of 

conquerors than that of friends. ‘lhe treatment of the inhabitants of ull classes, 
both princes and Boyars, as well a3 the labouring classes in this town, as regards 
billets, is most imperious, Austrian soldiers enter houses, turn out the 
servants, and occupy their rooms and beds, ‘They remove gentlemen's horses 
from their stables without speaking to their proprietors, and substitute their 
own in their places; and, in fact, if the undovbted stories I daily hear were 
repeated, your Lordship would seareely credit the treatment received by the 
people at their hands. 


I have heard from several respectable persons not at all well inclined ta

My Lord, Dresden, October 18, 1854. 


| HAD the honour of receiving, on the 26th of the preceding month, your 
Lordship’s despatch No, 38 of the 23rd of the same, transmitting to me, for my 
information, a copy of one addressed to Her Majesty's Chargé d'Affaires at 
Berlin, recording a conversation between your Lordship and Count Bernstorif 
on the policy now pursued by Prussia in Eastern affairs. 

M. de Beust is now exerting himself to draw nearer to the Cabinet of 
Berlin, but if Lam to believe what I hear, his success in that quarter will not 
be very great. Shortly after the reecipt of the despatch acknowledged above, 
his Excellency, in the course of conversation, began criticising the policy of 
Austria, as compared with that of Prussia, and saying that Austria was not 
acting wisely in Germany. 1 answered, that in this | could not agree with him, 


285 


and that, intimate as we were, | would not hesitate in saying that the latter 
opinion applied more to himself; that neither England nor France would nor 
eould give up the war, unless with some positive guarantee of its not being 
again begun by Russia the moment she was able, or that we bad withdrawn 
our forces; that with the experience of the Russian policy towards Turkey, and 
her cautious as well as insidious attucks on its independence, we must look to her 
weakness as the only safe assurance against a recommencement of what hail 
forced the war on us; and that Germany, in her own interest, ought to side 
frankly and openly with the Western Powers, and tuke steps at Frankfort to 
prove tt to Hurope. M. de Beust said, that if they were toarm, it would put them 
all to ereat expense, and without the slightest prospect of any advantage resulting 
to them. I answered, that he mistook the sense of what | had said, that there 
Was no present need of their arming, but that instead of making a third party 
in Germany along with M. Von der Plordten, they ought to join with Austria, 
anc use all their moral influence to destroy the illusions existing jn a high 
quarter in Prussia, so as to loree the latter ta uct on Wussia, and put an end 
toa war which Lassured him, if not terminated in the winter, would be carried 
into Germany: He said, that there was no asvertaining what we wanted, 
although Prussia was ready to re-open the Vienna Conference, which it appeared 
we were not, | saul that your Lordship hid set that question at rest, ina 
conversation with Count Bernstorii, and that although not exactly authorized, 
1 would take upon myscll to communicate to him the substance of it, as 
contuned in a despatch addressed to Lord Augustus Loftus, and which had 
heen shown te M. de Mantenttel. 

Ie read rowith great attention, saving, at the end, “ Voili ce qui est bien 
fort.” TP merely added, that Count Bernstori? had brought it down on himself, 
at which Twas not much surprised, from former personal acquaintance with the 
Count, ind that your Lordships admirable observations were not to be refuted 

In a subsequent conyversation—for they turn on no other subjert—l told 
M. de Beust that | had heard from two sources, and they were persons wha 
had their wits about them and their cars open, thit the idea of the re-establish- 
ment ofa Kingdom of Poland, as a barrier against Russia, had existed at Vienna; 
that Austria would not be tadisposed to give up Gallieia, which would entail the 
cession ef Posen on the part of Prussia; that each of these Powers would 
certainly not do it without indemmnities, aud Austria looked to the Principulities, 
Whilst Prussian had never since 1815 taken her eyes off Saxony, He suid, “If 
this be the case, all that we can do will not, in the long run, prevent it.” | 
said 1 could not agree in this; that by adopting the line of poliey I always 
recommended, the danger might be averted from Saxony for the present, and 
that others might later prevent what they were too weak to effect. T eould 
perceive that all this had struck him; tor two days later, | found him more 
reasonalile, excepting as regards Austria, whose publication of the last despatch 
(of the s0th September) to her Minister in Berlin, he blamed very much, 
saying it committed bier in an useless manner, 

I said that he must not indulee in any illusions as to either Austria or 
Prussia; that the former must now go on, for that if we all did not succeed in 
rendcnng Russia powerless for a time, the latter would naturally avail herself 
of the first opportunity and pretest to fall upon and revenge herself’ on Austria: 
and that what with her Rhenish provinces and Bultie ports, a very categorical 
answer as to her intentions and position must bir demanded from Prussia in the 
apring. 

My humble opinion is, that M.de Beust feels the false line he has been 
pursuing, but does not exactly see how he ean better the position of being 
situated between the two Great Powers of Germany, both of which lie lias 
Inanaged to indispose towards himself. lis despatch to Count Vitsthune of 
the th of July last, in answer to your Lordship's No. 24 of the 21st of June, 
(a sutmiiry of which wos given in my No, 42 of the 13th of July), lias been 
published in the “Augsburg Allgemeine Zeitung,” and a Germun translation 

of it is in several of the Saxon papers of this morning,

T HAVE taken means to inquire what ave the military reports received here 
as to the number and disposition of the Russian armies in Poland. ‘The ful- 
lowing report has been given to me as the latest correct intelligence received here 
by the War Department : 

Ist corps d’armeée, 50 battalions, contre of position at Wilna, 

2nd corps d’armnée, 50 battalions, centre of position at Zamosky, with its 
left wing extending to the Dnivster. 

32 battalions—Ist division of Grenadiers, centre of position at Minsk; 
Zod division of Grenadiers, between Bresletetfsky and Warsaw, 

‘Two divisions of 32 battalions of the Guards, now on their march inte 
Poland, amounting in all to 14 battalions. 

‘The nominal force of a battalion is 1,000 men, but its effective cannot be 
rated at above S00, 

The whole Russian foree in Poland may therefore be computed, inclusive of 
eavalry and artillery, at about 160,000 men 

[tis stated that the reserves “Sapazuy” have not hitherto proved them- 
selves to bean eflicient foree, and are only available for garrison duty, or for 
covering the communications of the army, 

The Austrian forces. concentrated on the Russian frontier, inclusive of the 
army in occupation of the Principalities, are estimated by the official authorities 
here at 240,000 men. 

As the foregoing information is derived from the official reports received by 
the War Office here, [do not hesitate to communicate it to your Lordship as 


means of corroborating the reports which your Lordship may receive from other 
quarters,

(Translation. ) 


(Extract.) October 17, 1854. 

IT was with great surprise that we learnt by the despatches from 
Constantinople of the Sth, thut Omer Pasha had encountered obstacles in 
carrying on his military operations from the Austrian Generals. We had 
supposed that all opposition on the part of General Hess would have ceased with 
the instructions sent to him and to General Coronini on the 21st of September, 
and which related to the movement of the Turkish troops on [braila and Galatz; 
and on the Gth of October we learnt from M. Ponjade that Omer Pasha had 
signed a Conyention with General Hess, by which he was to occupy Tbraila, and 
leave Galatz to the Austrians, and that this Convention had completely satisfied 
the Turkish Commander, You will see by this short statement that we have 
had difficulty in reconciling facts und dates with the reclamations we have had to 
address to Count Buol. After careful perusal of the account of the conference at 
Constantinople, | am well convinced that Baron Bruck has culpably ignored or 
neglected the views of his Government, and I trust that the steps which have 
now been taken by the Cabinet of Vienna, and the clear expression of its 
sentiments and policy, will prevent any further misunderstandings from taking 
place. | will not conceal from you that the conduct of certain Austrian Agents, 
both military and civil, has deserved great censure, but I reiterate my hope that 
future discussions will now be obviated, 

Although these disputes had already been the subject of grave discussion 
between Lord Westmorland, Count Buol, and myself, my English colleague and 
I repaired immediately to the Turkish Ambassador on receipt of our despatches 
from Constantinople, and we lent him every assistance in obtaining from Count 
Buol those full and satisfactory explanations which he transmitted by telegraph 
last night to Omer Pasha, Lord Westmorland and | transmitted similar 
information to our respective Agents at Bucharest.

: Pal capa PE ‘ount Buol to say, that we have found him as

2911 


have taken place between the Agents of his Government and those of the Porte, 
and while showing an earnest desire to put a stop to them, he has forcibly 
pointed out to us the serious obstacles which he las had to encounter in aaah bts 
out the policy of his Government. The revolution (for it is nothing less) which 
hes been accomplished in the alliances of Austria, has met with many and powerful 
opponents among certain ranks of the army and some portions of the civil 
administration, and although the continuous and decided expression of the 
Sovereign's willand sentiments has reconciled many to the new policy which has 
been adopted by his Government, there are still found some to resist it, and the 
Emperor, who had much to overcome in his own mind, feels indulgent to those 
who did not accept the conversion to this new policy as quickly as he did him- 
self, ‘These considerations do not mitigate the vexatious proceedings which have 
tended to disturb the good understanding between Austria and the allied Powers, 
but they miay serve to indicate the magnitude of those difficulties which have 
encumbered, and still do encumber, our path towards the object we wish to attain, 
and which | still hope we shall ultimately arrive at. 

The question is further complicated by the pretensions of the Austrian 
Generals, who require a certain liberty of uetion in order to secure the safety 
of their troops in the event of a sudden rupture with Russia, and to avoid com- 
promising the honour of their arms by SxpOniDg them to the attack of a belli- 
werent army before their own Government have declared war ; and acting under 
a sense of this responsibility, the Austrian Commanders have hazarded decisions 
which were at variance with the general spirit of their instructions. 

Count Buol both acknowledges and deplores this fact; and the only excuse 
he can offer for them lies in the conviction, which from their reports le believes 
them to have entertained, that Omer Pasha’s army would have been exposed to 
an almost inevitable check by an offensive movement in Bessarabia against the 
forees of General Liiders, which amount to 120,000 men, and have not as yet 
been weakened by a single detachment. 

Count Buol indulges the hope that the misunderstandings which have 
arisen may now be considered to have ceased, and that harmony may henceforth 
subsist between the Chiefs of the two armies in all that concerns the liberty of 
atrategical movements. With a view, however, of preventing the recurrence of 
those acrimonious discussions which have arisen in the Principalities, Count 
Buol has proposed to Baron Bourqueney and myself that any further dispute 
which may arise between the Austrian civil or military authorities and those of 
the Porte, or between the former and the Agents of the allied Powers, should be 
sent for settlement to Vienna, He proposes that orders should be transmitted 
to our Consuls-General to refer whatever differences may arise to their Missions 
here, and the Austrian Agents would receive similar instructions to refer to their 
Cabinet. He wishes that Baron Bourqueney and myself should assemble with 
him for the purpose of deliberation upon these matters, and that we should 
invite the Turkish Ambassador to join us, when we might examine in a spirit 
conformable to the amity of our policy, and to the text of the documents which 
regulate that policy, whatever question should arise between our Agents in the 
Principalities, and which oa should be unable to settle amongst themselves. 
The Porte would be requested to firnish her Representative with powers to this 
effect, and our Governments would be invited to authorize us to transmit to 
Bucharest the decisions which might result from our deliberations, excepting, of 
course, in such cases as would demand direct reference to our respective 
Governments. 

_ Count Buol, in submitting this proposal to your Lordship, trusts that it 
sufficiently indicates how far he is from entertaining any idea of exclusive pre- 
ponderance in the Principalities; and should it meet with your Lordship's 
npprobation, he thinks that it would be well to proceed forthwith to its 
execution. 

I have, &c.

WE add seme remarks on our position towards the belligerent Powers, 
to the contents of our previous despatch, ‘There are two points which are 
more or less decidedly required of us al Berlin, It is thought that we should 
close the Principalities against any offensive operations of the Turks or of their 
allies muguinst Russi, and an assurance is desired, that if Russian does not attack 
us, we, on our part, will not proceed to attack her. 

Both these requirements are, however, quite imcom vatible with our 
situation. We do not consider ourselves empowered to hinder the operations 
af the belligerent Powers, and we can in no case rive up the right of passing 
from our present position of armed expectation to that of a participator in 
the war. 

We will not discuss this last point any further. It is evident that we 
cannot expect to alitain the peace we should require hy the efforts and the ayme 
of others, and that we cannot engage ourselves to continue for an indefinite 
period to hear the heavy sacrifices which such a passive position entails on us. 
Lt is, therefore, only on the first point that we consider ourselves called upon to 
explain our reasons somewhat more fully. et

Inclosure 1 in No. 312. 
Instructions addressed to Omer Pasha, 


(Translation.) 

YOUR despatches of the 17th September have been received and laid 
hefore the Couneil, It would appear from them, that Marshal St. Arnaud and 
Lord Raglan having gone to the Crimea in the persuasion that your Highness 
was going towards the Pruth, and perhaps further on, the Austrian Commander- 
in-chiet opposed the passage even of the Gulonitza river by the Sultan’s forces, 
and stated that their further advance would be an obstacle in the way of the 
negotiations for peace; and that, as it would be ditlicult to divide the army in 
its present quarters, measures were being taken so as to enable it, if necessary, 
rapidly and easily to advance direct upon [braila and Galatz, It would appear, 
moreover, from all your Highness’ despatches, that the Austrian civil anid 
military oflicers come and go [between Bucharest) and the Russians. 

Explanations having been required of the Austrian Legation on these 
subjects, it was replied that the “negotiations for peace” meant the proposals 
lately made by Austria to the Russian Cabinet, and that the Austrian General 
had alluded to that subject betore the negative reply of Russia had been received; 
that although no value was any longer attached to this at present, the reason 
why your Highness’ advance was objected to is, that the troops under your 
command are not considered sufficient to encounter the Russian forces about 
the Pruth, and that Austria, not having yet declared war against Russia, would 
not be able to come to the assistance of the Sultan’s army, when a disaster might 
ensue; moreover, not to afford Russia any cause for returning into the two 
Principalities before their complete evacuation, that your Highness, without 
looking to the opinion of the Austrian Generals, ought, in the event of your 
advancing, to have considered beforehand [the chances} of coming into conilict 
with the Russians, as well as that the two provinces would have been left ta 
defend themselves ; and that they would not at all admit the assertion of the 
Austrian officers and employes being in communication with the Russians, 

In the opinion of the Porte, the main point is to devise the means of 
forwarding her own interest and of facilitating “the operations] of her two 

allies, ‘The provisions of the Treaty of Alliance, signed with Austria, are 
limited to the entry of the Austrian army into the Principalities, and to the 
restoration therein of the legitimate for of government; but the right of

made to your Highness, and, in like manner, all matters relating to the Austrian 
army should be referred to the Austrian Commander-in-chief. Those relating 
to the administrative or political aftiirs of the Principalitics would be naturally 
referred to the Commissioner of the Porte ; but while the question might have 
been adjusted in this sense with proper management, Dervish Pasha made it one 
of amour propre on the part of Austria by inserting the proposal for contradicting 
the proclamation. The Austrian Commander-in-chief demanded the eonfirma- 
tion in full of the first proclamation. A pretext was given to the Austrians for 
saving that while the previous letter of invitation had been sent to Stirbey (how- 
ever that may have happened), and while there was no mention of the con- 
ference whatever in the despatches from the Foreign Office, the assumption of 
such demands on the part of Dervish Pasha has leit no doubt in their minds 
that he would not act with impartiality in the inquiry which he was charged to 
make into the conduct of Prince Stirbey, and that they could therefore have no 
confidence in the Pasha’s statements. This proceeding [on the part of Dervish 
Pasha] is in truth to be regretted, und such disagreements must be adjusted as 
soon as possible. As the letter of invitation has been sent to Princes Stirbey as 
before stated, the subject of that Prince must not be again revoked until after 
the result of the inquiries to be made with respect to him, and. your Highness 
will ake the Pasha understand this. 

With respect to the proclamation, that subject has been written upon to 
Arif Effendi, our Minister at Vienna. You will, therefore, state this frankly to 
the Austrian Commander-in-chief at Bucharest; and if he does not consent, you 
must refer to Constantinople. It is inconsistent with the attributes of Govern- 
ments toact without the provisions of Treaty, and it is equally irregular that 
the Agents ofa Government should act beyond their instructions. 

We have afforded the Austrian Government every official assurance in this 
respect, and we expect of your Highness that Dervish Pasha will henceforward 
act in conformity with the provisions of the Treaty and with his instructions. 

This communication is addressed to you by His Imperial Majesty's orders. 


Inclosure 3 in No, 312, 


Instructions addressed to Dervish Pasha. 
(Translution.) 


WITH reference to the subject of complaints which have been made on the 
part of the Austrian Embassy here, relative to the disputes which have occurred 
with Count Coronini upon the demands that the questioned paragraph in the 
first Austrian proclamation should be reversed in the proclamation to be sub- 
sequently made, and that the subject of Prince Stirbey’s return should be 
referred to the Conference at Vienna, despatches have been addressed and sent 
to his Highness Omer Pasha by the Grand Vizier upon the subject, containing the 
necessary instructions and reflections, a copy of which, in order to avoid 
repetition of details, is herewith transmitted to you, and it will be necessary for 

ou to conform your conduct completely to the injunctions therein contained. 

our despatches, which have just arrived, state that, whereas it had been stipu- 
lated in the 3rd Article of the Treaty of Alliance with Austria, that the 
administrative system in the Principalities, in accordance with the privileges 
granted them by the Porte, should be settled and confirmed in concert with Austria, 
the desire of the Austrian authorities was to view this as meaning the restoration 
of the system in force at the time of the Russian occupation of the Principulities ; 
anil that the fourth paragraph of your instructions, setting forth that the system 
of adininisivation framed in accordance with the privileges granted by the Porte 
to the Principalities, having been destroyed by the Russian occupation, in order 
to avoid any disorder at the time of the present Russian occupation, the 
restoration of the above system with all possible speed was necessary,-—although 
apparcntly in accordance with the wish of the Austrinns,—was yet considered as 
contrary to then Treaty: and, in addition, that whereas your proclamation 
contuined astatement to the effect that the whole of the Treaties existing between 
the Porte and Russian were annulled, you were, nevertheless, in the apparent

With respect to the other points, it is agreed that Count Coronini’s draft 
shall be given in with one amendment, which, in my opinion, answers the 
principal objection advanced by Dervish Pasha. Instead of announcing the 
Turkish Commissioner's appointment, the note is so worded as to state that the 
Commissioner, having himself announced his appointment to the Administrative 
Council, is to be on equal terms with the Austrian General in matters ot 
communication. 

This | conceive to: be a correct principle during the period which precedes 
the complete restoration of what is called im the Tureo-Austrian Convention 
“the legal order of things in the Principalities.”

Porte’s instructions to Omer Pasha and the Commissioner; but I hope that 
Reshid Pasha has adhered to his previous intention of recommending frank- 
ness and cordiality in their dealings with the Austrian authorities, expected ta 
reciprucate the same.

Inclosure 2 in No. 313. 
Lieulenant-Colonel Simmons to General Lord Raglan, 


My Lord, Bucharest, September 24, 1854. 

1 HAVE the honour to inform your Lordship that his Excellency the 
Baron Hess arrived here yesterday from Cronstadt vid Plojesti. 

When at Plojesti his Excellency directed the Austrian troops which were 
stationed there upon Ibraila and Galatz, to which places | understand they are 
moving by forced marches. 

His Excellency was received upon his arrival here by all the troops of the 
Austrian and Turkish armies now in the garrison, which were drawn up outside 
the town to receive him, under their respective Commanders, with his Highness 
Omer Pasha and Count Coronini, 

This morning a telegraphic despatch in evpher from the Freneh Ambas- 
sador at Vienna reached Colonel Dieu, by which he was informed that a 
telegraphic despatch had been sent to Baron Hess, directing him not to oppose 
any obstacle to the occupation of Ibraila and Galatz by the troops of the 
Ottoman army, but only to reserve to himself the right of eventually occupying 
those places by Austrian troops if necessary. 

The French Ambassador adds, that the position of Aystria becoming more 
threatening towards Russia, renders it improbable that the Russians will weaken 
their forces much towards Bessarabia, but at the same time that the presence of 
the Turkish forces near the Russian frontier cannot fail to add to their 
inguietude in that direction, 

The above is the sense of the despatch, a copy of which will however be 
communicated by Colonel Dieu to Marshal St. Arnaud, 

lam, &c. 


(Signed) J. L. A. SIMMONS,

of such an attack tobe for the time well founded ; and when one of the Austrian 
circulars in this respect mentions the march of the Russian Guards to Poland, 
we submit the question to the impartial judgment even of those Powers who are 
at war with Twussia, whether the circumstance of Russia's drawing her military 
forces to her frontiers in the face of hostile troops displayed partly on her terri- 
tories, partly menacing it, aliords grounds to assume an intention on her part 
of returning from the defensive attitude she had assumed to the offensive. Never- 
theless we fully acknowledge the eravity of the present situation, and His Majesty 
the King is perfectly aware of the full extent of the duties which are imposed upon 
him by a solicitude in all eventualities for the salety of Germany in the East. 

With regard to the four points which should be the bases of the future 
peace, the attitude aesumed towards them by the Prussian Government has 
often been subjected to a perverted and unfavourable judgment. We have 
supported then i St. Petersburgh, although, as my circular of September rd 
says, we do not see from their general and vague character whether, and how 
far, they will be of any pract ical advantage to. the German interests. We did 
go, because we nevertheless thought that we perceived in them the germ of future 
negotiations of peace for the durable repose of Kurope. When Russia rejected 
these bases, perhaps more on formal than on material grounds, we declared to her, 
in spite of tle irritation which the Cabinet of St Petersburgh displayed on our 
first supporting them, that we could but regret this rejection, as we did not look 
on the four points as the only possible busis of peace, but as containing such 
elements whieh sooner or later would again be brought forward. 

We have communicated this confidentially to the Cabinets of London and 
Paris, and have expressed our readiness, if the other Powers wished it, to 
leclare ourselves in’ this sense in a fresh Protocol of the Vienna Conference, 
but particularly added, that neither in this Act, nor in the signing of the former 
Protocols, could we recognise an obligation by contract of military co-operation 
amninet Russia, ‘hese are the declarations of the 6th ultimo, which are men- 
toned in the Austrian despatch in a manner as if they were at varianee with 
cur intended attitude in the Diet, We totally deny the imputation. ‘The 
double whieh, in a German point of view, do. not sufliciently appear to relieve, 
<o as to recommend them to a binding acceptation of the Diet, and though 
Austria herself points out the clasticity of the separate Articles, still they cannot 
prevent us, in a Buropean pot of view, from giving them our moral support 
on every occasion, and under modalities which we may determine; and we 
attached greater importance to an attestation of our readiness to declare this 
‘na formal manner, as the erroneous opinion, which can only be explained by 
an intentional misconception, that Prussia had prevented the meeting of the 
Vienna Conference, has found its way not only into the public prints, but also 
‘nto the Cabinets, The European Powers buve not unfrequently reproached us 
with our German point of view, ina manner as if we, by maintaining it, under- 
mined the position of Prussia us a great European Power. We have inten- 
tionally avoided @ discussion of this point. We are perfectly conscious of our 
rights and duties as a great European Power, and we will not, for the purpose 
of fulfilling them® . . . . « but rather maintain them in undiminished vigour 
against all encroachments. We have too high an idea of the mission of 
Germany, which 18 60 closely united with the two great Powers, to perecive a 
diminution of our position in Europe in the fact that we look on the muinte- 
nance of the interests of Germany as one of our first duties in the present 
political complications. 

As the Cabinet of Vienna separates the four pomts, and only recommends 
two for the uceeptance of the German Governments, it acknowledges that the 
whole of the four points, as was expressed by the exchange of notes of the Sth 
August, are not required by those interests of which the Diet ought to consider 
itself’ the organ, and to express itself accordingly. That the free navigation of 
the Danube is a German interest, no German Government can deny, as little as 
that the former condition of the Protectorate of the Principalities could be 
replaced by a state of things more fuvourable to the German interests, To see 
this expressed in a suitable form by the Diet would, therefore, if Austrian and 
our allies attach any importance thereto, only coincide with the views and 
intentions of Prussia.

If, on the contrary, the confidential circular of Count Buol implies that 
the dignity of the Confederation demands that a decided attitude should now be 
assumed in the face of this European question, and that a binding declaration 
should be made, in order not to proclaim the total apathy and inactivity of the 
Central Organ, we can only concur with this opinion very conditionally. His 
Majesty the King has, on more oceasions than one, sought to vindicate for the 
Germanic Confederation & greater importance among the European States. 
Phese endeavours have been opposed more than onee, and more latterly have 
been foiled in a matter which affected the interests of Germany more closely 
than the present Oriental question in its original extent, by the nearly wnani- 
TOUS resistance of Europe. But also im the present European complications, 
His Majesty adheres to his opinion that an honourable and influential position 
is duc to the Germanic Confederation. Just this was and is the idea which 
suggested to His Majesty the Treaty of the 26th April. But His Majesty 
believes it his duty to hesitate before he considers this position as maintained and 
improved, if the Diet pronounces, in consequence of ticts which were carried 
out without its co-operation, and the cfleets of which it cannot fully foresee, a 
verdict ina binding manner, the practical value of which, for Germany, bas not 
been sufficiently explained, either as regards the object to be attained or the 
means ta be employed. 

— We believe that there is a tranquillity which is not a sign of weakness, but 

rather a pledge of unweakened strength, and we firmly trust that this strength, 
when called into vigour by a real danger of the rights and interests of the 
common fatherland, will be proved by unity and fidelity. 
‘The above remarks will sufficiently show to the Austrinn Cabinet how we 
judge of the position announecd by its list communication. We most sincerely 
regret that we cannot conceal from ourselves that differences in the Opinions On 
both sides have manifested themselves. But we believe that we are not mis- 
taken (and the Austrian despatch itself seems to be of this opinion), i! we 
assume that these differences linve arisen, not so much out of a diverging 
explanation of the Treaty of the 20th of April itself, as out of the circumstance 
that Austria, without consulting us or the Confederation, has taken decisions 
and contracted obligations, the importance of which can be acknowledged for 
the Empire, although the same would not be the case with the other parties of 
the ‘Treaty. ‘This does not appear to us to be the way of turning the Treaty to 
good account, to mect eventualities which will present themselves in the course 
of events, and in & manner corresponding with the great object for which it 
Wits concluded, We, for our part, are resolved, in spite of the reproaches and 
insinuations which we prefer not to reply to, to adhere to the Treaty, and. par- 
ticularly to Article II. : ; 

Should the other party desire some modifications, we will conscientiously 
examine the proposals addressed to us on this subject, and in doing so will not 
lose sight of our own interests and those of Germany; as also will we consider 
the great importance which we attach not only to the safe position of Austria 
but also to lier close connection with the rest of Germany, 

Whether Austria will now immediately make her proposals to the Diet 
alone, or whether such answers from our German allies as would correspond 
with our wishes, will afford matter and form for a common declaration of both 
Cabinets on this point, aud with regard to the question which Austria has 
framed for the German Governments in so decided a tone, we consider ourselves 
obliged, for our own part, to abstain from any initiative step, and rather to 
reserve our further decision on future proposals of that tendency, Fie

My Lord, Foreign Office, October 24, 1854, 
HER Majesty's Government adopt with much satisfaction the proposal of 
Count Buol, communicated in your Lordship’s despateh No. 393 of the I8th 
instant, that any further dispute which may arise between the Austrian civil or 
military authorities and those of the Porte, or between the former and the 
Agents of the Allied Powers, should be sent for settlement to Vienna; and they 
think, moreover, that the moment is happily chosen for such an arrangement, 
which will be a sequel to the instructions that Count Buol has lately addressed 
to the Austrian authorities, and will render more clear the character of the 


* No, 298, } No. 265. 


318 


occupation, and the harmonious feeling that exists between the four Powers with 
respect to the Principalities. 

Her Majesty’s Agent and Consul-General at Bucharest will accordingly be 
instructed to refer to your Lordship all questions of differences that may arise 
in Wallachia, and your Lordship will then, in conjunction with the Baron de 
Bourqueney and the Turkish Ambassador, examine them with Count Buol, 1m 
the spirit that will tend to promote a united policy; and you will then transmit 
to Mr. Colquhoun the decisions resulting from such deliberations, with the 
exception of those cases that may demand reference to the respective 
Governments. 

Her Majesty's Government gladly admit that this proposal indicates the 
absence of desire on the part of the Austrian Government to obtain exclusive 
preponderance + the Principalities, and they trust that it will put an end to a 
state of things which could no longer have continued without giving rise to 
serious discussions. 

L conclude that the arrangement will extend to Moldavia, and Her Majesty's 
Consul-General at Jassy will receive instructions gimilar to those addressed to"

Sir John Milbanke to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received October 25.) 


(No. 62) 
My Lord, Munich, October 20, 1854. 

‘THLE recent communications which have been interchanged between the 
Cabinets of Vienna and Berlin, on the eventualities which may arise out of the 
Eastern question, and especially the attitude assumed by the former in the 
despatches addressed to the Imperial Representative at the Court of Prussia on 
the 20th ultimo, which have been communicated to this and the other small 
Courts of Germany, seem at length to have fully opencd the eyes of all to the 
imminent danger of the position they have been at so much pains to create for 
themselves, and to have dissipated the iusions under which they have so long 
laboured, in spite of all the warnings they have received, It has at last beeome 
evident to them that the policy they have heretofore pursued is. no longer 
tenable; and they see with the utmost alarm, that unless something like a 
community of views can be re-established between the two Great German 
Powers, they must inevitably ere long be called upon to decide on which side 
they will range themselves, The alternative involves considerations of the 
deepest importance to them, both ina political and commercial point of view, 
since from the moment it is seriously put to them, the worn-out fabric of the 
CGormanic Confederation, which has been undermined by the events of the last 
few years, is virtually destroyed ; and the Zollverem will have received a blow 
which cannot fuil to shake it to its very foundations. 

To these two institutions most of the minor States are perfectly aware 
that they have, in latter times, principally owed their individual safety, as 
well as their prosperity; and it can therefore be by no means matter for 
wonder, if they perecive with dismay the rapid approach of a state of affairs 
which must peril their existence. Perhaps the only exception to this appre- 
ciation of their position is to be found in this country; for, 1 understand that 
ML. Von der Pfordten, who, four years age, waa most ardent advocate 
for giving u tore extended sphere of action to the organ of the Confedera- 
Hon at Frankfort, now declares that it fetters the Bavarian Government in 
nny ways; and maintains that the extent and importance of Bavaria quite

Colonel Hodges to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received October 26.) 
(No, 112.) 


My Lord, Hoamburgh, October 21, 1854. 
THE progress of the allied armies in the Crimea ts watched with the greatest 
anxiety by all classes in this town and neighbourhood, and the best wishes are 
expressed for their sucecss before Sebastopol. But, coupled with this sympathy 
the strongest indignation is felt against the Prussian Government for the jaliey 
they have hitherto pursued in the Eastern question, Indeed, I should be 
unwilling to repeat the very severe remarke that TI hear on all sides against that 
Government at the present time. And these censures are not limited to private 


circles, but they are openly and loudly spoken in clubs, reading rooms, and

places of public resort. Tt was no later than the day before yesterday, that I 
heard a conversation, in which the forbearance of England and France, in 
enduring the wavering and pusillanimous conduct of Prussia, was commented 
upon with great severity, and it was said, What have they, England and France, 
to dread from Prussia when they have the great mass of the German people 
with them? we know well that, at the last moment, the Prussian Government 
must follow Austria; for they dare not gratify their own selfish feelings by a 
coalition with Russia. ‘These observations were not made by men under the 
influence of passion and prejudice, but by sober-minded reflecting Germans, 
who have much to lose by war, and whose material interests must render them 
averse to it, In fact, amongst those best acquainted with the motives and 
syatem of the present rulers in Prussia, the general opinion is, that she will 
join Austria in the end, but not until every art of intrigue and persuasion has 
een tried in vain to induce that country to refrain from taking an active part 
uzainst Russia. 

It does, indeed, appear to me, that if Austria, or any other German Govern- 
ment, should at once commence active hostilities against Russia, the feeling of 
satisfaction in favour of such a step would be general throughout Germany, anil 
such a Government might, if she required them, count on multitudes of the 
bravest volunteers flocking to her standard, confident of success ; for the German 
people are well agreed that the alliance with England and France is to be relied 
upon. ‘The present anti-Russian feeling in Germany, | consider not the result 
of momentary excitement in the masses, but, founded on reflection, that it has 
originated with the leading intelligence of the country, and extended gradually 
downwards to the great body of the people; it will, therefore, in all probability, 
prove of a permanent and unflagging nature. | 

Connected with the preceding remarks is an article in the “ National 
Zeitung,” of Berlin, a liberal journal, with a large circulation; which appears 
to be again opposed to the policy of the Prussian Government, although lately 
it had, during a short time, endeavoured to encourage distrust of Austria. This 
article, which | inclose in original, has excited some attention; it declares to 
Germans, what | have before stated to your Lordship as my conviction, that 
the policy and inclinations of many of the German Governments in regard to 
the Oriental question, are in direct opposition to the feelings and sympathies of 
their people; and as it contains some striking observations on that point, it may 
be of some interest to your Lordship, and especially as they relate to a despateh, 
lately published of M. de Beust, in reply to a despatch of your Lordship, to the 
Saxon Government relating to the Bamberg Conferences, 

The article is headed, “The Note to Saxony of the Sth July,” and says: 
The publication of diplomatic documents, which, in the course of the compli- 
cation of Oriental affairs, has become absolutely necessary, is a complete 
acknowledgment that foreign policy, the questions of peace and war, and as to 
the position and relations of the State in regard to forcign countries, can no 
longer be withheld from the immediate participation of the public. 

By the publication of diplomatic documents the wide ¢ itference between the 
views of the Government and those of the people are very often shown, to 

whom their contents, when they become known, often appear as incomprehen- 
sible as if they had come from another world, or been diawn up in an unknown 
language. 

But such pulilications, and the discussions and opinions that they lead to, 
may bea means of bringing Government and people into a better understanding 
of each other, by showing them how widely they differ, and in what they differ, 
and how disadvantageous for hoth are, the want of a mutual understanding and 
the disharmony caused by each party taking direetly opposite ways, in positions 
and ut times when a co-operation of all their strength is inperatively required. 

Such reflections are suggested by diplomatic documents, that were formerly 
only communicated to Cabinets, being published and communicated during the 
last vent and a half to the people ; and this is especially the case with regard 
to the observations of M. de Beust, addressed to the Saxon Minister in London, 
in reply to the despatch of Lord Clarendon on the Bamberg Conferences, 

The Saxon Minister is considered as the zealous advocate of the claims of 
Russia to the thunks of Germany, and as the representative of the opinion that 
Germany, in the Oriental question, must stand at the side of holy Russia from 


das 


Christian motives, because Russia in her progress in the Orient was promoting 
Christianity, and advancing the cause of humanity, 

The writer of the article in question further says: In the despatch of 
9th July, M. de Beust declares the accusation against Russia, of having at all 
times sowed digsensions in Germany, as unjustifiable, ‘when he considers in 
what manner Russia occupied herself with Germany and her affairs during the 
years in which internal complications menaced the unity and tranquillity of 
Germany when all the efforts of the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh were directed 
to arrange the differences between the two German Great Powers.” 

‘The German nation, says the writer, in reply to the remark quoted, 
considers it as inadmissible as it is intolerable, that the Petersburgh Cabinet, 
whose 60,000,000 of subjects, 10,000,000 of whom are serfs, give it enough to 
do, should occupy itself everywhere, and on all sides, with German affairs. 

The “efforts” of the St. Petershurgh Cabinet in 1848 and 1849 were 
directed to prevent the realization of a Federative Union of German States ; she 
twice threatened Prussia that she would oceupy East Prussia; os if our provinces, 
like Moldavia and Wallachia, were to be held in pledge by her, and she 
demanded that England should blockade the coasts of the Baltic and North Sea, 
in order to bring about the settlement of the Danish-German differences 
according to Russian views, 

‘Through those “ efforts " nothing came of the Constitution of the German 
Empire, nor the Berlin Union, which M. de Beust, in need of protection and full 
of gratitude, had acceded to; that Prussian pioneers threw the bridge over the 
Elbe, across which Austrian troops advanced into Holstein; that, contrary to 
every German interest and only in favour of Russia, the way might be prepared 
for a state of things under which Schleswig-Holstein and Denmark suffer alike 
with Germany ; that in Hesse the Constitution might he set-aside, and a German 
race, remarkable fora sense of their rights, for their love of order and loyalty, 
might be kept to this day by M. von Hassenpflug under martial law. 

Thanks to those “efforts,” the old Federal Constitution, as to which 
numerous Representatives at the Diet, of many years standing, had expressed 
the most severe censures: which was generally allowed to be insufficient, and 
the principal cause of the catastrophe from 1845 to 1840, was reestablished 
unchanged, and no notice was taken of the representations of a German King, 
at the time of the Dresden Conferences, to Prince Sehwarzenberg, for the esta- 
blishment of German Parliament, on the grounds of the observations of a long 
life and many years’ experience asa ruler; that since then, in reality, nothing 
has been done by the Diet beyond reviving old objectionable laws in new forms, 
and allowing our having to witness, ata critical moment, what fruit the scttle + 
ment of the differences between the two German Great Powers has produced, 
brought about by the “efforts of the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh.” 

M. Von Beust, however (who, in regard to the principle, Sty pertinently 
remarks that where it is a question of German interests, the smallest German 
Government ean hetter judge than foreign Governments), is of opinion, and lets 
it be officially announced in London, “that the unity of Germany was never 
better secured, and that never had the principles of the Confederation better 
stood the proof.” 

The journalist remarks hereupon: 

The German nation has never stood before the world in its. dismemberment, 
its divisions, in insignificance of power and importance, so miserably as at the 
present moment; at a time when all the world is aroused, after long neglect; 
when the national enmity between England and Franee—which had become an 
article of Kurepean faith—has changed into a cordial understanding, mot a 
diplomatic or simulated one, but confirmed by facts; and when there is required 
action for magnanimous intentions, inspired by elevated impulses and high 
motives of national policy, and the wide perspective of the future is to be taken 
in at a view, 

Germany and the whole world remember the Bamberg and Weimar Con- 
ferences ; the peculiar and separate position of Wurtemberg; that deceased, she 
would never draw the sword against Russia; the fiberum veto that the twe 

Mecklenburgs gave at the last resolution of the Diet, as to the adhesion of the 
‘Treaty of April; and the Austro-Prussian differences. 

Germany might, and should be, so mueh; she should have taken the 
initiative against Russia, from which lower, as a frontier neighbour, since the

My Lord, Therapia, October 15, 1854. 

OUR latest advices from the camp near Sebastopol, instead of asnouncing 
the commencement of the attack, mention the increased security of our position, 
and the expectation that fire will be opened upon the place to-morrow, or next 
day. The difficulties of getting the heavy guns mto position, and completing 
the trenches, have been found, | believe, to be greater than we had originally 
expected, 

The want of reinforcements continues to be felt. The French army has 
been largely recruited from Varna; Bourgas, and Gallipoli. A large British 
steamer, of the transport service, went up this morning with a crowd of French 
soldiery on its decks. 

Lhave obtained 300 artillerymen from the Porte for Lord Raglan’s army. 
They entered the Black Sea yesterday. 1 despair of obtaining more Regular 
Infantry from here at present; and I have requested Admiral Boxer to send the 
steamers at his disposal to Volo, where the Seraskier promises to embark about 
5,000 men, of good troops.

Inclosure in No. 829. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to M. E. Pisani. 


Sir, Therapia, October 10, 1854, 

THE conduct of the ‘Turkish Ministers on certain points, whatever may be 
the cause of it, is quite inconceivable, and the more difficult to explain or to 
understand, because it is no less injurious to. the Empire than insulting to its 
friends and advisers. I use not this language without sufficient grounds to 
warrant it. My complaint is borne out: by facts, and it is become necessary to 
bring the matters complained of to an issue, While the Porte’s allies are 
sacrificing blood and treasure in her cause, they are entitled to satisfaction in 
those things which either affect the progress of the common cause, or the 
permanent welfare of that Empire for whose maintenance they are contending. 
It is not to be expected that they can consent to have their labours frustrated by 
the Porte’s perseverance in errors frequently pointed out, to have their counsels 
treated with indifference or sham respect, to look idly on while the grossest acts 
of inhumanity pass unpunished, and while the most obvious means of increasing 
the resources of the Empire, and bettering the condition of its inhabitants, are 
neglected or misapplied. 

Inquiries, Commissioners, and Councils, are mere mockeries, when they 
lead to no practical result. Since the introduction of the Tanzunat, the Porte 
and its suecessive Ministers have dealt largely in such expedients. The springs 
of that machinery are, however, too much worn to be kept longer in play. Those 
who have power expect realities, Corruption must be put down by punish- 
ment. Justice must be administered impartially. Public functionaries must be 


a a 


appointed and supported according to their merits. ‘The several departments of 


the Government must be carried on with more decision and activity. Sterile 
prejudices, and j wilousies, that obstruct the paths of improvement, must yield to 
the necessities of the State and the requirements of the time. 

Let us now look to facts: 

Sinope! What has been done? Where is the report ? 

Ahmed Pasha and Ali Ferik! What has resulted from their trial and 
conviction ? 

The massacre near Salonica! What has the Commission done? What 
punishment has been inflicted on the guilty ? 

The utrocitica in Bulgaria! Who has. been convicted? Who has been 
punished ? What local measures, preventive or remedial, have been enforced 4 

The more recent massacre near Damascus! What measures have been 
taken for redress or punishment? ; 

‘The Doojik Koord chiefs! Why have the repeated orders of the Porte for 
their return been neglected? What has become of them ' Why do they not 
‘ijipeare 

The outrage at Jerusalem! A proved offence; the culprit in custody; a 


5 


Consul's house, and the religion of England, openly insulted ; yet weeks allowed 
to pass without any public atonement adequate to the offence. 

Other examples may be cited, but the list is already too long; too long for 
any period, but more especially for one distinguished by events which make an 
irresistible appeal to every sentiment of justice and gratitude, while they afford, 
perhaps, a last opportunity for rescuing a great Empire from the natural 
consequences of misgovernment and its attendant evils. 

Ty no one better than to you can I address the outpourings of my 
disappointment and vexation on this painful topic. You ean bear testimony to 
the frequent remonstrances which I have addressed to Reshid Pasha and his 
colleagues. You have often laboured in vain, under my directions, to obtain the 
redress which the Porte is as much impelled by interest as justice to accord. 
You know that, in prosecuting a just claim, or declaring a monitory opinion, I 
express the sentiments of Her Majesty’s Government, and not unfrequently 
incur responsibility by too much forbearance. 

You will read my preceding remarks to Reshid Pasha. You will impress 
upon his Highness the serious intention with which they are made. The acts of 
justice which I have so often demanded, must be no longer withheld, Iam 
thoroughly convinced that no solid reasons exist for their indefinite postpone- 
ment. It is, otherwise, my firm resolution not to stop here. More efficient 
steps will have to be taken. Her Majesty’s Government will find it indispen- 
sable to come forward in a more decided manner, and full responsibility will be 
made to rest wherever it is justly due. 

I speak as a friend, and hope that my admonitions will be appreciated. 

Your faithful and obedient, 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clurendon.—(Recetved October 28.) 


(No. 596. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Therapia, Octoher 15, 1854. 

ATT a late hour to-night I received a message from Reshid Pasha, informing 
me that, out of deference for the Representatives of its allies, the Porte is 
willing to forego its claim to indemnity from Greece, for the losses sustained by 
Ottoman subjects during the late incursions into Turkey, 

This fresh concession, which reflects more honour on the Porte than it 
confers advantage on Greece, is to be understood with reference to what passed 
between Reshid Pasha, the French Chargé d'Affaires, and myself, at our last 
collective interview on the subject of Greck affairs. It has still to receive the 
Sultan’s formal confirmation. ‘ 

I mean to propose another conference, which may be expected to take 
place in two or three days, ond at which | hone we shall be able to settle 
completely the course of proceeding in so far as’ urkey is concerned, As your 
Lordship has done me the honour to sienify the approval by Her Majesty's 
Government of our preceding steps, and has, moreover, instructed Mr. Wyse to 
the same eflect, 1 entertain a sanguine hope of our being able before long, with 
the concurrence of our colleagues at Athens, to replace the friendly relations of 
‘Turkey and Greece on their former footing, with a fair prospect of their acquiring 
in time a greater degree of firmness and cordiality, 

[abstain from trespassing further on your Lordship’s time at this stage of 
the proceedings. and reserve whatever may be needed in the way of explaination 
for my report of our next collective interview. 

T have, &e. 


(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

Inclosure 11 in No, 232, 


Dervish Pasha to Reshid Pasha. 


(Translation. ) October 4, 1854. 
YOUR Highness is already aware that the invitation to Prince Stirbey 
has been sent. Having ascertained that a party of men and disreputable women 
had been hired by Prince Stirbey’s partisans, consisting of eight or ten persons, 
to raise triumphal arches on his read on the day of his arrival, to scatter 
flowers from the windows on his passage through the streets, and to express the 
public rejoicing by having his horses unharnessed and his carriage dragged by 
men, &e.; and informed that the opposite party would likely take measures 
for counteracting this display in the event of its taking place, I felt strongly 
that there were many serious objections to such irregularitics taking place, and 
the Commandant of the place, Mazhar Pasha, with my knowledge and by my 


direction, addressed the order, copy of which is inclosed, to the Chief of the 


Police. 

On Saturday afternvon, the 30th of September, Count Coronini came: to 
me and said, with much violence of manner, “If you are going to act in this 
way on every oceasion, | will now throw up my commission and go away.” 
tasked him what he meant, when he took out a copy of the order to the 
police and read it, stating that it was my intention to cause it to be published, 
1 sail that such an order had certainly been sent to the volice, but that it was 
not to be printed and published: by ‘being posted in the streets, but to be 
communicated to the pee concerned. ‘The Count said, “ You gave orders for 
its being printed. How is this? You invite Prince Stirbey to come here to 
assume the government, aud why do you at the sanie time make such statements 
to the public against him? ‘This is a proceeding by which the Austrian forces 
here are completely set side,” &e. (and other violent langitaye to the same 
effect), Lobserved to him, that 1 not only did not order, bat that it never 
entered my thoughts that it should be Bes, und publishet, and that it wis 

4

‘
