not to be published; that it was simply an order to the police ; that there was 
nothing in that order which could afford a cause for such violent language; 
that the object was to prevent a conflict between the partisans and the enemies 
of Prince Stirbey, and all the evil resulting therefrom, so a3 not to necessitate 
the interference of the Ottoman, and perhaps of the Austrian troops; and that 
| was surprised that, instead of approving of my proceeding, he condemned it in 
such violent terms. 

Count Coronini replied, “Is it not necessary that I should use strong 
language when you have recourse to such proceedings on your own account 
without communicating with me in the first place? You look upon us as 
nothing. ‘The Sublime Porte engaged to restore the tranquillity and the 
administration of the Provinces, in conjunction with my Government, and you, 
hy thus acting on your own bottom, desire to do the business yourself. Let 
me, at all events, withdraw and go, and do you proceed to act as you please.” 

I said that I could see nothing in this which required any communication 
with the Count; that, moreover, when the objections to the publication of the 
proclamation were made known to him, with the request that it should be 
deferred for a short time, he had not consented, and that I had been therefore 
under the necessity of protesting. The Count observed that my protest was 
wounding to the honour of the Austrian army, upon which I replied that, 
setting that aside, 1 had represented the matter to my Government, and would 
act in conformity with the answer 1 received; that, although the Count had 
said that he was content to act in harmony with the orders received by me, he 
did not do so on my making them known to him; that no advantage had 
proceeded out of our discussions for acting conformably with the orders received 
by me from the Porte relative to the invitation to Prince Stirbey ; that when 
Thad, on several occasions, discussed with him the impropriety of receiving the 
Prince with military honours on his entry to Bucharest, when he was about to 
arrive and to be put on his trial, the Count had not agreed ‘to this; and that, 
finally, the Count had sent to tell me that he was going to do military honours 
to Prince Stirbey by sending a company of cavalry as far as the town gate, and 
a detachment of troops to his house, I said that I had thus seen no advantage, 
hitherto, in the discussion we had held together, and that how could 1, therefore, 
confer upon a discussion on such a trifling matter as the present; that according 
to the third Article of the last Conyention, Austria 1s engaged, conjointly with 
the Porte, to establish the form of Administration which proceeds out of the 
privileges granted by the Porte to the two Principulities; that the establishment 
of local order was one thing, and the legitunate form of Government deriving 
from the privileges was another; that, in my opinion, the time had not yet 
come for establishing the legitimate forni of administration as deriving from the 
privileges ; that the Porte had hitherto sent ime no instructions on this subject 5 
that 1 did not know whether Lor another person was to act with the Austrian 
Commissioner for restoring the legitimate Government, but that any attempt 
proceeding from any quarter whatever to impair the sovereiga rights of the 
Porte over these Principalities would be resisted by me, 0s | officially stated ta 
the Count, 

His Excellency replied: Tf, in that case, any troubles should break out 
here, do you suppose that I, backed by so many troops, am to remain a quict 
spectator? According to the late Convention the rights of the two Governments 
are equal here.” 

i observed that 1 did not understand what he meant by this equality of 
rights. 

(We must act conjointly,” said the Count, * for restoring local order and 
tranquillity. We cannot act separately for this purpose. 

I replied that 1 was the Agent of the Sovereign and Muster of these Princi- 
valities, and that the Count was the Commander of the forees of another 
SR that this was my appreciation of my own, us well as of his position ; 
that I was commissioned personally to preside over the consolidation of the 
local order and public tranquillity ; that nothing had yet taken place to disturb 
order, and that it was necessary, above all things, to see that nothing should ; 
that if unfortunately any disturbance should arise, the Ottoman forces here 
would take measures to quell them, and that the Austrian troops might assist 
them ; but that such interference on the part of the Austrian forces must always 
take place with the concurrence of the Sublime Porte.

with which Sweden was not particularly concerned, - = ie

Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon.— (Received October 29.) 


‘No. 185.) 
My Lord, Berlin, October 27, 1854. 

| HAVE the honour to inform your Lordship that M. Von der Pfordten, 
the Bavarian Minister President, arrived in this capital on the 22nd instant, 

The differences existing between the two creat German States, and thie 
jmminent danger to which the minor States of Germany are exposed in conse- 
quence of a threatened rupture, have occasioned the visit of this statesman to 
Berlin. 

lt cannot be said that his presence here, under existing circumstances, can 
be avrecable to the Prussian Government, who have at all times repudiated the 
mediation of the minor German States when differences have arisen with their 
German ally. But on the present occasion the presence of this Minister is 
received with more than ordinary suspicion and dissatisfaction, as it is evident 
that the object of the Bavarian Minister is to exereise a pressure on the decision 
and poliey of the Prussian Government. 

| arn informed that M. Von der Pfordten has declared, both to His Majesty 
and Baron Manteutfel, that in the event of any separation between Austria and 
Prussia, the geographical position of Bavaria would oblige her to remain in 
allianee with Austria, He is reported to have clearly laid before the King the 
necessity of an understanding between the two German Powers, in failure of 
which lie foretells a dissolution of the Confederation, and that the minor States 
will be driven to ally themselves with their nearest and most natural ally. 

I am further ‘informed that M. Von der Pfordten, in striving to induce 
Prussia to yield to the demands of Austria, is also desirous that Prussia should 
require reciprocal concessions from Austria; and that his proposals are that,— 
1. Austria should promise to take no offensive part against Russia; and 2. That 
Austria should engage herself to enter into no alliance with the Western 
Powers. 

These ave, as fur as I can ascertain, the principal objects of M. Von der 
Pfordten’s mission. Your Lordship will perceive that the firm and consistent 
language held by Austria towards Prussia and the German States have heen the 
means of completely counteracting the evil effects of the Bamberg Coalition; who 
in view of a triple alliance between England, France, and Austria, entertain very 
just fears that they may be exposed to considerable dangers and defeat by allying 
thhemeclves with Prussia. 

No direct proposals have been as yet submitted to the Government by 
M. Von der Pfordten, He has been anxious to await the return here of Count 
Esterhazy from Vienna, and to be informed of the reply of the Austrian Cabinet 
to the last Prussian communication of the 13th instant. 

From information which has reached me from another quarter, Tam induced 
to believe that the Bavarian Minister is endeavouring: to influence both the 
Austrian avd Prussian Cabinets towards the ends he is anxious to obtain, by 
holding cut the Bavarian support or threatening its withdrawal, as may suit his 
purpose. ‘The object he has in view is evidently to produce such an under- 
standing between Austria and Prussian os shall effectually restrain the former 
from uny olfensive action against Russian and prevent her from entering mto any 
separnte alliance or Treaty with the Western Powers. 

I entertain confident hopes that the mission of M, Von der Piordten will 
prove fruitless, in as fitr as he aspires to utilising the action of Prussia for the 
purpose of fettering and restraining the free action of Austria. 

Count Esterhazy informed me this morning, in the most positive and 
decided terns, that the Austrian Cabinet were determined to bind themselves by 
no engagement which would prevent them acting offensively towards Russia ; 
and that they were further resolved to pursue the course of policy which they 
had expressed to their German confederates in their late communication, 

It is probuble that the Prussian ‘overnment will courteously but decisively 
decline any mediating endeavours of M, Von der Pfordten, and that they will 
bring about by direct means an arrangement of their diflerence with Austria. Tt

be, but Tam of opinion that whatever understanding is arrived at, it will be but 
ephemeral, and will only last until a fresh crisis shall arrive, anc when the active 
co-operation of Prussia is required.

Lord A, Loftus to the Earl af Clarendon. —( Received October 29.) 
(Na. 141.) 


My Lord, Berlin, October 27, 1854. 

THE Marquis de Moustier, the French Minister at this Court, informs me 
that he had, a few days ago, a very interesting conversation with M. Von der 
Prordten. 

In the course of this discussion, during which M, Von der Pfordten was 
very animated, he expressed himself in hitter terms against Austria, stating that 
she had shown ingratitude towards those who had rendered her such signal 
service, and restored her influence in Germany. He particularly alluded to. the 
Treaty und engagements into which she had entered both with Turkey and the 
Western Powers, without any previous consent with the Confederation, He 
spoke in deprecatory terms of Prussia, and very strongly against England. With 
respect to the German press, he remarked that it did not represent the opinions 
of the great majority of the people, but only the revolutionary party ; and he 
stated that for half-a-million he would buy it up, and change completely its tone. 
He asserted that none but the revolutionary party in Germany were anti- 
Tussin: and that were there “six hommes de moins” in Austria, her pohey 
would be quite changed. ‘To this latter remark M. de Moustier replied, that 
one of those six was the “Emperor;” and on M, de Moustier remarking that 
the Austrians could searcely be called the revolutionary party in Germany, he 
exclaimed, “ Pareequ’ils marchent entigrement avee vous.” , 

M. Von der Ptordten then defended the policy which he had pursued. He 
suid all he desired was the independence of Germany ; that as for the domination 
of Russia, it was not indore to be feared than the preponderance of England and 
France, - 

With respect to the Bamberg Coalition, he said that those States had only 
inet to exchange opinions; that undue importance had been given to that micet= 
ing; and that with respect to the “ memorandum’ drawn up, it was only i 
secret paper intended for the German States, and he expressed great anger at 
its publication, 

He-stated that if Austria and Prussia did not come to on understanding, 
that the Confederntion would be dissolved, and that each member would have to 
provide for his own safety, 

Haron de Malzen, the Bavarian Minister at this Court, was present during 
this conversation, and repeatedly attempted to check the animated and inflisereet 
language of M, Von der Pfordten, and on the following morning he called on 
M. de Moustier to exeuse the imprudence of his chiet.

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received October 29.) 


(No. 398.) 
My Lord, Vienna, October 25, 1854, | a.m. 


THE reports received from the Austrian head-quarters in Bucharest state 
that the Russian advanced posts on the Danube are at Matchin, Isatcha, Babadagh, 
and Tulteha. 

General Liiders and his staff, and a brigade of Infantry, are at Satarrof, 
General Engelhardt with the 15th Division and a brigade of Hussars, are at Reni 
and Wadoul Isaki. General Ouchakolf is at Ismail with three regiments of 
Infantry, and three regiments of Cossacks. ‘The rest of the 5th corps d’armée, 
and a division of the 4th, are on the line of the Danube and the Pruth. General 
Aurep has been sent with his division, some Dragoons, and a brigade of Lancers, 
and two regiments of Cossacks, to Chotzine, to form a cordon towards Gallicia 
and the Bukovine. 

It also stated that Prince Gortchakoff is at Kicheneff, where he has 
received the Russian Grand Dukes, and that General Dannenberg 1s likewise 
there. 

According to these accounts the force of the Russian army in Bessarabia 
has lately been increased by reinforcements from the interior, so that, including 
the troops in the Dobrudscha, it amounts to from 100,000 to 120,000 men. 

The Russians have begun to transport their magazines and hospitals to the 
left bank of the Dniester. Their flotilla is at Isatcha and Ismail, and a part 
at Kilia, [tis said that the Russians mean to pass their flotilla into the mouth 

of the Dnieper, and that it is for that purpose that they keep possession of the 
Dobrudseha.

No, 342. 


The Eurl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 
(No, 660.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, October G0, 1604. 


| HAVE received your Excellency’s despatch No, 590, containing copies 
of correspondence bearing on the diseussions which have taken place at Bucharest 
between Dervish Pasha and Count Coronini. 

Her Majesty's Government trust that these painful and unseemly differences 
ave now at an end, but the fault does not appear to he exclusively with the 
Austrian authorities. ‘The Porte determined to have a judicial inquiry into the 
conduct of Prinee Stirbey. Her Majesty’s Government and the Austrian 
Government considered this to be both proper and necessary. — But instead of 
wroceeding with it at once, an invitation was sent by Dervish Pasha to Prince 
Stirbey to return to Bucharest, and resume his functions; and then a notice 
was published by the Turkish authorities there that the Prince was not to be 
reoeived with honour, and in such a course there was neither consistency nor 
prudence, 

Count Coronini appears to have conducted himself throughout in an 
arrogant manner; still Her Majesty's Government cannot forget that Dervish 
Pasha was the man who, when acting as Commissioner for settling the Tureo- 
Persian boundary, forcibly seized upon Kotoor, in defiance of the British Com- 
missioner, and in disregard of the obligations of his own Sovereign, He is 
violent and unscrupulous, and should not have been selected for the office he 
now fills, which is one of a delicate natare, and requiring tact and moderation 
for dealing with the various embarrassing questions that were certain to arise 
out of a joint occupation of the Principalities, 

Tam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 1. 


(No. 1,307.) 


My Lord, Paris, October 31, 1854. 

IT’ was next to impossible that, with the opinion I entertained of the 
Emperor’s letter to the widow of the late Marshal St. Arnaud, 1 should see 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys without mentioning the subject to him. Accordingly, 
during the first interview which | had with his Excellency after its publication, 
[ pointed out to him the effect which | feared the expression of ‘* timides avis” 
must have in England and among the English Generals in the Crimea, I was 
quite certain, I said, that the Emperor had not seen the sense which must 
necessarily be given to them, or he would have avoided employing the words ; 
but that | trusted there would be greater cireumspection in future, for 1 could 
not answer for the consequences if such language was repeated. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys was profuse in his assurances that no imputation 
upon any Englishman was fntanded by the expressions to which I alluded. He 
said that he would write to the Emperor upon the subject, who, he was certain, 
would confirm these assurances, 

I heard no more on this matter until this morning, when I saw the accom- 
panying article in the “ Moniteur,” explaining that the obnoxious words apphed 
only to the diversities of opinion respecting an expedition to the Crimea, which 
were known to have existed in the French military and naval services. 

I saw M. Drouyn de-Lhuys this afternoon. His Excellency said that he 
had written to the Emperor after his conversation with me, and that His 
Majesty had ordered, in consequence, the insertion in the '* Moniteur™ of the 
explanatory article to which T have the honour to call your Lordship’s notice, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY.,

My Lord, Stuttgardt, October 25, 1854. 

BARON DE TALLEYRAND, the French Minister at Baden, showed me 
at Carlsruhe on the 17th instant, a despatch from M. Drouyn de Lhuys of the 
4th, which he was about to communicate to Baron de Riidt, setting forth with 
great clearness and ability the mischievous effect upon the Eastern question of 
the want of unanimity in Germany ; maintaining the impossibility of Germany's 
neutrality in the existing struggle ; and forcibly recommending the Government 
of Baden to give full support to Austria in th Oriental discussions which might 
take place at Frankfort. 

My departure from Carlsruhe prevented me from seeing Baron de ‘Talleyrand 
after hia interview, but he informed me that not long since Baron de Riidt had 
told him that he Serine of the Prussian distinction between German and 
European interests, and that he had instructed the Baden Minister at Frankfort 
to speak in that sense. 

With me Baron de Ridt lamented the want of practical views in the 
King of Prussia, but strongly praised His Majesty's conscientiousness, whilst his 


Excellency passed the highest eulogy on the good sense and loyalty of the 
Prince of Prussia. 
I have, &c. 
(Signed) G. §. 8, JERNINGHAM,

Inclosure 1 in No. 356. 
Lieutenant-Colonel Simmons to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


(Private and Confidential.) 
My Lord, Bucharest, October 11, 1844. 


IN a communication which | had yesterday with his Highness Omer Pasha, 
he expressed his intentions as to his mode of procedure here now that Prince 
Stirbey has returned, and desired me to communicate them confidentially to 
your Lordship. 

His es gaid that he considered the Prince's return entirely as a con- 
cession to Austria, and although he could not personally approve of the 
resumption of authority by the Prince, still, as he had returned under arrange- 
ments entered into between the Porte and her allies, he felt himself bound to 
aceept that condition, and visits have accordingly been exchanged between the 
Prince and himself, 

He added that it was not his intention in any way to interfere with or 
to counsel the Prince as to the operation of his government, which, being left 
entirely free to himself, he would have an opportunity of showing his inclina- 
lions unfettered, and proving whether hencetorth he desired to promote the 
interests of his Suzerain or those of a foreign State. 

His Highness intends therefore to maintain a strict attitude of observation. 

If no amelioration in the government takes places, or if it continue as 
formerly, and Russian agents, or those strongly inclined towards the interests 
of Russia, are introduced into power, it will be his duty as a military Com- 
mander to represent the circumstances to his Government, and to the allied 
Commanders, and to declare the impossibility of acting with his army in the 
field, that is, if the operations continue in this quarter of the Empire, so long as 
its movements are liable to be known in detail to the enemy, and to have 
obstacles placed in their way by the local authorities, with whom he will have to 
communicate in utilizing the resources of the country. 

His Highness, assuring me that he was incapable of deceiving your Lordship, 
and that he used all possible means to prevent his being deceived, so that he 
might not unintentionally deceive, desired me to inform your Lordship that he 
was perfectly satisfied with the honesty and loyalty of Dervish Pasha’s acts and 
intentions towards Austria, He desired me to point out to your Lordship that 
Austria holds two distinct languages at Constantinople and at Bucharest, and 
that by her representations at the former she endeavours to make it to be 
believed that Dervish Pasha has already acted in such a manner that any report 
which he may make with reference to Prince Stirbey will not be free from 
prejudice, and therefore not worthy of that credit which would ensue from an 
impartial judgment of the matters brought to his attention. 

His Highness desires me to assure your Lordship on the contrary that the 
vonduct of Dervish Pasha here has heen most loyal towards Austria and the 
interests committed to his charge, and he is perfeetly satisfied of the purity and 
coodness of his intentions in these respects. 
~ With respect to the instructions which have been sent to him as to the 
movement of his troops to the front, his Highness desires me to inform your 
Lordship that the time has now passed when such a movement could be useful 
with reference to what is taking place in the Crimea, and that, therefore, he 
cannot now make any proposition to that effect to the Austrian Commander-in- 
chief, especially as the movement at this season would entail much fatigue, and 
probably considerable loss, on the troops. He feels that he has done all that 
was possible towards making the movement, and that itis solely due to Austria 
that it was not made, and therefore Uiat Power must bear the entire responsi- 
bility, ifany portion of the Russian army of the Danube has been transferred to 
take part in the operations of the Crimea, 


roles 


x 


* - pana re ai F s> iii- dans t Po ra wee et a ax 1 i S 2 (es 


55 


His Highness added, that after the late satisfactory information received 
from the Crimea, he has every confidence that the Russian reinforcements will 
not arrive in sufficient time or strength to be brought to act efficiently against 
the allies, although he has strong reason to believe that large bodies of troops 
have been for some time in march from the army of the Danube to the Crimea, 
under the command of General Liders. 

In the communications which his Highness has had with Count Coronin, 
the Count has pressed upon him the advisability of his taking measures to 
compel the small body of Russians, which may amount to 4,000 or 4,000 men, 
now in the lower part of the Dobrudscha towards Isaktchi and Toultcha, to 
recross the Danube. 

His Highness desired me to inform your Lordship that he does not take, nor 
wish to take, any steps against these troops, as he does not consider their position 
dangerous or very injurious. Moreover, as Austria has declared her object to 
be to obtain for Germany the free navigation of the Danube, he does not con- 
aider that this object is obtained so long as the Russians occupy both banks of 
the Danube, including all its mouths, and therefore he considers it desirable ta 
leave this small force of Russians unmolested in the Dobrudscha pending the 
assumption of a more decided attitude by Austria; and he added, that unless 
Austria interferes to procure the abandonment of this position by the Hussians, 
it cannot be considered that the military occupation of the Principalities by 
Austria hag secured one of the conditions which Austria, as well as the allied 
Powers, deem essential to a re-establishment of peace, viz., the free navigation 
of the Danube. 

Tam, &e. 
(Signed) J. L. A. SIMMONS, 


Inclasure 2 in No. 356, 
Lieutenant-Colonel Simmons to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe, 


(Extract.) Bucharest, October 11, 1854. 

OMER PASHA thinks it absolutely necessary that decided measures 
should be taken for the enlistment of the army from the Christian subjects of 
the Porte, as he conceives there is a prospect of a continuation of the war, and 
unless such measures be taken, the Ottoman army will within a short period 
cease to exist. 

He considers it impossible that the Mahomedan subjects of the Porte can 
supply the necessary numbers for the recruitment of the army, and that the 
present moment is particularly favourable to commence drawing from the 
Christian element, especially as there are a number of foreign officers who are 
anxious to serve in the army, who could be usefully employed in organizing and 
commanding these troops until officers can be formed from among the Christian 
subjects of the Porte themselves. | 

The outline which he proposes for adoption in the first instance, is to 
form a fourth battalion of Christians to serve with every three battalions of 
Mahomedans, a proportion which he considers could not be dangerous to the 
Empire, and which the Christians, after the liberties which have lately been 
conferred upon them by the Sultan, may reasonably be called upon to supply. 
The experiment has been tried by the Pasha, and to a certain extent suecess- 
fully, by the measure he adopted about four months azo, when he formed two 
companies from the Christian Miridites, who were compulsorily converted from 
irregular into regular troops for leaving the fortress of Silistria without orders 
during the siege, 

A second measure which he intends to propose for consideration is to raise 
a force of 15,000 men in Wallachia, and probably some in Moldavia, either as 
inaugmentation to the local militia, or to serve with the armies of the Porte. 

Che other measures which he considers as requiring immediate attention 
are the recruitment of the Mahomedan battalions, and the formation of depots 


pk the maintenance of the army on the footing upon which it may be decided to

Sir Stephen Lakeman to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Bucharest, October —, 1554. 


[ HAVE taken the liberty to send your Lordship the following letter, 
because ils contents are not only an explanation of my conduct, but relate also 
to public matters. . 

When I took the post which I) at present occupy, namely, that of Com- 
mandant of the town of Bucharest, a bitter feeling had already sprung up between 
the Turkish and Austrian authorities ; this | considered it my duty to allay by 
every possible means: thus by visits that were never returned, by courteous 
letters that were not answered, I attempted the difficult task; before however 
any good results could be obtained, Prince Stirbey announced his carly arrival at 
Bucharest. Omer Pasha having previously lef town without giving me any 
orders as to the line of conduct | was to pursue, T was left entirely to my own 
resources, and therefore determined to be muided by that common justice to all 
parties which an Englishman always supposes evel y one is entitled to. If I there- 
fore forbade triumphant public demonstrations (by order of the police), it was 
because public opinion condemned them. If I prevented military honours being 
paid the Prince, it was because he had not thought proper to inform the 
Ottoman authorities of his intended arrival; and it was to carry out this line of 
conduct that | sent the following letter to the Pretect of Police ; 


“M. le Prétet, 

“44 les accusations graves, nombreuses, et officielles qui pesent aujourd’ hui 
sur le Prince Stirbey ; vi la répugnance de la majeure partie des notabilités ct 
des habitants de la ville 4 voir méme lo retour du Prince dans les circonstances, 
jai cru de mon devoir de déférer an sentiment public. 

« En eonséquence je vous invite, M. le Préfet, d’empécher 4 ce qu'on éleve 
des ares de triomphe, donner des adresses, &c., &ec., afin Wempécher par tous 
les moyens possibles & ce que des manifestations intempérées ne viennent aigrir 
les esprits et faire dclater des désordres, 

(Signe) !Maaian Pacna, 
« Commandunt Militaire de la ville de Bucharest.” 


Before Lsent this letter | had had a long conversation with Dervish Pasha, 
who told me that he should consider any deinonstration of joy an insult to the 
Sublime Porte, for he knew that the people would raise no triumphal arches, &c., 
aud, therefore, he would not allow a false triumph, in which it might be 


557 


supposed that his Government took no part, and he desired me to send a letter 
to that effect to the police. { must here beg to remark to your Lordship that 
my letter bears no resemblance to a proclamation, neither had | the remotest 
‘ntention that it should be taken as such if the police thought proper to get it 

rinted, it was their act and not mine, although Tam quite willing to take the 
responsibility, as I see nothing reprehensible in the wish to spread an order that 
was evidently intended to prevent disturbances. 

Count Coronini, being informed that such a letter was to be published, 
sent General Popoviteh to the printing office, who attempted to obtain possession 
of it in the name and by the order of Count Coronini; in this he failed, as the 
printer refused to give it up, unless upon a written order of the Prefect of Police, 
by whom it had been left with him. ‘The Austrian General, however, at length 
succeeded in the following manner; “ Mais, M. I'Imprimeur, si vous ne voulez 
pas me la donner, laigsez-moiau moinsla lire.” ‘This the printer allowed him to 
do: when the Austrian General said, * Crest tres bien; bon jour,” puts the 
manuseript in his pocket and walks away. 

Count Coronini having thus obtained the letter, went to Dervish Pasha, 
and asked him what it meant, at the same time threatening to leave Bucharest. 
Dervish Pasha, ignorant of the exact wording, although he knew its purport, 
asked to sec the letter, and, after reading it, told Count Coronini that it met 
with his decided approval. ‘Thus thwarted he left Dervish Pasha, who imme- 
diately sent for me, and desired that I should go and see Count Coronini, and 
endeavour to appease him. I went; and tried every means in my power to do 
so, [said that the letter was dictated by no other motives: than those of 
preventing a disturbance, that 1 knew positively, from official and other sources, 
that if any demonstrations were made in favour of Prince Stirbey, counter ones 
would also tuke place. This, Count Coronini denied: he said, that he was 
determined to put down all demagogues with a strong hand; that he had just 
received-a letter from his Ambassador at Constantinople, in which he was told 
that they held him responsible for any political disturbances, which they had 
good reason to believe would be attempted when the Prince entered Bucharest ; 
he was therefore fully prepared for them, nnd 1 need not be afraid of any 
counter demonstration suceecding. | told him that I thought he took a 
position which virtually deprived the Ottoman Government of its sovereignty in 
the Principalities ; that, however, Dervish Pasha must decide upon; | merely 
obeyed his orders, and | trusted they would not, for the sake of ill parties, be 
found on a closer examination to differ much from his own. Ile said that if 
disturbances took place, he should not wait to see if our orders agreed, but 
should act independently, He was pleased further to say, that men had ne 
right to judge the conduct of Princes; that letters like mine had brought Louis 
XVI to the scaffold; that ‘il faut toujours agir avec beaucoup de délicatesse 
en matiére politique; and many other things of the same nature, to which | 
considered it unnecessary to reply; for little did I think, whilst he was reading 
over and making his remarks upon my letter, that it was the manuscript he held 
in his hand. 

1 then left Count Coronini, and reported his conversation to Dervish 
Pasha; who said that it was becoming a very serious matter, and he thaught L 
had better suspend the publication, ‘and even withdraw the letter altogether. 
'’o the latter course 1 demurred, on the plea that it was derogatory to himself, 
and to me, thus to eat our own words; but that, as I hud never given orders to 
have the letter printed, | would willingly consent: to prevent its being done. 
‘To the latter course he at last agreed; and I gave the necessary orders to stop 
the printing. It was then only, when my aide-de-camp went to the printer’s, 
that I became aware of General Popovitch’s proceedings before-mentioned, I 
now considered it necessary, for the honour und dignity of the Sublime Porte, 
that the letter should be published ; and accordingly sent a detachment of 
‘Turkish soldiers to the printer's oflice, wrote the letter n second time, and had 
it printed. An Austrian oflicer mresented himself at the door whilst the printing 
was going on; but on being told that any attempt to enter would be resisted by 
foree, contented himself with protesting. 

The Prefect of Police now came to me, and said that he plainly saw a 
conflict would take place, for the friends of the Prince, supported by the 
Austrians, were determined to make a demonstration in his favour, and he could 
not then answer for the results: he further said, that he saw but one way to

everybody shrinking from responsibility, 1 decided upon allowing him to go. 
Things remained in this state until the Prefect returned ; when he told me that 
le had been charged officially, by Prince Stirbey, to imform Count Coronini 
that it was his (the Prince’s) earnest wish that no Austrian troops should be 
sent to meet him; but that, nevertheless, Count Coronini persisted in doing so; 
which, however, he did not do to any great extent (three regiments only): but 
still, this was in opposition to what he had told Dervish Pasha a few days 
previously, viz., that he intended to send one squadron only to the Barriére, and 
a guard of honour to the palace. The Prince was received by the inhabitants in 
the deepest silence. ‘ 

These are the facts, my Lord, relating to this ease; and 1 trust your 
Lordship will find in them a sufficient justification for my asking for your 
support should any unfair charge be brought against me at Constantinople.

Inclosure 2 in No. 357. 
Lieutenant-Colonel Simmons to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Bucharest, October 11, 1854. 

YOUR Lordship is aware, by letters from Mr. Colquhoun, and also from 
one which has lately been addressed to your Lordship by Mazhar Pasha (Sir 
Stephen Lakeman), of the circumstances relating to a certain letter written by 
Mazhar Pasha to the Aga of Police here, having reference to the return ot 
Prince Stirbey to this city. 

It having been the subject of conversation yesterday with Omer Pasha, he 
desived me to inform your Lordship that he was aware that the conduct of 
Mazhar Pasha was being made the subject of representations to the Ottoman 
Government at Constantinople, and therefore he was desirous your Lordship 
should know that he attributed it entirely to Mazhar Pasha’s letter that there 
were no disturbances when the Prince entered the capital. 

His Highness is certain that in the prospect of a favourable demonstration 
being prepared by the Prince's partisans, counter demonstrations were meditated, 
and actually in course of preparation, which would probably have been the signal 
for Hot and disorder. For instance, he stated that bouquets of onions were 
prepared to be thrown upon the Prince, in return for any similar demonstration 
of Howers. 

As your Lordship is aware, the day passed off in perfect tranquillity; and 
ulthough, perhaps, the language in the letter in question, which Mazhar Pasha 
never intended for publication, may be strong, the fact of the order which reigned 
must be taken as most satisfactory, especially as, in the present state of the 
feclings of the inhabitants, it cannot be doubted that any demonstration against 
the Prince would have been equally directed against the Austrians, who are, as 
they themselves are perfectly aware, unpopular to a degree almost amounting to 
iletestation. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) J, L. A, SIMMONS,

My Lord, Vienna, October 31, 1854. 

IN pursuance of your Lordship’s directions as contained in your despatch 
No. 240 of the 24th instant, I communicated to Count Buol the information 
contained in the despatch of Lord Augustus Loftus No. 181, as to the States 
of Germany who are believed to be in the mtention of supporting Austria, a 
lier appeal to them in the Diet of Frankfort, to agree to the propositions s ie 
has brought before them. Count Buol told me that he considered Lore 
Auumsts. Loftus’ report to be perfectly correct, except that since the 
that report the Duchy of Brunswick, the Saxon Duchies of Thuringia, the 
Town of Frankfort, and the Hanse Towns, had given in their adhesion. ; 

Count Buol has received notice from M. Von der Pfordten that he will 
arvive from Berlin in Vienna on Thursday next, and that the great object of 
his mission to the Prussian Court has been the settlement of the existing: 
differences between Austria and Prussian as to the proposition to be submitted 
to the States of Germany. Count Buol stated that he should wait for the 
communication of the resultof M. Von der Pfordten’s mission with the attention 
which was due to it; that he had not yet received any indication of it, but that 
he should not be swaved froin the line of conduct which, in conformity with the 
decision of his Government, had been agreed upon. 

Thave; &e.

No. 362. 
The Barl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon,—{ Received November 6.) 


(No. 409.) 


My Lord, Vienna, November 1, 1854, 

COUNT BUOL, to whom I read your Lordship’s despatch No, 333 of 
the 20th ultimo, expressed to me his great satisfaction at the language in which 
it was couched, and at the assurance it contained that the question of a Treaty 
with Austria was one to which Her Majesty’s Government attached the highest 
importance, and earnestly desired to arrange in a manner alike honourable and 
advantageous to the Contracting Parties. 

Count Buol stated that. there was a great deal in your Lordship’s despatch 
to which he entirely subscribed, and to which he would give his most serious 
attention; that the postponement of the signature of a Treaty such as he had 
suggested he did not object to, but his reason for the proposition he had made, 
was, that if any sudden event had placed Austria in hostility with Russia, the 
sve) providing for mutual support would already have been determined upon 
and signed, 

Count Buol will reply to your Lordship’s despatch through Count Colloredo, 
to whose conversation with you it refers, but he will delay doing so until he is 
able to ascertain what is the position in which Austria is likely to be placed 
with Prussia, and which, as he expected the arrival of M. Von der Pfordten this 
evening, he will be able more clearly to understand than he has hitherto been 
able to do from the communications that have reached him, 

Count Buol has learnt from Paris that your Lordship has suggested some 
new form of Treaty, and | have not in any way coriatea this impression, 
although in an official form I was not authorized by your Lordship to commu- 
nicate it; but I cannot augur from the feelings Count Buol expressed upon the 
subject that he would at all object to the general stipulations it would propose, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND.

My Lord, Vienna, November 1, 1854, 
WITH reference to your Lordships despatch No. 337 of the 24th ultimo, 
L have the honour to inform you that 1 have stated to Count Buol, without 
naming the quaszek from whence the information was derived, the language 
which Baron Hess is reported by Colonel Simmons to have held both as to the 
strength of Austria as compared with Turkey, und as to the expedition of the 
allies to the Crimea, and his Excellency replied that he could not for one 
moment believe that General Hoss had been so imprudent and unwise us to 
have held the very foolish language which was attributed to him, and he could 
not persuade himself that these and similar stories had anything but rumour to 
reat upon, He said that the conduct of ne Agents of the Austrian Government 
5 


364 


was sometimes, as he had had oceasion lately to remark upon in the late tran’ 
actions in the Principalities, not in accordance with the intentions of their 
Government ; this required to be put right, and at the same time he felt that the 
Agents of other Governments required equally to be restrained from the expres- 
sion of their individual opinions, which differed from the courteous and friendly 
expressions of their Governments. He had himself received many complaints 
of such language; but he had never taken any notice of them, as it might lead 
to the annoyance of ‘ndividuals; and he felt satisfied that in the end the opinions 
of these persons would be brought to coincide with the feelings and policy 
declared by their Governments. 

In remarking upon this subject Count Buol again alluded to the conversa- 
tion of the Chevalier de Prue, upon which I had spoken to him when T received 
the report of it direct from Sir Henry Ward : he said he condemned it as foolish 
and as altogether in opposition ta the feelings of his Government ; but that 1 
was impossible to eontrol the unofficial language of persons who had nothing to 
do with the political conduct of their Governments, and it was impossible to 
deny that there were some officers both of the navy and army who. still were 
indisposed towards England by the recollection of her supposed hostility 
towards Austria in the years 1848 and 1849. ae | 

With respect to the burthen of the Austrian troops on the inhabitants of 
the Principalities, Count Buol said that when all the expenses of an occupation 
were paid by the Government of the troops employed upon that service, there 
could not be much to complain of ; the Austrian soldier certainly was, accus- 
tamed to a better bed, and to a more substantial nourishment, than a Russian 
soldier ; he had these luxuries, if they are-to be called so, in his own country, 
and as every other expense belonging to him was paid for by his Government, it 
was hard if the Municipalities were not able to compensate the peasants. OF 
householders for the bedding and the other trifling articles which they f urnished 
to the soldiers that were pilleted upon them, and it 18 hardly to be believed that 
the general population would allow such inconveniences 10 weigh in the scale 
as compared with the advantage of having been relieved from the presence af 
the enemies of their legitimate Sovereign,

Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 6.) 
(No, 610.) 


My Lord, Therapia, October 23, 1854. 

THE frontiers of Turkey, near Seutari, having been disturbed by incursions 
from Montenegro, the Porte has resolved on applying to Austria for assistance. It 
docs not appear that there is any urgent necessity for the measure. The Monte- 
negrins have been hitherto repulsed. But, on the other hand, their attacks 
may be renewed; they find sympathy with a portion of the neighbouring popu- 
lation, and there are subjects of djesension in that quarter which might be made 
to operate in their favour. 


a 


Inclosed herewith is a translated copy of a note prepared by Reshid Pasha 
for transmission to the Austrian Internuncio. Your Lordship will learn from its 
contents the motives which have determined the Porte to apply for assistance, 
the limitations which accompany the request, and the manner in which the 
Porte proposes that assistance should be given. 

The occupation of Montenegro by Austrian troops would be dependent in 

pint of time on circumstances of which the Porte reserves the appreciation for 
fiself, Such an occupation ought in reason to operate to the exclusion of 
Russian influence; it would secure the Turkish frontier from disturbance on that 
side ; and, even if it were continued beyond the intended term, 1 question whether 
any well-established right of the Porte would be thereby violated. 

These considerations have weighed with me in deciding not to offer any 
opposition to the proposed measure Without receiving instructions from your 
Lordship to that effect.

(No. 615.) 
My Lord, Therapia, October 25, 1854. 


MY latest advices from the Crimea are of the 19th; and from the squadron, 
off Katschu, of the 2lst instant. It is to be hoped that later accounts will be 
received before the departure of the messenger. Even in that case it is probable, 
however, that they will not come to my knowledge so soon. 1 am, unfor- 
tunately, exposed to the frequent disappointment of secing vessels, dispatched 
from the scene of action, pass down the Bosphorus without communicating with 
Her Majesty’s Embassy, though it is situated within thirty yards of the line of 
passage, 

The fire of the allied batteries had undergone a certain degree of inter- 
ruption on the side of the French lines, owing to more than one explosion there; 
and the consequence had been a concentration of the Russian fire on our 
trenches, with very much less effect, providentially, than the terrific appearance 
had led those who witnessed it to apprehend. | 

According to general expectation, an assault has taken place by this time ; 
but, if such be the case, its result is not yet come to our knowledge, : 

The French batteries, with the addition of two fresh ones, had reopened 
their fire on the 19th, after a whole day's unavoidable silence; but, owing to the 
hazy state of the atmosphere, the effect produced by their fire had not been 
ascertained, 

_ Thave reason to believe, on good naval authority, though not official, that 
the squadrons are intended to be called into action again on the occasion of an 
assault by the land forces. On the 2lst instant the “ Agamemnon” was with 
the British fleet off Katscha, 

Her Majesty's ships “ Albion” and “ Arethusa” are already in the Arsenal 
at Constantinople. ‘The result of close examination was an impression that the 
repairs might be completed without taking the vessels into dock, which, as 
avoiding delay, is to be desired, 

Since writing what precedes, I learn officially from Rear Admiral Boxer, 
that the “ Arethusa’ is “found to be so rotten” as to necessitate her going to 
Malta; and that there is reason to hope, that the “ Albion” may be repaired 
« alongside the wharf, at the Arsenal.” 

I have, &e.

My Lord, Therapia, October 25, 1854. 

| HAVE reason to believe that up to the latest dates from the Crimea a 
great want of reinforcements continued to be felt by the allied armies. 

It is satisfactory, therefore, to know that fresh detachments from France 
arrive, and that Rear-Admiral Boxer is able to aecelerate their passage by means 
of the steam force at his disposal. He writes me word to-day that application 
having been made to him for the conveyance of 1,000 men, arrived here from 
France, he ig able to comply with the request. 

He had sent up about the same number of men from the sick depot to 
Lord Raglan, with the expectation of adding 500 or G00 in two or three days. 

With respect to Turkish reinforcements, Lord Raglan has under his com- 
mand 4.400 Infantry and 300 Artillery, all young and promising soldiers. He 
has dispatched a steam force for the detachment awaiting his orders at Batoum. 
The battalions from Volo may be expected from day to day. Six thousand 
men, under Omer Pasha’s command, are announced by Colonel Simmons as 
ready for conveyance from Varna to the Crimea, as soon as Lord Raglan'’s 
pleasure is known. More may be spared hereafter, if Omer Pasha adheres to his 
intention of regarding the campaign as terminated on the Danube. 

The Seraskier has promised, at my instance, to do whatever depends upon 
him to prepare a further reinforcement here, and the execution of this promise 
may be facilitated by the arrival of the troaps from Egypt, about 2,500 of whom 
have reached Constantinople. . ees 

To complete the information on this subject I inclose herewith, in copy, 
my last despatch from Colonel Neale, by which your Lordsiip will perceive 
that the full complement of 6,000 men had not reached Varna at the period of 
its date.

| expressed myself as unwilling to enter into any discussion with his

losses ineurred in the Crimea, and that it was naturally felt that if Prussia had

Although his Excellency, during this interview, conversed with calmness

referred to the invitation transmitted to St Petersburgh for the purpose of 
extracting some observations or reply from me in return, but [allowed it to 
pass in silence, refraining from addressing to his Excellency any remarks

M. E. Pisani to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Pera, October 25, 1854. 


1 HAVE the honour to report that Reshid Pasha requested me to acquaint 
your Excellency with the intentions of the Ottoman Government regarding the 
difficulties that had lately arisen in the Danubian Principalities. 
The Porte attributes the conflicts which originated at Bucharest to the 
erroneous interpretation of an ill-defined and complex position; it earnestly 
wishes to prevent any such recurrence, and for that purpose desires, in concert 
with England, France, anid Austria, to seek for an arrangement which, in detin= 
ing the general attributions of the several foreign or native Agents, would at the 
same time reestablish between them the good understanding which should never 
have ceased to exist. This arrangement ought to be founded on certain prin- 
ciples resulting from the state of things themselves. Legal order being restored 
in the Principalities, the exclusive aiministration would be entrusted to the 
Hospodars, upon whom alone the Moldo-Wallachian functionaries would be 
dependent, and upon whom the task of giving them orders, and seeing to the 
execution of the existing administrative regulations, would also devolve. The 
Generals commanding the troops of occupation would then only have to provide 
for the wants of their armies, and their intercourse with the Hospodars would 
be circumscribed to that object ; this being, however, the implied result of the 
Convention concluded between Turkey and ‘Austria on the 14th of June. 
It would be established that, during the present war, the allied, as well as 
the Ottoman armics, would be ut liberty to oceupy such points in the Prinei- 
palities as would be considered of strategical importance for them to take 
possession of, and move without impediment wherever the exigency of war 
might eall them, after giving due notice to the Commanders-in-chief of the other 
allied armies. ‘The Porte, in remaining faithful to its declaration to respect the 
rerogatives granted to the Danubian Provinces, would, besides, maintain the 
ull right, which it exercised during former occupations, of sending Commis- 
Oe us Bos to ascertain the position of affairs, and watch over the

‘his arrangement, which might be recorded in a diplomatic nf

and its allies have never ceased to be in perfect agreement, notwithstanding 
certain deviations on the part af some of their Agents. 'This measure could 
only nee 3 peneteey character, and would be so described. |

No, 378. 
The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland, 


(No, 352.) 
My Lord. Foreign Office, November 7, 1554, 


COUNT COLLOREDO on the 3rd instant read to me a despatch from 
Count Buol to Count G. Esterhazy, dated the 23d ultimo, in which, alter 
expressing his satisfaction that Prussia should, in accordance with the wishes of 
Austria, have submitted the communication made by the latter to a careful 
examination, he proceeded to show that whatever may be the causes of the 
existing divergence of opinion between the two Powers, such divergence, and its 
possible consequences, can in no manner be ascribed to anything which Austria 
lias done. His Excellency states it to be in no way the desire of Austria to 
fetter the independent decisions of Prussia as opposed to the independent 
measures taken by herself; for Austria had, in fact, taken care to secure for 
herself, both by the Treaty of April and by anterior engagements, the right of 
independent action, as well as the power of forming independent allmnees, 
provided such action and such alliances should not be at variance with the provi- 
sions of the Treaty of April. Why should it, therefore, Count Buol asks, be 
made a matter of reproach to Austria that she should in certain eases have 
acted independently? Why is it not first ascertained whether she could have 
proceeded in any other way with a view to the carrying out the principles of the 
Treaty of April, and to the attainment of the objects she had in view! 

Count Buol considers the Treaty with the Porte, and the present position of 
Austria in the Principalities, as only results necessarily proceeding from the 
‘Treaty of April. At the time this Treaty was concluded, Prussia did not require 
that if Russia should consent to evacuate the Principatities, Austria should in 
such case not cooperate with the adversaries of Russia. Tn fact, Count Buol 
argues, Prussia must have foreseen that the very reverse would be the ease. 

Count Buol farther expresses himself unwilling to believe that the difference 
between Austria and Prussia is one of principle as to the bearing and extent of 
their reciprocal engagements. He rather considers that difference to arise from 
a divergence in her estimate of the bearing of the actual events and cireum- 
stances of the times; and Count Buol expresses the hope that as these events 
and circumstances assume a further development, this difference between confe- 
derate States will ecase, Count Buol instances, in illustration of his argument, 
the circumstance that Prussia attributes to the evacuation of the Principalities 

by Russia a value to which Austria is unable to consider it entitled as a purely 
strategical measure, Prussia further considers that the declaration made b 
Russia of er intention to remain on the defensive, affords a security which 
Austria is unable to discover therein. Prussia sees no cause of alarm in the 
concentration of Russian forces in Poland, Austria, on the contrary, considers 
that concentration as involving a threat, oe 

Count Buol finally informs Count Esterhazy that Austria still attaches the 
wreatest value to the cooperation af Prussia at the Diet, and accordingly instructs 
lim to use every effort to attain this end ; and with this vicW, Count Buol 
furnishes Count Esterhazy with the draft of an instruction which his Excellency 
proposes to address to the Austrian Minister at the Diet, and directs him to 


submit the same to M. de Manteuffel, with an assurance that the Austrian 
Government have no intention to dispatch it until they shall have discussed its 
contents with the Prussian Government. 
lam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON. 


No. 379. 


The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 


(No, 353.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, November 7, 1854. 

COUNT COLLOREDO has read to me a despatch from Count Buol, 
inclosing a copy of a despatch from the latter to Baron Bruck, upon the subject 
of the differences which have arisen between the Austrian Commanders in the 
Principalities and Omer Pasha. 

In his despatch to Count Colloredo, Count Buol states that, in consequence 

of these differences, the Porte had entered upon direct explanations with the 
Austrian Government, in order to come to a complete agreement as to the 
reciprocal right and duties of the Commanders of the armies which occupy the 
Prineipalities. 
_ Count Buol expresses his sincere regret that this agreement should have 
been disturbed by misunderstandings, and expresses the hope that all cause for 
these misunderstandings will he entirely removed when the principles laid down 
in the instructions to Baron Bruck are taken as the rules for the guidance of 
both parties. 

Jount Buol declines to enter into the causes of the disagreements; he 
remarks, however, that it is not accurate to allege that Omer Pasha has been 
prevented by the Austrian Generals from making a diversion in Bessarabia, 

In the despatch to Baron Bruck, Count Buol replies in detail to certain 
questions which the Porte had addressed to the Austrian Government with 
regard to the intentions of Austria, and the position of the Austrian troops in the 
Principalities. 

In reply to the first question, whether Russia having rejected the last 
Austrian proposals, the Austrian troops would march with the Ottoman army 
against the enemy, or would remain inactive in the Principalities, Count Buol 
observes, that the Porte must haye been aware that Austria had never engaged 
to compel Russia by force to accept the four points; and he cannot, therefore, 
conceal his surprise that such a question should be asked. By the Convention 
with the Porte of the 14th of June, Austria engaged to obtain the evacuation of 
the Principalities by the Russian army, to reestablish the legal order of things 
in these Provinees, and to withdraw her troops from them as soon as peace 
should be concluded. This object has been completely accomplished, and a 
sien service thereby rendered to the cause of the integrity of the Ottoman 

AT piInG, 

Count Buol states that he has equal difficulty in finding a reason for the 
second question, namely, whether, in case the Russian army should attempt to 
recross the Pruth, the Austrian Government would oppose them, since the 
Austrian Government has repeatedly declared, in the most positive manner, that 
they looked upon the obligation to detend the Prineipalities against, all hostile 
igeression as inherent in their engagement to occupy them; and it is precisely 
on this aecount that it is indispensable for the Austrian General to be entirely 
free as to his own movements, and also to be kept acquainted with the move- 
ments of the Anglo-French and Ottoman forces upon the territory occupied by 
the Imperial forces. The Austrian Commander-in-chief, therefore, whilst he 
has orders not to embarrass the operations of the allies, must insist upon their 
not acting without previous concert with him. 

If it was thought necessary for the Anzlo-French armies to enter the 
Principalties, Austria would have nothing to object to such a measure in prin- 
ciple, supposing there had been # previous conecrt upon this point with the 
Imperial General, .

In the opinion of Austria, the resolution of the Diet ought to be so framed 
as to strengthen her in her endeavours to carry the specitied bases of peace; and 
outht further to adopt specially as its own, the two points as to the freedom of 
the navigation of the Danube, and the cessation of the Russian Protectorate, as 
the indispensable groundwork of a future peace. : an 

In accordance with the above considerations the Austrian Minister 1s 
directed to endeavour: ee 

1. That the Diet should declare that an attack on Austria, whether on its 
territory or in the Prineipalities, would oblige the Confederation to come to her 
assistance. : 

2, That the Dict recognizes the four points as appropriate bases for peace; 
and adopts, more especially, the two first, as bearing on the interests of 
Germany. 

3 ‘That the Diet should take measures to carry into effect the necessary 
military preparations, : 

Finally, the Austrian Cabinet informs M. de Prokesch that, should a 
resolution in conformity with the above not be adopted, nothing would be left 
for Austria but to declare that, while she renounced all responsibility as to the 
consequences, she would abstain from making any further proposition to the 
Confederation, and would contine herself to the exercise of her rights as one of 
the independent Great Powers of Europe.

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 
(No. 667.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, November 7, 1854. 

| HAVE received your Excellency’s despatch No, 599 of the 19th ultima, 
in which you report the communication made to you by the Mrench Chargé 
d’ Affaires, respecting a proposed special agreement by which the several positions 
of the parties now called upon to take an immediate interest in the affairs of 
the Principalities should be regulated, 

I have to state to your Excellency that Her Majesty’s Government hope 
that the objects contemplated by the French Government will be better secured 
by the Mixed Commission established at Vienna, which will constantly watch 
aver the proceedings in the Prineipalities, and receive authentic reports respecting 
them, than by a formal instrament which could not embrace all contingencies, 
atid would be liable to constant evasion. 


lam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

Turkish armies.

rendered necessary by the neglect of the Turkish Government.

No. 389. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved November 10.) 


fo. 1,847. 
a Lord, Paris, November 9, 1854. 


THE advices received yesterday by the French Government from Berlin 
mention the confident hope entertained there that the Emperor of Russia may 
at length yield to the reiterated recommendations of the Prussian Government, 
and accept the four points as a basis of negotiation for peace with the Western 
gai) Drouyn de Lhuys does not doubt that under such an eventuality the 
Prussian Cabinet will call upon the Western Powers to sus end all further 
hostilities, since the cause for which these hostilities were unc ertaken will, in 
the opinion of that Cabinet, cease to exist. It is not altogether impossible, ue 
Excellency thinks, that Austria may take a similar view, anil super ne 
demand of Prussia. He is, therefore, extremely desirous that the Cabinets o 
London snd Paris should be prepared for such an eventuality, and si tony, 
through a previous interchange of opinions, to mect at once any demand of the 
kind whieh may be made, by language which shall show that there is no 
liverge T views between them. Bs 
a Se pear. de Lhuys assumes that the action of the two Powers is diplo- 
matically and morally unfettered: he argues that they have always reserved to 


389 


themselves entire liberty to diminish or to reinforce the obligations contained in 
the four points, and to insist on any other conditions which the progress of the 
war might render expedient or necessary. 

France, M. Drouyn de Lhuys said, had even gone further, for in her com- 
munications with Austria in respect to the four points, he had pointed out that 
it might become as necessary to curb the power of Hussia in the north as in the 
east, and that the allied Powers might determine on requiring an indemnity for 
the expenses of the war in whieh they were engaged. 

Furthermore, the two Governments had declared that the simple acceptance 
of the four points by Russia would not be sufficient to put a stop to hostilities ; 
that war might be carried on while negotiations were pending ; and that nothing 
like an armistice could be thought of until the preliminaries of peace had been 
signed. It was clear, then, that Great Britain and France were free to act as 
their interests pointed out, although Russia might accept the four points, and 
express her willingness to negotiate a peace upon the basis of them; and the 
question which remained for them to decide, and on which he desired to consult 
your Lordship was, what course should be pursued by the two Governments 
should an attempt be made to open negotiations on the basis of the four 
points, 

Now, although the two Governments had taken care to secure to them= 
selves entire liberty of action, this was a fact not known to all the world, and 
a crude refusal to treat, though justifiable in reality, would be considered by 
Russia, and perhaps by Austria, as proving that we had other views than those 
which we had in general put forward. Germany also would tuke the alarm, 
and we should find ourselves to be the objects of suspicion and distrust, 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys thought, therefore, that the two Governments should 
(if Russia expressed herself willing to treat upon the four points! ugree to name 
Plenipotentiaries, but declare at the same time that hostilities would be continued 
util the preliminaries of peace had been signed, and that the allies would now 
have other conditions to make in addition to those, the acceptance of which 
would at an earlier period have satisfied them, 

[f Her Majesty’s Government agree to this course, it might be advisable 
to examine, not only in what those other conditions should consist, but in what 
the guarantees for the future, alluded to in the four points, should be sought. 

With regard to the first of these questions, he seemed to think that, con- 
sidering the gigantic plains which it was evident Russia entertained in the Bultic, 
and which, had they been carried out in the Islands of Aland, would have made 
her mistress of the north of Europe, the ‘Treaty of Peace should contain an 
engagement that no fortifications were to be erected on those islands. M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys remarked that such a stipulation could not but be pleasing both to 
Sweden and Denmark, and even to Prussia, 

The French Government seems bent on demanding indemnities for the 
expenses of the war. . 

With regard to the guarantees to be obtained through the four points, 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys is of opinion that Russia should engage to erect no more 
fortifications at Sebastopol, or on the coasts of the Black Sea, such works not 
being required for purposes of defence, 

Furthermore, the maritime Powers should bind themselves by Treaty never 
to have above a certain force in the Black Sea, such foree to be neither 
menucing to Russia, nor dangerous to Turkey. 

In order to exercise a proper control over the actions of Russia, the English 
and French Governments should have a right of establishing Consuls at Sebas- 
topol, Nicolaey, and such other points in the Russian dominions as they might 
Judge advisable. 

These were the points which M. Drouyn de Lhuys considered offered the 
greatest difficulties, and on which he thought an exchange of opinions between 
the two Governments desirable, The solution of the future condition of the 
Principalities, and the navigation of the Danube, did not regard them alone, 
and must be considered in conjunction with other Powers. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys expressed his intention of writing in this sense to 
Count Walewski at an early day, having, he said, received the E*nperor’s orders 
60 to do.

Mr. Buchanan to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved November 10.) 


(No. 818. Most Confidential.) 
My Lord, Copenhagen, November 4, 1854. 
~ COUNT ERNEST MOLTKE, the Secretary of the Danish Legation in 

Russin, has arrived here, having left St. Petersburgh on the 24th ultimo. He 
has been good enough to call upon me, and | venture to report to your Lordship 
the account which | have received from him of the state of public feeling at 
St. Petersburgh, and the opinions which he expressed on the state of affuirs 
there, in the hope that they may not prove uninteresting to your reir 

He represented the news of the battle of the Alma to have produced much 
depression upon all ranks, and particularly upon the Eimperor himself, who, in 
common with the public, is now much affected by the intelligence from the 
army, his spirits rising or falling according to the character of the lust despatches. 
When Count Moltke left, the general feeling was hopeful, and it was believed 
that the Crimea was safe; that Sebastopol und the flect might probably be 
destroyed, but that the allies would not be able to establish themselves perma- 
nently in the country, or even within the walls of the fortress He also said 
that Prinee Menchikoff had instructions to sink all the fleet if he despaired of a 
sucecsstul resistance, 

[asked what effect he thought the fall of the fortress would lave upon the 
public and the Emperor. 

He said it would at tirst cause exasperation, and 4 more obstinate determi- 
nation to prosecute the war, but that a few weeks, he believed, would bring 
ubout a reaction, and that despondency would eventually be the prevailing 
sentiment among all classes. ; | 

Ile suid that the Government had entirely failed in their endeavours to 
exeite the fecling which had existed in 1812, and that whenever a disaster 
occurred, o disposition was evinced to consider the Emperor as its Cause, not a0 
much however from his having been the author of the war, as from his having 
hoon deficient in talent and energy in conducting it, While such were the 
felines of the people, he said, the Emperor appeared also to have lost the 
firmness of charwcter which he was formerly supposed to possess. He was much 
aced, and had feltsp keenly the disasters which had already attended his arms, 
that it would excite no astonishment if he did not survive the effect of 
such a blow us the complete triamph of the allies in the Crimea. ‘The fall of 


ee ee eee ETRE NTT (site tLe eee en whet ee Rte 


391 


Bomarsund had produced a deep impression upon him, as he had received a letter 
from General Bodisco, a few days previously to the intelligence reaching 
St. Petersburgh, stating that “he could die but would never surrender ;” an 
incident which, taken with many others of a similar tendency, has led him to 
mistrust every one around him, and to lose confidence in all those in whose zeal 
and devotion he had formerly trusted. 

Count Moltke said that the war had not produced so great an effect on the 
prices of commodities as might have been expected, but that the higher classes 
made no secret of the falling off which had taken place in their incomes; while 
it was generally acknowledged that the Government would be seriously embar- 
rassed to find the funds necessary for prosecuting the war next year, the issue 
of paper having been carried as far as it was possible to do so. 

Count Nesselrode however, appears to take a more favourable view of the 
future than others, and assures every one that peace will be restored in the 
course of the winter. As | asked whether the Chancellor was equally commu- 
nicative as to the means by which this desirable object was to be effected, the 
Count replied that he believed the Emperor would not make any great objection 
to two of the guarantees demanded by the allies, namely, the abandonment of 
the protectorate in the Principalities, and of his claim to that of the Greek 
Christians in Turkey; but that he saw no probability of His Imperial Majesty 
ever consenting to arrangements involving a cession of territory——a condition 
which would not even be easily obtained in the eyent of His Imperial Majesty’s 
death, as the Hereditary Grand Duke had lately affected great ardour for the 
prosecution of the war, and for the maintenance of the integrity of the Empire. 

On my referring to the visit of the English fleet to Cronstadt, Count 
Moltke said that its appearance had created great-alarm in St. Petersburgh, and 
that it had been generally believed that Sir Charles Napier would have contrived, 
hy attacking the forts in succession, to get sufficiently near to destroy the 
Russian fleet and the arsenal of Cronstadt. He did not speak positively on the 
subject, but he believed the masonry at Cronstadt to be of the same dezeription 
as that of Bomarsund: and he assured me that from the nature of the founda- 
tion of Fort Menchikoff, the whole edifice shakes when the guns are fired, 
He also said that on the submarine mines being inspected in June, it was found 
necessary to replace many of them which had suffered and been rendered 
ineffective from two months’ immersion in the water. 

With regard to the higher classes, Count Moltke said, as 1 have already 
mentioned, that their opinions are unsteady, being influenced by the favourable 
or unfavourable incidents of the day, and that they have ceased to see much of 
the Diplomatic body, all foreigners being more or less objects of suspicion ta 
them, 

The English Government and people are the subjects of much obloquy, 
but the notional hatred is principally directed against Austria, the most 
opprobrious epithets being applied to the conduct of that Power. 

I ought to add, however, that Count Moltke fully confirms the reports 
which have already reached your Lordship of the admiration which Her 
Majesty's troops at Alma excited among the Russian officers who were opposed 
to them. 

I asked what position Baron Werther, the new Prussian Minister, occupied 
in society, and what language he held respecting the present state of affairs in 
Germany. Count Moltke said that he was extremely prudent in the expression 
of his opinions, but though he was made much of fy the Imperial family and 
the Court, it was well known that he and Count Munster, who may be 
considered the representative at St. Petersburgh of the Russian party in Prussia, 
racials in their views of public affairs, and acted in direct opposition to each 
other,

Mr. Buchanan to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recewved Nobember 10.) 


(No. 319. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Copenhagen, Noverber 5, 1854. 

WITH reference to my despatch No. 118 of yesterday's date, | have the 
honour to add, that a gentleman mentioned to me this morning that Count 
Moltke, during the two days which he spent at Copenhagen before proceeding 
to the country, had generally spoken of the war as being extremely unpopular 
at St, Petersburgh. pan 

‘My French colleague, also, to whom J communicated the information 
which I have reported to:your Lordship in’ my above-mentioned despatch, has: 
since obtained from a friend of Count Moltke a complete confirmation of all his 
statements to’ me,'and’ some further particulars which may not be unworthy of 
your Lordship’s notice. “a 

The Count ts said to have represented the Emperor’ ‘as spending much of 
his time in ‘the inspection of recruits, and occupying himself even with such 
details as fixing’ on thé shoulders of the men the number of the regiments to 
which they are appointed. He also appears: to have said that many members 
of the nobility openly show their dissatisfaction with the war, and declare “ that 


Russia is large enough, and does not require to aggrandize herself by seeking’ 


‘nfluence: in ‘Turkey ;” and he expressed an’ opinion that the higher orders 
cenerally would be indisposed to make further sacrifices for the maintenance of 
the war, if the disasters which have hitherto attended the Russian arms were 
not sodn retrieved by some important successes. 

The’ clergy likewise were described by him as being no longer willing to 
place funds at the disposal of the Emperor. ' 

With regard to the feeling prevalent at St. eb when Count Moltke 
left, that the Crimea was safe, he appears te have added to his: friend, that 
Count Esterhazy had expressed in his presence a conviction that if Sebastopol 
did not fall now, the Emperor would strain every nerve to make it unassailable 
in the spring, and’ that His Imperial Majesty would, if necessary, contrive to 
throw 200,000 men into the Peninsula in the course of the winter. 

M. de Botezac’s informant ‘understood, from what he learnt from Gount 
Moltke, that there was disposition to make the Emperor alone responsible! 
for the war; but as I particularly inquired of the Count what he meant by using 
this expression to me, I still’ think T was correct in stating that it isnot so much 
the war itself, as the manner in which it has been ‘conducted, that is exposing 
His Imperial Majesty to the:criticism of his subjects. 

I ought to add that this information appears to have beet communicated 
by Count Moltke to M. de Bluhme, and that his Excellency expressed some. 
surprise that he should never have heard anything of the kind from Baron 
Plessen—a statement which | think very probable, as M. de Bhihme, in reply to 
the inquiries which I have from time to time made of him as to the nature of 
his reports from St. Petersburgh, has always assured me that Baron Mlessen 
appeared to consider it imprudent under present circumstances to write much 
respecting the state of affairs in that capital. His Excellency may possibly now,’ 
if he places credit in M.de Moltke’s report, attribute the Danish Minister's: 
silence to some other cause, Baron Plessen has received much kindness from 
Count Neaselrode, is a great favourite in Russian society, and may not therefore 
be disposed to see matters in 80 unfavourable a light as Count Moltke has done. 


It wes understood at the time of Count Moltke’s departure, that at the 


earnest entreaties of the Empress, orders had been sent to the young Grand 
Dukes to return from the South and to join the Hereditary Grand Duke at 
Warsaw. 

M. de Moltke seems also to be of opinion that the Grand Duke Constan- 
ting las shown himself to be so self-willed since the commencement of the war, 
that he does not enjoy so much of His Impenal Majesty’s favour as the 
Hureditary Grand Duke. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) ANDREW BUCHANAN.

My Lord, Varna, October 26, 1854. 

ISLAM PASHA, the Military Governor of Varna, called upon me this 
morning, and communicated to me that he had received orders from Omer 
Pasha to hold in readiness for immediate embarkation, should such be required, 
the whole of the ‘furkish Infantry now stationed at Varna and at Pravadi. 

Islam Pasha stated that the number und distribution of the troops referred 
to was as follows :—In Varna 9 battalions, 5,820 men; in Pravadli 4 battalions, 
8.400 men; total, §,320; with three batteries of field artillery. 

The Pasha, therefore, stated that he was prepared to embark those troops 
for the Crimea without further reference to Omer Pasha, and requested 1 would 
inform your Lordship that, in case you should deem it desirable that these 
troops should proceed to the Crimea, the would be ordered immediately to 
embark by such transports as may be provided for them, 

The Pasha further informs me that, in the event of their so embarking, 
Omer Pasha had directed that an equal number of troops should be directed to 
supply their place in Varna from Shuma,
