Consul Neale to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Varna, October 28, 1854. 


I HAVE the honour to acquaint your Lordship that [have been placed m 
possession of the following information respecting the number of the Russian 
forces in the Dobrudscha, by a British-protected subject, named Giovanni Anino, 
who left Toultcha on the 14th instant. | 

M. Anino states that he left Toultcha in company with Mr. Charles 
O'Connell, a British subject, who has been for a considerable period settled in 
Toultcha asa ship chandler, and with whom he was in partnership. He states 
that they experiened much difficulty in obtaining permission to leave Toultcha ; 
but having eventually reached Zatoka, opposite Galatz, they succeeded in 
crossing to the latter place by bribing the Cossack guard at Zatoka, 

1 questioned M. Anino particularly respecting the Russians i the 
Dobrudseha, and he assures me that, when he left, the following was the number 
and distribution of the troops still remaining there. 


Toultcha.—The Commandant and Staff, with a few Cossacks. 

Babadagh.—About 2,700 Infantry (chiefly composed of Greek and 
Bulgarian volunteers), and B00 Cossacks. 

Isaktcha.—3,000 Infantry, and 17 gun-boats in the river protecting the 
bridge. 

Matehin,—2,000 Infantry. 


M. Anino very positively states that the foregoing are the whole of the 
Russian troops in the Dobrudscha, Up to the 15th of September, however, he 
states that there were upwards of 15,000 men in Toultcha, but that they 
crossed the Danube and proceeded to Ismuil about that period. 

M. Anino also assures me that the Russian batteries in Toultcha have all 
been dismantled. 

According to the best information M. Anino possessed, the Russian troops 
stationed between Ismail, Tchatal, and Reni, amounted to about 30,000 
men. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) EDWD., ST. JOHN NEALE.

My Lord, Therapia, October 30, 1854. 

1AM informed by a message from Reshid Pasha that Baron de Bruck has 
sent him a printed paper, in German, purporting, as the interpreter stated, that 
the Austrian Government had declared the port of Cattaro to be a military 
port. His Highness was at the same time requested to sign a paper, drawn up 
beforehand in French, in acknowledgment of the said notification and its 
contents. The Pasha, unwilling to sign as proposed, made the best excuses he 
could, and the matter lies open for another day. He expressed to M. Pisani 
a suspicion that the intention of Austria, in declaring Cattaro to be a military 
port, is to comprise the Turkish issues of Kleck and Sutorina, with the view of 
excluding British trade from those channels of intercourse, as had been avowed 
on a former occasion, by denying the right of the Porte to any power over them. 

The question thus raised is not unworthy of attention; and the Porte, 
which looks upon the Austrian proposition as a snare, is not likely to give into 
it without a knowledge of your Lordship’s opinion, of which I beg to be 
apprised at a convenient season. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 13.) 
(No. 422.) 
My Lord, Fienna, November 9, 1854. 


| HAVE the honour to invite your Lordship's attention to an article in the 
* Allgemeine Zeitung,” in illustration of the treatment which Austrian commerce 
on the Danube has experienced at the hands of the Russians, as the statements 
it contains give a correct idea of the facts of the case. 

The article in question begins by quoting a statement from the “ Journal de 
St. Pétersbourg,” to the effect that “although the hostilities between the 
Russians and Turks had to a certain extent inconvenienced the navigation of the 
Danube, yet that it had met with every facility on the part of the Russians com- 
patible with the requirements of military operations; that friendly explanations 
on the subject had passed between the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh and Vienna ; 
and that in accordance with the Emperor's orders, the Russian Commanders had 
always as much as possible protected the interests of Austrian commerce and 
navigation, as their proclamations could show.” 

In refutation of this statement, the writer observes that “although it was 
well known that when Russia declared war with Turkey, her Generals gave the 
assurance that the commerce of neutrals, and more especially the exportation of 
corn to Austria, would not be interfered with, vet that in direct contradiction to 
this, Prince Paskiewitch proceeded to prohibit all exportation of corn down the 
Danube, closed the non-Russian ports of Galatz and [braila, where six millions 
of Austrian property in corn (destined for the ports af the Adriatic, and which 
therefore could not be transported up the Danube) was stored, and to complete 
the total destruction of all liberty of commerce, and the abrogation of all inter- 
national rights, proceeded ta block up the Sulina mouths. It was in this manner 
that the proclamations were attended to. 

“The friendly explanations,” adverted to by the Russian paper, ended by 
Count Esterhazy, in a note dated May the 8th, complaining of the injury done 
to Austrian and German commerce, and on the l4th by expressly reserving to 
Austria the right todemand at the proper time compensation tor the losses sustained 
by the forcible interruption of the navigation of the Danube. The permission to 
continue the navigation was a pure illusion, as it was clogged by the condition not 
to touch the right bank of the Danube—a condition which any one acquainted 
with the conformation of the river and its bunks in the Principalities knows it 
would be impossible to observe; and consequently the navigation of the Danube 
had to be given up de faeto until the Russians chose on pure strategical 
grounds” to evacuate the Principalities. Indeed, how could neutral ships 
navigate a river where they were fired upon by a Russian battery, the com- 
mander of which alleged in exeuse that he did not know the Austrian flag; and 
that on the Danube, on which the Austrian flag is the predominant one. Such 
was “the peculiar protection of the interests of the Danubian navigation,” 
of which the Russian journal speaks, [t extended, however, to the commerce 
of neutrals beyond the Danube. 

In contradiction to the assurances above adverted to an Imperial Deeree of 
the 12th of February prohibited the exportation of corn from the ports of the 
Black Sea and the Sea of Azoff. Urgent application was made that what had 
already been bought by the Austrians in these ports might be allowed to be 
removed: this was not granted, but a promise was given that it would be 
repurchased hy the Russians. A small proportion was accordingly repurchased 
at Odessa, but by fur the greater portion remained unsold.and was yet not allowed 
to be removed, by which the greatest injury was caused to miny Austrian

No. 412. 


Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Karl of Clarendon.—( Received November 16.) 
(No. 647.) 


My Lord, Therapin, November 5, 1854. 

_ OUR advices from Balaklava and before Sebastopol come down to the 3rd 
instant, It appears that nothing remarkable had taken place subsequently to 
the 26th ultimo. The batteries kept up their fire, with more or less effect ; and 
the French approaches, reinforced by new batteries, were gradually advancing 
towards the outward defences of the town. I presume that despatches are 
forwarded by the messenger from Lord Raglan and Admiral Dundas. Those 
from General Rose, which pass through my hands under flying-seal, will convey 
to your Lordship a general idea of the state and progress of the operations. 

I collect, in general, that the prevailing expectation is in favour of an early 
and successful assault, to be made, in all probability, from the French extremity 
of the lines. Your Lordship must, 1 fear, be prepared for a desperate resistance 
on the part of the Russians; and the allied forces may have to deal with a 
Rugsian army in the field, at the same time that they are engaged in overcoming 
the resistance at Sebastopol. 

[ learn from a naval officer, who came in from Balaklava this morning, 
that the late violent gales from the north were not attended with any damage or 
danger to the squadrons. 

I have. &e. 


(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

Inclogure 3 in No. 413. 


Prince Ghika to Reshid Pasha. 


Rucharest, le 26 Septembre, 1854. 
POUR satisfaire A un ordre exprés de son Excellence le Commissaire 
Impérial Ottoman, Dervisch Pacha, j'ai Vhonneur de remettre entre ses mains 
ma déposition comme suit: 

Le Prince Stirbey ayant regu la lettre de son Altesse Réchid Pacha, qui lui 
enjoignait de quitter le pays, fit. convoquer extraordinairement le Divan institué 
depuis le Traité de Balta-Liman pour provoquer une opinion de cette assembler 
sur la circonstanec. 

Quelques jours avant la réunion, M. Toanides, dont je n’étais pas habitué a 
recevoir les visites, se présenta chez moi et me dit que M. Khaltchinsky 
entendait que V'adresse qui serait presentée au Divan, fut adoptée, sous peine, 
pour ceux qui feraient opposition, Pen -courir les eonséquences les plus graves. 

A la séance, le Secrétaire d’Etat, M. Jean Mano, lut la lettre de son 
Altesse Réchid Pacha au Prince Stirbey; puis feu Georges Philippeseo, Président 
du Conseil des Ministres, invita les Membres du Divan a faire une adresse au 
Prince pour le supplier de ne pas quitter le pays, et désigna plusieurs membres 
goi-disant pour rédiger cette adresse. Je fus un des membres chargés de cette 
rédaction ; nous passimes dans une chambre séparée pour delibérer. 

La, M. le Seerétaire d'Etat, Jean Mano, nous lut la minute de l'adresse 
prepare d’avance. Sur le phrase qui termine l’adresse, “ L’unique but que Sa 
Majesté le Sultan s'est toujours proposé, et auquel tend incessamment lin 
paternelle sollicitude des deux hautes Cours Suzeraine et Protectrice,”” je fis 
observer qu'il était inutile de faire mention de la Cour Protectrice, quise trouvait 
on guerre ouverte avec la Turquie; le Seordtaire d’Etat répondit peremptoire- 
ment, “On ne doit rien changer a la redaction; elle est trés bien combinée, et 
c'est moi qui, de concert avec le Consul-Général de Russie, ai ajouté cette 
phrase afin de rappeler aux ‘Tures qu'ils ne sont pas seuls a décider de nous.” 

Le Réglement Organique preserit, que si la majorité accepte une proposition, 
lu minorité eat tenue de la signer avec tous les membres; conséquemment 
‘adresse fut signée par tous dans un morne silence. 

Le Ban, 
(Signe) PRINCE CONSTANTIN GHIKA.

The Barl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received November 20.) 
(No. 429.) 


My Lord, Fienna, November 15, 1854. 

IN reply to your Lordshijp’s dezpatch No, 348 of the 7th instant, and 
tiarked Confidential, | have to state that I inquired of Count Buol whether 
Count Coronimt in demanding the recall of Dervish Pasha was acting upon 
instructions from his Government. . 

Count Buol replied that he hati issued no instructions to that effect; but 
he had looked upon the conduet which Dervish Pasha hud maintained tn the 
Principalitics as subject to animadversion, and lie was aware that this opinion was 
shared by Reshid Pasha, and he also believed that the general proceedings of 
Dervish Pasha had not been approved by Lord Stratford, 

Count Buol, however, stated that he had since learnt that Dervish Pasha 
had become more conciliatory in the manner in which he carried out his duties, 
and he also understeod that Prince Stirbey, who had complained of his pro- 
ceedings upon his arrival at Bucharest, was not disinclined to his retaining his 
eituntion, Count Buol expressed his hope that such was the case, ns his great 
object was the establishment of harmony and good understanding between the 
official authorities employed by the different Governments in the Principalities, 
where questions of differcnee must necessarily arise.

No, ‘119, 
Tie Earl of Westmorland to the Burl of Clorendon,— (Received November 20.) 


(No. 492, Confidential.) 


My Lord, Vienna, November 15, 1854, 

T HAVE already announced to your Lordship by telegraph, on the 13th 
instant, that M. de Bourqueney and myself attended a meeting at Count Buol’s 
ut which we presented to his Excellency the project of an Offensive and Defensive 
Treaty between the three Powers, which we had received from our respective 
Governments. 

I have now the honour of inclosing for your Lordship'’s consideration a 
copy of the dia! of this ‘Treaty, in the form in which, after the discussions which 
took place, Count Luol tins himself drawn it up. 

Your Lordship will observe that the first advantage which the Austrian 
Government has taken of the entire freedom of action which they have main- 
tained in their late discussions with the Government of Prussian and the States 
of Germany, has been to make to the English and Vrench Governments the 
declaration of the couduct which they are determined to adopt, and which they 
consider the present position of alfiirs ne longer will allow them to postpone. 

Count Collovedo is instructed to communicate to your EG as M. de 
Hithner is directed to place, before M. Drouyn de Lhuys, the despatch by which 
Count Buol annonnces the definitive determination of the Imperial Government; 
and at the same time those Ministers will submit the projeet of Treaty to 
which | have above alluded. 

‘The resolutions of the Imperial Government may be resumed in the 
following manner : 


2 415 


The Austrian Government consults with those of England and France as to 
the immediate objects of the war, the progress of which tends to bring them 
nearer to those Powers, but without considering themselves in any way entitled to 
limit the conditions which our Governments inay consider themselves called upon 
to fix for the re-establishment of peace. 

The Austrian Government ask of those Powers, their allies, to point out the 
conditions which, according to their views, would now render the re-establish- 
ment of peace possible. Belore taking up arms the Austrian Government 
desire to know upon what conditions they may expect to be able to liy them 
down. But they clearly admit that the prolongation of the war would annul the 
basis which had been discussed between the three Powers, and established by 
the notes of the 8th of August. ‘They consider that the terms of peace must 
vary with the duration of the war. 

* These communications once exchanged between the three Governments, 
Austria will sign with England and France the Offensive and Defensive Treaty 
now proposed, and immediately afterwards, without mission from any of the 
parties engaged in the Treaty, in her own name alone, and, in consideration of 
the interests of the Empire which ean no longer accept the prolongation of the 
present state of tension, she will transmit to St. Petersburgh her final demands 
and summons. 

Upon their rejection by the Russian Government, Austria will break off her 
diplomatic relations with that Government, and the Treaty of Alliance fixes the 
date of the Ist of January, 1855, for the definitive settlement of the military 
arrangements and the cooperation and distribution of the respective forces for 
the ensuing campaign. 3 

Count Buol stated that he considered it necessary to make'a communica- 
tion to the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh as marking the date of the final resolution 
of Austria in passing from the menacing attitude she has hitherto maintained 
to that of belligerent, and 1 do not believe that any effort would have induced 
him to have abandoned this mode of proceeding. It is considered by the 
Austrian Government as the fulfilment of their efforts for the attamment of 
peace and the justification of their appeal to arms ; and Baron Bourqueney and 
myself were satisticd that any attempt to avoid the embarrassment these pre- 
vious communications may occasion to our Governments would certainly have 
been without success. 

[ distinctly pointed out, however, to Count Buol that no question could be 
addressed to our Governments upon the conditions of peace, without a simul- 
taneous engagement on his part to bind his Government by the signature of an 
offensive and defensive alliance, and that the completion of this Treaty eould 
in no way be made dependent upon the Russian reply to the Austrian summons, 
and that the signature should take place according to the form which had been 
agreed upon. 

With respect to the modifications which have been introduced in the project 
of Treaty, as it was transmitted to M. de Bourqueney and myself, Count Buol 
has adopted a form in Article IT relative to the Principalities, which has the 
advantage of placing the duties of Austria in connection with the means by 
which she would be enabled to carry them out, while our rights in the Princi- 
palities are expressly defined, and the freedom of the movements of the troops 
of England, of France, and of Turkey, is distinctly established. 

The most important modification, however, which has been introduced, is 
the substitution of the date of the end of the year for that of the Ist of April, 
for entering upon the deliberation without delay of the most effective means 
of obtaining the objects of the alliance, and the Seeret Article, which fixes for the 
beginning of next year the conclusion of the military arrangements.

(Signed) WESTMORLAND,

Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Recetved November 20.) 


(No. 170.) 
My Lord, Berlin, November 17, 1864. 


COUNT ESTERHAZY, the Austrian Special Envoy at this Court, commu- 
nicated on Sunday lust to Baron Manteuftel the answer of the Austrian Cabinet 
to the last Prussian note, with a copy of the instructions to be addressed to 
Baron Prokesch, and also a copy of a confidential despatch addressed to him by 
Count Buol. 

I have not yet seen these documents, but I am informed that their 
substance is as follows: 

Austria desires to suppress the phrase, “4 maintenir de tous les ebtés,'’ 
with reference to the acceptution of the four points. She wishes that the Diet 
shall declare their readiness to afford their aid without making it dependent on 
any question which might be raised by the Committee of the Diet. Anutria will 
communicate with Prussia and her allies previously to taking the offensive. 

But Austria reserves her liberty of action if the Western Powers should 
refuse to enter into negotiations on the four points, She will contract no 
obligatory engagements having for object their extension. On the contrary, she 
will use her best endeavours to support the four points. 

A simple assurance given by Russia of a desire to enter into negotiations on 
the four points, offers no sulficient guarantee for Austria, Russia must declare 
her acceptation of them in the most precise and positive manner, and the 
conclusion of peace ought to follow immediately, 

The Emperor of Austria cordially desires that the confidential communica- 
tion lately made by the Cabinet of Berlin to the Government of Russia may be 
attended with success. If they should be fruitless, His Imperial Majesty does 
not doubt of the assistance of Prussia in that contingency. 

Austria reserves to herself, under all circumstances, to confer with the 
Western Powers with respect to the answer from St, Petershurgh, and to learn 
their views before she takes any decision. She cannot guarantee that the 
Western Powers will not extend the conditions of peace, as she herself has 
reserved the right of making her own conditions in case of war. She cannot 
accept a forced neutrality: on this subject she has fully expressed her views in 
her note of the 6th August. 

She has given very wide instructions to M. de Prokesch : she hopes that 
Prussia, on her part, will do the same, 

_, Austria points out certain passages which might be omitted in the propo- 
sition to the Diet. For instance, it would not be necessary to say, “ when the 
Austrian territory shall be in danger ;" it might be said, “ when the Confederation 
shall be in danger.” . 

5 Q 


420 


In the confidential despatch of Count Buol to Count Esterhazy, it is stated 
that it is superfluous to add another Additional Article to the Treaty of Berlin, 
aa that Convention will suffice for the purpose required. The Austrian Cabinet 
will be satisfied with the confidential communications of the different Governments. 

The instructions to Baron Prokesch, to which reference is made at the 
commencement of this despatch, are the same as those of which your Lordship 
is already in possession. 

Count Esterhazy has informed me that these instructions will be sent to 
Baron Prokesch, with directions to communicate and concert, if possible, with 
AI. de Bismark Sch@nhausen. If the latter should propose any unimportant modi- 
fications, Baron Prokesch will apply to Vienna for further instructions ; but that 
“’ M. de Bismark refuses his cooperation, Austria will then take the course she 
has decided upon. 

Lhave, &c. 
(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS.

No. 423. 
Lord A, Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recewed November 204 


(No. 171.) 
My Lord, Berlin, November 17, 1854. 


THE Russian Minister, Baron Budberg, and the members of the Russian 
Legation here, were unable to repress the exultation in which they confidently 
indulged that a signal victory would be shortly obtained by Prince Menchikoff 
aver the allied armies in the Crimea. Baron Budberg expressed loudly on 
Sunday last his conviction that the English and French armies would be driven 
from the plateau before Sebastopol, and that there was no longer any danger to 
be feared for the fortress. 

On the evening of Sunday, Baron Budberg hastened to the Minister Pre- 
sident to communicate a despatch he had received through St. Petersburgh from 
Prince Menchikoff, stating that two sorties had been made on the Sth from 
Sebastopol; that they had been most successtul, and that an assault had been 
made by the French on the town, but vigorously repulsed, 

Your Lordship may imagine how completely disconcerted the Tussian 
party were, on the arrival here of General Canrobert's telegraphic despatch on the 
following Monday ; for they had fully hoped to gull the public for a certain time 
with their false reports. Asa last resource, they even denied the authenticity 
of General Canrobert’s despatch, saying that it had been fabricated at Paris. 

[am informed by a person who sees the onginal telegraphic despatches 
whieh arrive at the Russian Legation, that they are never published as they are 
received, and frequently are in direct contradiction to the original intelligence. 

I have the honour to incioce to your Lordship herewith, in original and 
‘a translation, an article which appeared in the official Prussian paper (the “ Cor- 
respondenz ”) written clearly under the impression that the siege of Sebastopol 
would be raised, intending to prove that the military honour of neither party 
was at stake, and that negotiations for peace might be resumed. As this article 
was evidently written under Ministerial inspiration, I have thought it of sufficient 
interest to bring to your Lordship’s notice.

[nclosure in No, 423. 
Extract from the “ Preussische Correspondens.”” 


(Translation.) 
Bastenn Avrains. 
SEVERAL papers are discussing the question, what influence the fall of 


Sebastopol will have on the diplomatic negotiations; and, according to their point 
of view, declare the success or failure of the expedition to be fatal to the hopes 


AT * oe Pe a a te is lam Tt ‘oe. 
LST Tt aL RE eo ee 


42 


of peace, as it would be a point of honour for the vanquished party to continue 
the war, ‘This discussion is futile, as the disputing parties are probably not 
aware of the intentions of the different Governmeuts, and also forget that other 
things, besides the siege of Sebastopol, come into consideration ; and, above all, 
beeanse their arguments are too partial. If, indeed, the military honour of the 
belligerent Powers was so closely concerned in the expedition, then a decision 
would make it impossible for one of the parties to commence negotiations of 
wace, 

Fortunately, the facts are different. The bloody events in the Crimea have 
wiven a favourable turn to the state of things. The daring and vast expedition 
against Sebastopol, whatever may be its result, will always form a bright episode 
in the military annals of England and France. The Battle of the Alma has 
vindicated the military fame of the allies; and the political position of the 
Western T’owers is rendered more free and independent, because they have now 
given effect to their alliance with the Porte and carried the war into the enemy's 
territory. ‘The deeds of the Russians are also worthy of honourable mention ; 
and even the fall of Sebastopol will not erase the fact that the Russian forces 
have fought well against the chosen troops of England and France. 

The point of honour, therefore, will not be affected on either side by the 
final fate of Sebastopol, and it is not in contradiction to eventual negotiations of 
peace, The question ts, on what basis they could be carried on so as not to 
appear at once hopeless, Certainly not on one which is simply dependent on 
the fortunes of war, and which every casual event would change ; for then the 
end of the struggle is only to be expected after the complete exhaustion of the 
mighty nations epposed to each other. On the other hand, the conditions of 
peuce which were proposed a few months ago by the Western Cabinets, which 
Austria accepted in a binding manner, und which Prussia has repeatedly sup- 
ported, are worthy of general attention. We cannot believe that the Porte and 
her allies, either by a partial success or by a momentary misfortune, could be 
brought to enter into the strange plan of a change of all the territorial arrange- 
ments of Europe, and to give up 4 programme which, in essence, affords good 
securities fora durable peace in the East. On the other hand, we have reason 
to believe that also the Russian Cabinet would at present be found more inclined 
to negotiate on proposals which they previously rejected, principally on grounds 
of formality. We are far from explaining this readiness as arising out of a real 
exhaustion or discouragement of Russia; but we see in it the woof that they 
have come to a conviction in St. Petersburgh, how Suivallable the basis 
proposed in the four points has become for an attempt to mediate, and how 
much, not only the attitude of the Western Powers, but also the position of the 
whole of Germany, depends on an agreement on this subject. 

The first result of the siege of Sebastopol appears to be only of secondary 
importance in the state of things which we have alluded to above, and the 
immense sacrifices which the conflict has entailed and will entail on both 
patties, will impart weight to the exhortation, that a solution of the question at 
issue will be attained more easily on the field of diplomacy than by arms.

No, 425. 
Lord A. Loftus to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved November 20.) 


(No. 176. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, November 17, 1854. 

ISTATED to your Lordship in my despatch No. 160 of November 10, 
that the text of the official answer of the imperial Cabinet to the Prussian note 
of the 22nd ultimo, had been received by this Government. I am now informed 
that the reply (which will be forwarded by the Russian Minister at this Court) 
has not yet been received, and that the intelligence to which I referred solely 
related to communications received from Baron Werther, who has only expressed 
his own opinion that the Emperor was disposed to accept the four points, 

I have been secretly informed to-day, however, that this Government is in 
receipt of indirect but positive information that the Emperor Nicholas will 
consent to accept the four points, and that Prussia will be charged to submit 
them to the Western Powers. 

Lam also given to understand that the Government here are very much 
embarrassed to know how to execute this commesion, and in what manner to 
convey the aeceptation of the Emperor of Russia to the allied Governments. 

n this subject 1 would venture to submit two observations to your 
Lordship, 

First, Prussia is very interested, as well as Russia, to prevent at this moment 
any aggressive action of Austria, and she will gladly eatch at any means afforded 
her to restrain a common hostile attitude on the part of Germany against Russia. 

Secondly. Prussia in her present isolated position will be anxious to secure 
herself a part and a position in any conferences or negotiations which might 
take place consequent on an acceptation of the four points by Russia. She will 
seck thereby to re-enter the European concert, and will avail herself of these 
means to prevent her exclusion at the conclusion of peace. 

T have likewise some suspicion that secret promises have been given by the 
King of Prussia to the Emperor Nicholas, that in the event of his acceptation, 
Prussia will do her utmost to further and promote his views on the resumption 


of negotiation. 
I have, &e. 


(Signed) AUGUSTUS LOFTUS.

Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 22.) 


(No. 654.) 
My Lord, Therapia, November 10, 1854. 


| RECEIVED Iast night from Reshid Pasha the two papers inclosed in 
copy herewith, one purperting to be a despatch addressed to that Minister by 
the Turkish Ambassador at Vienna, the other a translated instruction from your 
Lordship to Her Majesty's Agents and Consuls in Wallachia and Moldavia. 

T learn from this communication that, acting in concert with the French 
Cabinet, your Lordship purposes that all differences arising between the Austrian 
und Ottoman authorities, whether’ civil or military, in the two Prineipalitics, 
shall heneeforth be referred to Vienna, and submitted to the deliberation of a 
Commission composed of Count Buol, who will naturally preside, and of the 
inglish, French, and ‘Turkish Representatives there. 

Copy of M. Pisani’s report, communieating the papers in question, 18 also 
inclosed herewith. It appears from the language held to M. Pisamt by Reshid 
Pasha, that his Highness views with regret the measure thus announced, and 
not the less so because it has the appearance of being already definitively 
adopted. 

No official instruction has hitherto reached me on this subject. I feel 
myself, therefore, at liberty, as indeed it is my duty, to remark that the Porte, 
ulive to the captions proceedings of the Austrian authorities at Bucharest, 
‘formed of the overweening spirit exhibited on many occasions by the officers 
and soldiers under their command, and not unreasonably mistrustful of the 
policy of the Austrian Cabinet, when viewed through the medium of those 
proceedings, which, us there is strong reason to apprehend, have enabled the 
Russians to obtain reinforcements productive of a most heavy loss of life to the 
allies before Sebastopol. can hardly he expected to adopt the declared measure 
with confidence and satisfaction, Should Auf Effendi be instructed, us he 
probably will be, in the sense prescribed by the Karl of Westmorland under 
your Lordship’s instructions, the Porte’s compliance may be furly interpreted 
ag an act of submissive deference to the two belligerent Governments who have 
go just a claim to ber respect and gratitude. It can hardly fail of occurring to 
the ‘Turkish Ministers, as I confess it does to me, that the differences to be 
adjudged at Vienna, relate to matters which immediately concern a portion of 
the Sultan’s dominions, and take place within the circuit of his sovereign 
jurisdigtion, 

even with respect to Ter Majesty's Embassy, the proposed course of 
proceeding is new and anomalous. Her Majesty's Consuls in the Principalities 
have been hitherto in the habit of reporting to the British Iepresentative at 
Constantinople, as being-the eapital of that Empire, of which the Principalittes 
form an integral part ; and, with the eneral sanction of your Lordship’s office, 
they are Hable to be called upon fo act under his direct instructions. | faa not 
how far it may be intended to continue any relations at allofthis kind between the 
‘Turkish capital and the ‘Turkish provinees north of the Danube; but it ts 
evident, respecting that class of questions now vreferred to Vienna, that. the 
innovation if complete. 

In conclusion, your Lordship need hardly be reminded that hitherto the 
difficulties whieh it is proposed to remove by submitting them to a collective 
arbitration at Vienna, have not arisen 80 much out of contradictions between 
the ‘Turkish Government and its Agents, a8 from the inconsistency which has 
go remarkably prevailed on certain important points between the assurances of 
the Austrian Cabinet and the pretensions of the Austrian officers in Wallachia. 


Unhappily, too, for our impressions on the subject, these embarrassing 


407 


discrepancies have been allowed to subsist at a time when they tended manifestly 
to impede the operations of the Turkish army, and to afford the Russians an 
advantage from which they appear to have derived no little profit.

(Signed) | STRATFORD DE REDCLI PEE.

(Translation.) 


SINCE the entry into Wallachia of the Ottoman and the Austrian forces 
great dissensions have arisen between the Agents of those Powers at Bucharest, 
and it appears requisite that measures should be taken under these cireum- 
stances for framing regulations for defining the special duties of the Agents of 
all perties and of the Princes of those provinces. and for securing constant 
harmony and good understanding between them,as for preventing the recurrence 
of all discussions and difficulties in future. ‘The English and French Embassies 
at this place have therefore come to a joint decision with the Porte on the points 
which it would appear necessary to establish and define between the Sublime 
Porte, Great Britain, France, and Austria, respecting the two Principalities ; the 
assistance for prosecuting the war to be afforded by those provinces, as well as 


by Servia, if necessary, being comprised in that decision; and the chief inter- 


preters of the two Embassies having addressed a report to their respective chiefs

according to Treaty concluded with Austria in April last, was the object of the

No. 454, 
The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 
(No. 372.) 
My Lord, 


Foreign Office, November 22, 1854, 

COUNT COLLOREDO has read to me a despatch from Count Buol, 
stating that Baron Bourqueney and your Lordship had communicated to him 
the project of Treaty with Austria agreed upon by Her Majesty's Government 
and that of the Emperor of the French. . 

Count Buol remarks upon Article V, that to fix at this moment in a public 
Act the precise date at which Austria should conclude with the belligerent 
Powers all the arrangements for her active participation in the war, if peace 
should not previously be concluded, would be, in his opinion, to provoke Russia 
to anticipate the arrival of the period so fixed, by taking the initiative against 
Austria, cither at once, or whenever she may think it most for her advantage. 

Count Buol considers it, therefore, better thot this stipulation should he a 
Separate and Secret Article, a draft of which is transmitted. 

On the other hand, Count Buol proposes to modify Article V_ by fixing the 
end of the year, if it should not then be certain that peace will be speedily 
concluded, as the period for the mutual understanding with regard to the military 
arrangements, in case of Austria engaging in the war, instead of the month of 
April, which Count Buol thinks too distant for the objects intended. 

Tam, &e. | 
(Signed) CLARENDON, 


No. 435, 
The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland, 
(No. O73.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, November 22, 1854, 
YOUR Lordship's despatch No. 432 has been received and laid before the 
Queen, 

Count Colloredo yesterday communicated to me the project of a Treaty 
which Austria is prepared to sien with England and France, and he read to me a 
despateh from Count Buol announcing the course which the Cabinet of Vienna 
proposes to adopt. I have recorded the substance of that despatch in my 
No. 471 of this day’s date. 

Count Buol is well aware of the value and importance attached by Her 
Majesty's Government to the alliance of Austria, and you will assure his 
Lixcelleney that the prospect which now presents itself of her active cooperation 
Ing contest upon which the future destiny of Europe may depend, and which 
vitally affects the best interests of Austria, is the cause of sincere satisfaction to 
Her Majesty’s Government. 

_ Your Lordship states that the Austrian Government desires to know, and 
Count Buol in his despatch to Count Colloreda also inquires, what are the 
imimediate objects of the war, the progress of which tends to unite Austria with 
the maritime Powers, and what are the conditions upon which England and 
France would now consider the re-establishment of peace to be possible, and it is 
both prudent and reasonable that Austria before taking up arms should desire to 
know upon what conditions she may expect to lay them down; but as England 
and France, when they took up arms to defend the threatened independence of 
Turkey, entered into no engagement with each other asto the terms on which 
they would consent to make peace with Russia, and as Count Buol frankly 
idmité that the prolongation of the war would wnnul the bases which have been 
agreed to between the three Powers, and that the terms of peace must vary with 
the events of war, his Excellency will doubtless also admit the difficulty of 
giving # definite answer to his inquiry. 

Her Majesty's Government, however, have no wish for concealment. Their 
policy is disinterested, and their objects are those which concern Austria even 
5 U 


456 


more deeply than England and France, who, having exerted and exhausted every 
effort to maintain peace, were under the necessity of declaring war against a 
Power which menaced the existence of the Ottoman Empire; which forcibly 
occupied a large portion of the Sultan’s territory ; and converting into depen- 
jencies of its own the countries bordering on the Black =e, seriously endangered 
the balance of power in Europe. 

Tivseia assumed a@ supremacy Over the whole Greek Chureh, and based 
upon it a political protectorate over the Christian subjects of the Porte, in virtue 
of Treaties obtained by violence, and worded with inten ional ambiguity, 

Russia has injured European comments in the Black Sea, by obstructing the 
navigation of the Danube. Russia has erected a stupendous naval and military 
establishment at Sebastopol, and possesses a powerlul fleet, which, not being 
required to protect her commerce, or to guard against an cnemy, can only be 
intended for purposes of AgeresslOn, Russia has gradually transferred from 
Turkey to herself the allegianee of the Danubian Provinees ; and on the eastern 
shores of the Black Sea she seeks constantly to extend her power and influence. 
Such a state of things cannot exist without danger to the independence of 
Europe; and mo peace can he solid or lasting that is not founded upon effectual 

uarantees against its recurrence. 

Regarding such guarantecs as are contained in the four conditions of the 
notes of the 8th of August, Her Majesty's Government would not be indisposed 
fo enter upon negotiations on this basis, reserving to themselves the right to 
discuss their practical application, and to propose such further conditions as the 
events of war may render necessary, inthe same way that Austria has reserved to 
herself a similar right in the event of hostilities occurring between her and Hussin. 

Upon the question of territorial changes, if any such should hereafter arise, 
Her Majesty’s Government will be prepared to confer with the Governments of 
Austria and France, as the union which will then exist between the three 
Powers by the proposed ‘Treaty will impose upon them the obligation of 
frankly communicating their ‘ntentions to cach other. 

Her Majesty’s Government learn with regret that it ts the determination 
of the Austrian Government to make a farther a ypeal to Russia, which they 
apprehend will either be fruitless, oF be met with evasion for the purpose of 
defeating the objects which the three Powers have in view, but your Lordship 
will distinctly inform Gount Buol that Her Majesty's Government desire no such 
communication, and can be no parties to it; and that even if the Emperor of 
Russia were to consent without resety® to negotiate upon the terms proposed, it 
must be understood that the allied Powers are not thereby in any Wy bound to 
aurrec tO a suspension of arms during the progress of negotiations. 

Your Lordship will read this despatch to Count Bual, and inform his Excel- 
lency that you are empowered to sign the Treaty of which the project was 
communicated to me by Count Colloredo. 

Tam, &e. 


(Signed) CLARENDON.

Sir J; Milhanke to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 35.) 


(Na. 71.) 
My Lord, Munich, November 20, 1854. 

M. VON DER PFORDTEN has arrived here from Hohenschwangau, 
whither he had proceeded on the day following his return from Vienna, for the 
purpose of laying before the King the results of his double mission to that, and 
to the Prussian capital. 

Little has, as yet, transpired as to the real position of the different German 
States towards one another, but that little indicates a much stronger desire to 
come to a common understanding on this Eastern policy than has hitherto 
marked their conduct; and Iam told that the latest accounts, from Berlin in 
particular, afford fair ground for hope that the difference of opinion between the 
two principal Federal Powers, whieh has until now caused so much hesitation 
and delay, is about to disappear, and that they are in fact on the point of 
coming to ah agreement as to the terms and nature of the communication to be 
made to the Diet of Frankfort. ; 

As L have reason to believe that M. Von der Pfordten was unable to obtain 
from the Cabinet of Vienna any very essential concessions, | must presume tliat 
that communication will differ but little in substance from the despatch 
addressed by the per Cabinet to the President of the Diet a few weeks ago, 
and that consequently it will be ealled upon to declare that an attick upon 
Austrian, whether within her own frontiers or against her troops in the Danubian 
Principalitics, would impose on the whole of Germany the duty of aiding her by 
every means in its power; that the Germanic Confederation, a8 an European 
Power, recognizes the four preliminary pomts in substance, as calculated to 
serve os the busis of a peace which shall secure the rights of Europe, and os a 
German Power especially, identify itself with and hold to the first point; and 
that lastly, it should adinit the existence of the danger of attack, and acconlingly 
instruct the Military Commission, in virtue of the Convention of the 20th of 
April, to make such preparations as would, upon the demand being made, 
render possible the immediate employment of the forces of the Confederation ; 
whilst, at the sane time, the Political Committee should be authorized, in the 
event of their services being required, to propose in the proper quarter that the 
contingents should be actually called out, and placed in those positions which 
might be designated. Upon the nature of the support to be given to these 
propositions mainly turn the negotiations which are ut this moment actively 
carried on between all the German Cabinets, and everything [ hear on the 
subject loads me to conclutde that an understanding upon them, or something 
nearly approaching it, is not far distant. Up to the present time, however, 
this Government has not formally signified ils intention to adhere uncondition- 
ally to the policy of Austria on the Eastern question; but T cannot suppose 
that this important act will be much longer delayed, if any flith is to be put in 
the language of M. Von der Pfordten, who appears to have been so thoroughly 
converted at Vienna—whether from conviction or apprehension L will not stop 
to examine—that he now holds the pure and simple acceptance of the four 
points by Russia to be the unalterable groundwork of any arrangement to he 
ontered into with her on the part of the Confederation. | 

Now, if it were possible ut once to take advantage of the existing favourable 
dispositions of most of the minor German Cabinets, and have the question 
instantly brought before the Diet, some expectation might be reasonably indulged 
sn that the demands of Austria would be acceded to without much further dis- 
cussion; but il the negotiations between the Cubinets of Vienna and Berlin be 
protracted until the answer of the Emperor of Russia to the last Prussian 
appeal, which will in all probability be suseey tible of more than one interpreta. 
tion, shall reach Berlin, it can seareely be doubted, I think, that the Russian 
party, as well there as in other parts of Germany, will make fresh und strenuous 
tfforts once more to fan those embers of jealousy whieh appear to be inextin- 
ruishable on both sides, and thereby occasion much further delay, if not 4 tinal 
severance of apinion.

Lord Bloomfield to the [earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 27.) 


(No, 4723) 
My Lord, Berlin, November 24, 1854. 

| PAID my first visit, since my return, to Baron Manteuffel this day. His 
Excelleney appeared but little disposed to give any information which could 
enlighten me on the various negotiations said to be pending at Bertin, and 
ecemed desirous to give as few details as possible respecting these affairs, and 
evidently expected that I had been charged with communications which would 
force Prussia to take some decision, He was, therefore, areally relieved when 
he found that I had as little to say to him on public affairs as he had to 
communicate to me. 

Lasked his Excellency if it were true that Prussia and Austria had agreed 
as to the terms in which their next communications on the Eastern question 
would be made to the Dict itt Frankfort: he replied that it was so. Baron 
Manteutfel remarked, with reference to the four points which Russia ts said now 
necept as the basis for negotiation, that he thought something was to be done 
with them, and that Count Buol had communicated them to your Lordship. 
Lis Excellency said nothing more on the subject, seeming to feel that it was 
vecloss for him to urge the matter on the consideration of Her Majesty's 
Government, 

We conversed on the war in the Crimea, The Prussian Minister spoke of 
the hardships to which the British army were exposed, and expressed the highest 
sdmiration of their conduct; be alluded to the privations they had so cheerfully 
undergone; he spoke of the gallantry of. their conduct in unmistakeable terms : 
when [suid that England was truly proud of the brave men who had gone to 
fiht her battles in'so just a cause, and that Leould assure him it had been no 
crnull satisfiction to me, in leaving England a few days ago, 10 learn that my 
country fully appreeiated the conduct of our soldiers, and that the rapidity with 
which the recruiting wis going On, proved that there would be no want of men 
to tight our battles and to insure the suecess of our arms. I then asked his 
Excellency whether Prussia intended to continue in her passive condition ; that 
| presumed it could not be, for | was told that the Government was about to 


. ‘ > rT 1 tl 
daa a2 i 


441 


propose to the Chambers, at the opening of the sessions next week, the realisation 
of the other half of the loan for the mobilisation of part of the army. 

His Excellency replied that it was true that this money would be asked for, 
but he added that the King continued to be as averse to war as ever, and that 
His Majesty had but lately observed that he felt the greatest repugnance to take 
arms against Russia, #8 a campaign would of necessity commence in Poland, 
where friends and foes would be mixed together in undistinguishable masses. 

From all that fell from Baron Manteuffel in the course of this conversation 
it is clear that the opinions of this Court have not undergone the least change, 
and, indeed, | regret to hear that the language of persons about the Palace is as 
favourable to Russia as it ever has been.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 27.) 
(No. 474.) 


My Lord, Berlin, November 24, 1854. 

A COMMUNICATION has been made by Baron Budberg, the Russian 
Minister at this Court, to Baron Manteuffel, of a despatch from Count 
Nesselrode, conveying the reply of the Imperial Cabinet to the Prussian despatch 
cof the 22nd ultimo, I have the honour to inclose to your Lordship an extract 
of this document, in which the four conditions are laid down which the Russian 
Cabinet are ready to accept as the basis of negotiations. . 

In terminating the despatch to Baron Budberg, T am informed, from a 
private source, that Count, Nesselrode states that Russia has been induced to 
make these large concessions in furtherance of the wishes and interests of 
Germany, in whose welfare she feels so great a solicitude. Russia trusts that 
Germany will oppose any further extension of demands. that might be made on 
her; and she likewise expects that Germany will maintain a perfect neutrality. 
It is vaguely hinted that Russia has been induced to this pacific course by a 
wish to preserve those relations with the Cabinets of Vienna and Berlin which 
are so necessary to the peace and welfare of Germany, 

have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

TInclosure 1 in No. 449. 
Dervish Pasha to Reshid Pasha. 


(Translation. October 21, 1854, 

I HAVE already reported Prince 5tirbey’s arrival at Bucharest. “The 
moment he arrived he proceeded to devise the appointment of the Ministry, and 
broached the subject to me in order to feel his way. 

Having considered that if he appointed Ministers faithful to the interests of 
the Porte, the Porte would be able to carry into better effect hereafter anything 
now in contemplation with respect to this province, while it would be promotive 
of its prosperity, | commenced by stating that if he appointed Ministers from 
among the adherents of the Porte, he would confirm his devotion to the Porte, 
and would create a favourable change in public opinion with respect to himself; 
and I gave him some advice on the subject. But the Prince, nevertheless, made 
frivolous excuses with reference to the individuals put forward by me—that 
some were incompetent, from want of sufficient capacity, to fill office; and that 
others were not of sufficient rank to hold high office, 

I inclose a list, to your Highness, of individuals, with notes to cach name, 
by which it will appear that the Prince accepted only two of the persons put 
forward by me, and made the ether selections and appointments himself. 1 
inclose likewise a return, drawn up in French, of the individuals proposed by 
me: of those whom the Prince was desirous of appointing; and of those whom 
he has now appointed.

Inclosure 4 in No. 449. 
Dervish Pasha to Reshid Pasha. 


(‘Transiation.) October 21, 1854. 

I INCLOSE to your Highness the copy of a memorandum drawn up by Count 
Coronini, and sent to the Commission, composed of Austrian officers and Boyars, 
for making the necessary arrangements for lodging and supplying the Austrian 
forces in the Principalities, in order that it might be discussed therein, It will 
appear by that memorandum that it is demanded that the lodgings, stabling, 
candles, wood, hay, beds and bedding, and other furniture, &e,, required for the 
‘Austrian soldiers, officers, and horses, should be supplied gratis by the inhabi- 
tants. Although this question has not been decided yet, the demand is in 
opposition to the proclamation just issued by me, and will cause & eommotion 
among the inhabitants. IT will continue to keep your Highness informed on this 
subject, having stated thus much for your information.

Inclosure 5 in No. 449. 
Omer Pasha to the Grand Vizier. 


( Translation.) October 21, 1854. 

AS most of the Wallachian authorities—perhaps all of them—are Russian 
partisans and traitors to the Porte, Dervish Pasha sought to change them 
through Prince Stirbey, and haying approved of some of the men in office at 
Bucharest, they were appointed. ‘The Prince, disregarding the Pasha's opinion, 
appointed others conformably with his own, and made changes. Some were 
confirmed in office, and however much the Pasha endeavoured to have them 
changed, it was decided that they should be confirmed in office, as there were 
no other suitable persons to take their place. Dervish Pasha reported me the 
above information, and added, that out of respect to Prince Stirbey, and not to 
give him eause of offence, he had approved of the appointment of his brother- 
in-law, as “ Postelnik” for Affairs. it would have been more appropriate if all the 
appointments had been made with the Pasha's sanction; he states that the 
“Ispetar Herisco, the Head of Police, and the Comptroller Otodelasiaus, who were 
confirmed in office, being notoriously Russian partizans, it was highly expedient 
that. they should be dismissed, and would be also advantageous to the Prince. 
Dervish Pasha went again to the Prince, and:spoke to him on the subject, and 
Stirbey called on me yesterday, and opened the conversation by sa ing that he 
hewmed 1 would not be hostile to him, but be his sineere friend. said, if the 
Prince would change the Ministers who surrounded him, and those in the 
districts who were known partizans of Russia, and appoint honest men ani 
well-wishers to the Porte in their place, | would be his best friend, but if he 
confirmed them in office 1 could not be friendly towards him. 

The Prince replied, “ Yes, the Ministers have been changed, but as there 
was no one fit to fill the office of * Spathar,’ Head of Police and Contréleur, who 
have been confirmed, you choose some one, and we will change them.” 

I proposed that as there was no one capable of filling the otlice of Head 
of the Police, that as it would not be suitable unless all those who came forward 
fiom among the army could be distinguished from each other, and that none 
of them could be appointed, as they were avowed Russian partisans, his son in 
Paris bein young, with the rank of Colonel, belonging to no party, neqnainted 
with the high position which the Porte held in| European estimation, should be

The Prince replied that his son knew that all he possessed was acquired 
under the auspices of His Majesty, and he hoped his son would render good

educated, that it required another half-year to eomplete that ohject, that it

| observed to the Prince that 1 was of the same opinion, but that it was not 
requisite to recall his son now, that the lace might be held by deputy. 

The Prince returned an unfavourable answer. Having appointed one of 
the Colonels of the Wallachian Militia to be “ Viee-Postelmk” for A fairs, however 
unworthy to fill that office, he may be sail to be the best of the lot, that is, he 
las done less misehicl than the others, and | therefore assented to his appoimt- 
aent, ‘The Controleur Otodelashius is every bad mun, but this does not exactly 
come under my competency. Dervish Pashn 1s, moreover, conducting matters 
very ably, and these things can be looked to later without entering now into 
trivial discussions. Our dispute was therefore brought to a close here, and we 
shall ly degrees come to the settlement of more important matters still. 

With reference to my despatch of the 88th Septeniber, and to your 
Highness’ reply, requiring the enrolment and services of a body of Watliehian 
volunteers, | discussed the means of carrying this into operation with the Prinee. 
He observed that, if the volunteers were to be enrolled now, it would require a 
long time to assemble and drill them properly, 

I replied that the real object of the Porte, in incurring the burden of this 
war against Russia, was to save the two Principalities from Russian occupation 
and seeure the repose of the people; that it was clear that this object was 
attained, and that as the people, sensible of the humane and upright rule of 
their legitimate Sovereign, were anxious to show their devotion and tender their 
serviees to the Porte, he, the Prince, ought also to evince his attachment and 
veal in this matter, I said, if other troops were levied, the Wallachian militia, 
who had completed their period af service, might be called under arms, and that, 
by adding them to the 5,000 troops now under arms, it would constitute a body 
of 10.000 men; that is, twelve battalions of Totuntry, and two regiments of 
Cavalry, forming one division, That | would then ask the Porte to grant me a 
battery of Horse Artillery and two of Foot Artillery ; that the “ Dorobacey ” and 
a body of select police could look to internal order, and the division in question 
he employed wherever the Porte thought proper. 

The Prince agreed to this plan, and we both decided that it should be so. 
With reference to the clothing, arms, and other necessaries for the troops to be 
o called under arms, and for other incidental expenses, it was agreed that the 
raonasteries here, which possess. cnormous wealth and revenues, should contri 
bute ta their assistance. It was slso thought desirable that some of the sons of 
the nobility who were volunteers should be joined to the army with the rank of 
Knsign und Captain, which was approved by me. 

If this scheme meet with your Highness’ approbation, and His Majesty the 
Sultan's sanction; if Prince Stirbey keeps to his word, and has not been deceiv- 
ing me with idle talk, and holds firm te the execution of the project, it might 
he undertaken in due time, and completed in early spring. 1 request to have 
your Highness’ orders with reference: to discussing the raising of a similar 
division in Moldavia with those authorities. 

If His Majesty approves of these two divisions being raised and organized, 
they might he anited to a division of Ottoman troops, and placed all three 
ander the command of a Mushir at one’ plice, and ieapleved wherever 
required, 

Although Abdi Pasha, ex-Mushir of the army of Anatolia, was not const. 
dered fitting for that command, the disorders which ensued there arose rather 
ont of a want of harmony among the subordinate officers, than out of any igno- 
rance on the part of Abdi Pasha, There is nothing to be said against him as an 
officer ind engineer, and he might be advantageously employed. If His Majesty 
upproved of t, the three divisions in question might be placed under Abdi 
Pasha’a command, and attached to my army.

sugeestions ta their most serious and immediate attention. 

Later portions of the same correspondence have heen conveyed ina similar 
form and with similar recommendations to the Seraskier Pasha and his 
colleagues. 

Lam assured by M. Pisani that, on the side of the ‘Turkish Ministers, there 
is every appearance of a sincere intention to comply with my demands, As soon 
as I um eatisticd that the supplies are actually sent, and orders corresponding 
with the suggestions of Colonel Williams issued in stringent terms, I shall not 
fail to apprize your Lordship of so gratifying « result. 

The subject being now relicved of much superfluous and exaggerated 
matter, the course is made clearer to Turkish apprehension; and T trust that 
the experience of last year, which certainly was painful enough in its most 
reduced proportions, will have its effect in contributing to the suecess of my 
endeavours, grounded on the strenuons exertions of Colonel Williams, and aided 
hy the pecuniary supplies derived from the loan, 

I have, &e.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 28.) 


(No. 1,425.) 
My Lord, Paris, November 27, 1854. 

WITH reference to your Lordship’s despatch No. 1,142 of the 93rd instant, 
inclosing copies of two despatches from Her Majesty's Ambassador at Constan- 
tinople, relative to the means proposed by the Porte for preventing future dis 
agreements In regard to the administration of the Principalities, and to the 
proceedings of the Commanders of the Austrian and Turkish troops, and desir- 
ing me to ascertain what instructions the French Government proposed to give 
upon the subject, I have the honour to state that M, Drouyn de Lhuys coincides 
in the opinion expressed by your Lordship in the same despatch that the Com- 
missioners at Vienna should not be unduly interfered with, | 

His Excellency proposes instructin M. Benedetti to inform the Porte that 
they have mistaken the objects which the three Governments had in view in 
desiring to establish, in concert with the Ottoman Government, a Commission or 
Board at Vienna; that there was no intention of discussing any question con- 


cerning the sovereignty of the Sultan, or the admiuistration of the Principalities ; 


nor, indeed, any other desire but that of facilitating the operations of the war by 
rectifying any misunderstandings that might arise between the Generals com- 
manding the Austrian and Ottoman forces, and that this could be more easily 
accomplished at Vienna than at Constantinople. ; 
I have, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

The Karl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 


(No, 382.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, November 28, 1854. 

COUNT COLLOREDO has read to mea despatch addressed by Count 
Ruol to the Baron de Bruck, respecting the position of the Hospodars of 
Wallachia and Maldavia, and the causes of complaint which the Porte has 
against them. , A 

Count Buol states that he is far from intending to advocate the cause of 
those Princes, and he declares that Austria has no other wish than to sce the 
administration of the Principulities confided to men of ability who are worthy 
of the Sultan’s confidence ; but his Excellency expresses a hope that the pro- 
ceedings against Prince Strbey will be con ucted in w spirit of justice and 
impartiality, and that the report of the Turkish Commissioner will be communi- 
eated to the Austrian Government. oa : | 

Count Buol further expresses a hope, that if upon this subject, as well as 


upon other questions concerning the affairs of the rincipalities, an agreement 


camot be obtained at Constantmople, the Porte will not object to refer them to 
the Commission at Vienna. p~*. 

| thanked Count Colloredo for this communication, and again told him my 
reasons for thinking that the return of Prince Stirbey to his former government 
waa an unfortunate event for the Principalities, and | took the liberty of strongly 
recommending that he should not be upheld by the Austrian Government, if the 
report of the Turkish Commissioner was adverse to him. 


457 


1 said that all matters connected with the Austrian occupation of the 
Principalities and the requirements of the Austrian army, might with advantage 
be referred to the Commissioners at Vienna; but that the case was different 
when a question arose so nearly affecting the sovereign rights of the Sultan as 
the deposition of a Hospodar and the appointment of his successor, and that a 
settlement of such questions elsewhere than at Constantinople could not be 
attempted without impairing the power and lowering the dignity of the Sultan. 


ain, ec, 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

No, 453. 
The Karl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


(No. 750.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, November 29, 1654. 

I HAVE weeived your Excellency’s despatch No. 677 of the 15th instant, 
in which you report the steps taken by you to call the atten tion of the Porte to 
the suggestions offered by Colonel Williams for the improvement of the Turkish 
army at Kars. 

I have to state to you that I approve of your proceedings in this 
matter, and that Her Majesty's Government hope that measures will be taken for 
at length abandoning the systematic neglect with which the army at Kars bas been 
treated, and of which up to this moment no explanation has been received by 
Her Majesty’s Government. 

Her Majesty's Government place entire confidence in the reports of Colonel 
Williams, and when they find that the most shameless robbery existed in cvery 
department ; that the soldiers were deprived of their proper rations, because their 
officers cheated them; that even on the 25th of October, the authorities at 
Frzeroom were issuing daily 35,000 rations for a force that does not exceed 
14,000 men: that the hospitals were generally in a miserable condition, the 
medicines of the worst or most useless kind, the surgeons who knew something 
of their profession rejected for men who knew nothing ox it, but had bought their 
places 5 that Zarif Pasha is now leaving his command gorg with plunder; that 

hitual and notorious drunkenness prevailed amongst the officers to such an 
extent as to invite the enemy to surprise the army ; that the soldiers were with- 
out proper elothing or shoes; that the cauldrons in which their food was cooked 
were in such a state as to render it poisonous; that the muster-rolls ex ceeded 
wreatly, often one half, the numbers really present ; and Instly, when there is 
reason to believe that nearly 18,000 men perished last year through the want af 
ordinary care and precautions, Her Majesty's Government cannot consider that 
there has been any superfluous or exaggerated matter in the reports which have 
reached them during the last twelve months, and respecting which they have so 


often and ineffvctually remonstrated with the Turkish Government. 


Iam, &e 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

Inclosure 1 in No, 455. 
The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon. 
( Telegraphic.) Vienna, November 16, 1804, 
WE received by a telegraphic message this morning the letters of Omer 
Pasha and Count Coronint of the 6th and 9th instant, as to the movements of 
the Turkish troops towards Bessarabia. Although they were transmitted to us 
without any remark by the Consul-General Mr. Colquhoun, M. de Bourqueney 
and myself immediately waited upon Count Buol to inquire of him what was 
meant by the expressions of Count Coronini, which appeared to indicate that the 
road to Foxchani had been refused to Omer Pasha. 


Count Buol assured us that that road not only had not been refused to the 


Ottoman troops, but that a feeropnle despatch just arrived announced that 
those troops, to the number of 10,0 


Omen, were traversing Foxchuani. 

As to the terms of the letters of Count Coronini they were only the 
repetition of the instructions sent from Vienna, which had recorded the adherence 
of the Austrian Government to the original demands of Omer Pasha, and which 
for all further reclamation indicated the Commission of Vienna as the authority 
to be referred to. Omer Pasha has addressed no complaint to his Ambassador,

(Telegraphic.) Vienna, November 20, 1854. 

COUNT BUOL has received a communication this day from Count 
Esterhazy from St. Petersburgh of the 17th, by telegraph, which announces that

Buol, who was anxious that you should not remain uninformed of this news 
from himself, although he does not attach much importance to it. Count Buol 
stated distinctly that he did not consider this communication ought in any 
way to interrupt the negotiations proceeding between our Governments.

The Karl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 27,) 


(No. 440.) 
My Lord, Vienna, November 22, 1854. 
IN compliance with the instructions contained in your Lordship’s desputeh 
No. 858 of the 14th instant, I asked Count Buol whether any wish had been 
expressed by the Turkish Government that Austria should contribute to the 
repression of the Montenegrins, and whether there would be any objection on his 
part to fulfil this wish if it should be found to be desirable so to do. Count 
Buol stated that he liad no reason to oppose this wish, exeept from the principle 
that it was not desirable to oceupy the territory of a neighbouring State without 
a proved necessity for such a measure. He believed that in some of the late 
transactions upon the Turkish and Montencgrine frontiers, there had been faults 


committed on both sides, and for his own part he had not failed to point out 


continually to the Prince of Montenegro the expediency of his remaining on good 
terms with the Government of the Porte. The Austrian Government, he said, 
had lately furnished the Pasha of Scutari with some ammunition which he 
required, and froin the recent reports which he had received from those countries 
he was in hopes that the disturbances which had existed on their frontiers had 
now ceased,

Brigudier- General Du Plat to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received November 27.) 


(No. 10.) 
My Lord, Vienna, November 18, 1854. 


THE so oft reported “retreat behind the Piliea ~ on the part of the 
Russian troops stationed in the Kingdom of Poland, which supposed fact has, 
for some time past, played so prominent a part in the journalistic argumentations 
upon the real present state of the political relations between the Courts of 
‘Austria and Russia; that supposed fact, | say, 1 looked upon by military men 
hore us of no real military importance, even if it were certain that it had taken 
place, the less so, as not the slightest intimation has ever been given of any corre- 
sponding retreat from the Austrian frontier on (he left of the Russian position, 
between the Vistula and the Bug. But, | believe, the fact is, no retrograde 
movement whatsoever on the part of the Russians has been made, 

In the official statement of the distribution and strength of the Russian forces 


—————————— 


461 


generally, which has been recently given tome, and of which Tsent your Lordship 
(in my letter No. 9 of the 15th instant) a partial abstract relating to the Crimea, 
the foree under Paskiewitch's command is mentioned at 180,214 men, with 472 
cuns, including 45,400 men and 56 guns newly formed reserves: 17,504 men, 
with 64 guns, of this total force are stationed in the Baltic Provinces, leaving in 
the Kingdom of Poland Proper, for active operations, 120,810 men, with 306 
cuns ; 28,710 men, with 100 pieces of Artillery, form the centre of the present 
dislocation of this foree, with head-quarters at Warsaw ; 27,800 men, with Ub 
runs, form the left wing between the Bug and the Pilica, with the head-quarters 
at Lublin; and 28,900 men, with 10+ guns, the right of this. position between 
the Vistula and the Prussian frontiers, with head-quarters at Radom, a town 
still considerably in advance of the Pilea towards the Austrian frontier; and 
the accompanying very detailed exposition of the distribution of every part of the 
whole force will show that the extreme advanced Russian outposts towards the 
most vulnerable part of the Austrian frontier are still at Olkutz, Michalowiee, 
and Czentochow. In short, the only real:symptoms of a desire on the Her 
of Russia to assume a less menacing attitude towards Austria is the halt of 
the Guards on their march, although the Emperor had so  ostentatiously 
informed Count Esterhazy that these troops “ furent expédi¢es 4 Vadresse directe 
de Autriche,” 

The extreme minuteness of the details given in the Austrian statement 
induces me to believe that they have excellent sources of information on the 
subject of the real strength of the Russian army, it least in such parts as come 
in contact with their own frontiers; nor is it surprising that such should be the 
case, considering the great stake the Austrians themselves now have in the 
question, and the comparative facility they possess, through the similarity of the 
idioms spoken by the inhabitants of the limitraph provinces of the two States for 
acquiring such information. 

I beg leave, therefore, to point out to your Lordship on this occasion that 
the strength of the Guards destined for Poland ts stated at only 28,780 men, 
with 104 guns; whereas, in almost every other report emanating fram con- 
tinental authorities, I have seen it estimated at nearly double, nay, im some, 
at almost three times that amount, . 

Including these Guards at the figure just stated, and the troops, principally 
Cavalry, amounting to 5,440 men, with 1G guns, in Volhynia near Sutzh; 
besides the foree in Podolia of 7,880 men, with 32 guns (all of which your Lord- 
ship will find detailed with great precision in my inclosure), the total force of 
Paskiewitch amounts to 180,214 men, with 572 guns. “The whole of the reserves, 
[ perceive, is allotted to the fortresses, and these troops cannot, therefore, be 
supposed to be ina very effective state, Moreover, I observe, that such garrisons 
are sent lack as far as Gobowick and Vilna, and that, therefore, this very great 
position of Paskiewitch’s present army is not very aviilable for aggresive 
purposes, It is also of great importance to our own and our allies’ interests in 
the Crimea, and in the south of Russia generally, to know that Paskiewiteh hus 
declared he cannot spare a single man if he is to be expected successfully to 
maintain his position against the preparations and demonst rations which Austria 
has already effected along the whole line of the Russian frontier, 

In another part of the repeatedly mentioned Austnan statenient of the 
Russian forces, it appears also that Count Ostensacken (with his head-quarters ut 
Kicheneff) has in Bessarabia 44,720 men, with 120 guns, composed of the Gth, 
Sth, and 9th Divisions of Infantry, the 4th Light Cavalry Division, and of the 
battalion of Sappers and of Sharpshooters belonging to his own corps, besides three 
pulks of Cossacks, Further it is mentioned that General Liders on the Lower 
Danube, with head-quarters at Ismail, has the 7th, bOth, and 15th Divisions of 
Infantry, the Srd and Sth Light Cavalry Divisions, the oth Sharpshooters and 
ith Sapper battalions, besides eight pulks of Cossucks, under his Goma, aud 
composing a force of 40,240 men, with 180 pieces of Artillery.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received November 29.) 


(No. 1,429.) 
My Lord, Paris, November 28, 1854. 
M. DROUYN DE LHUYS has reecived a telegraphic despatch of the 24th 
instant, from Bucharest, announcing that the allied Commanders in the Crimea 
had written to request Omer Pasha to send 90,000 of his best troops to Varna, 
to hold themselves in readiness to embark for the Crimea. Under these 
circumstances M, Poujade inquires whether he 1s to support this demand, or 
to continue to evgage Omer Pasha to advance towards the Pruth. He alludes, 
at the same time, to fresh difficulties raised by Generals Coronini and Augustin 
to the advance of the Ottoman army, force even having been talked of to 
event it In transmitting this despatch to M. Drouyn de Lhuys, M. de 
Jourqueney adds, that whatever decision the Freneh Government may take, he 
hopes that it will not be influenced by the upp ot hostility of the Austrian 
Generals to the advance of Omer Pasha's army, for that he ean affirm that the 


M, Antonini, the Neapelitan Minister, thought proper to place this state- 
ment of Count Nesselrode before M. Drouyn de Lhuys in the form of a memo- 
randum, and to press him for an answer upon it. 

His Excellency stated to M. Antonini this morning, that although he had 
not been able to take the Emperor's orders, he might at once reply that this was 
not the first attempt made by the Russian Government to engage Franee in a 
separate negotiation to terminate the Eastern question, but that it wolild be 
well for Connt Nesselrode to understand that any overtures for peace which he 
might think it expedient to make must be addressed simultaneously to the 
Governments of France, Great Britain, and Turkey; that any such overtures, 
however, to command success, must be far more explicit than that now made ; 
and that he (M, Drouyn de Lhuys) was convinced that the whole object of the 
Russian Government in making it was to gain time, and prevent the continua- 
tion of hostilities while the state of the roads in Russia rendered the passage of 
troops and ammunition difficult. 

I said to M. Drouyn de Lhuys that I saw from his answer that he consi- 
dered the Neapolitan Minister to have been authorized to make a communication
