No. 466. 
The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 30.) 


(No. 441.) 


My Lord, Vienna, November 26, 1854. 

YOUR Lordship will have learnt by my telegraphic despatch of this day, 
that a meeting took place yesterday evening at Count Buol’s, upon the report 
made by the French Consul at Bucharest of the conduct of General Augustini. 
I will now give your Lordship a more detailed account of what took place, 

Count Buol, after inquiring of the Turkish Ambassador if any complaint had 
reached him from Omer Pasha, and, being answered in the negative, asked 
General Hess if he had any reason for believing that General Augustini had (as 
reported by M. Poujade) addressed a letter to Omer Pasha refusing to permit the 
Turkish troops to pass the Sereth, and even threatening to oppose the attempt 
to do so. 

General Hess replied that he had not heard of such a letter, and that tt 
appeared to him that it could not have been written, for, in the first place, he 
had notice that the Turkish troops had passed the Sereth; next, the orders he 
had transmitted to Count Coronini were, to give up the whole country from 
Galatz to Formosa for the offensive operations Omer Pasha had announced his 
intention of undertaking against Bessarabia. Consequently, General Augustini’s 
interference would be in direct opposition to those orders; and, thirdly, he 
(General Hess) had just received a report from Count Coronini, announcing that 
he had been in communication with Omer Pasha as to his passage through 
Formosa and his advance upon the Pruth, between the mouth of that river and 
Formosa. General Hess detailed the orders he had given to Count Coronini, and 
stated that he conceived that by the arrangements he had made, as to the passage 
into Bessarabia, he had met every wish Omer Pasha had expressed, namely, to 
have a free passage from Ibraila through Galatz to the Pruth. He added, that 
should Omer Pasha wish now to enter Bessarabia on any other point, and would 
transmit his wish through the Ambassador in Vienna, he (General Hess) would 
make such arrangements for his own troops as would be required to facilitate it. 
The Turkish Ambassador stated he had not received any notice of a desire of 
Omer Pasha's to that effect, 

Baron Bourqueney and myself both represented that if such a letter as 
M. Poujade reported had been written by an Austrian Commander, it was in 
direct opposition to all which had been repeatedly declared to us by Count Buol, 
and which we had in full confidence and on his authority transmitted to our 
Governments. We therefore accepted the assurances now given by himself and 
General Hess, and | most strongly urged the censure which should mark the 
conduct of any Anstrian officer using language for which he eould not have 
received any authorization, 1 also took the opportunity of animadverting upon 
the letter by which Count Coronini announced to Omer Pasha the arrangements 
proposed by General Hees for the attack on Bessarabia, of which I had seen a 
copy. | stated that I could not but regret the tone in which it was written, 
which was anything but conciliatory, and I warmly urged the necessity of 
instructing all the Austrian Generals to use in their communications with Omer 
Pasha more courteous language, and to conform themselves to the spirit of 
friendly cooperation which existed between the four Governments and which 
characterized our present meeting. 

It was then decided that General Hess should transmit M. Poujade's report 
to General Augustini, and should it appear that it was grounded on thet, we need 
not doubt its complete disavowal by the Imperial Government. 

L have, &e. | 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND,

Kirst. The Protectorate hitherto exercised by the Imperial Court of Russia 
over the Principalities of Wallachia, Maldayia, and Servia, shall cease for the

on their Empire be placed under the collective guarantee of the Powers, in virtue

dispositions should, ut the same fine, resulate all cjuestions ot detail. 

The guarantee of the Powers, whieh it is proposed to substitute for the 
Protectorate of Russia in Wallachia, Moldavia, and Servia, differs widely from 
the system under which those provinces have of late years suflered, "The object 
is to guarantee the privileges which have been granted to them by the Sultans, 
torether with other rights which it may be desirable to extend to them; and 
this object is European, and is sought for in the same spirit that dictated the 
notes of August 8; for it is manifestly a European interest to create upon the 
Danube a barrier against Russian encroachments; but it is not by foreign 

Proteatorates, it is not by a renewal of tho ‘Treaties of Jossy, Bucharest, 
Ackerman, and Adrianople, that Governments possessing freedom of action cin 
be established, or the Prath again become the boundury of Russia, instead of 
the Danube, to which of late years her power and influence have in reality been 
extended, 

Secondly. Unless the navigation of the Danube to its mouths be freed from 
all obstacle, and subjected to the application of the principles recorded in the 
Acts of the Congress of Vienna.

Thirdly. Unless the Treaty of 1841 be revised in concert by all the High 
Contracting Parties in the interest of European equilibrium. . 

The object is to give effect to the policy of the Powers who signed the 
‘Treaty of 1841, which is recorded in its preamble, and thereby to carry out the 
intentions announced in the notes of August 6, to attach the existence of the 
Ottoman Empire to the general system of Europe. It is intended that the 
maritime preponderance of Russia in the Black Sea shall cease; that political 
and commercial agents shall there, as clsewhore, be established ; and that the 
vast military and naval establishments of Russia, which could only be required 
for purposes of agyression, shall no longer endanger the existence of Turkey nor 
menace the peace of Europe. 4 

Fourthly. Unless Russia abandons her claim to exercise an official Pro- 
tectorate over the subjects of the Sublime Porte, to whatever rite they may 
belong; and Austria, France, Groat Britain, Prussia, and Russia, mutually 
eoneur to obtain, by the initiation of the Ottoman Government, the recognition, 
vatablishment, and observance of the religious privileges of the several Christian 
communities, and turn to account, for the common interest, the generous 
intentions manifested by His Majesty the Sultan, without injury to his dignity 
or the independence of his Crown. 

The intention of the three Powers 1s clearly expressed in this Article, and 
requires no further elucidation; but in order to give full effect to 1t Her Maj esty's 
Government are of opinion that, as all Treaties between Russia and the Porte 
have been annulled by war, the stipulations of the Treaty of Kainardji, and of 
other Treaties inconsistent with these bases, must not be renewed, Tt was by 
giving to the Treaty of Kainardji an interpretation that it did not bear, that the 
Emperor of Russia claimed a right of Protectorate over the Greek subjects of 
the Porte that no Sovereign could submit to without a complete abdication of 
his independence ; a pretension which, as is well known, would have enabled the 
Emperor of Russia to ‘iterfere between the Sultan and his subjects in temporal 
as in spiritual affairs, to arrest the progress of improvement, and in effect to 
exercise a power in the Sultan's dominions which the Sultan himself does not 
possess. 

'The Sultan has already given proofs of his enlightened desire to meet the 
views of the Christian Powers, and it will be their duty to aid him by their 
counsels, to procure the redress of acknowledged wrongs, and to prepare the 
way for a system which shall place under the same laws the people of different 
origin and creeds who now co-exist in Turkey, 

Having now explained the manner ‘1 which the bases of negotiation con- 
tained in the notes of the 8th of August are regarded by Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment, it only remains for me to add that Her Majesty's Government have every 
reason to believe that their views are in accordance with those of the Cabinet of 
Vienna; and it will be to them a-cause of much satisfaction if, on reading this 
despatch to Count Buol, your Lordship should find that there do not exist any 
important points of difference between the two Goren

No. 469. 
The Eurl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 


(No, 389.) 
My ford, Foreign Office, November 30, 1854. 


WITH reference to your Lordship's telegraphic despatch of the 26th instant, 
and Mr, Colquhoun’s a Ue Nu. 97, which. passed through your Lordship’s 
hands under flying seal, | have to inform your Lordship that Her Majesty's 
Government have learnt with pain and surprise that a determination to obstruct 
the movements of the Turkish army appears to exist on the part of the Austrian 
Generals. Explanations have been repeatedly asked of the Austrian Govern- 
ment, assurances have been received that na such intention existed, and Her 
Majesty’s Government cannot doubt that orders in conformity with such 
assurances were duly sent, although they appear to liuve been invariably 
disregarded. 

The question, however, 1s one of serious importance, and it must he 
definitively solved, for it not only involves the good faith of Austria, but effects 
the operations of the allies in the Crimea. 

The army of Omer Pasha has, for several months remained inactive, and it 
was the desire of the Porte, of the English and French Governments, and of the 
Commanders-in-chief of the allied forces, that a diversion should be made by 
the Turkish army, and that an offensive movement towards Bessarabia should 
serve to check the sending of the reinforcements which the Russians have poured 
into the Crimea; but so far from this movement having been assisted, as it was 
natural to expect, by the Austrian Generals while occupying a portion of the 
Sultan's territory, and bound by Treaty to defend it against the Sultan's chemy, 
it hag been absolutely prevented; and so lately as the 9th mstant, General 
Coronini informed Omer Pasha, when about te eross the Pruth, that he was not 
authorized to let the Turkish troops pass beyond a prescribed limit, while more 
recently General Augustini ‘s said to have forbidden their mdvanee beyond the 
Serethi. A signal service has thus been rendered to the Emperor of Russie by the 
Austrian Goverment, and a disservice has been done to the allies that is hardly 
to be distinguished from an act of overt hostility. 

The possibility of such a course being adopted by Austria, was foreseen by 
Her Majesty's Government, and stated to your Lordship in my despatels 
No. B01, and it was distinctly disavowed by the Austrian Government, as 
reported in your despatch No. 962: and Her Majesty’s Government have now 
therefore an additional claim to ask for a frank explanation of the intentions af 
Austria. Your Lordship will therefore request Count Buol to state on what 
ground and by virtue of what right the movements of the Turkish army have 
been obstructed, whether precise orders will be given to the Austrian Generals 
not in any way to interfere with the operations of Omer Pasha, and whether the 
General who disobeys these orders will be immediately recalled.

I may also observe that this Additional Article contains the two points for 
which Austria has been long striving to obtain the concert of Prussia ; viz., the 
aceeptation of the four points as the basis for future negotiations of peace ; and, 
secondly, the promise of suecour if her armies were attacked in the Prin- 
cipalities. 

No reference is made to the event of Austria taking the offensive, nor has 
Prussia renewed her desire that Austria should bind herself not to exceed 
the demands made on Russia in the four points. 

The concessions, therefore, made by Austria, to Prussia are of a real and 
substantial nature; wherens Austria has merely ceded, in a matter of form, in 
agreeing to a second Additional Article to the Convention of the 20th April, in 
lieu of a simple exchange of confidential notes. 

This matter of form is, however, of some importance to Prussia, more par- 
ticularly at this moment, on the approaching meeting af the Chambers. The 
signature of an Additional Article to the Treaty places her on a more equal 
footing with Austria, and it bears to the publie eye the character ofa spontaneous 
and voluntary act, rather than what it really is, that of a forced concession to 
Austrian. 

The complete understanding which is now established between the two great 
German Powers will insure the immediate adoption, by the whole of Germany, 
of the poliey of Austria and Prussia. 

Baron Manteuffel informed me further, that he had forwarded instructions, 
by telegraph, to M, de Bismarck-Schinhausen, at Vrankfort, to communicate 
this Additional Article to the Diet, and to invite its adherence to the principles 
laid down in it, adding that this would probably be done at the next sitting of 
the Diet, on Thursday next. .

Inclosure in No. 471. 


Praject of Additional article to the Treaty of April 20, 1854, between 
Austria und Prussia. 


(Translation.) 

THE. state of European affairs daily becoming more menacing, has induced 
the Courts of Berlin and Vienna to take into more immediate consideration the 
nveessity of an agreement in completion of the stipulations of the ‘Treaty of 
April 20, 1854. The Sovereigns coneur in the conviction that it is, above all, 
necessary for the participators of the alliance extended by the Decree of the Diet 
of July 24, to bring about in common the aceeptation of a basis which they 
consider suitable for future negotiations of peace. ‘They recognize this basis in 
the four preliminary points, for the acceptation of which Austria and Prussia 
have already addressed themselves to. the Imperial Court of Russia, and will 
therefore do their best ta. give effect to this basis. Though on this rests the 
hope of paving the way to a pacific solution, still the serious state of Europe in 
general, and the necessity of pursuing with effect the object of the peace in view, 
demand the security of an united action on the part of all Germany, Guided by 
this idea and appreciating the dangers which an attack on the Austrian troops, 
not only by an invasion of the Imperial territory, but also by an attack in the 
Danubian Principalities, could cause to Germany, His Majesty the King of 
Prussia hereby enters into an engagement with his august ally the Emperor of 
Austria, respecting a common defence even in the latter case, und confidently 
trusts that a similar readiness to accept the present Additional Article will be 
evineed by the other German allies, and, if necessary, that they will carry the 
samie into effect.

No, 475. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Bart of Clarendon.—(Received December 2.) 


(No. 684.) 


My Lord, Therapia, November 20, 1854, 

ON the night of the 18th instant Mr. Pisani reported to me, in a secret 
form, that the Cabinet Council had deliberated on the proposal confided by me 
to Reshid Pasha in the morning, and that the Porte was in consequence ready 
to send YO,000 men to Eupatora, under the command of Omer Pasha; that 
Ismail Pasha would take the command on the Danube during his Highness’s 
absence; that he would be temporarily replaced at Kars in the manner I have 
already stated elsewhere ; that the troops under Ismail Pasha would be encamped 
in Bulgaria, for the defence of that country, after leaving a portion of the army 
at Bucharest, and another portion of it in Galatz or Tbraila; and, finally, that 
the Porte would look exclusively to the allies for means of transporting the 
expeditionary troops to the Crimean, together with at least six months’ 
provisions. 

This decision is understood to be confidential, awaiting a joint communica- 
tion in the same sense from the two Embassies. 

I have in consequence directed a confidential overture to be made to 
M. Benedetti, but it is hardly possible for me to know his reply before the 
departure of the messenger. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Inclosure 4 in No. 477. 
Omer Pusha to the Serashier. 


(Translation. ) November 13, 1854- 

1 HAVE already addressed a detailed report to your Excelleney, inclosing 
eopies of the telegraphic despatches from the Minister of War in Paris to the 
French Ambassador at Vienna, and from thence to this place, respecting the 
desire of the Emperor Napoleon in favour of a forward movement of the Turkish 
army, and I stated that | had taken the necessary steps for this: purpose. 

Your Excellency is aware that in consequence of the correspondence which 
took place respecting the obstacles interposed by the Austrians to the advance 
of the Imperial army, the subject was represented to the Ottoman Embassy at 
Vienna; and I received firstly a telegraphic message, and afterwards a despatch 
from the Ambassador, stating, that in the event of any further difficulties or 
opposition, L was, by the Grand Vizier’s, as well as your Excellency’s, directions, 
to act according to the instructions sent from the Embassy ut Vienna, and that 
there would be no further obstacles to my operations ; but that if the army wus 
to be moved beyond Ibraila or Galatz, the Austrian Commander-in-chief was to 
be apprized thereof, in order that he might take his own measures, I therefore 
took my measures on this occasion in pursuance of the communications fron) 
the Ottoman Enibassy at Vienna; and Count Coronini being at Jassy on the 
oceasion of Prince Ghika’s imminent arrival at that place, | informed his 
Excellency of the movement of my troops. In the meantime, I received & 
despatch from the Count, written before the receipt of my communication to 
his Excellency, requesting to he informed, in the first pliee, with respect to my 
movements, in the event of an advanee on my part bemg necessary. There was 
no opposition made to my movement in this despatch; but it was simply 
inquired what part | intended to moye from. The despatch, however, sent in 
uiswer to my late one, is of a different tonour from the first, and sets a limit to 
the movements of my army. In that despatch special limits are lnid down for 
the movements of the Inperial army, and he stutes that he has no authority 
for granting me any further latitude for my movements, and that in the event of 
my requiring it, reference must be made to the Embussy at Vienna, 1 think 
that the contradiction whieh appears in the tenour of the two despatches is the 
result. of iresh instructions from Vienna, because the son of Dibescon, an 
Austrian officer who arrived here very lutely from Vienna, left this to joi 
General Coronini at Jassy. ‘The country to which my movements are limited, in 
the despatch in question, is swampy, lying on the banks of the Pruth and the 
Danube, with neither wood, so necessary in winter, nor villages to quarter the 
troops in. It is, moreover, on the left bank of the Pruth, und has been much 
strenzthened by the Russians. Part of it, on the right bank, extending over 
five or six miles, is a pure marsh, without any villages, and it is impossible to 
move an army on it. This proposition 16 tantamount simply to leading us into 
the position which the Russians would like best to see us in. ‘The Austrians 
knew that we were not so stupid as to be blind to the great injury [which would 
have acerued to the army], and the proposal was made in order to prevent our 
moving, to deceive ws, and to gain time. 

This is the third time that they haye prevented the Turkish army from 
marching. In the first instance we moved at their own request, but when we 
reached the Yalonitza river they would not consent to our going beyond. Se- 
condly, seven days after the arrival at Vienna of the rejection of the four articles 
by Russia, Count Coronini, in a despatch which I inclosed at the time to your 
Excellency, was altogether against our moying. ‘This is the third time. Inde- 
pendently of the fatigue to which the army has been put on each of these 
occasions, a considerable expense has been incurred for provisions, transport, &e., 
and as Russia has been all the time pouring reinforcements into the Crimes from

(Translation.) November 6, 1854. 


(An Imperial Reseript has been issued in conformity herewith.) 


ON the examination and trial of his Excellency Mahmoud Pasha and the 
other naval authorities, relative to the catastrophe of Sinope, bemg submitted 
to His Imperial Majesty, a Royal Order was issucd for their fresh examination, 

ons had respecting 
that occurrence, as well as upon other points, has been brought several times 
before a special meeting of the Cabinet. In bringing Mahmoud Pasha to Ee 
and confronting him with the other naval authorities, the pomt sought to be 
investigated into. and established was the bovd fide cause and origin of we 
catastrophe in question. Other points bearing on this subject were not pe : 
and an inquiry was therefore entered into of the causes of the lamentable 


and the detailed report of the Supreme Council on the discuss 


occurrence at Sinope. ‘The following is the réumé of the discussions had. 
It is still in recolle 


ction that about the period when war was coing to bedeclared 


war was subsequently declared, it was reported that some Russian vessels were 
cruizing off Heraclea and Amaseri, and threatening the merchant steamers ; and 
come more vessels were added to the first, and sent to show themselves and 
eruize off the Bosphorus as guard-ships. In the event of their falling in with 
the Russians they were to engage them, if they thought themselves a mateh for 
the enemy; otherwise, they were to avoid danger by flight. Such were the 
measures which were discussed in Council, and communicated to Mahmoud 
Pash. It would have been like courting danger for these vessels to have 
undertaken an extensive ordinary cruize in the Black Sea, and more so for the 
squadron to go into port in time of war, and remain there; and pemeen was 
never granted for them to enter a port like Sinope, insufficiently fortified against 
an enemy—a circumstance corroborated by Mahmoud Pasha throughout his 
examination, 

His Excellency declares that he never gave instructions, either written or 
verbal, to the captains of the vessels sent to sea, to go and lic in the port of 
Sinope; and that he is willing to undergo any degree of punishment on the 
production of any such instructions from him; that their orders were to sail 
out of the Bosphorus and eruize off the coast; to engage any Russian vessel 
which they thought they could beat, and to return into the Bosphorus when 
pressed by weather or want of supplies; and that he gave them a short 
instruction to the foregoing effect. ‘The naval commanders likewise stated, and 
it would appear also from the record of the despatches previously addressed by 
Mahmoud Pasha to Hussein Pasha, who was killed al Sinope, and to Osman 
Pasha, who was carried prisoner into Russia, that they were authorized by the 
orders and instructions given to them to go into Sinope, if it were expedient. 

On the occasion of a flotilla, like that in question, going to sea, the same 
form and rule is observed, with respect to its fundamental operations, as with 
regard to those of the Imperial army: namely, a written instruction is, in the 
first place, drawn up, discussed in the Cabinet, and then issued, if sanctioned by 
His Imperial Majesty. But Mahmoud Pasha did not observe this course, and 
it is considered that he was wanting in having issued instructions on this subject 
de propria motu, without any record thereof being made in the registers of the 
Admiralty, But although he was somewhat cule in this respect, neither 
Osman nor Hussein Pashas, with whom it would be necessary to confront him, 
were forthcoming; neither are the instructions drawn up and issued to them, 
or the record thereof, in existence; and it is thus impossible to establish how 
far he is culpable. It would require the presence of Osinan Pasha and the 
production of the original instructions to establish the real fucts of the case, 
and complete the trial: but Osman Pasha's return depends upon the conelusion 
of the present war, and it appears suitable and conformable with the justice of 
His Imperial Majesty that the completion of Mahmoud Pasha’s trial and his 
sentence should be deferred until that period. 

It must be observed, however, that the order for returning into the 
Bosphorus for watering, &e., as above set forth, rests on @ verbal assertion. 
while it appears on record that authority was granted for entering the port of 
Sinope in case of expediency, which was. the origin of the catastrophe. Any 
further dilatormess im punishing this clear and palpable fault would appear 
wrong and unbecoming in the eyes of the world. Whien, on the happy solution 
of the present question, Osman Pasha returns, further inquiries can be made, 
and the trial brought to a conclusion, and a heavy punishment awarded, or not, 
according to the result. In the meanwhile, Mahmovd Pasha might be exiled 
to Boli, without assigning any term, in punishment of the wilfulness and neglect 
of which he stands convicted. 

‘As it would be inconsistent with the merciful disposition of His Tnperial 
Majesty that the Pasha’s fumily should be reduced to want by depriving him 
now of his salary, which was previously conferred to enable him to maintain his 
family, it has been sinadered by the Cabinet that the salary in question might 
continue to be issued in the name of his family. 

The subject is therefore submitted for His Imperial Majesty's commands, 
together with the aecompanying report,

"Her Majesty's Government do not conee 


al from themselves that the Porte 


483 


has hitherto evinced an unreasonable reluctance to take full advantage of the 
profferred services of European officers, and has preferred to allow its. armies to 
eo to ruin rather than subject its soldiery to the control of the officers of other 
Powers, and its Generals to the supervision which might serve to bring before 
the Sultan, in a light too strong to be disregarded, the competency, to say the 
least of it, of the Commanders to whom His Highness has entrusted his armies. 
Her Majesty’s Government are also fully aware that Omer Pasha, not long ago, 
expressed himself in regard to the employment of European officers in the 
Sultan's service, in terms which they are unwilling to characterize. 

But your Exeelleney will perceive from Major-General Cannon's letter, of 
which I inclose a copy, that Omer Pasha’s sentiments in this respect have 
entirely changed, and that he is now as desirous for such assistance, for the 
conduct and organization of the troops under his command, as he was previously 
averse to accept it. 

The proposal, however, which your Excellency will have to submit to the 
Porte, involves an arrangement different from any which have hitherto been 
brought under its notice. The Porte has already consented to the enrolment, 
under Colonel Beatson’s orders, of the Bashi-Bozouks, to be attached as an 
Irregular Corps to the British army. 

Her Majesty's Government now desire to take into the British service, 
during the present war, a portion of the regular Turkish army, to be organized, 
disciplined, and commanded by British officers, and to be armed, elothed, paid 
and fed by the British Government. The Porte may not be aware that this system 
was afopted, to a great extent, during the last war in which this country was 
engaged, when it was applied to the troops of Portugal, a part of the officers of 
each Portuguese regiment being English ; and the sucecss of the experiment at 
that time renders it probable that a similar suecess will attend the adoption of 
the same measure with regard to Turkish troops. The example of Portugal, in 
placing her troops under the orders of British officers, may serve to satisly the 
Porte that there would be nothing in the proposed scheme derogatory to the 
dignity or independence of Turkey ; and as regards any religious scruples whieh 
may be alleged against subjecting Mahomedans to the control of Christian 
officers, your Excellency may, it is to be hoped, easily dispel them by calling 
attention to the practice of the British Government in India, where Mahomedans, 
and Hindoos, and Sikhs, are indiscriminately enrolled in the ranks of the British 
army, and commanded by British officers, and where the religious feelings: and 
opinions of each particular sect are as scrupulously regarded by their Christian 
officers as they could be if no such control was exercised over them. As is the 
case with regard to the Mahomedans serving in British regiments in India, so 
would it be with regard to the Turkish soldiery whom Her Majesty's Government 
are desirous of engaging in their service. 

By far the greater part of the officers in each resiment would necessarily be 
Turks. If there were any comforts or observances which might not be deemed 
necessary for British troops, and therefore escape the «tention of British 
ofticers, the requirements of the Turkish soldiery would be made known to the 
British officers in command by the Turkish soldiers; and, if made known, the 
Porte may feel sure that they would be instantly attended to, 

Her Majesty's Government hope, therefore, when the matter is fairly 
brought before the Turkish Government, the offer which your Excellency is 
‘nstructed to make to the Porte will be thankfully acce ted and it will be 
wroper that your Excellency should point out to the Porte that the benefit which 
it will derive from the proposed arrangement will not be confined to the present 
war. It may certainly be expected that a salutary influence will be exerted over 
the whole Turkish army by the spectacle of a ‘Turkish contingent, in British 
pay, acting in honourable emulation with their European comrides, and earning 
for itself that honourable distinction which effective organization and proper 
discipline can alone secure for an army’; but, beyond this, when the wir shall 
be brought to a close, and the Turkish contingent be restored to the Turkish 
army, the Porte will possess a body of well-disciplined OnE to whose model it 
may adapt the bulk of the Turkish army, and, above all, a number of well- 
instructed Turkish officers, who, having served with British officers, will be able 
to turn to good account, for the Sultan's service, the experience which they will 
have thus acquired of the mode in which troops cin be rendered really cifective. 

Her Majesty's Government would wish in the first instance'at least to offer

Inclosure in No, 454. 


Extract from the “ Oest. Deutsche Post Gazette” of November 28, 1854. 


(Translation.) 


THE Treaty concluded yesterday between Austria and Prussia, is one of the 
most fortunate events at this critical moment, We were on the brink of a great 
danger. A split in Germany would have carried the Eastern question far beyond 
its original dimensions ; the war would have been brought into the heart of 
Germany and would have destroyed all the sources whence flow its wealth, its 
culture, and its unity. 

This threatened peril has now been averted, thanks to the firmness which 
the Austrian Cabinet has united with an inexhaustible patience, and thanks also 
to the better counsels which have at length prevailed in Berlin. 

We were not wrong when we prophesied that Austria would not prove 
obstinate in matters of form, as long as they (lid not affect: the spirit of her 
demands, the chief objects of her efforts, The Vienna Cabinet has willingly made 
the concession that the co-operation of Prussia and of the other members of the 
German Confederation should be defined in a new, additional Article to the 
Treaty of April. 

Prussia has bound herself to make, in common with Austria, the following 
proposals to the Confederation :—l. That the four points should be taken as 
erounds for negotiations of peace. 2, That not only an attack on the Austrin 
territory, but also any attack on the Austrian Lroops on this side the Pruth, 
should bind the Confederation to defend Austria, 3. That the Co. :ederation 
should desire the Military Commission to commence the eventual pr arations 
for war. 

We hear that a sitting of the Diet is appointed for the 30th instant, a: [it is 
hoped that the Committee, which has been provided with all the doct » ents 
concerning this question, will be able to make its report. In this case, the 
common proposal of the two great Powers would be made in this sitting, There 
can he no doubt as to the result. Most of the smaller States, especially the 
Thuringian Duehies, have long ago expressed their desire for the strongest sup- 
port being given to Austria, and the consent of Bavaria, Saxony, and Hanover is 
no longer doubtful, ; 

Russia’s position towards Europe is now, therefore, as follows :— 

France and England, being engaged in active warfare with her, will no longer 
content themselves with the four points established in August. 

Austria, who is perfectly prepared to go to war, still considers the four 
wints sufficient, but has given the well-known declaration, that in the event of 
ier finding herself obliged to take an active part in the war, she reserves to 
herself the right to put forward further special demands, 

Prussia, who has hitherto only given her moral support to the four points, 
has now fully appropriated these four demands as bases of peace, and the same 
course ig ubout to be taken by the Confederation. Austria las therefore the 
merit of having brought the views of Prussia and the Confederation, on the 
chicf question, in accordaunee with those of the Western Powers.

My Lord, Munich, November 28, 1894. 


| AM bound to confess that I approach with infinite repugnanee the 
unprofitable subject of the jealousies and intrigues which in these countries are 
dignified with the name “policy,” and L shall in consequence confine myself to a 
simple narration of the ettect produced and the hopes aroused here, as far as 
| am capable of comprehending them, by the simultaneous arrival of the news 
of the agreement of Austria and Prussia on the Eastern. question, and the 
acceptance by Russia of the four joints which were laid down tn the Vienna 
Protocol of the Sth of August as ee able of future negotiations, 

With respect to the first of these events, I may be permitted to express my 
apprehension that when the discussions to which the latter will give rise shiall 
commence, the supposed cordiality of the understanding just arrived at will be 
put to a severe test, for it is impossible to conceive that the embarrassments 
caused by the Prussian Government are, even in part, to be explained by the 
miserable feelings of jealousy of Austria to whieh it is now sought to attribute 
them. However, such as it 1s, the Bavarian Minister for Foreign Affnirs takes 
ho stall credit to himself for haying in a great degree contributed to bring it 
about, and in a recent conversation he avowed that the German portion of the 
question was, for the minor States, of immeasurably greater importance than the 
rest. ‘To this 1 replied that I could not assent, Tnasmuch as if a convulsion, 
whieh should be violent enough to overthrow the existing European super- 
structure, should occur, there would, in my opinion, be but amall chance that 
purely German interests, as he sought to explain them, would withstand the 
shock. Baron von der Pfordten seemed to be so. deeply impressed with the 
notion that this new-born anion of Germany would produce such immense 
effect on the minds of the belligerent. part ies, and especially on the Emperor of 
Russia, that 1 felt myself justified in refreshing lis memory by an allusion to 
the confidential conversations of His fmperial Majesty with Her Majesty's 
Minister at St, Petersburgh. He dwelt with the most self-satisfied confidence 
us to its results, on the prospects of pence opened to Europe by the recent 
acceptance of the four points by the Czar, and though he appeared to wish to 
elicit from me an opinion as to whether the British and French Governments 
would be prepared to adhere to them still, I thought 1 could discover that his 
satistaction proceeded much more from the hope that the new turn thus piven 
to the question would afford some loophole by which Austria, and consequently 
Germany, would -be able to escape from a closer ullianee with the Western 
Powers, and from any participation in the war aainst Russia. 

told M. von der Plordten that T entirely concurred with him in all le 
euid about the blessings of peace, and that I was sure Her Majesty’s Govern- 
ment would be at all times ready to enter into: any negotiations whieh would 
offer a fair prospect of a lasting and honourable termination of the deplorable 
strugele now golly ON, and whieh England and Franee had been driven to under- 
take, against their wish, in defence of a great European principle which had 
heen trodden under foot by the Emperor of Russia. T said that until Thad seen 
‘he terms in which the acceptance of the four points was couched, [could not 
venture any judgment as to their proving satisfuetory to the allied Governments, 
nor could Utake upon myself to pronemnee whether they still considered themselves 
hound by them; fort reminded him that at the time when they were pub forward 
they were described as the minimum of the conditions to be imposed upon Russia, 
and [ added that [saw no redson at any rate to demand less, whilst the results 
already attained might, 1 thought, fairly justify us in claiming more. Baron 
von der Pfordten here interposed the observation, that at all events, from the 


= % 


manner in which they had been originally put forward, they must be deemed to; 


eonstitute the essential conditions af peace, Having perceived, as it atruck me 1 
tye course of our interview, that his Excellency interpreted the acceptance af the 
four points as necessarily involving o discussion on them, | endeavoured to show 
that the Protocol of the Sth of August did not warrant any such construction, 


487 


gince it was therein distinctly stated, that unless the preliminaries enumerated in 
‘+ were unconditionally accepted, peace could not be concluded at all, and the 
parties to it had actually bouud themselves not even to negotiate upon any other 
basis. “In order to gain time for the examination of them, your first step 
must,’ I said, ‘be to attempt to obtain cessation of hostilities, but the events 
that may from day to day arise out of the continuance of them may possibly £0 
alter the relative positions of the belligerents so as to dell all calculation ; and is 
it likely,” I asked, “that England and France would consent to pause in the 
course they are pursuing, upon no better security than vague and probably 
insincere propositions for negotiations that would have to be conducted in con- 
junction with Governments which, up to the present time, have shown but little 
geal in the cause of right and justice, as understood by the Western Powers ?”” 
I was induced to speak thus because, ina preceding conversation, Baron von der 
Pfordten had recurred to the subject of the joint protectorate of five Great Powers 
over the Christian subjects of the Porte, and hinted that a modification in that 
sense might be introduced into the fourth point; and upon my observation that 
any protectorate of this nature would amount to a direct encroachment upon the 
independence of the Sultan, his Excellency thought proper to ridicule the fiction 
that his Highness was any longer an independent Sovereign, 

| will not detain your Lordship with a comparison between the language 
now held by M, von der Pfordten in reference to the four points, and: his sieve 
as expounded in his famous memorandum presented to the Bamberg Con- 
ference, for the two appear to me altogether irreconcileable. | za

LES informations que nous recevons de différents cétés nous prouvent que

Hons ci-dessous indiquées serviraient de point de départ, telles qu’elles sont

des populations Chrétiennes de Empire Ottoman sans distinction du culte.

% Revision du Traité de 1841, La Russie ne s'opposera pas 4 son

Cette détermination est fondée comme de raison sur la supposition que les

déclaration, sont appréciés en Allemagne, comme nous devons le supposer, nous 
croyons pouvoir nous livrer A lespoir que la Confédération réunie sur le meme 
terrain, et entitrement rassurée sur les intéréts Allemands engagés dans ln 
question, mettra A profit son unanimité pour peser dans la balance de l'Europe 
en faveur d'une paix dont l’Autriche et la Prusse nous ont présenté spontanément 
duns lea quatre points, une base qui les satisferait complétement. 

Si, au contraire, on youlait se servir de cette union, maintenue encore une

COUNT GEORGE ESTERHAZY received instructions from Vienna this 
morning, to communicate confidentially to the Prussian Government the 
substance of the Treaty which Austria is about to conclude with England and 
France, witha view to re-establish the general peace. The Austrian Minister 
had an interview this afternoon with Baron Minteuffel, and has just informed 
me that, in conformity with his instructions, he read to his Excellency a paper 
in which the main points of the ‘Treaty were enumerated, adding that a 
rapprochement had taken place between his Government and the Western 
Powers, and that the terms of a Treaty had been agreed upon, but that before 
signing it, his Government wished to know if Prussia would not also become a 
party to the transaction, and thus resume her position with the Powers, 

Count Esterhazy observed to mo that Baron Manteuffcl received the 
communication apparently without surprise, replying that he would take the 
King’s ordres on the subject, and inform him of the result, He requested to be 
allawed to keep the memorandum, but this Count Esterhazy declined doing, 
having been especially instructed not to leave the paper out of his hands, upon 
which the Prussian Minister for Foreign Affhirs took notes af its contents, and 
has promised to give an early answer, Count Esterhazy added that if the King 
were disposer to join in this transnetion, he would immediately request Count

No. 491. 
The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley. 


(No. 1,194.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, December 4, 1854. 


ON the 2nd instant Count Walewski informed me that a proposal had 
been formally made to M, Drouyn de Lhuys by M. Hiibner, that the Austrian 
jossessions in Italy should be cuaranteed by France, and his Excellency then 
confidentially read to me the draft of a Convention for that purpose, which the 
Government of the Emperor was prepared to sign with Austria as soon as the 
opinion of Her Majesty's Government on the subject was ascertained, 

Count Walewski said that this proposal had occasioned much embarrass- 
ment to his Government, who ndimitted, however, that Austria was fairly 
entitled to make the demand, as the Emperor had some months ago told 
M. Hibner, that if Austria took part with Russia she must be prepared for the 
uncompromising hostility of France, but that if she joined with France against 
Russia she might rely upen the active aid of France in any quarter where she 
might be attacked, or find herself exposed to danger, and the French Government 
were further of opinion that if Austria declared war against Russia it would be 
for the interest of the Western Powers that her attention should not be 
Jistracted, nor her forces divided, hy insurreetionary movements in Italy « anil 
that if France altogether declined the proposed engagement her good faith and 
her intentions might be liable to suspicion, and the knowledge that she had so 
declined might serve to excite the movement that Austria so much drended. 

Count Walewski added that an exchange of notes might have been suflicient 
for the purpose, but that the form of Convention had been preferred us likely to 
be more agreeable to Austria, and also, that it gave greater facility for making 
the assistance of France conditional on the signing of the Tripartite Treaty and 
the active co-operation of Austria in the war. 

Count Walewski. concluded by saying, that M. Drouyn de Lhuys thought 
he had best consulted the wishes of Her Majesty’s Government by avoiding 
all reference to England in hus communication with M. Hibner on this 
subject, and by not inviting Her Majesty's Government to take part in the 
Convention. 

1 requested Count WWalewski to convey to M. Drouyn de Lhuys the 
thanks of Her Majesty's Government for not having imposed upon them the 
uecessity of declining to become party to any such arrangements but the 
Government of the Emperor having determined on grounds they thought 
sulficient to agree to it, they appeared, [ said, ta have given elect. to thei 
decision with caution, and as the Convention involved the previous signuture of the

fee plete

‘Tripartite ‘Treaty, tt entailed no obligation on France, beyond using her influence 
to prevent attempts against the territorial integrity of Italy, unless Austria was 
engaged in hostilities with Russia, its duration would terminate with the war, and 
France only engaged to employ the foree that was already stationed in Italy. 
I am, &c.

| cannot feel that this new alliance with Austria has strengthened that which 
previously existed between France anid England, and tam much tistaken if one 
of the objects of Austria is not to weaken the latter. Without then fecling any 
immediate anxiety, or wishing to inspire any in Her Majesty’s Government, 
vet venture to think that it would be prudent to profit by the present favourable 
moment, and that Her Majesty’s Government should endeavour to pledge the 
Fiench Government to the course to be pursued in common, before Austria is 
admitted further into the counsels of the two Governments. M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys is quite ready to enter into a confidential exchange of opinions on the 
subject, 

[ had written thus far when I received your Lordship's authorisation to 
communicate to M, Drouyn de Lhuys the despatch to Lord Westmorland 
to which I have alluded above. fis Excelleney, in passing a high encomium on 
its contents, in which, he said, he entirely agreed, expressed some regret that 
your Lordship should have allowed Lord Westmorland to give a copy of it to 
Count Buol. He observed that the object of the Maritime Powers should be to 
engage Austria to take the lead in developing the three points which were of 
nearest interest to her, in order that she might have less right to dispute the 
pretensions of England and France, to whom the fourth point—namely, the 
revision of the Trenty of 1841—was of paramount importance. But in your 
Lonlship’s despatch to Lord Westmorland the contrary course had been adopted. 
The three points which chiefly interested Austria and Germany were explained 
inso falla manner, that they might serve as the text for the preliminaries of 
peace, while the guarantees to be demanded for the limitation of Russian power 
‘athe Blaek Sea were left almost in their pristine vagueness. His instructions 
to M. de Bourqueney were, if was true, ually explicit upon the same three 
points, and vague upon the fourth, but he had expressly stated to M. de 
Bourquency that those instructions were merely intended as a guide for his 
language in conversation with Count Buol, and were on no account to be officially 
communiented to that Minister, His reasons for this reserve were, first, us he 
had suid before, to excite Austria to put forward the most stringent conditions on 
those points which concerned her, and thus to make it more difficult for her to 
counteract the Western Powers on the point which interested them, Secondly, 
if Austria was furnished with. copies of those despatches, she might communicate 
them to the Cabinet of St, Petersburgh, and a bad impression might be ereated 
in Europe, if Russia accepted the terms of the two Powers as signed by them- 
selyes, aid peace was ufterwants rendered impossible by what Austria and 
Germany might declare tobe the undue pretensions of the Maritime Powers to 
cripple the naval means of Russia. Moreover, it would be difficult, M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys thought, to refuse a suspension of hostilities, if Russia agreed 
without reserve to terms so distinetly set forth, on condition of hostilities being 
suspended, For these reasons his Excellency was most desirous that as little als 

possible should passin writing between the Western Powers and Austria, until 
the future intentions of the litter were more clearly developed. 

I venture to think that your Lordship will consider M. Drouyn de 
Llhuys' observations as worthy of your consideration, ‘They led naturally with 
me to a further conversation respecting the nature of the guarantees to be 
demanded of Russia in the Black Sea, and that conversation confirmed mein the 
opinion that the two Governments should come to an early understanding on 
this very important matter, M. Drouyn de Lhuys repeated that he did not 
think that we could be satisfied with less than what I have specified in the former 
part of this despatch. With regard to anything that we might ask in addition to 
the four points, his Execlleney said that it would probably have reference to 
the Baltic, and to the limitation of Russian power in the north. 

I have, &e,

The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 

(No. 402.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, December 7, 1854. 

WITH reference to your Lordship’s despatch No. 454, inclosing the Treaty 
between Austria, England, and France, which was signed on the 2nd instant, 
I have to inform you that Her Majesty’s Government have learned the signature 
of that Treaty with much satisfiction, and earnestly hope that it may lead to 
the happy results which an intimate alliance between the three Powers is 
calculated to produce at this moment, 

I have the pleasure to convey to your Lordship the entire approval of Her 
Majesty's Government for your conduct in this matter.

Lord Cowley to the Eart of Clarentlon.—( Received December 4.) 


(No, l ot 75.) 
My Lord, Paris, December 7, 1854, 


M. DROUYN DE LHUYS has reevived a telegraphic despatch from 
M. de Moustier, stating that Count Esterhazy had invited the Prussian Govern- 
inent to adhere to the Treaty signed between Austria, England, and France, on 
the 2nd instant, and inquiring whether he was to support this invitation. 

M. Drouyn de Liuys replied, that as soon as the Governments of England 
and France had come to a decision upon this point, thew Representatives at 
Berlin would receive instructions for their guidance, 

After giving me this intelligence, M. Droayn de Lhuys said that sinee he 


had spoken to me on this subject yesterday, it had-struck him that the Prussian 
Government might offer to adhere to the Treaty, and not to the Secret Article, 
whieh, he observed, would be placing Prussia in the position of having a voice 
it the deliberations for peace, without subjerting her in any way to the chances 
of war contemplated by the Treaty; that he had therefore instructed M. de 
Bourqueney, by telegraph, to state to Count Buol that Prussia must be asked ta 
adhere ta the Seeret Article as well as to the Patent Articles of the Treaty, and 
that no reservation or condition of any sort would be permitted—she must 
adhere without observation, or not-at all.

M, de Moustier.

My Lord, Bucharest, November 22, 1854. 

THE Spathar Keresko having given in his resignation, it has been accepted, 
hut no successor has been appointed. Colonel Pasnausky, chief of the Military 
Chancelry (a Russian hy birth), has also been removed, and Colonel Vladoyano 
appointed his successor, to the scandal of the country. This Colonel commanded 
the Regiment of Wallachs at Buseo, in August last; when the year-guard under 
D’Aurep left Buseo, he disarmed the Wallach regiment. ‘This Colonel 
Viadoyano asked if any would volunteer to accompany the Russians, No 
answer being made to this appeal, he said, they were ‘un fis d'ingrats et quils 
rouvaient aller au diable.” Colonel Viadoyano ig succeeded by a Russo-Greek, 
a Major Macedonski, as Colonel of the Srd Regiment, who thus: passes over 
several meritorious officers, his seniors, The Spatharship is, tt is said, reserved 
for the Prince Guorge Stirbey, son of the Hospodar.

Inclosure in No, 519. 


Instructions given to Osman Pasha, of the Imperial Guard, sent wr Command 
of the Ottoman Forces at Sebastopol, 


(Translation.) 

THE Imperial troops now at Sebastopol with the forces of the allies, and 
those to be sent hereafter, will amount to_ thirty battalions. His Imperial 
Majesty is very anxious that these troops should be firm in battle, and distinguish 
themselves by a proper spirit of religious zeal, patriotism, and military ardour : 
of which he has no doubt while under the able command of Osman Pasha, 

The Pasha will, on his arrival, put himself in communication with the two 
allied Commanders-in-chief, and, alter being informed by them of his duties, he 
will, in pursuance of his orders, employ his efforts for conducting himself as 
above laid down, the foundation of all military undertakings, and for fulfilling 
his duties properly on other more important matters, He will in this respect 
conform himself strictly with the instructions which he may receive from the 
Commanders-in-chief relative to the operations and administration of his forces, 
and carry them into immediate execution, 

The Pasha will be careful to preserve discipline among his troops, and to 
inspire them with courage, &c. He will act towards the inhabitants of any 
places which may be taken, according to the injunctions of the Commanders-in- 
chief, and be careful in avoiding the commission of anything wrong, by express 
order of His Imperial Majesty. ‘The Pasha will attend herein to the strict 

performance of justice. 

The Pusha will make prompt and full reports to the Seraskier of any 
advantages gained over the enemy, or other military matters; and will be 
eareful not to proceed beyond the jimits of his present instructions. He will 
always be on terms of good fellowship with the allied troops with whom he is to 
act, and do nothing contrary toa spirit of good comradeship. 

The Pasha will attend to the good administration and comfort of the troops. 
He will have to superintend himself the discipline and order of all the Ottoman 
troops, those already there and those to be sent out: but as the collective force 
at Sebastopol consists of the troops of the auxiliary and allied Powers, he must, 
under the circumstances, carry into immediate execution any instructions he may 
receive from the Commanders-in-chief relative to matters of war or military 
operations, and, in short, attend implicitly to their directions in all his military 
movements. 

The Pasha will, therefore, act as above set forth in the execution of his 
duties and movements, in conformity with the exigencies of the times, and 
conduct himself bravely and uprightly.

Sir, Constantinople, November 30, 1854. 


BEING informed by the Earl of Clarendon that a military force might be 
ordered from India in aid of the British army employed in this quarter, | have 
thought it desirable to obtain the removal of any obstacle which might by 
possibility retard its jmssage from 8uez to Alexandria, that being the route by 
which the troops would find it most convenient to puss. poet tees 

It must in fairness be presumed that Said Pasha would be little inclined to 
make any difficulty, but his Highness might think it. proper to have the Sultan s 
sanction before he consented to the passage of a foreign force, however small in 
number, through a part of the Ottoman dominions. 5 

In anticipation of this contingency, | have applied for letters to apprise the 
Viceroy of His Imperial Majesty's assent to the proposed passage ol British 
troops, and 1 am happy to inform you that my request has been met with 
w ready and cordial compliance. 

‘he Grand Vizier’s letter to Said Pasha is inclosed herewith, and a trans- 
lation accompanies it, You will observe that it is yery considerately worded, 
You will, no doubt, find a convenient as well as an early opporrunity for 


ols 


presenting it to his Highness; and TI eannot anticipate any but a favourable 
reply, which, I need not add, should be made known to Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment, and also to the Government of India, with the least practicable delay.

No. 524. 


Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Kecetved December 11.) 
(No. 720.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, November 30, 1854. 

IT is painful to observe that irritating differences continue to arise between 
the Commanders-in-chief of the Austrian and Ottoman armies in Wallachia, 
The correspondence, inclosed herewith in copy or translation, will show your 
Lordship on what points the disagreement more particularly turns. 

[t appears, moreover, that the conduct of the Austrian officers and soldiers, 
whenever they come into immediate contact with the inhabitants of Moldavia 
and Wallachia, is marked with circumstances of insolence and outrage tending to 
rouse a dangerous fecling of resentment and indignation among the inhabitants. 

[ derive my information on this subject principally from Mr, Colquhoun, 
who, no doubt, transmits to your Lordship the same information which he sends 
to me. The Internuncio, in conversation with me, refers the want of harmony 
which unfortunately prevails between Omer Pasha and Count Corronini, to 
military susceptibilities, and is unwilling to admit that any fundamental difference 
exists between his own opinions and those of Count Buol. He is now insisting 
on a demand of satisfiction from the Porte, on account of Siw Stephen 
Lakeman’s proceedings at Bucharest, and on that plea he requires the with- 
drawal, if not from the whole of Wallachia, at least from its capital, of such 
refugees as are still employed in Omer Pasha’s army, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFIVE,

Inclosure 2 in No, 525. 
Memorandum. 


LES rapports les plus récents des Prineipautés ayant donné licu de craindre 
que les chefs des différentes armées ne se fassent pas complétement entendus sur 
leurs positions respectives et sur les lignes de démareation nécessaires aux opera- 
tions de chacune d'elles, la Commission composce des Représentants des quatre 
Puissunces, et 4 laquelle avaient éte invités a se rendre les Généraux De Hess et 
Létang, s'est rassemblce pour rechercher et établir les moyens les plus propres & 
prevenir tout espéce de conflit, 

Aprés mir examen la Commission est tombée d’accord sur les principes 
suivants pour régler Voecupation des Principautés Danubiennes, tant sous le 
rapport de la Convention conclue entre PAutriche et la Turquie, que sous celui 
de Vopération offensive de larmée alliée vers la Pruth: 

|. Liemaplacement et la position militaire de larmeée Autrichienne, comme 
foree principalement: destinée & la défense des Principautés en cas de besoin, doit 
étre assuré de mani¢re que, par une position de flanc, clle puisse remplir ce but 
aussi bien en Moldavie qu’en Valachie. 

Les. troupes Autrichiennes cn Moldavie doivent done occuper une ligne qui 
ne permette pas seulement leur communication libre et continuelle de lune des 
Principautés 4 Pautre, mais couvre en méme tems le dos de leurs propres pro- 
vinees et ait la profundeur nécessaire pour ces: positions et cantonnements, 

2, Larmée Turque, de son cote, a besoin de Vespace nécessaire pour la 
marche et le développement d'une masse de 60,000 hommes entre le Sereth, la 
Byrlat, et le Pruth, pour se mouvoir avec aisance et pouvoir faire ses operations 
pour le passage de ce fleuve. 

Ces deux principes posés, une ligne allant de Faltsehi sur le Proth par 
Bolesh et Dokolemy jusqu’i la Byrlat, et de li le long de cette riviére jusqu’é 
Tekush, est la seule qui peut encore remplir ce double but ci-dessus indiqué, en 
laissant A Varmée Turque la libre action de presque quinze milles Allemands en 
longueur le long du Pruth et toute la largeur nécessaire pour ses opérations et 
pour leur base, tandis quelle est en méme tems pour VAutriche la seule et In 
plus reculée que ses troupes pourraient prendre pour ne pas abandonner tout-i- 
fait cette Principauté et retarder par cela, de leur edté, toute action 4 un terme 
incalculable, 

lin conséquence les Représentants d’Autriche, de France, de Grande Bre- 
tazne, et le Général de Létang, ont demande a |’ Ambassadeur Ottoman de vouloir 
bien transmettre i son Altesse le Généralisime Ottoman le présent memorandum 
comme contenant lexpression des veeux de la Commission si¢geant 4 Vienne, 
tandis que le Général Baron de Hess s’est chargé de son efté de faire parvenir 
aux Commandants Autrichiens lordre d’oecuper la ligne indiquée pour les troupes 
Autrichicnnes. 

Vienne, le 4 Décembre, 1854.

effect this in as short a time as possible, we have submitted to a most searching

Decree of the Dict. In doing so we have taken into account as much as possible 
the considerations which Austria owes to her European position, and her obliga- 
tions arising therefrom. 1 believe I may pass over the details. One assumption, 
however, | must point out as resting ecnerally on a misconception, namely, that 
we had intended to declare the four points, under all circumstances, as exclusively 
binding for us and our allies, and thus to fetter Austria to this extent. On the 
contrary, Article IIL of our Project had the case in view in which new demands 
would hiave to be made in the interests of the countries of Central Europe, and

that, if Austria were to agree to this in the form of a Decree of the Confederation, 
she would be only acting in the spirit of the Treaty of April 20, But we appre- 
ciate, as has been already said, the objections raised by the Cabinet. of Vienna, 
and we have therefore taken care, as faras the adherence to our own opinions 
permitted, to expunge from the new Project which is herewith inclosed, and 
which His Majesty the King has specially sanctioned, everything which could be 
in contradiction to the Austrian view ; and, on ihe other hand, to adopt nearly 
verbatim the three points as Austria herself has worded them in the draft of an 
instruction to the Imperial Minister at the Diet communicated ta us, so that we 
may confidently count on Daron Prokeseh being authorized to pronounce himsel!’ 
in the Committee for the adoption of this project, 

His Majesty the King, in declaring his concurrence with such a Decree of 
the Diet, as has been ulready frequently remarked, is nevertheless penetrated 
with the conviction that, to avoid discussions and dissenting votes, it can only 
be taken, if an Additional Article has been previously nereed to, pronouncing the 
protection of Austria in the Danubian Principalities, which the Imperial Cabinet 
itself acknowledges as going beyond the origmal principle of the Treaty of April. 
His Majesty has also ordered everything to be avoided in the drawing up of this 
Additional Article which could possibly delay an understanding, 


This is the leadins consideration which has given rise to the inclosed Project, 
which has also been sanctioned by His Majesty, and your Excelleney will commu- 
nicate it to Count Buol, observing that, it it meets with the concurrence of His 
Majesty the Emperor, your Excelleney 1s aut horized to sign it with Count Buol 
without loss of time. Should they prefer in Vienna that the signature should 
take place here, Count Esterhazy can be easily authorized by telegraph to sign 
with me, The formalitics of giving the full powers ean be fulfilled afterwards, 
But when the Additional Article has been signed, it will be immediately cominu- 
nicated to our German allies, a8 well us to our Representatives in Frankfort, and 
its general adoption will not only not he attended with any difficulties, but it will 
also materially simplify the labours of the Committee connected with ity for the 
latter would only have to frame their propositions with reference to it, which, 
arising out of a Project agreed to by Prussia and Austria, will be certain of being 
unanimously adopted in the Committee as well as by the Diet, 

Your Excellency will, without delay, communicate: this despatch and its 
‘nclosures to the Imperial Cabinet. His Majesty attaches great value in bringing 
this matter—in which he has been guided by the most lively care for the interests 
of Prussia and Germany, und at the suine time of those of Kurope in general—to 
a speedy conclusion in the sense implied above, and confidently calculates on the 
cooperation of his august ally His Majesty the Emperor of Austria. 

I look forward with the greatest interest to your Excellency’s report on hie 
result of the steps taken by you.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received December 11.) 
(No. 497.) 


My Lard, Berlin, December 8, 1554. 

IN the course of conversation to-day with Baron Manteuffel, he alluded to 
the question of the proposals for peace which had been made at Vienna. I asked 
his Excellency if he had received any further information on the subject from 
St. Petersburgh, when his Excellency replied that despatches had reached him 
this morning from Baron Werther, from which it certainly appeared that the 
Emperor of Russia was desirous for peace, and that His Imperial Majesty was 
a He to make great concessions to obtain it; but headded that no new light 
had been thrown on the subject by Baron Werther, and that the only tangible 
points were to be found in the note which had been addressed to Count Buol by 
Prince Gortchakoff on the 28th ultimo, a copy of which, together with his 
Excelleney’s answer, had been forwarded for the consideration of Her Majesty's 
Government, which he sincerely hoped would lead to negotiations. Lreplied that 
Her Majesty's Government would certainly not be disposed to take the simple 
acceptance of the four points by Russia as a‘ point de depart” for negotiations, 
and that we should require some guarantees from Russia of the sincerity of her 
intentions before we consented to meet in conference with a@ Russian Pleni- 
potentiary,

According to the details given by General Hess, it appears that the first 
upplication of Omer Pasha for the passage of his troops for the purpose of 
invading Bessarabia contained the proposal that the Austrian garrisons of Tbraila 
and Galatz should retire from those positions, in order to allow his army to move 
forward upon the Prath. My despatches to your Lordship of the 16th and 18th 
of October will explain what took place at that period, and in my despatch 
No. 399 of the 25th of the same month, | report that when Mr, Colquhoun and 
M. de Poujade informed Omer Pasha of the decisiou of the Austrian Govern- 
ment, ‘that he was entirely unfettered as to carrying into effect the movement 
he contemplated,” his reply was, “that he considered any movement of 
importance upon the Pruth as now useless, and that the season was too far 
advanced to allow of a campaiga in Bessarabia,” &c.

himself und Omer Pasha as to the occupation by the ‘Turkish troops of Ibraila

above veferred, General Hess stated that since his arrangement with Omer 
Pasha in October, the Ottoman Commander-in-chiel had again announced his 
intention of advancing to the Prath in a different direction by Fokschani and ta 
Jassy. ‘This proposed operation | referred to in my despatches Nos, 441 of the 
26th of November, and 462 of the 6th of December; and upon the same 
oceasions I had likewise the honour to report General Hess's declaration made

Pasha to allow Lim to pass through the districts oceupied by the Austrian troops

orders upon the subject, and he then proceeded to detail the decision which the

No. 637. 


Précis of « Despatch from Count Buol to Count Colloredo, dated Vienna, 
December 3, 1854, communicated to the Earl of Clarendon by Count 
Calloredo, December 13. 


COUNT BUOL, after referring to the telegraphic despatch by which he 
had informed Count Colloredo’ that Count Nesselrode had declared to the 
Austrian Minister at St. Petersburgh the acceptance by Russia of the four points 
‘dicated in the Notes of the 8th of April, and to conversations which he had had 
with Prince Gortchakoff, incloses for the information of Count Colloredo copy of 
a note which Prince Gortchakoff had addressed to hin on this subject, together 
with copy of his own reply, 

In Submitting to the serious consideration of Her Majesty's Government 
this overture of Russia, Count Buol remarks, that in the eyes of the Austrian 

tovernment the note of Prince Gortchakoff amounts to a complete adhesion to 
the four bases of peace ; and he considers it capable of affording the ground for 
the commencement of serious negotiations, 

This opinion is confirmed by the announcement made to him by Prince 
Gortehukoff, that the acceptance of these four bases by Russia implies the 
necessity of her renouncing the religious protectorate of the Greek subjects of the 
Sultan and the political protectorate of the Danubian Principalities, and of her 
recognising the principle of the free navigation of the Danube, and the revision 
of the Treaty of 1841. Count Buol proceeds to examine possible objections to 
opening negotiations. 

It may be said that Russia may not be sincere, and that she has accepted 
the four bases only for the purpose of detaching Austria from her adhesion witht 
the Western Powers. 

In answer to this, Count Buol points to the signature of the Treaty of the 
ond of December, Since Russia, he argues, must in face of this Treaty 
renounce the hope of detaching Austria from the alliance so long as the objects 
of that alliance are not completely attained, what interest can she haye in com- 
inencing fictitious negotiations, or in delays which will be injurious rather than 
advantageous to her, since delay increases the chance of the number of her 
enemies being added to, Count Buol thinks the tone of Count Gortchukoff"'s 
converea On with him an argument in favour of the sincerity of the Russian 

sourt. 


A SOT Rar TNC ha Os ol Oa se ee 
TP abe MRE owe aor et SE thes 


525 

Believing then that it is improbable that Russia wishes to open negotiations 
only to gain time, Count Buol thinks no time should be lost in taking her at her 
word, if only to test her sincerity, 

The first interchange of ideas between the Plenipotentiaries would, Count 
Buol thinks, be enough to show whether Russia would agree to the practical 
application as well as to the definitive sanction of the guarantees which Europe 
has a right to require. ; 

Kither Russia will make the sacrifices required of her, or she will not. If 
she does, peace will follow; if she does not, the Western Powers will have the 
satisfaction of avoiding the reproach of having rejected an honourable opportunity 
of terminating the present contest, and Austria, having exhausted every attempt 
at conciliation, will be more than justified, from that time, in coneerting with the 
allied Powers the most efficient means of restoring peace. What risk could the 
Western Powers have in opening negotiations? Iussia does not demand the 
suspension of hostilities before the opening of negotiations, which, however, does 
not exclude the hope that if the negotiations should take a favourable turn, an 
armistice may be agreed to,

No. 545. 
Sir A. Malet to the Earl of Clarendon,—( Received December 14.) 

(No. 142.) 
My Lord, Frankfort, December 11, [854. 

| FIND an expression of opinion, very nearly to the following effect, in 
several different organs of the German pubhe press in relation to the effect likely 
to be produced by the working of the Tripartite Treaty of the 2nd of December : 
That the alliance of Austria with the Western Powers will prove that no 
third party or Power exists in Germany, and that all the efforts of M. Von der 
Pfordten and his associates to found a terlium quid of any weight, are fruitless. 

The understanding now arrived at, compels all minor German Sovereigns to 
take a decision, and either to unite with Austria, or to remain floating at the 
mercy of eventualities, a prey to all the evils of internal impotence and external 
isolation. 

The accession of Prussia to the Treaty is generally expected, but not 
without well-founded suspicions that in so dog that Power will still endeavour 
to hinder and thwart all action against Russia to the utmost of her ability. 


I have, &c. 
(Signed) A. MALET,

No. 546. 


The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley. 
(No, 1,284.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, December 15, 1854. 

| INCLOSE the abstract of a despatch from Count Buol, which was read 
to me by Count Colloredo, who at the same time placed in my hands the copy 
of a note from Prince Gortehakoff announcing that the Emperor of Russia 
aceepted the four propositions of the Cabinet of Vienna as the “point of 
departure” for negotiations for peace, and of Count Buol’s note in answer to 
Prince Gortchakoll, ; 

Count Buol, in his despatch to Count Colloredo, states his reasons for 
thinking that the Emperor of Russia is sincere in his offer to negotiate for peace, 
and strongly expresses his desire that this offer may not be rejected by Her 
Majesty's Government, | 

I told Count Colloredo that I did not share Count Buol'’s opinion as to the 
sincerity of Russia, that I did not consider the note of Prince Gortchakof! was 
an offer to treat for peace, and that a hollow and illusory negotiation would be 
alike repugnant to the Government and people of England; but that upon a 
matter of such importance | could cive him no answer until I had obtained the 
Queen's sanction, after consulting with my colleagues, and having ascertained the 
views af the French Government, 

On the 10th instant, Count Walewski communicated to me the draft of an 
‘dentic note, copy of which | herewith inclose, which M. Drouyn de Lhuys 
proposed should be delivered by the Ministers of England and France at Vienna 
to Count Buol, who, if he coneurred in its terms, was to be invited to give an 
identic reply ; that these notes should then be communicated to the Russian 
Minister, as containing the interpretation given by the three Powers to the 
bases, and it would then be for Prince Gortchakolf to say whether he was 
authorized to adopt that interpretation of the bases, and accept them so 


uxplained as the " point of departure for negotiations. . 
On the following day I informed Count Walewski that, in the opinion of 


f 


531 


Her Majesty's Government, no further eommunication to the Austrian Govern- 
ment was neeessary, as Count Buol was fully in possession of the views of the 
English and French Governments respecting the bases, which we had every 
reazon to believe were in accordance with those of the Cabinet of Vienna, and 
that he had only to make them known to Prince Gortchakoff, and ascertain 
whether they would be adopted by Russia, The two Governments would thus 


‘he spared the necessity of entering upon a negotiation with the Russian 


Minister which was unlikely to lead to any useful result, and which might give 
rige to much misunderstanding, and be difficult to explain satisfactorily in the 
present excited state of the public mind, Her Majesty’s Government, however, 
being desirons to meet the wishes of the Government of the Emperor, which 
were so earnestly pressed on them by Count Walewski, would not object to the 
course which M, Drouyn de Lhuys proposed to pursue, and they were prepared 
to agree to the Ist, IInd, and IVth Articles in the project of note; but the 
frd appeared to them open to serious objections, as it referred to the revision 
of the ‘Treaty of 1841, which was by far the most important of the four bases, 
and the only one on which we could rely for effectually securing the objects of 
the war. It had hitherto not been defined with sufficient precision ; but as the 
note of M. Drouyn de Lhuys left it more vague und uncertain than before, 
++ was the wish of Her Majesty's Govermnent that the conditions to be required 
of Russia, with reference to the Black Sea, should be distinctly stated. 

Count Walewski said he would communicate this to his Government, and 
he yesterday placed in my hands a copy of a despateh from M. Dronyn de Lhuys, 
copy of which is inclosed, stating at great length and with much ability the 
grounds on which his Excellency hopes that Her Majesty's Government will 
adopt the draft as originally proposed. 

The views of Her Majesty’s Government remain unchanged; they still 
think that no further notes are necessary; but your Excellency ts instructed to 
inform M. Drouyn de Lhuys that Mer Majesty's Government. will adopt his 
project of note. ‘They must, however, request that his Excellency will agree to 
substitute in the I!lrd Article, for “diminuer” the words “ faire cesser,” or 
“mettre fin,’ and to omit the word “ maritime’ after “ prépotence.” 

It is obvious that the words “ diminuer la prépotence maritime” imply a 
consent on the part of England and France to a maritime ascendancy of Russia 
‘n the Black Sea. From the moment such an admission 1s nade it is of little 
consequence whether that maritime preponderance is maintained by ten line-of- 
battle ships or twenty. “Ten line-of-battle ships escorting fifty transports would 
effectually overcome Turkish resistance at the Bosphorus and put un end to the 
Turkish Empire in Europe. 

Nor would it be just and right to Austria to leave her in the belief that 
England and France would consent to a security so illusory. 

Her Majesty’s Government consider it quite indispensable that the expression 
of a desire to treat for peace should proceed from Russia, and be formally com- 
municated to the Ministers of England and France at Vienna, and they trust that 
the Government of the Emperor will be of opinion that upon no other ground 
could the proposed course of proceeding be justified or defended. 

Her Majesty’s Government likewise consider It an object of extreme import- 
ance that their views and those of the Government of the Emperor respecting the 
revision of the Treaty of 1841, should be recorded in a formal document. The 
honour of the two Governments, the real issue of the war, and the future tran- 
quillity and equilibrium of Burope, are all involved in the conditions that are to 
be imposed on Russia; and 1 accordingly inclose u note which embodies the 
opinions of Her Majesty's Government on this subject, and your Excellency will 
address it to M.Drouyn de Lhuys, who, Her Majesty's Government do not doubt, 
will address to you # similar note in answer, 

Lam, &c, 
(Signed) CLARENDON,
