Inclosure 6 in No. 446, 
Draft of Note to be presented by Lord Cowley (a M. Drouyn de Lhuys. 


HER MAJESTY’S Government, considering it of great importance that a 
clear understanding should exist with the Government of the Emperor of the 
French as to the interpretation of the third basis of negotiation, which provides 
for the revision of the ‘Treaty of 1841, and the conditions to be required of 
Russia: the Undersigned has been directed to make known to M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys that, in the opinion of Her Majesty's Government, Sebastopol is the seat 
of danger to Turkey, as it is from thence that Russia is always able to menace 
the existence of the Ottoman Empire, which itis the policy and the determi- 
nation of England and Franee to maintain, Itussia, however strictly she may 
be bound by Treaties, may, at any moment when it suits her purpose, declare 
war against Turkey; and, being in possession of Sebastopol, with a powerful 
fleet and a numerous army, she may, in forty-eight hours, reach Constantinople, 
and seize upon the heart of the Ottoman Empire, 

The Porte would be too weak, and the allies of the Sultan too distant, to 
oppose any eflectual resistance to such a coup de mam. The Bosphorus and the 
Dardanelles would be in the possession of Russia, and, long before any hostile 
furces could be brought against her, she would be in a position “to defy 
them. 

‘Turkey, thus held firmly in her grasp, and the Black Sea then really a 
Russian lake, it is manifest that the countries hordering on that seu—Cirenssia, 
Georgia, Persia, and Asia Minor—must at once fall under her dominion, and it 
is equally clear that the power of Russian must extend over Greece, Thessaly, 
Albania, and the Danubian Principalities. 

Russia would then be in a position to dictate the law to Europe; every 
evil that England and France hoped to avert by the war might occur; every 
object they mean to attain might be frustrated, and these calamities would be 
directly deducible from the retention of Sebastopol by Russia, and her great 
naval and military preponderance, that would be the natural and certain result 
of such an error on the part of England and France—an error that would render 
null all the sacrifices they have made, the treasure that has been expended, and 
the blood that has snrat eu) 

England and France must, therefore, insist upon the demolition of Sebas- 
topol, and, if possible, also of the other Russian fortresses ov the enstern const 
of the Black Sea. Russian must be bound by Treaty uot to reestablish them, 
nor at any other point in the Black Sea to establish a great naval arsenitl, 
Russia must not have more than four ships of war to be employed hereafter in 
the Bluck Sea. } 

Other wations, melding Turkey, must be limited to the same number, 1 
the Porte consents to annul the Treaty of 1841; but no final decision can be 
taken on this point until the Porte has been consulted.

My Lord, Vienna, December 18, 1854. 
COUNT BUOL requested Baron Bourqueney and myself to call upon fim ; 
when he stated that he had received a report from Bucharest, according to which 
it appeared that it was the mtention of the Ottoman authorities in the Princi- 
palities to require the expulsion of several Moldavian and Wallachian subjects. 
and that it was understood that the property of some of the Boyar nated 
in the list of those to be expelled, was to be confiscated. | 
Count Buol stated, he was most anxious that any harsh measure of that 
nature should not take place at this moment; that the privileges of the Danubian 


Pay ry eae 1p 4 1a i F 
Provinces had been secured by the proclamation of the Government of the 
Sultan upon the entry of his ped 


Is, designated 


ul 6 into the Principalities, as well as by the 
nSSUrANces given, both by Omer Pasha and Dervish Pasha, of a general amnesty ; 
and that the proclamations upon the entry of the Austrian troops into those 
Provinces were in conformity with those declarations. . 

Count Buol said that he in no way would wish to enter upon any discussien 
as to the sovereign rights of the Porte with reference to the privileges accorded 
to the Principalities ; but what he was desirous of obtaining, was the postpane- 
ment of any measures of severity, even if at a later period they should be consi- 
dered necessary. He therefore requested M. de Bourqueney and myself to write 
in that sense to our respective Consular Agents in Bucharest. 

_ Baron Bourqueney said he was convineed that such a proceeding was one 
which his Government would approve, and therefore that he would write to 
M. de Poujade in the sense which Count Buol desired, stating always that he was 
well aware that the feeling of the Austrian, as well as of the allied ‘Governments 
Was distinctly in fayour of upholding the sovereign rights of the Porte, ; 

W ith the expression of the same sentiments, | consented to write to 
Mr. Colquhoun, and 1 herewith have the honour of forwarding to your Lordship 
a copy of the letter I addressed to him. | : 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND.

‘ a ROM information recently received from Bucharest and Jassy by the 
ustrian Government, it appears that not only decrees of exyulsion had been

Sublime Porte, which subjected twenty-three Boyards im Wallachia to the

As | have not heard anything from you upon this subject, 1 am inclined to 
believe it may not have been correctly reported; but, as you are well aware, the 
paramount object of the Commission established in Vienna, of which | form a 
part, and which is recognized in the Treaty signed on the 2nd instent, is the 
upholding the sovereign rights of the Porte and, according to the public acts 
which have been previously entered into, the privileges of the Principalities, and 
this Commission, when it is officially constituted, will naturally desire the con- 
ciliation of the respective interests existing in the Principalities. 

As the promises of aninesty made by the Porte when she marched her army 
into the Principalities will undoubtedly be maintained, and although exceptional 
cases may arise as mentioned in my last letter to you as to the arrest of 
persons by the different millitary authorities, yet | am sure you will agree with 
me that the more extensive measures which [ have above alluded to, had 
better if possible be postponed, cven if ultimately they might be found to be 
neccessary. 

Your French colleague, M. de Poujade, will receive a letter from M. de 
Bourqueney upon this subject, and upon this occasion, as upon all others, 
I conceive that you would desire to act in consultation, and in combination 
with him,

(No. 478. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Vienna, December 14, 1854, 

IT HAVE reported to your Lordship in my despatch No 477 of this day, 
the exchange of Her Majesty's matifieations with those of His Imperial and 
Royal Majesty the Emperor of Austria, and’ His Imperial Majesty the Emperor 
of the French. 

Before exchanging these documents I brought before Count Buol ancl 
Baron de Bourquency, your Lordship’s ‘nstructions contained in your despatch 
Nig. 403 of the 7th instant, by which T am directed to return to you certificates 
of the exchange of the ritifications (the forms of which you transmit to me), ani 
which were to be signed by the Austrian and French Plenipotentiartes, 

Upon my producing to Count Buol and to M,. de Bourqueney these 
instructions, they both stated that the ngual form which had been followed on 
euch occasions was, that the Plenipotentiaries should sign a joint procés-verbal, 
by which they attested the exchange of the ratifieations which had taken place, 
and that as the Treaty and the Secret Article could only be considered as 
forming one instrument, it was natural that the exchange of the ratifications of 
the Treaty and of the Secret Article, should be recorded in the same document 
by the Plenipotentiaries who had signed both those instruments. 

Upon my appeal to my two colleagues, to take into consideration the pre- 
cision of the instructions 1 had received, they both replied that they would most 
willingly agree to any form which would be agreeable to the British Government, 
and which would-answer the purpose required, but Count Puol appealed to the 
head of the Austrian Chancery, as to the usage established in transactions of 
this nature by the Imperial Government, and he stated distinctly, that it was im 
jecordance with the procés-verbal which had now been drawn up and prepared, 
Count Buol and M. de Bourqueney ‘mmediately said, that under these cireum- 
stances, they could not but press me fo adopt the form which appeared to be of 
ao established a character, and which fulfilled entirely all the requirements of my 
Government; but to relieve me from all responsibility, they proposed to address 
me a letter, signed by them, which would give me the ussurance that if [ was 
directed by my Government to ask for an acknowledgment in a different form of 
the act just completed, they would be quite ready to accede to any wish | might 
express upon the subject. 

In consequence of this declaration, and being unwilling to obstruct the 
exchange of the ratifications by an appeal to your Lordship, which must have 
taken several days, I consented to sign the procés-verbal, a copy of which 1s 
‘nelosed in my despatch No. 477 of this Hay. [have now the honour to forward 
to your Lordship a copy of the letter addressed to me by Count Buol and 
M. de Bourqueney, to which I have above referred, 

L have, &ec. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND,

My Lord, Paris, December 17, 1854. 

I WAITED upon M. Drouyu de Lhuys this afternoon by appointment, and 
read to him your Lordabip's despatch No. 1,264 of the 15th instant, giving a 
narrative of the proceedings of Her Majesty’s Government on the question of 
opening negotiations with Russia 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys recognised the aecuracy of your Lordships statement, 
and he consented at once to make the alterations desired by your Lordship in 
the note which it is proposed by his Excellency the Governments of England 
and Franee should offer to exchange with that of Austria. 

His Excellency agreed also that ib was indispensable that the expression of 
a desire to treat for peace should proceed from Russia, and be formally 
communicated to the Ministers of England and France at Vienna. He assured 
me that all his instructions to M. de Bourquency, the last of which were sent off 
on the 15th instant, and all of which he promised me should be communicated 
to your Lordship, insisted on this necessary preliminary to all further 
negotiation. 

I then read to M. Drouyn de Lhuys the text of the note which your 
Lordship instructs me to address to him. He said that it coincided perfectly 
with his own views, and was in fact but a repetition of what he had constantly 
stated himself,

addition of a paragraph inviting an answer of idherence to the principles which 
it sets forth. | have the honour to inclose a copy with this addition.

Inclosure in No. 56. 
Lord Cowley to M. Drouyn de Lhuys. 


Paris, Decenber 17, 1854. 

HER Majesty’s Government considering it of great importance that a clear 
understanding should exist with the Government of the Emperor of the French 
as to the interpretation of the third basis of negotiation, which provides for the 
revision of the Treaty of 1541, and the conditions to be required of Russia, the 
Undersigned, Her Majesty's Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to 
the Emperor of the French, has been directed to make known to his Excellency 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys, His Imperial Majesty's Secretary of State for the Foreign 
Department, that, in the opimon of Her Majenty's Government, Sebastopol is 
the seat of danger to Turkey, as it is from thence that Russia is always able to 
menace the existence of the Ottoman Empire, which it is the policy and the 
determination of England and France to maintain, Russia, however strictly she 
may be bound by Treaties, may at any moment when it suits her purpose, 
declare war against Turkey, and being in possession of Sebastopol, with a 
powerful fleet and numerous army, she may in forty-eight hours reach 
Constantinople and seize upon the heart of the Ottoman Empire. The Porte 
would be too weak, and the allies of the Sultan too distant, to oppose any 
effectual resistance to such a coup de main; the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles 
would be in possession of Russia, and long before any hostile forces could be 
brought against her she would be in a position to defy them, 
‘Turkey thus held firmly in her grasp, and the Black Sea then really a 
Russian lake, it ig manifest that the countries bordering on that sea, Circassia, 
Georgia, Persia, and Asia Minor, must at once fall under her dominion ; and it 
is equally clear that the power of Russia must extend over Greece, Thessaly. 
Albania, and the Danubian Prineipalities.

This, then, lies in the balance of strength, and space protects them from 
aggression by Russia. 

Austria, then, has oniy to take care to retain the road from Cracow to 
Lemberg, on the north side of the Carpathians, in order not to lose the power of 
free circulation, 

Prussia must look out to maintain the communication between her territories 
ooris Vistula and on the Oder, so that the belly be not cut out of her body 
politic. 

Austria, then, requires for her security nothing more than what she possesses 
of Poland, and can rather do without Lemberg, and be bounded by the Vistula, 
the Sar, and the Dniester ;—nay, if Russia gives back to Poland all that she has 
taken from her, Austria can even do more than the above: she can draw 
a boundary-line which, starting from the Carpathians, would join the Vistula 
after passing over Dukla and Tarnow, thus rendering the Carpathians her proper 
boundary. 

Prussia, however, would gain her object if with the Drewenz she joins the 
Vistula ; and from thence, over Sempolno, she meets the Wartha near Kolo, so 
following this river as far as Silesia. 


Cosxenusion anp Appexpix—These are the military boundaries, supposing 
that Poland hecomes a Russian province, or that it becomes once more an inde- 
pendent State, And only in this way can the security of the States in the East 
he assured. Should, however, it become clear, from the course of the political 
negotiations followed up to this moment, that the above indicated houndaries 
against Russia cannot be obtained, but, at most, those indicated against Poland, 
it follows thence that the security of the States requires that in such case nothing 
should be neglected in order that Poland, with the exception of the necessary 
exceptions for her security indicated in the above views, may be com letely 
restored: that is to say, sincerely and energetically to endeayour to make it a 
sel{-subsisting, independent, self-governed State, ruled by its own rulers, who do 
not sit upon foreign thrones, For J repeat it, the boundaries lastly indicated 
only afford security against Poland, not against Russia. 

On the contrary, should Russia refuse the complete restoration of Poland, 
and yet extend herself as far as the Wartha, let it be under what pretext il may, 
her plans for the dominion of the world are then clear, the freedom of Europe is 
threatened from that quarter, and in a short time we may look forward to a fresh 
war to rescue the independence of the other States. 

Nothing remains for us, then, but even now to devise means of meeting this 
impending war, ‘These means are, that— 


|. Austria and Prussia shall unite still more firmly together. For this 
purpose, however, Austria must assist more 0 enly, more candidly, and more 
readily towards the consolidation of Prussia. She should further this matter as 
aclaim in the interest of the world on which, in after time, the salvation of 
Europe will depend, and not as an act that she reluctantly performs, in which 
she shows distrust} that she accedes to only conditionally, and upon which she 
not even yet expresses herself openly and sincerely, notwithstanding the condi- 
tions she attaches thereto. Let her be convinced that, when she acts freely and 
openly towards Prussia, and meets her views in a friendly spirit, the infallible 
consequence of this must be to obtain what she now requires in advance as a 
condition, without even at the same time declaring herself clearly respecting the 
consolidation of Prussia. This, however, can only be a consequence of Austria's 
mode of acting; it cannot precede it, because Prussia would cast aside its sole 
support, and would stand completely isolated, without finding a new support in 
Austria, | 

What Austria requires lies certainly in the nature of things, Whereas she 
throws Prussia, by concessions ambiguously framed, conditional and reluctantly 
made, unavoidably into the arms of Russia, because no other support remains for 
Prussia on the continent. Generally, in polities, all declarations are reluctantly 
made, and betraying reserve, advance no cause and only produce in alliances, 
ilistrust, isolation, trouble, and disturbance, and are therefore not suited to great 
ideas, great plans, and great States. 

Let any one ask himself, if Austria does not express herself clearly, openly, 
and freely with regard to Prussia, what else has the latter to do but to ally

Te u 4% 


bepress 


nono 


herself with Russia? Does Austria wish this? No. She wishes to found a 


central Europe. To effect this, Prussia must be independent of Russia, But 
that it may be independent, it is requisite that her strength should be consoli- 
dated und increased. Does Austria do this? No. On the contrary, it 
participates with difficulty and reluctance in all that concerns Prussia’s con- 
solidation, or explains herself indefinitely upon what regards Prussia. Instead 
of drawing Prussia towards her, she makes her apprehensive, and forces her to ally 
herself with the East. Austria thus acts quite contrary to her proposed object, 
nnd forces Prussia to do that which Austria wishes to prevent, and which Prussia 
certainly does unwillingly. May she then, for the welfare of Europe, become 
sensible of the wrong course she is pursuing. If this happens, then it is— 

9. Necessary that Germany be organized on a military footing, and ally 
herself with both Powers, both as a Power and as a Confederation. 

3. That these Powers should themselves well organize their military forces 
and prepare everything for war; that Austria erect a fortress &@ cheval between 
Jablunken aud Teschen. Prussia, a strong place in Posen. 

4. That Austria, Prussia, and Germany, should ally themselves firmly with 
England. 

5. That the policy of each of these Powers should be directed to prevent 
an alliance between Russia and France, 

&. That the above-mentioned Powers should ally themselves with the 
‘Turks, and endeavour, in case of a war with Russia, to set the ‘Turks and also 
the Persians in motion. 

= ‘That this war should be avoided if possible, until the Turks, and if 
possible the Persians, take q part in it 

8. ‘That in case of this war, the Poles should not be neglected, but that the 
above-named Powers should solemnly guarantee to them their deliverance from 
the Russian yoke, as well as their freedom and independence on the abave- 
mentioned boundary improvement. 

If no one of these points be neglected, but if they be all followed up with 
spirit and prudence, such as the importance of the case requires, then will the 
freedom of Europe be as secure against the East, as it is now happily secure 
ugainst the West.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received December 18.) 
(No, 508.) 


My Lord, Berlin, December 15, (B54. 

A DISCUSSION took place to-day in the Second Chamber on the question 
of voting an address to the King, thanking His Majesty for his speech from the 
Throne. ‘The Government wished to avoid a debate with respect to the foreign 
relations, and it was decided that no address should be voted. 

The opposition parties, composed chiefly of the Liberal and Constitutional 
Conservatives, have, notwithstanding, moved addresses, which were submitted 
in the sitting of to-day, the one being proposed by M. de Vineke, the other by 
M. de Bethmann-Hollweg, 

I have the honour to inclose to your Lordship an extract of that portion of 
the address moved by M. de Bethmann-Hollweg which refers to the present 
foreign relations of Prussia. 

The principal object of these motions was to enable these members to 
express their disapprobation of the foreign policy of the Goyernment. M. de 
Vincke, M. de Bethmann-Hollweg, and M. Reichensperger spoke at great length, 
and were answered with equal warmth by M.de Gerlach. On a division the 
address of M. de Vincke was rejected by a majority of about forty, and M. de 
Bethmann-Hollweg subsequently withdrew his motion. 

I shall have the honour to forward to your Lordship a précis of this 
debate, which has not yet appeared in public print. 

L have, &e. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received December 19.)

My Lord, 7 Paris, December 18, 1854. 
M. DROUYN DE LHUYS received in the course of last night a tele- 
graphic despatch from M. de ourqueney, dated yesterday evening, stating that 
he could take upon himself to affirm that Count Buol would make no objection 
to the course proposed to be pursued by the Western Powers, namely, that 
Prince Gortchakoff should make a formal demand to treat with those Powers 
on the basis of the four points; that on his doing so, the explanation of the 
four points, as understood by those Powers and Austria (for M. de Bourquency 
is convinced that Count Buol will make no objection to the exchange of notes), 
should be laid before him, and should he still express his intention of continuing 


the negotiations, that he should be informed that no further step can be taken 
before the arrival of a Turkish Plenipotentiary.

Lord Bloompeld to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received December 21.) 


No. 510, Confidential.) 

Me Lord, Berlin, December 17, 1854. 
COUNT ESTERHAZY called upon me yesterday, and informed mie tet 

he had now received from Count Buol instructions to communicate officia y to 

the Prussian Government a copy of the ‘Treaty of the 2nd of December, ingest ver 

with the Secret Article, and that he proposed at once to cull upon Baron 


“4 ~ ne Pes? wrieesr ps = 
A PeAT Teton Sate 


561 


Manteuffel, read to his Excellency Count Buol’s despatch, inviting the accession 
of Prussia to the ‘Treaty, and leave it with him. This he appears to have done; 
and further to have stated to the Minister President that an accession to the 
Treaty would enable the King to resume his place at the Vienna Conference, 
und that the Austrian Government trusted this invitation would be well 
received, 

Count Esterhazy in vain expected some answer from the Prussian Minister; 
his Exeelleney, however, said nothing in reply to this communication, and 
turned the conversation to another subject. 

Last evening I saw Baron Manteuffel by appointment, I delivered to his 
Exeellency the copy of the Treaty which 1 had received from Lord Westmorland, 
and told. him that, in requesting his Excellency in the most earnest manner to 
recommend the King to accede to it, | might add that His Majesty by thus 
meeting the wishes of the allies, would no longer find himself isolated amongst 
the Great Powers, whilst his accession would increase the chanees of the 
restoration of peace. I then added that | had been told that the King felt 
deeply annoyed that Austria had become a party to this Treaty without having 
made any previous communication to him, and that I begged His Majesty 
to consider the impossibility in which we found ourselves of making confidential 
communications to him, when we knew that every office at Court was filled 
by persons whose political opinions were hostile to us, and whose efforts were 
perpetually direeted to advance the interests of Russia. Under these citeum- 
stances, | said, it was really impossible for us to propose the Treaty to Prussia 
until the three Powers had first. agreed to it, more particularly as we felt certain 
that, if the Court party became aware of the negotiation, not only would they 
set all their engines at work to prevent its adoption here, but would endeavour 
to influence the opinion of the smaller States, seck to draw them away from 
Austria, and urge the establishment of a neutrality in Germany, adapted to call 
forth the entire approlaition of the Imperial Court of Russia. 

I then drew Baron Manteuttel’s attention to the Secret Article, as one of 
the important parts of the document, and observed that it was my duty to 
inform him that we expected Prussia would either accede or decline our 
invitation, for that we could not admit of any half measures. I said further 
that, in a fortnight from this time we should, unless Russia agreed to prelimi- 
naries of peace, he in consultation with Austria as to an Offensive and Defensive 
Alliance, and that it was almost needless for me to say that the Treaty of the 
2nd of December was only a first step, and that we looked forward, if Prussia 
were inclined to join us, to establishing a coalition in Europe which might insure 
un eurly restoration of peace, and that. if this failed, a general war might be the 
consequence, 

Baron Manteuffel said he could not give me any definitive answer to this 
communication; that, however, he could assure me that, though the King was, 
for the moment, indisposed to accede to the Treaty, he was willing to agree to 
stipulations of the sume purport in another form. I rejoined, if the King were 
so disposed, might we then expect that His Majesty would pass over this 
prelimimury arrangement of the 2nd of December, and enter at onee inte an 
Offensive and Defensive Alliance with the Three Powers? To this Baron 
Manteuffel replied that. he could say no more than that ho thought such a 
negotiation would, at the present moment, be more likely to succeed than the 
Treaty to which we wanted his simple secession, 

I then said, But if the King wishes his Envoy to attend the Conferences that 
ay shortly be held at Vienna, he of course cannot do so unless he aceedes to the 
Treaty, and enters into’ engagements with us which will prevent his holding any 
separate communication with St. Petersburgh, 

Baron Manteuflel’ appeared aware of all the difficulties of the present 
position; but he nevertheless observed to me with some degree of surprise, that 
Count Nesselrode had complained that Count Buol had not mide known to 
Prince Gortchakoff, the Austrian interpretation of the four points. I explained 

that Count Buol most naturally felt himself bound to communicate with London 
and Paris on the subject before offering any opinion, and that same little time 
might be consumed in doing this; but I said, all will be ready long before the 
end of this month, and then our positions will be more clearly detined, 

Buron Manteuftel remarked that if our interpretation of the four points was 
as it had been represented to him, he did not believe Russia would subseribe to

General Gerlach had tendered his resignation, which was not accepted ; and the 
General and Count Dohna have both declared to Baron Manteuffel that he will 
forfeit the confidence of their party if the mission succeeds. 

It is difficult to believe that the King will continue long in his present 
mood, with such open opposition to his apparently altered views: but still I 
would venture to suggest that it may be advisable to give His Majesty some 
encouragement. The opinions of many adherents of the Court party will be 
shaken, and the waverers may come round—indeed, the change already effected 
is quite remarkable. Moreover, the negotiator selected is deserving of confidence ; 
alliance with England is his political creed ; and he has assured me that he will 
never take office, if asked to do so, under present circumstances, unless the King 
consents to a cordial union with the Western Powers, and to the adoption of 
warlike measures in support of this policy, 

T understand that one of the reasons which has induced the King to take 
this sudden decision of sending Baron Usedom to England, is his continual 
apprehension that Protestantism is threatened, and that the union of England 
and Prussia is essential to the maintenance of the principles of the Reformation.

My Lord, Berlin, December 18, 1854. 
WITH reference to my despateh No, 508 of the 15th instant, I have now 
the honour to inclose an extract, in translation, of the debate in the Prussian 
Chamber on the address. 
| I have, &e. 
(Signed ) BLOOMFIELD. 


Inclosure in No, 579, 


Précis of Debate in Prussian Second Chamber, on Question of Voting an Address 
in reply to the Speech from the Throne, 


THE Minister President, in remarking that the Government in no way 
admitted the grounds on which an address was proposed, stated that the advisers 


of the Crown, when consulted whether an address should be consequent upon 
the opening of the Chambers by the King in person, decided in the negative. 


The competency of the Chamber to vote an address was incontestable, and the 
explanations to be given in the debates are clearly in the hands of the Chamber. 

In the state of suspension in which negotiations are now, it is impossible 
to give any detailed information concerning the political position. I must also 
abstain from the rectification of false statements, in case they should be advanced. 
| would also remind the members of this Chamber an take part in this 


debate, that we are at the present moment at peace with all States, and request 
that they will have due regard to this consideration, 


M. Reichensperger spoke in favour of an address. The German Diet had 
always had an ancient right to assent to peace or war, The States-General 
(vercinigte Landtag) of 1847 affords a precedent of the participation of the 
Chambers in the foreign policy. From the writings of Professor Stahl, he 
(M. Reichensperger) proves that in Constitutional States the Representatives 
have the right to express their wishes on questions of forcigit policy. He hoped 
and expected that the address would be voted. 


M. de Vincke commences by explaining the motives for an address. He 
remarked that it was said that the address was of no political consequence; the 


form, however, was of importance, for it was the only direct connection of the 
Chamber with the Throne.

Ata still earlier period, two years before the commencement of the war, 
L submitted to the Sultan himself an idea which might, 1 conceive, have been 
carried into effect with advantage, and also without much difheulty. It was 
this: to form into certain Hal the various Pashaliks of which the Empire 1s 
composed, and to place at the head of each eroup—without otherwise disturbing 
the present distribution—a Governor-General or High-Commissioner, selected 
from among the most experienced and best disposed of the Porte’s servants, 
enjoying the full confidence of his Government, und charged with the special 
enforcement of the new administrative system by means of the revular subor- 
dinate authorities placed for the purpose under his superintendence. [ also 
eave in a list of fifteen individuals qualified more or less, in my opinion, for the 
trust. The suggestion was graciously received, and I heard no objection from 
Reshid Pasha, who was Grand Vizier at the time; but nothing followed, and 
the plan has in all probability floated into that limbo which here, as elsewhere, 
is ever filling and never full.

My Lord, Pera, December 3, 1854. 


THE Ottoman Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs communicated to-day 
in confidence to M. Pisani, for my information, a despatch just received from 
Veli Pasha at Paris. 

The Ambassador reports that having had oceasion to sce M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys, the conversation fell upon the Crimea, when the rench Minister said, 
We shall probably get possession of that country, and it is worth while for your 
Government to consider what is to be done with it, He then went on to say, as 
Veli Pasha asserts, that Omer Pasha might be installed there in the same manner 
us the Viceroy of Pgypt now stands towards the Porte. igs 

I do not understand that any distinct proposal was made by M. Drouyn ce 
Lhuys, and Aali Pasha, when showing the despatch to M, Pisani, said that he 
merely thought it right to bring the statement to my knowledge in a confidential 
manner. " Bie 
1 can well conceive that the idea might be palatable to the Turkish 
Government apart from Omer Pasha, who 1s by no means in favour equal to his 
merits,

My Lori, Varna, November 22, 1854. 


I HAVE the honour to report to your Lone that the number and 
distribution of Turkish contingent destined, if required, to proceed from Varna 
to the Crimea, is as follows :-— 


In Varna, 10 battalions at 650 men eae eins) OOOO 
In Pravadi, Abattalionsat G50 6 6 6 we ee ee 2600 
In Yasi Tepe (8 hours from Varna), 4 battalions at 660. . 2600 


Men .« « 12700 


ea am batteries of Field Artillery, one of which is at Varna, and the other at 
ravac, 

I took occasion to converse with Tefik Bey, the brother-in-law of his 
Highness Omer Pasha, who is appointed to command a division, or one half of 
these troops (Mehmet Pasha having the command of the other division), 
respecting their numerical strength and condition as to equipments. He 
confirms my computation as to the number of effective men per battalion ; and 
with respect to their equipments, he states that they are in much need of winter 
clothing, especially great-coats and trousers, He spoke of various arrangements 
which had been made to supply, as far as possible, this deficiency, by temporarily 
appropriating for the troops destined for the Crimea, some great-coats from the 
Artillerymen stationed in Varna, and of some clothing for other corps on the 
Danube. But he said, in reply to my inquiry as to what clothing it was 
absolutely necessary should be supplied from Constantinople, that 5,000 great- 
coats and 6,000 pairs of trousers were indispensible. 1 have, therefore, the 
honour to bring this fact to your Lordship’s knowledge, and respectfully to 
suggest that the Turkish Government be urged to supply this deficiency as 
speedily as possible. 

Tefik Bey said that there would be a sufficiency of tents, as it was 
purposed to take 300 belonging to the Egyptians, besides those that remained 
serviceable, 

Shoes and other articles of clothing, he informed me, would be procured in 
Varna; and, he added, with respect to provisions, that these troops would take 


with ten from Varna, if they went to the Crimea, a sufficient quantity for one 
month, 


I have, &e. 
(Signed) EDWD. S'l’. JOHN NEALE.

Inclogure in No. 587. 


Consul Neale to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Varna, December 6, 1854, 


IT HAVE the honour to report to your Lordship that the British hired 
steamers “Simla,” “Colombo,” and “ Queen of the South,” and the sailing 
transport * Shooting Star,” having arrived at Varna within the last three or 
four days for the purpose of conveying the first detachment of the ‘Turkish 
contingent to the Crimea, the troops are im course of being actively embarked. 
One of the steamers, the “ Queen of the South,” has already left with 1,200 


Infantry on board. : P 
Seri axke number of troops of the several arms which will be embarked 


o7l 


is as follows: Infantry 10,800, Cavalry 1,000, Artillery 380; total, 12,180, with 
twelve guns. 

Four steamers and four large sailing transports have been ordered by Vice- 
Admiral Dundas to proceed to Varna to embark these troops, and which they 
would have effected in two trips; but from some causes unexplamed one of the 
steamers and three of the sailing transports have not arrived. It will, therefore, 
be necessary that those which are at present disposable perform four trips, in 
order to convey the whole of the troops. 

Some clothing has arrived ‘for these troops from Constantinople, but they 
consist chiefly of jackets; the great-coats and trousers so much wanted have not 
arrived, 1 understand, however, that Omer Pasha has communicated to the 
military authorities here that he has forwarded 6,000 pairs of trousers and as 
ey pairs of shoes from Bucharest, and that they expected shortly to arrive 

1ere. 

The troops in course of embarkation are the corps recently commanded by 
Hassan Pasha, and, I understand, are entirely composed of the Rediff, who do 
not, however, differ in any matenal degree from the troops of the regular 
Turkish army. ‘These troops have also seen active service on the Danube, and 
some of the battalions were engaged in the defence of Silistria, They are 
commanded by Mehmet Pasha, who served at Giurgevo, and who 1s favourably 
spoken of, and the two brigades which form the division are respectively com- 
manded by Behram Pasha (General Cannon) and Shefik Pasha, the nephew of 
Omer Pasha. General Cannon will embark to-morrow; he 1s accompanied by 
Colonels Ogilvy, Hinde, Morgan, and Ballard, and Lieutenant Cadell of the 
Madras Artillery, all attached to his Staff. The troops take with them one 
month’s supply of provisions. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) EDWD. 8ST. JOHN NEALE. 


P.S.—The latest intelligence received from the seat of war is up to the 
Ond instant, but ne event of importance had occurred.

No. 588. 
Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved December 23.) 


(No. 743.) 
My Lord, Therapia, December 10, 1854. 

INCLOSED herewith in copy is a despatch, which I received this morning 
fron Field-Marshal Lord Raglan, It relates to the Turkish troops detached, 
or proposed to be detached, from the army of Omer Pasha for service in the 
Crimea. Your Lordship will observe that the Commanders-in-chief of the allied 
armics agree in requiring more reinforcements from that quarter, and in desiring 
that Omer Pasha should take the command of the expedition in person, 

The Porte’s instructions, by order of the Sultan, directing the Generalissimo 
to take the command, were sent off by express four days ago. 

I avail myself of this opportunity to bring under your Lordship’s notice 
an official application for French and English steamers, to be employed in 
conveying provisions and ammunition from Bulgaria to the Crimea, on behalf 
of the Turkish army destined for Eupatoria, 

[shall lose no time in recommending this demand to the attention of Rear- 
Admiral Boxer; but I question whether the means ut his disposal will be found 
equal to the occasion, while reinforcements and supplies, principally under the 
British flag, are daily passing into the Black Sea, and absorbing o large 
proportion of the steam-power now in hand, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

Inclosure | in No. 588, 
General Lord Raglan to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Before Sebastopol, December 8, 1854. 

COLONEL SIMMONS arrived here the day before yesterday, and returned 
to Bucharest vid Varna yesterday, He was the bearer of letters from Omer 
Pasha, and he was charged by General Canrobert and myself with despatches 
for his Highness, in which we again urged him to repair to the Crimea, ant to 
bring with him as many of the troops belonging to his army as he may be able 
to withdraw from the Principalities. 

ft would appear that an advance towards the Pruth would be useless, the 
creater part of the Russian force having been withdrawn from Bessarabia, and 
put in march for the Crimea, 

The first ships I sent to Varna for Turkish troops arrived here three days 
ago, and are now gone up to Eupatoria. They should have been directed there 
straight from Varna, but by an extraordinary oversight they were ordered here 
by the superintendent of the transport service, Captain Christie. 

T find from General Canrobert that his intention of feeding the Turkish 
troops to be landed at Eupatoria was limited to the period at which arrange- 
ments for their supply by their own Government could be made. 

| entreat your Excellency to impress this upon the Seraskier Pasha, and to 
urge him to make every exertion to send them provisions and warm clothing. 
If he fail to do this either as regards food or clothing, the Ottoman troops will 
be wholly inefficient, and be deprived of the power of creating a diversion that 
shall be useful, and which otherwise they may be able to effect, particularly if 
commanded by Omer Pasha in person. 

I have, kc. 
(Signed) RAGLAN.

It can hardly be intended to call into existence throughout the whole of the 
Turkish Empire. not even in its Huropean provinces, a state of things such as 
that in Servia; for that state of things owes its existence to repeated success In 
eme, and represents a degree of national independence which the Porte can 
hardly be called upon to recognize in other portions of its dominions. It will 
consequently only be neccssary to lay down certam conditions, without which ih 
peacelul and secure, even ‘f subordinate, personal existence for the Christian 
population cannot be secured. , 

As the first of these conditions we will specify the right to property ; that 
‘s to say, to secure and legally guarantee possession of real property. In order 
iully to understand what is meant, we must recollect that within the last decade 
the removal of the Christian population from their possession has constantly 
heen carried on, especially in Bosnia. It is a matter of course that the old 
feudal retainers of the Sultan, the Spalis, are considered as the proprietors in 
the villages, and draw their rents and emoluments from the lands of the Christan 
population. But as landed property, notwithstanding this charge upon Mt still 
afforded a not inconsiderable surplus, a new class has in later tines intruded into 
its possession. ‘These were generally adventurers of Mahomedan ereed, who 
under one form or another, or by open violence, took possession of the land, 
and have thus reduced the ‘nhubitants to a condition devoid of law, such as 
renders a peaceable existence, as is required by men even in the lowest grade ol 
society, almost an impossibility. ; 

Theseintruders are called Tshithik or Tshitlik-Sesebris. ‘They have not 


power which so frequently accompany the collection of imposts, it might not be 
expedient to depute the Kneses or other authorities of the Christian commu- 
nities to collect these imposts in the aggregate or in detail, as has been done at 
Jadar, For the Christian. must remain liable to the Sultan’s taxes and the legal 


rent due to the Spahi, 

Tn aceordance with the above, the proposition im a nezotiation for peace 
might be worded as follows ; 

“The free exercise of their religion, as well as the enjoyment of their 
sroperty, shall be guaranteed to the Christian inhabitants of Durkey for ever. 

hey shall have judges and chiefs of their own creed and nations.” 

It remains, however, a question of some difficulty whether with such insti- 
tutions the integrity and sovereignty of the Porte can be maintained. 

We answer, the Porte will have fall power and liberty to garrison its 
fortresses exclusively with Turks; for those fortresses which guard the frontiers 
of the province, will, without exception, as well as those provinces themselves, 
remain in its possession, It would, however, be of advantage as regards the 
desirable separation of the two nationalities, were the Turkish population to

No, 598. 


Sir A, Malet to the Earl of Clarendon —(Received December 23.) 


(No. 145.) 
My Lord, Frankfort, December 20, 1854, 


THE impression produced here by the text of the Treaty of the 2nd of 
December is, that Austria has taken one step farther towards an open breach 
with Russia. 

That such is the prevailing opinion is to be gathered not only from the 
Janguage of those who desire to look forward to such a solution of the long 
hesitations of Germany, but still more from the unconcealed anger and vexation 
of the decided partizans of Russia. 

Amonust these, certain Prussian members of a party calling itself national, 
are foremost in denouncing what they assert to be bad faith on the part of 
Austria, in not having sooner made the Cabinet of Berlin acquainted with the 
negotiation which was being earried on with Great Britain and France, and 
with discourtesy in hastening to sign the Treaty, when the Prussian Government, 
on receiving a partial intimation of its objects, signified a desire to participate im 
the negotiation. 

If the opinions of this party should unfortunately prevail at Berlin, not 
only would that Government abstain from ‘accession to the Treaty, but there 
would be considerable risk of their allying that country with Russia. 

The policy of Austria is represented by its advocates as being perfectly 
sincere, but necessarily cautious, having to provide against great risks and 
dangers. 
 Austrin sought in the first place, not to separate herself from Prussia and 
Jermany, but to bind these to community of action, and this object has to some 
extent been effected by the Additional Article to the Treaty of the 20th of April. 

In the next place, it was necessary to secure, or at least to fortify certain 
eints on the Austrian frontier, which were wholly open to ® Russian attack. 
This has now been in a great measure effected at Saat Przemisl, and one 
other important point in Galicia, the name of which escapes me. 

Thirdly. Austria desires to avoid a winter campaign. 


581 


By the course pursued she hopes to carry all Germany with her, and to be 
fully prepared to act on the offensive in the spring, im case the obstinacy of the 
Emperor Nicholas renders it necessary. 

Your Lordship is of course better ‘nformed than I can be, of what is the 
animus of the Berlin Cabinet, but no one here seems to anticipate a frank anc 
unconditional accession to the Treaty. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) A. MALET.

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received December 24, 
5°15 P.M.) 
(Telegraphic.) Vienna, December 24, 1854. 
COUNT BUOL objects to adopting the form of an identical note, while he 
entirely adheres to the spirit and letter of the terms and interpretations contained 
in the one sent by your Lordship, He writes to Count Colloredo and M. Hiibner, 
to offer to declare his adherence in a responsive note, or he is ready to sign 
a Protocol with the French Ambassador and myself, recapitulating the words 
of the interpretation of the four Articles, as declared in the identical note, and 
stating the perfect agreement of the three Governments. He prefers this mode 
as more suited to the dignity of the Emperor of Austria, considering that the 
one proposal implies a want of confidence in good understanding no longer 
existent.

There are, no doubt, objections and difficulties to proceeding in this way,

The Emperor having stated to me that he would be glad if this, or any 
other, expedient could be found to prevent a communication to the Russian 
Government of the intentions of the allies, | spoke in the same sense this 
afternoon to M. Drouyn de Lhuys, at the same time giving his Excellency to 
understand that he must not consider meas muking any proposition from your 
Lordship. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys expressed great satisfaction at the plan | laid before 
him. He said, however, that it ought not to be brought forward until Austria 
was committed to our interpretation of the four points, for that if the two 
Governments showed misgivings previously they might shake her good intentions 
at the present moment. Nor, indeed, after the signatare of a Protocol or other 
instrument could the two Governments act as [ proposed without the con- 
vurrence of Austria; but he was quite of opinion, his Excellency said, that the 
proceeding which I advocated should be proposed to Austria as soon as the 
Protocol was signed, and that Count Buol should then be asked whether, in the 

resent state of the war, it would not be advisable for Austria, as for the 
belligerent Powers, to avoid unnecessary explanations with Russia, and merely 
to meet Prince Gortchakoff for the purpose of refusing his propositions (which 
eould never be acceptable to the allies), without needlessly exposing our own, 
He added that he should write on this subject to Count Walewski to-morrow, 
and that, in the meantime, if he received your Lordship's agreement to a 
Protocol, that he should direct M.de Bourqueney to sign it, and to abstain from 
all further proceedings until he received further instructions. 

It is exceedingly difficult to explain as I would desire, within the limits 
ofa despatch, a plan of this nature, but your Lordship will understand that the 
foundation of itis “yes” or “no” to what Prince Gortchakotf has to propose, 
and a simple statement that we have ne propositions to make ourselves, 

[ have again to appeal to your Lordship's indulgence in travelling beyond 
the sphere of my duties, by offering suggestions when | ought only to be the

struck, unnecessarily perhaps, with the danger of aiding the cause of Russia by 

utting forward demands, however yague, which we must ourselves admit. we 
ave no right to expect Russia to concede at the present. moment, that my 
anxiety makes me outstep-my diseretion, 

That anxiety is not a little increased by a feeling which | may impart to 
our Lordship, though | could neither express it to the Emperor nor to his 
linister, that if Russia could declare openly that peace had been prevented, 

after she had satisfied all the legitimate demands of the allies, by the require- 
ment of conditions incompatible with her honour, and which an belligerent 
Powers were not in a condition to enforee, a sympathy for her would be aroused 
in France, as embarrassing for the Emperor as it would be perilous to the 
allianee.

(No. 523.) 
My Lord, Berlin, December 22, 1804, 

AN artiele, of which I inclose herewith a copy in original and in translation, 
lately appeared in the ‘Kreuz Zeitung,” giving the “analysis” of a despatch 
which was stated to have been addressed by the Prussian Government to the 
Cabinets of London, Paris, and Vienna. . 

At a late interview with Baron Manteuffel, I took occasion to refer to this 
subject and to inquire whether he had written any such despatch. 

His Excellency at once stated that this analysis was a pure invention and 
he promised that a reputation of its authenticity should be published. In con- 
formity with whieh, an article to that intent was inserted in the ministerial organ, 
the ‘Preuasische Correspondenz,” of which I transmit to your Lordship herewith 
a copy and translation. 

The original text, however, of this despatch to which the © analysis ”’ 
referred, has been since published by the © Allgemeine Zeitung” and re roduced 
in the Berlin papers, and | have the honour to forward to your Lordship, 
herewith, a copy of it accompanied by a French translation. 

Your Lordship may be enabled to judge by this transaction how sedulously 
the “Kreuz Zeitung” seeks to poison the public mind, without any regard to 
facts or truth.

(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

Inclosure 1 in No. 618. 


Extract from the“ Kreuz Zeitung. 
(Translation.) 


WE have received from Paris the analysis of a Prussian cireular despatch 
to the Prussian Minister at the Courts of London, Paris, and Vienna. We 
reproduce it here without being answerable for its authenticity, although our 
correspondent is generally well informed. The despatch is suid to have stated 
something near the following :— 

«Tn the difficult cireumstances in which Europe ig placed, the German 
Government have hitherto been solely guided by their love for peace. In the 
interest of all Europe and for the attainment of a great end, they have urged the 
Russian Cabinet to accept conditions which a year ago no one would have 
thought possible that Russia could accept. The Emperor of Russia yielding to 
the urgently expressed wishes and desire of his old ally, has given @ proof of an 
extraordinary moderation. ‘The concessions which he has made go to the 
furthest limit of what is compatible with his dignity. If the monstrous demands 
which are put forth in certain organs should be submitted at a Conference, the 
terman Government would in no way support them, and the responsibility of 
an European conflict would recoil heavily on the authors of such pretensions.

Inclosure 2 in No. 618. 


Extract from the “ Preussische Correspondenz.” 


(Translation.) 


THE “ Preussische Correspondenz” states as follows;—In several news- 
papers (not in the ‘ National Zeitung’) has been inserted from the new Prussian 
Gazette, or ‘Kreuz Zeitung, a reported analysis of a Prussian circular 
despatch to their Ministers at the Courts of London, Pans, and Vienna. The 
‘Krenz Zeitung’ has with perfect, reason added to this intelligence the cautious 
remarks that they did not guarantee the menuineness of it, On our part we cun 
give the certain assurance that no document of the said nature exists.”

No. 620, 
Consul-General Colquhoun to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recewwed December 25.) 


(No, 112;) 
My Lord, Rucherest, November 30, 1854. 


YOUR Lordship is aware that, after the occupation by the Russians of 
the Provinees in 1849, Russia exacted from the Prineipalities eae of the 
expenses of that occupation; the Turks declined making any such demand on 
the country. 

To enable the provinces to micet thig extraordinary and very onerous 
demand, a communication was made by the Imperial Chancelry at St. Peters- 
burgh to the Russian Commissioner, and by him communicated to the Prince, 
who acknowledges its reeeipt in the note of which copy 1s inclosed, sanctioning 
the imposition of a tax on all the “contribuables: and possessors of lan 
throughout the: country. Appended to the above note will be found the office 
of the Prince Hospodar conlirming the said proposal ; consequently the matter 
passed inte a law. 

This tax, collected under the fille of “ Amortissement de la Dette envers 
la Russie,” amounts to three piastres, « tenth of the capitation changed on all the 
peasants, of the six piastres which the proprietors pay for each family of 
heasants on their estates, and ol five per cent. of the revenues of the uninhabited 
ands. ‘his tax is collected halt-yearly; it amounts to something near 
5,000,000 piastres (46,0000) annually: i has been regularly collected from 
1849 to June 1854, and has heen appropriated to the purpose for which it was 
destined, ‘lhe proceeds of the last haltyear of 1852, and the whole of that 
of 1853, amounting to about 4,140,000 piastres (68,0001), were paid into the 
Chancelry of the Russian Consulate here, ‘4 terms of a note from Count 
Nesselrode. 

For the last half-year this tax ‘= now in course of collection, and is being 
deposited in a chest of the ‘Treasury specially set apart for this purpose. 

| was waited upon, a few days ago, by some large landed proprictors who 
told me that summouses have been issued to the administrators of the districts, 
ta collect the tax for the identical purpose, in virtue of a princely ordinance. 
Many have refused to pay it. 

L think it right to call your Lordship’s especial attention to this fact, —that 
such a tax should be mmposed and collected, at such a period, for such a 
purpose. | have set inquiries O1 foot to ascertain up to what period the tribute 
due by the provinees to the Sublime Porte has been paid, and what measures 
have heen taken to pay Up the arrears. 

In 1849, Fuad Effendi, then Ottoman Commissioner, complained not only 
of General Duhamel, who did not even consult him on the subject of this war 
tax, but also of the Prinee Stirbey, who adopted the measure without bringing 
it before the Turkish Commissioner; nay, further, when the Turkish forees were 
pressed for money about the same time, and Fuad pro osed that a year’s tribute 
to the Porte should be paid ‘ny advance, General Duhamel hy note to the 
Wallachian Government refused to consent to the proposal, and formally 

wrotested against it. Wive years have now contributed nearly 15,000,000 
af piastres ; the total required from the twe provinees was about 30,000,000, 
of which Wallachia was to contribute 16,000,000, and Moldavia 14,000,000, 
Russia, during the last cighteen months, has largely drawn upon this 
exhausted ‘Treasury, whose different chests are much dilapidated. It would 
now be an act of but common justice that the sum now in the Treasury should 
he sequestrated ; thet the sums taken from the peasantry should be restored 
to those particulur districts which have most suffered during the late occu- 

ation, such as Viaska (Giurgevo), Jalonit#a (Calarash, opposite Silistria), 
aettss and Fokschani; that part of the fund taken from the proprietors 
may be retained and ‘wpplied to various useful purposes, such as forming 
roads, the increase of the militia, &e. But under the present ruler there is 
little chanee of anything of the kind being done, except by the means of 
a firman from the Porte; and if this be obtained, a committee of proper upright 
eaple should be appointed to su erintend the distribution of the returned fund 
ro the hands of the peasantry, maependent entirely of the Boyards or governors 


597 


of districts, who seldom or never disgorge any funds which once have reached 
their hands. | abstain from further comment, and leave the matter in your 
Lordship’s hands. ; é 
T have, &c. 
(Signed) ROBERT G. COLQUHOUN.

No, 623. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received December 28.) 
(No. 1,572.) 
My Lord, Paris, December 26, 1854. 

| HAVE been informed confidentially that Count Hatzfeldt had received 
instructions, under date the 19th instant, to explain to M. Drouyn de Lhuys 
that the Prussian Government, though admitting that the Treaty of the 2nd 
‘netant is based in terms which have received the sanction of the King of 
Prussia, cannot meet the wishes of the English, Austrian, and French Govern- 
ments, that His Majesty should adhere to that ‘Treaty. M. Manteuffel adds, 
that the King would have less objection to enter into some separate arrangement 
with the Western Powers, and he expresses a wish to be inade acquainted with 
the interpretation which they give to the four points, on which the Treaty of 
Vienna is founded. 

~— M. Drowyn de Lhuys being indisposed, 1 have been unable to see his 
Excellency to ascertain the answer which he returned to Count Hatefeldt’s 
communication, but Tam informed that the substance of it is, that it will be 
Haley for the French Government to enter into any Treaty with the King 
of Prussia which contains less than the Treaty of Vienna, but that if the Prussian 
Governmetit should do that which 1s most unlikely, viz., offer to enter into more 
stringent engagements against Russia, there could be no longer any objection on 
the partof the French Government to enumerate such engagements by ‘Treaty. 

T understand that Count Matzfeldt observed to M, Drouyn de Lhuys, that 
to ask Prussia to adhere to the Treaty of the 2nd instant, was to ask her to do 
that which had not common sense, for that in no way could the 2nd Article 
relating to the Principalities he made applicable to her, and that M. Dronyn de 
Lhuys admitted that if Prussia adered to the sense of the political part of that 
Treaty, a new instrument to be signed by the four Powers would become 
necessary’. 

It may not be impossible that Prassia may have something of this kind in 
view, so as not to have the appearance of adhering to an Act which was already 
signed.

No. 627. 
The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—{ Received December 29.) 


(Telegraphic. ) Vienna, December 28, 1854. 

WIE signed the Protocol this day. ‘The express meeting with the Russian 
Minister, a8 settled by Count Buol, took place shortly afterwards, the object 
being only to inform him of the interpretation put by our Governments on the 
four Articles. Each hada memorandum containing this interpretation, which 
was read out by the French Ambassador. ‘The Russian Minister declared that 
he was unable to adhere to our interpretation, particularly of the third guarantee. 
Nevertheless, he attempted to: separate the Austrian Pienipotentiary from the 
other two, but Count Buol remained firmly united to his colleagues. ‘The 
Russian Minister asked if we could communicate to him the document we had 
read. ‘The French Ambassador agreed to do so, statins expressly that no name 
was attached to it, and that it was intended only to aid lis memory. He sends 
it by courier to St. Petersburgh, and conformably with your Lordship's mstruc- 
tions, in your despatch No, 422, we fixed a delay of fifteen days for a reply. 
We agreed to this, because the Russian Minister, whilst refusing to adhere to 
our interpretation, declared that he could not reject it without reference to hie 
Court, ‘The firmness of Count Buol appeared to produce a painful TMpression 
on the Russian Minister.

The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 


(No. 445.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, December 30, 1854. 

[ TRANSMIT to your Lordship a copy of adespatch* from Her Majesty’s 
Consul-General at Bucharest, reporting the continued levy of a Russian war-tax 
by the Hospodar of Wallachia; and I have to observe that it is really disgraceful 
that the Hospodar should be collecting a tax for Russia from the exhausted and 
impoverished peasantry. A tax imposed in 1849 for the repayment of Russia 
ought certainly not to be collected in 1854, either for Russia or for Prince 
Stirbey. Jf any doubts existed before as to the unfitness of Prince Stirbey for 
the post he occupies, and of his faithlessness to the Suzerain Power, and of his 
understanding with Russia, they must now be removed. ‘The allies of the 
Sultan must not permit the supreme authority in Wallachia to be entrusted to 
such hands, 

You will communicate to Count Buol the sentiments of Her Majesty's 
Government on this subject. 


Lam, &c. | 
(Signed) CLARENDON.
